front: Pyruvate dehydrogenase processing yields a two-carbon unit that enters the citric acid cycle. What is that product called?

front: Why is “Succinyl CoA” wrong here? Pyruvate dehydrogenase processing yields a two-carbon unit that enters the citric acid cycle. What is that product calle…

front: Why is “Phosphoenolpyruvate” wrong here? Pyruvate dehydrogenase processing yields a two-carbon unit that enters the citric acid cycle. What is that product calle…

front: An allosteric inhibitor typically binds where on the enzyme?

front: Why is “Only to ribosomal RNA in the cytosol” wrong here? An allosteric inhibitor typically binds where on the enzyme?

front: Why is “First destroys the substrate in solution” wrong here? An allosteric inhibitor typically binds where on the enzyme?

front: Why is “Covalently on the catalytic nucleophile only” wrong here? An allosteric inhibitor typically binds where on the enzyme?

front: What directly powers ATP formation during oxidative phosphorylation?

front: Why is “Spontaneous ADP joining without a gradient” wrong here? What directly powers ATP formation during oxidative phosphorylation?

front: Why is “Direct phosphate transfer from NADH to ADP” wrong here? What directly powers ATP formation during oxidative phosphorylation?

front: Why is “Photon capture by mitochondrial chlorophyll” wrong here? What directly powers ATP formation during oxidative phosphorylation?
back: Chemiosmosis here is redox-driven.

front: The central dogma of molecular biology describes macromolecular information flow as which sequence?

front: Why is “Glucose to glycogen as the usual forward path” wrong here? The central dogma of molecular biology describes macromolecular information flow as which sequence?

front: Why is “Protein to RNA to DNA as the usual forward path” wrong here? The central dogma of molecular biology describes macromolecular information flow as which sequence?
back: Forward flow is DNA to RNA to protein.

front: Why is “Lipid to carbohydrate as the usual forward path” wrong here? The central dogma of molecular biology describes macromolecular information flow as which sequence?
back: Not the dogma; see the cited source passage for detail.

front: Per turn of the citric acid cycle, which reduced electron carriers are formed according to the standard textbook accounting?
back: Three NADH and one FADH2

front: Why is “Six NADPH molecules” wrong here? Per turn of the citric acid cycle, which reduced electron carriers are formed according to the standard textbook account…

front: Why is “One NADH molecule only” wrong here? Per turn of the citric acid cycle, which reduced electron carriers are formed according to the standard textbook account…

front: Why is “Four FADH2 molecules” wrong here? Per turn of the citric acid cycle, which reduced electron carriers are formed according to the standard textbook account…
back: FADH2 yield is one per turn.

front: In competitive inhibition, how does the inhibitor reduce enzyme activity?
back: It competes with substrate for active-site binding
extra: OpenStax: the inhibitor competes with substrate for active-site binding.

front: Why is “It binds DNA enhancers and blocks transcription” wrong here? In competitive inhibition, how does the inhibitor reduce enzyme activity?
back: Different mechanism; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Transcriptional regulation, not catalytic inhibition.

front: Why is “It digests the enzyme into free amino acids” wrong here? In competitive inhibition, how does the inhibitor reduce enzyme activity?
back: Competitive inhibition is binding competition.
extra: That would be proteolysis, not classic competition.

front: Why is “It pumps protons to starve ATP synthesis” wrong here? In competitive inhibition, how does the inhibitor reduce enzyme activity?
back: Not enzyme active-site competition.

front: Watson and Crick proposed which structural description of DNA?
back: Two strands twisted into a helix
extra: OpenStax recounts two strands twisted around each other.

front: Why is “A hollow tube made of membrane lipids” wrong here? Watson and Crick proposed which structural description of DNA?
back: Irrelevant; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Membrane fantasy — does not match the cited teaching point.

front: Why is “One peptide strand in an alpha coil” wrong here? Watson and Crick proposed which structural description of DNA?
back: DNA is nucleic acid; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Confuses protein structure with DNA.

front: Why is “A branched sugar polymer network” wrong here? Watson and Crick proposed which structural description of DNA?
back: DNA is polynucleotide.
extra: Wrong polymer class — does not match the cited teaching point.

front: What critical catalytic task do almost all enzymes perform inside cells?
back: Lower the activation energies of chemical reactions
extra: OpenStax: enzymes lower activation energies of cellular reactions.

front: Why is “Replace ATP as the universal energy currency” wrong here? What critical catalytic task do almost all enzymes perform inside cells?
back: Enzymes catalyze its use.
extra: ATP remains the phosphoryl currency.

front: Why is “Change the equilibrium constant of reactions” wrong here? What critical catalytic task do almost all enzymes perform inside cells?
back: Catalysis is kinetic.
extra: Enzymes speed rates; they do not alter delta-G equilibrium.

front: Why is “Supply the net free energy for endergonic processes without coupling” wrong here? What critical catalytic task do almost all enzymes perform inside cells?
back: Enzymes do not create energy.
extra: Endergonic work still needs energetic coupling.

front: During electron transport in mitochondria, what happens to protons that enables chemiosmotic ATP synthesis?
back: They are pumped from the matrix to the intermembrane space
extra: OpenStax: protons are pumped from the mitochondrial matrix to the intermembrane space.

front: Why is “They freely equilibrate across an unsealed outer membrane only” wrong here? During electron transport in mitochondria, what happens to protons that enables chemiosmotic ATP synthesis?
back: Complexes pump across the inner membrane.
extra: Outer membrane is porous; the relevant barrier is the inner membrane.

front: Why is “They diffuse into the nucleus to activate transcription” wrong here? During electron transport in mitochondria, what happens to protons that enables chemiosmotic ATP synthesis?
back: Nuclear signaling is separate.
extra: No such ETC coupling.

front: Why is “They are consumed as the carbon skeleton of glucose” wrong here? During electron transport in mitochondria, what happens to protons that enables chemiosmotic ATP synthesis?
back: CO2 carbons come from substrate carbons.
extra: Protons are not incorporated into CO2 carbon.

front: If aerobic respiration does not occur, why must NADH be reoxidized to NAD+?
back: NAD+ must be regenerated as an electron carrier
extra: OpenStax: NADH must be reoxidized to NAD+ for reuse as an electron carrier so glycolysis can continue.

front: Why is “ATP synthase consumes NADH as its substrate” wrong here? If aerobic respiration does not occur, why must NADH be reoxidized to NAD+?
back: NADH feeds the ETC when available.
extra: ATP synthase uses ADP+Pi and proton flow.

front: Why is “Oxygen can oxidize glucose without any carriers” wrong here? If aerobic respiration does not occur, why must NADH be reoxidized to NAD+?
back: Carrier regeneration is the point.
extra: Oxygen is not a direct glycolytic oxidant.

front: Why is “NADH must become NADPH for biosynthesis only” wrong here? If aerobic respiration does not occur, why must NADH be reoxidized to NAD+?
back: The issue is NAD+ availability for GAPDH.
extra: Wrong cofactor story.

front: What is glycogen in animals?
back: A polymer of glucose used for energy storage
extra: OpenStax: glycogen, a polymer of glucose, is an energy storage molecule in animals.

front: Why is “Dietary cellulose in humans” wrong here? What is glycogen in animals?
back: Cellulose is plant fiber.
extra: Humans do not store cellulose as glycogen.

front: Why is “A mitochondrial electron carrier like ubiquinone” wrong here? What is glycogen in animals?
back: Glycogen is cytosolic storage.
extra: Wrong compartment/function.

front: Why is “A protein hormone from the pancreas” wrong here? What is glycogen in animals?
back: Glycogen is a polysaccharide.
extra: Confuses glycogen with glucagon/insulin.

front:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to the emergency department with crushing substernal chest pain for 45 minutes. Electrocardiography shows ST-segment elevation in leads V2 through V4, and cardiac catheterization confirms occlusion of the left anterior descending artery. Biopsy of the ischemic myocardium reveals depleted mitochondrial ATP and accumulating lactate despite continued glucose uptake.

Which of the following best explains why substrate-level ATP production can briefly continue in this tissue without oxygen?
back: Glycolysis proceeds in the cytosol and does not require oxygen
extra: Glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate in the cytosol and can proceed without oxygen; under ischemia it continues briefly to supply substrate-level ATP while mitochondria cannot run oxidative phosphorylation.

front: Why is “Glycolysis relocates into mitochondria when oxygen delivery falls” wrong here? A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to the emergency department with crushing substernal chest pain for 45 m…
back: Glycolysis remains cytosolic; mitochondria run the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, which fail without oxygen.
extra: A compartment shift is being invented for anaerobiosis.

front: Why is “Hexokinase begins to consume oxygen as an alternative substrate” wrong here? A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to the emergency department with crushing substernal chest pain for 45 m…
back: Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose with ATP; it does not use oxygen, and ischemia does not convert it into an oxidase.
extra: The glucose-trapping enzyme is being given a respiratory role.

front: Why is “PFK stops so that all ATP is spared for ion pumps” wrong here? A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to the emergency department with crushing substernal chest pain for 45 m…
back: PFK regulation modulates glycolytic rate; the reason ATP can still be made without O2 is that glycolysis itself is anaerobic, not that PFK stops.
extra: Regulatory shutdown is being treated as the reason ATP continues.

front: Which statement best describes glycolysis with respect to oxygen requirement and cellular location in eukaryotes?
back: It does not use oxygen directly and occurs in the cytoplasm
extra: OpenStax states glycolysis is termed anaerobic and takes place in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells.

front: Why is “It requires molecular oxygen in the mitochondrial matrix” wrong here? Which statement best describes glycolysis with respect to oxygen requirement and cellular location in eukaryotes?
back: Oxygen is the terminal acceptor of the electron transport chain, not a glycolytic substrate.
extra: Confuses glycolysis with oxidative phosphorylation.

front: Why is “It occurs only on the inner mitochondrial membrane” wrong here? Which statement best describes glycolysis with respect to oxygen requirement and cellular location in eukaryotes?
back: Inner-membrane complexes belong to oxidative phosphorylation.
extra: Misplaces the pathway on the ETC membrane.

front: Why is “It is strictly aerobic and mitochondrial” wrong here? Which statement best describes glycolysis with respect to oxygen requirement and cellular location in eukaryotes?
back: Glycolysis proceeds without direct O2 use in the cytosol.
extra: Opposite of the actual oxygen independence and location.

front: In eukaryotic cytoplasm, what are the net carbon products of glycolysis starting from one glucose before mitochondrial oxidation?
back: Two pyruvate molecules
extra: OpenStax Biology notes glycolysis begins with glucose and produces two pyruvate molecules (plus ATP and NADH carriers).

front: Why is “Six CO2 molecules” wrong here? In eukaryotic cytoplasm, what are the net carbon products of glycolysis starting from one glucose before mitochondrial o…
back: Full oxidation to six CO2 requires pyruvate processing plus citric acid cycle turns.
extra: Jumps to complete aerobic oxidation of glucose.

front: Why is “Two acetyl-CoA molecules” wrong here? In eukaryotic cytoplasm, what are the net carbon products of glycolysis starting from one glucose before mitochondrial o…
back: Acetyl-CoA forms after pyruvate enters mitochondria and is processed by the pyruvate dehydrogenase path.
extra: Skips the mitochondrial pyruvate-to-acetyl-CoA step.

front: Why is “One pyruvate and two CO2” wrong here? In eukaryotic cytoplasm, what are the net carbon products of glycolysis starting from one glucose before mitochondrial o…
back: CO2 release occurs during pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle, not glycolysis itself.
extra: Confuses glycolysis with pyruvate dehydrogenase oxidative decarboxylation.

front: Hexokinase catalyzes the first committed trapping step of glycolysis. What does it do to glucose?
back: Phosphorylates glucose using ATP
extra: OpenStax: hexokinase phosphorylates glucose using ATP, producing glucose-6-phosphate.

front: Why is “Exports glucose via GLUT transporters” wrong here? Hexokinase catalyzes the first committed trapping step of glycolysis. What does it do to glucose?
back: GLUT facilitators move glucose; hexokinase modifies it.
extra: Transport is not an enzymatic phosphorylation.

front: Why is “Cleaves glucose into two trioses” wrong here? Hexokinase catalyzes the first committed trapping step of glycolysis. What does it do to glucose?
back: Cleavage occurs after fructose-1,6-bisphosphate formation.
extra: That is later aldolase chemistry.

front: Why is “Oxidizes glucose to gluconolactone” wrong here? Hexokinase catalyzes the first committed trapping step of glycolysis. What does it do to glucose?
back: That oxidative step is not the hexokinase reaction.
extra: Describes glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase in PPP.

front: Which enzyme regenerates NAD+ by reducing pyruvate under anaerobic conditions?
back: Lactate dehydrogenase , LDH
extra: OpenStax identifies lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) for this reaction.

front: Why is “Citrate synthase” wrong here? Which enzyme regenerates NAD+ by reducing pyruvate under anaerobic conditions?
back: Citric-cycle entry, not lactate.
extra: Condenses acetyl-CoA with OAA.

front: Why is “Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex” wrong here? Which enzyme regenerates NAD+ by reducing pyruvate under anaerobic conditions?
back: Not the fermentation enzyme.
extra: Makes acetyl-CoA aerobically.

front: Why is “Hexokinase” wrong here? Which enzyme regenerates NAD+ by reducing pyruvate under anaerobic conditions?
back: Upstream of pyruvate.
extra: Phosphorylates glucose.

front: In aerobic mitochondrial electron transport, what is the final electron acceptor?
back: Oxygen
extra: OpenStax: oxygen is the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain.

front: Why is “Cytochrome c only” wrong here? In aerobic mitochondrial electron transport, what is the final electron acceptor?
back: Electrons continue to complex IV and O2.
extra: Cytochrome c is an intermediate carrier.

front: Why is “Water-splitting photosystem II” wrong here? In aerobic mitochondrial electron transport, what is the final electron acceptor?
back: Respiration consumes O2.
extra: That is photosynthetic O2 production, opposite direction.

front: Why is “Carbon dioxide” wrong here? In aerobic mitochondrial electron transport, what is the final electron acceptor?
back: O2 becomes water after accepting electrons.
extra: CO2 is a carbon waste of decarboxylation, not an ETC acceptor.

front: When DNA damage is detected, what does normal p53 do according to the OpenStax cancer chapter?
back: Triggers repair mechanisms
extra: OpenStax: if damage is detected, p53 triggers repair mechanisms.

front: Why is “Builds the mitochondrial proton gradient” wrong here? When DNA damage is detected, what does normal p53 do according to the OpenStax cancer chapter?
back: Unrelated; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: ETC, not p53 — does not match the cited teaching point.

front: Why is “Silences all classical conditioning memories” wrong here? When DNA damage is detected, what does normal p53 do according to the OpenStax cancer chapter?
back: Unrelated; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Psychology confusion.

front: Why is “Immediately phosphorylates glucose via hexokinase” wrong here? When DNA damage is detected, what does normal p53 do according to the OpenStax cancer chapter?
back: p53 is a checkpoint/tumor-suppressor response.
extra: Wrong pathway — does not match the cited teaching point.

front: Which statement about glycolytic regulation matches the OpenStax account?
back: A few key enzymatic steps set the pace
extra: OpenStax: glycolysis is primarily regulated at three key enzymatic steps.

front: Why is “Oxygen level is the sole metabolic input” wrong here? Which statement about glycolytic regulation matches the OpenStax account?
back: Multiple inputs exist.
extra: Oxygen affects aerobic fate, but nucleotide regulators also act.

front: Why is “There are no regulated enzymatic steps” wrong here? Which statement about glycolytic regulation matches the OpenStax account?
back: Regulation concentrates at committed steps.
extra: False; key steps are control points.

front: Why is “Only ATP synthase sets the sugar-breakdown rate” wrong here? Which statement about glycolytic regulation matches the OpenStax account?
back: Glycolysis has its own control enzymes.
extra: ATP synthase is mitochondrial oxphos.

front: What are proto-oncogenes?
back: Genes for positive cell-cycle regulators
extra: OpenStax: genes for positive cell-cycle regulators are called proto-oncogenes.

front: Why is “Genes that only trigger apoptosis programs” wrong here? What are proto-oncogenes?
back: Opposite class; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Overlaps tumor-suppressor roles like p53.

front: Why is “Ribosomal RNA molecules with no protein product” wrong here? What are proto-oncogenes?
back: They are typically protein-coding genes.
extra: Wrong molecule class.

front: Why is “Dietary antioxidants stored in adipocytes” wrong here? What are proto-oncogenes?
back: Genes, not nutrients.
extra: Nonsense — does not match the cited teaching point.

front: After glycolysis in a eukaryotic cell with oxygen available, where are the pyruvate molecules transported next?
back: Into mitochondria for further oxidation
extra: OpenStax: pyruvate produced at the end of glycolysis is transported into the mitochondria when oxygen is available.

front: Why is “Into the Golgi for glycosylation” wrong here? After glycolysis in a eukaryotic cell with oxygen available, where are the pyruvate molecules transported next?
back: Glycosylation substrates are nucleotide sugars.
extra: Golgi processes proteins, not pyruvate oxidation.

front: Why is “Out of the cell as lactate only” wrong here? After glycolysis in a eukaryotic cell with oxygen available, where are the pyruvate molecules transported next?
back: Aerobic cells oxidize pyruvate in mitochondria.
extra: Lactate export is a fermentation alternative, not the aerobic default.

front: Why is “Into the nucleus for transcription” wrong here? After glycolysis in a eukaryotic cell with oxygen available, where are the pyruvate molecules transported next?
back: Transcription uses NTPs, not pyruvate import.
extra: Pyruvate is not a nuclear metabolite for gene expression.

front: During DNA replication, what role does each parental chain play?
back: It templates a new complementary chain
extra: OpenStax: each strand serves as a template for a new complementary strand.

front: Why is “It binds oxygen as the terminal acceptor” wrong here? During DNA replication, what role does each parental chain play?
back: Unrelated to replication.
extra: ETC confusion — does not match the cited teaching point.

front: Why is “It is discarded and replaced by RNA only” wrong here? During DNA replication, what role does each parental chain play?
back: Semiconservative copying uses each chain.
extra: Parental chains remain as templates.

front: Why is “It is converted into glycogen stores” wrong here? During DNA replication, what role does each parental chain play?
back: Nucleic acid remains nucleic acid.
extra: Category error — does not match the cited teaching point.

front: Relative to glycogen, triglycerides in animals are best described as which store?
back: Long-term caloric reserve in adipose tissue
extra: OpenStax describes triglycerides as long-term energy storage in animals.

front: Why is “Oxygen carriers circulating in blood” wrong here? Relative to glycogen, triglycerides in animals are best described as which store?
back: This option does not match the cited source passage for the stem.
extra: That is hemoglobin/myoglobin territory.

front: Why is “Immediate synaptic transmitter pool” wrong here? Relative to glycogen, triglycerides in animals are best described as which store?
back: They are long-term fuel stores.
extra: Lipids are not neurotransmitters here.

front: Why is “The only anaerobic ATP source in muscle” wrong here? Relative to glycogen, triglycerides in animals are best described as which store?
back: Not anaerobic; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Fat oxidation is aerobic.

front: In the genetic code, what is the nucleotide triplet that specifies an amino acid called?
back: A codon
extra: OpenStax refers to the triplet codon.

front: Why is “An Okazaki fragment” wrong here? In the genetic code, what is the nucleotide triplet that specifies an amino acid called?
back: Replication, not coding unit name.
extra: Lagging-strand DNA pieces.

front: Why is “A ligand” wrong here? In the genetic code, what is the nucleotide triplet that specifies an amino acid called?
back: This option does not match the cited source passage for the stem.
extra: General binder term, not the code unit.

front: Why is “An intron” wrong here? In the genetic code, what is the nucleotide triplet that specifies an amino acid called?
back: Not the amino-acid specifier name.
extra: Introns are intervening sequences removed from pre-mRNA.

front:
In a hypothetical cell system, glucose is converted to glucose-6-phosphate by hexokinase using ATP. A variant markedly reduces that enzyme's activity. Later reactions function normally, and investigators can introduce metabolites directly into the relevant compartment.

Which of the following interventions most directly bypasses the defective conversion while supplying its downstream pathway?
back: Supply glucose-6-phosphate directly to the cell system
extra: Glucose-6-phosphate is the product of the impaired reaction. Direct delivery supplies the next pathway step without requiring the defective hexokinase conversion to function first.

front: Why is “Supply additional glucose directly to the cell system” wrong here? In a hypothetical cell system, glucose is converted to glucose-6-phosphate by hexokinase using ATP. A variant markedly r…
back: Glucose is the substrate upstream of the impaired conversion. Increasing its availability does not bypass the requirement for hexokinase to form the downstream metabolite.
extra: Confuses adding more upstream substrate with bypassing the enzyme required to convert it.

front: Why is “Supply a competing active-site ligand to hexokinase” wrong here? In a hypothetical cell system, glucose is converted to glucose-6-phosphate by hexokinase using ATP. A variant markedly r…
back: An active-site competitor opposes substrate access rather than supplying the missing product. It therefore does not provide a bypass around the impaired enzymatic conversion.
extra: Treats an active-site competitor as a source of the missing downstream product.

front: Why is “Remove glucose-6-phosphate from the cell system” wrong here? In a hypothetical cell system, glucose is converted to glucose-6-phosphate by hexokinase using ATP. A variant markedly r…
back: Removing the product further reduces material available for the downstream reactions. It acts in the opposite direction from the requested restoration of pathway input.
extra: Removes the downstream input while attempting to restore supply to later pathway reactions.

front:
A hypothetical isolated pathway is X → Y → Z. Enzyme 1 converts X to Y, and enzyme 2 converts Y to Z; there are no alternative routes. After a sequence variant reduces one enzyme's function, X accumulates while Y and Z fall.

Which of the following best explains this pattern?
back: Reduced activity of enzyme 1 converting X to Y
extra: Blocking the first conversion permits X to accumulate while limiting Y formation. The shortage of Y then also restricts the downstream formation of Z.

front: Why is “Reduced activity of enzyme 2 converting Y to Z” wrong here? A hypothetical isolated pathway is X → Y → Z. Enzyme 1 converts X to Y, and enzyme 2 converts Y to Z; there are no alter…
back: A block at the second conversion would restrict consumption of Y. That does not explain the stated combination of accumulating X with depletion of Y.
extra: Places the block after the depleted intermediate instead of before its impaired formation.

front: Why is “Increased activity of enzyme 1 converting X to Y” wrong here? A hypothetical isolated pathway is X → Y → Z. Enzyme 1 converts X to Y, and enzyme 2 converts Y to Z; there are no alter…
back: Increasing the first conversion would favor X consumption and Y formation. That direction conflicts with the measured accumulation of X and reduction of downstream products.
extra: Predicts substrate accumulation from increasing the reaction that consumes that substrate.

front: Why is “Increased activity of enzyme 2 converting Y to Z” wrong here? A hypothetical isolated pathway is X → Y → Z. Enzyme 1 converts X to Y, and enzyme 2 converts Y to Z; there are no alter…
back: Enhanced conversion of Y to Z does not explain why Z is depleted. It also does not directly account for accumulation before the first reaction.
extra: Uses increased conversion into the final product to explain depletion of that same product.

front:
In a study model, event X has probability 0.20 and event Y has probability 0.30. The model explicitly assumes the two events are independent.

Which of the following probabilities should it assign to both events occurring in the same participant?
back: A probability of 0.06
extra: For independent events, the joint probability is the product of their individual probabilities. Multiplying 0.20 by 0.30 gives 0.06, or a 6% chance of both.

front: Why is “A probability of 0.00” wrong here? In a study model, event X has probability 0.20 and event Y has probability 0.30. The model explicitly assumes the two ev…
back: Zero would mean the events cannot occur together. Independence instead permits joint occurrence and specifies that its probability equals the product of the two individual probabilities.
extra: Confuses independence with events that cannot occur together.

front: Why is “A probability of 0.10” wrong here? In a study model, event X has probability 0.20 and event Y has probability 0.30. The model explicitly assumes the two ev…
back: Subtracting the individual probabilities gives 0.10 but does not calculate their joint occurrence. For independent events, the appropriate operation is multiplication rather than subtraction.
extra: Subtracts marginal probabilities instead of multiplying them for the joint event.

front: Why is “A probability of 0.20” wrong here? In a study model, event X has probability 0.20 and event Y has probability 0.30. The model explicitly assumes the two ev…
back: This is the probability of event X alone. Requiring event Y to occur as well changes the probability to the product 0.20 × 0.30.
extra: Uses the probability of X alone without also requiring Y.

front:
A trial compares the mean change in a measurement between a new intervention and a control. The planned statistical test evaluates whether the population means differ.

Which of the following statements is the null hypothesis for this comparison?
back: The difference in population mean changes is exactly zero
extra: For this comparison, the null hypothesis states that the two population mean changes are equal. A difference of zero expresses that no-difference claim on the measurement scale.

front: Why is “The intervention produces a larger population mean change” wrong here? A trial compares the mean change in a measurement between a new intervention and a control. The planned statistical test…
back: A larger mean change is a directional difference, rather than the no-difference claim being tested. It describes one possible alternative to equal population mean changes.
extra: Substitutes a directional increase for the population no-difference claim.

front: Why is “The intervention produces a smaller population mean change” wrong here? A trial compares the mean change in a measurement between a new intervention and a control. The planned statistical test…
back: A smaller mean change is also a directional difference. The null hypothesis for the stated comparison specifies equal population mean changes rather than choosing either direction.
extra: Substitutes a directional decrease for equality of population means.

front: Why is “The difference in population mean changes is nonzero” wrong here? A trial compares the mean change in a measurement between a new intervention and a control. The planned statistical test…
back: A nonzero difference is the two-sided alternative hypothesis for this comparison. The null retains equality of the population mean changes, corresponding to a difference of zero.
extra: Confuses the two-sided alternative with the no-difference null.

front:
A screening program contacts everyone with a positive result. Before confirmatory testing, the program wants to estimate the fraction of these people who actually have the condition.

Which of the following quantities answers that question?
back: True positive results divided by all positive results
extra: Positive predictive value uses the positive-test group as its denominator. It describes the fraction of those positive results that represent actual disease, which is the program’s question.

front: Why is “True cases detected divided by all people with disease” wrong here? A screening program contacts everyone with a positive result. Before confirmatory testing, the program wants to estimate…
back: This describes sensitivity, the fraction of actual cases the screening test detects. It starts with people known to have disease, rather than the group contacted after positive results.
extra: Confuses detection among actual cases with disease among positive results.

front: Why is “True negatives divided by all people without disease” wrong here? A screening program contacts everyone with a positive result. Before confirmatory testing, the program wants to estimate…
back: This describes specificity, the fraction of disease-free people correctly testing negative. It does not estimate the fraction of positive results that correspond to actual disease.
extra: Substitutes disease-free negative classification for positive predictive value.

front: Why is “False positive results divided by people without disease” wrong here? A screening program contacts everyone with a positive result. Before confirmatory testing, the program wants to estimate…
back: This describes false-positive results among people without disease. The requested quantity instead starts with everyone testing positive and asks how many of them truly have disease.
extra: Uses false positives among noncases instead of true disease among positives.

front:
A study records two binary results for each participant: whether an exposure is present and whether an outcome occurs. Each combination is possible.

Which of the following sets is the sample space for one participant’s paired record?
back: Exposure and outcome; exposure only; outcome only; neither
extra: There are four possible combinations of two binary results: both present, exposure alone, outcome alone and neither. This set includes every possible record described by the study.

front: Why is “Exposure present with outcome; exposure absent without outcome” wrong here? A study records two binary results for each participant: whether an exposure is present and whether an outcome occurs. E…
back: This set contains the two matching combinations but omits the discordant combinations. A sample space must include every possible paired record, not only selected patterns.
extra: Omits discordant exposure-outcome combinations from the possible outcomes.

front: Why is “Exposure present with outcome; exposure present without outcome” wrong here? A study records two binary results for each participant: whether an exposure is present and whether an outcome occurs. E…
back: This set restricts attention to exposed participants and omits both possibilities for unexposed participants. It is a subset of the full sample space for one paired record.
extra: Restricts the sample space to exposed participants.

front: Why is “Exposure absent with outcome; exposure absent without outcome” wrong here? A study records two binary results for each participant: whether an exposure is present and whether an outcome occurs. E…
back: This set restricts attention to unexposed participants and omits both possibilities for exposed participants. The sample space must include all four combinations allowed by the study.
extra: Restricts the sample space to unexposed participants.

front:
A test evaluation labels the four groups as A = true positive, B = false positive, C = false negative and D = true negative.

Which of the following ratios measures the fraction of actual cases that the test detects?
back: A / (A + C)
extra: Actual cases consist of true positives plus false negatives, A + C. The detected cases are A, so sensitivity is A divided by A + C.

front: Why is “D / (B + D)” wrong here? A test evaluation labels the four groups as A = true positive, B = false positive, C = false negative and D = true negat…
back: This ratio is specificity, since it counts true negatives among all people without disease. The requested detection fraction instead starts with the actual cases, represented by A and C.
extra: Uses the specificity formula when detection among actual cases is requested.

front: Why is “B / (A + B)” wrong here? A test evaluation labels the four groups as A = true positive, B = false positive, C = false negative and D = true negat…
back: This ratio counts false positives among all positive results. It measures errors within the positive-test group rather than the fraction of actual cases successfully detected.
extra: Counts false discoveries within positives instead of detected cases within disease.

front: Why is “C / (C + D)” wrong here? A test evaluation labels the four groups as A = true positive, B = false positive, C = false negative and D = true negat…
back: This ratio counts missed cases among all negative results. Sensitivity instead asks how many actual cases are detected, using the case group rather than negative results as the denominator.
extra: Uses missed cases among negative results rather than detected cases among all cases.

front:
A surveillance team already knows which patients truly had a disease from an independent assessment. It asks how successfully a new case definition identifies those patients.

Which of the following quantities directly evaluates this goal?
back: True positive results divided by all people with disease
extra: Sensitivity is the proportion of true cases identified by a test or case definition. Divide the detected true cases by all independently established cases to evaluate this goal.

front: Why is “False positive results divided by all positive results” wrong here? A surveillance team already knows which patients truly had a disease from an independent assessment. It asks how success…
back: This asks how many positive results are false alarms. Sensitivity instead starts with all people known to have disease and measures how many the definition detects.
extra: Counts false alarms among positive results instead of detected actual cases.

front: Why is “True negative results divided by all negative results” wrong here? A surveillance team already knows which patients truly had a disease from an independent assessment. It asks how success…
back: This starts with negative results and measures how many are truly disease-free. The surveillance question instead concerns detection among the independently established group with disease.
extra: Uses the negative-result denominator rather than the actual-case group.

front: Why is “True negative results divided by all disease-free patients” wrong here? A surveillance team already knows which patients truly had a disease from an independent assessment. It asks how success…
back: This is specificity: correctly excluding disease among people without it. Sensitivity uses the group with disease as the denominator and counts the cases detected.
extra: Confuses exclusion among noncases with detection among cases.

front:
A test evaluation labels the four groups as A = true positive, B = false positive, C = false negative and D = true negative.

Which of the following ratios measures correct negative classification among people without disease?
back: D / (B + D)
extra: Disease-free people consist of false positives and true negatives, B + D. Correct exclusions are D, so specificity is D divided by B + D.

front: Why is “A / (A + C)” wrong here? A test evaluation labels the four groups as A = true positive, B = false positive, C = false negative and D = true negat…
back: This ratio is sensitivity, since A and C together represent all actual cases. Specificity instead evaluates correct negative classification among the group without disease.
extra: Uses the diseased-group sensitivity formula to assess disease-free classification.

front: Why is “A / (A + B)” wrong here? A test evaluation labels the four groups as A = true positive, B = false positive, C = false negative and D = true negat…
back: This ratio is positive predictive value, since A and B together represent all positive results. The requested measure instead begins with people independently known to be disease-free.
extra: Substitutes PPV for specificity by conditioning on positive results.

front: Why is “B / (B + D)” wrong here? A test evaluation labels the four groups as A = true positive, B = false positive, C = false negative and D = true negat…
back: This ratio is the false-positive fraction among people without disease. It uses the right denominator but counts incorrect positive results rather than correct negative classifications.
extra: Uses the correct noncase denominator but counts false positives as successes.

front:
A new surveillance rule is tested in a group confirmed to be free of the target disease. Investigators want to know how well the rule avoids incorrectly classifying these people as cases.

Which of the following quantities measures that ability?
back: Negative classifications divided by all disease-free people
extra: Specificity measures correct negative classification among people who do not have the disease. The disease-free group is the denominator, and correctly negative results are the numerator.

front: Why is “Positive classifications divided by all disease-free people” wrong here? A new surveillance rule is tested in a group confirmed to be free of the target disease. Investigators want to know how …
back: This measures the false-positive fraction among people without disease. It complements specificity but counts errors, rather than the successful exclusions requested by the investigators.
extra: Counts false-positive errors instead of successful disease exclusion.

front: Why is “True positive classifications divided by all positive results” wrong here? A new surveillance rule is tested in a group confirmed to be free of the target disease. Investigators want to know how …
back: This is positive predictive value, which starts with positive results. The specified study instead asks about correct classification within a group already known to be disease-free.
extra: Confuses disease among positive results with negative classification of noncases.

front: Why is “True positive classifications divided by all people with disease” wrong here? A new surveillance rule is tested in a group confirmed to be free of the target disease. Investigators want to know how …
back: This is sensitivity, the detection fraction among people with disease. The investigators are assessing exclusion among people without disease, so a different denominator is required.
extra: Substitutes detection among diseased people for exclusion among disease-free people.

front:
A screening test is evaluated in 1,000 people whose disease status is established independently. Of 100 people with disease, 90 test positive. Of 900 people without disease, 90 test positive.

Which of the following pairs gives the test sensitivity and the probability of disease among those testing positive?
back: Sensitivity 90%; probability of disease after a positive test 50%
extra: Sensitivity is 90 true positives divided by 100 people with disease, or 90%. Positive predictive value is 90 true positives divided by 180 positive results, or 50%.

front: Why is “Sensitivity 50%; probability of disease after a positive test 90%” wrong here? A screening test is evaluated in 1,000 people whose disease status is established independently. Of 100 people with dise…
back: Sensitivity uses all actual cases as its denominator, giving 90/100 rather than 90/180. The probability of disease among positive results uses all positive tests, giving 90/180 rather than 90/100.
extra: Swaps the actual-case and positive-result denominators.

front: Why is “Sensitivity 90%; probability of disease after a positive test 90%” wrong here? A screening test is evaluated in 1,000 people whose disease status is established independently. Of 100 people with dise…
back: The 90% sensitivity is correct, but it does not give the probability that a positive result represents disease. The positive group includes 90 people without disease, reducing that probability to 50%.
extra: Treats sensitivity as the probability of disease after a positive result.

front: Why is “Sensitivity 10%; probability of disease after a positive test 50%” wrong here? A screening test is evaluated in 1,000 people whose disease status is established independently. Of 100 people with dise…
back: Ten percent is the proportion of actual cases missed, since 10 of 100 people with disease test negative. Sensitivity measures detected cases instead; the stated positive predictive value is correct.
extra: Substitutes the missed-case fraction for the detected-case fraction.

front:
An independently classified sample contains 200 people with disease and 800 without disease. A test is positive in 160 people with disease and 80 without disease. An analyst reports 160/240 as specificity.

Which of the following calculations should replace that value?
back: 720 divided by 800, yielding 90%
extra: Among the 800 people without disease, 80 test positive and 720 test negative. Specificity is therefore 720/800, or 90%, using the disease-free group as its denominator.

front: Why is “160 divided by 200, yielding 80%” wrong here? An independently classified sample contains 200 people with disease and 800 without disease. A test is positive in 160 p…
back: This ratio measures sensitivity: detected cases divided by all people with disease. Specificity instead concerns correctly negative results among the independently identified group without disease.
extra: Uses detection among diseased people to estimate specificity.

front: Why is “160 divided by 240, yielding 67%” wrong here? An independently classified sample contains 200 people with disease and 800 without disease. A test is positive in 160 p…
back: This is positive predictive value, because it divides true positives by all positive results. Specificity requires the disease-free group as the denominator and true negatives as the numerator.
extra: Substitutes the positive-test denominator for the disease-free denominator.

front: Why is “720 divided by 760, yielding 95%” wrong here? An independently classified sample contains 200 people with disease and 800 without disease. A test is positive in 160 p…
back: This ratio asks what fraction of negative results come from people without disease. Specificity instead divides true negatives by all people without disease, including those who tested positive.
extra: Confuses negative predictive value with specificity.

front:
A 50-year-old woman with type A blood inadvertently receives type B blood during surgery. Within minutes she develops fever, flank pain, and hypotension, and the transfusion is stopped immediately.

Which of the following best explains why this reaction began immediately, without any prior sensitization to type B cells?
back: Her preformed anti-B antibodies bound the transfused cells
extra: In contrast to antibodies against the Rh antigen, which are produced only after exposure, ABO group antibodies are preformed, so a type A recipient already carries anti-B antibodies that react immediately with donor B cells.

front: Why is “Donor T lymphocytes attacked her tissues” wrong here? A 50-year-old woman with type A blood inadvertently receives type B blood during surgery. Within minutes she develops fe…
back: Graft-versus-host reactions mediated by donor lymphocytes develop over days to weeks and cannot explain a reaction within minutes.
extra: A delayed cellular reaction is being used to explain an immediate hemolytic one.

front: Why is “The donor blood contained high-titer anti-A antibodies” wrong here? A 50-year-old woman with type A blood inadvertently receives type B blood during surgery. Within minutes she develops fe…
back: The dominant reaction is the recipient's preformed anti-B antibodies attacking transfused B cells; donor plasma antibodies are diluted and are not the principal driver.
extra: The direction of antigen-antibody reactivity is being reversed.

front: Why is “Her plasma cells rapidly produced new anti-B antibodies” wrong here? A 50-year-old woman with type A blood inadvertently receives type B blood during surgery. Within minutes she develops fe…
back: New antibody production after first exposure takes days; the immediate reaction implies antibodies that already existed.
extra: A primary adaptive response is being credited with minute-level kinetics.

front:
A 24-year-old medical student reviewing a normal ECG tracing identifies distinct deflections corresponding to atrial depolarization, ventricular depolarization, and ventricular repolarization, but cannot find any deflection corresponding to atrial repolarization.

Which of the following best explains why this deflection is not seen?
back: It is masked by the larger QRS complex at that moment
extra: Atrial repolarization occurs at about the same time as ventricular depolarization, and its small signal is masked by the much larger QRS complex.

front: Why is “Atrial repolarization generates no measurable electrical current” wrong here? A 24-year-old medical student reviewing a normal ECG tracing identifies distinct deflections corresponding to atrial dep…
back: Repolarization is an electrical event and does generate current; the deflection exists but is buried in the contemporaneous QRS signal.
extra: Absence of a deflection is being taken to mean absence of the electrical event.

front: Why is “It occurs after the T wave and is therefore not recorded” wrong here? A 24-year-old medical student reviewing a normal ECG tracing identifies distinct deflections corresponding to atrial dep…
back: Atrial repolarization occurs during the QRS interval, well before the T wave (which reflects ventricular repolarization), and within the recorded tracing.
extra: The timing of atrial repolarization is being placed outside the recorded cycle.

front: Why is “It is conducted too slowly through the atria to summate” wrong here? A 24-year-old medical student reviewing a normal ECG tracing identifies distinct deflections corresponding to atrial dep…
back: The issue is not slow conduction but timing: the small atrial repolarization signal coincides with the dominant ventricular depolarization signal.
extra: Conduction velocity is being blamed for a signal-amplitude problem.

front:
A 22-year-old woman stands up quickly from a supine position and experiences a transient decrease in arterial blood pressure, which is corrected within seconds and she does not faint.

Which of the following sequences correctly describes the immediate baroreceptor reflex response to this decrease in pressure?
back: Decreased baroreceptor firing, increased sympathetic outflow, increased heart rate and vasoconstriction
extra: Decreased blood pressure produces slower rates of baroreceptor firing; reduced afferent input increases sympathetic drive, raising heart rate and constricting peripheral vessels to restore pressure.

front: Why is “Increased chemoreceptor firing, hyperventilation, increased pressure” wrong here? A 22-year-old woman stands up quickly from a supine position and experiences a transient decrease in arterial blood pres…
back: Chemoreceptors monitor oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH; the acute response to a postural pressure drop is mediated by baroreceptors, not ventilatory chemoreflexes.
extra: The chemoreceptor reflex is being substituted for the baroreceptor reflex.

front: Why is “Increased baroreceptor firing, increased parasympathetic outflow via the vagus nerve, decreased heart rate” wrong here? A 22-year-old woman stands up quickly from a supine position and experiences a transient decrease in arterial blood pres…
back: Increased firing with vagal slowing is the response to an increase in pressure; this patient's pressure fell, so firing decreases and sympathetic output rises instead.
extra: The reflex response to rising pressure is being applied to falling pressure.

front: Why is “Decreased baroreceptor firing, increased vagal outflow, decreased heart rate” wrong here? A 22-year-old woman stands up quickly from a supine position and experiences a transient decrease in arterial blood pres…
back: Although falling pressure does decrease firing, the reflex response to hypotension is sympathetic activation and vagal withdrawal, which raise rather than lower the heart rate.
extra: The afferent limb is correct but the efferent limb is inverted.

front:
A healthy 28-year-old medical student has a resting heart rate of 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 75 mL. During a treadmill study, his cardiac output rises with exertion, as expected in a nonathlete, toward a maximum of about 20 L/min.

Which of the following values best approximates his resting cardiac output?
back: 5.25 L/min
extra: Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume: 70 × 75 mL = 5,250 mL/min, or 5.25 L/min, the mean resting value cited for adults.

front: Why is “3.5 L/min” wrong here? A healthy 28-year-old medical student has a resting heart rate of 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 75 mL. Duri…
back: Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume: 70 beats per minute times 75 mL gives 5,250 mL/min, not half that value.
extra: The stroke volume is being halved before multiplying by heart rate.

front: Why is “14.0 L/min” wrong here? A healthy 28-year-old medical student has a resting heart rate of 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 75 mL. Duri…
back: Outputs approaching 14-20 L/min occur during exercise, when rate and stroke volume both rise; the resting computation gives 5.25 L/min.
extra: An exertional output is being reported as the resting value.

front: Why is “7.0 L/min” wrong here? A healthy 28-year-old medical student has a resting heart rate of 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 75 mL. Duri…
back: At 70 beats per minute, 7.0 L/min would require a stroke volume of 100 mL; with the measured 75 mL, output is 5.25 L/min.
extra: A stroke volume of 100 mL is being assumed rather than the measured 75 mL.

front: When arterial blood pressure rises, baroreceptor firing rate most likely does which of the following?
back: Increases because greater vessel wall stretch activates the receptors
extra: Increased blood pressure stretches carotid and aortic baroreceptors, producing increased rates of baroreceptor firing.

front: Why is “Decreases because stretch receptors are inhibited by higher pressure” wrong here? When arterial blood pressure rises, baroreceptor firing rate most likely does which of the following?
back: Baroreceptors increase firing when arterial pressure rises; decreased firing occurs when pressure falls.
extra: The pressure–firing relationship is inverted.

front: Why is “No change because baroreceptors respond only to oxygen tension” wrong here? When arterial blood pressure rises, baroreceptor firing rate most likely does which of the following?
back: Baroreceptors sense arterial stretch and pressure; chemoreceptors monitor blood gas and pH.
extra: Chemoreceptor function is being substituted for baroreceptor function.

front: Why is “Complete cessation of firing until pressure normalizes” wrong here? When arterial blood pressure rises, baroreceptor firing rate most likely does which of the following?
back: Baroreceptors fire continuously at a rate proportional to pressure; rising pressure increases, not abolishes, firing.
extra: Baroreceptors are being treated as on–off switches rather than graded sensors.

front: When a healthy person stands up quickly and arterial pressure falls transiently, baroreceptor afferent activity to the brainstem most likely does which of the following?
back: Decreases, reducing inhibitory input and permitting increased sympathetic outflow
extra: Decreased blood pressure produces slower rates of baroreceptor firing; reduced afferent input permits increased sympathetic drive to raise heart rate and vascular tone.

front: Why is “Increases, triggering increased parasympathetic outflow and bradycardia” wrong here? When a healthy person stands up quickly and arterial pressure falls transiently, baroreceptor afferent activity to the b…
back: Increased firing with vagal slowing follows a rise in pressure; when pressure falls, firing decreases instead.
extra: The response to rising pressure is being applied to falling pressure.

front: Why is “Remains unchanged because chemoreceptors compensate within seconds” wrong here? When a healthy person stands up quickly and arterial pressure falls transiently, baroreceptor afferent activity to the b…
back: The immediate correction to an orthostatic pressure drop is mediated by baroreceptors, not ventilatory chemoreflexes.
extra: Chemoreceptor reflexes are being substituted for the acute baroreceptor response.

front: Why is “Increases, causing reflex vasodilation in skeletal muscle beds” wrong here? When a healthy person stands up quickly and arterial pressure falls transiently, baroreceptor afferent activity to the b…
back: Falling pressure decreases, not increases, baroreceptor firing; the efferent response is sympathetic vasoconstriction, not vasodilation.
extra: Both the afferent direction and efferent limb are inverted.

front:
A 67-year-old man with long-standing hypertension undergoes left heart catheterization with simultaneous phonocardiography and left ventricular pressure-volume recording. Immediately after the end of ejection, ventricular pressure falls rapidly while ventricular volume remains unchanged and no blood enters the ventricle. A sharp sound is recorded at the onset of this interval.

Which of the following valve events most directly produces this sound?
back: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
extra: When ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure at the end of systole, the semilunar valves close, producing the second heart sound and beginning isovolumic relaxation with all valves shut.

front: Why is “Simultaneous opening of all four heart valves” wrong here? A 67-year-old man with long-standing hypertension undergoes left heart catheterization with simultaneous phonocardiograp…
back: All four valves never open together in the normal cycle; the second heart sound is produced specifically by closure of the semilunar valves.
extra: An impossible valve configuration is being proposed for a normal sound.

front: Why is “Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves” wrong here? A 67-year-old man with long-standing hypertension undergoes left heart catheterization with simultaneous phonocardiograp…
back: Mitral and tricuspid valve closure produces the first heart sound at the start of systole; the sound recorded after ejection ends reflects semilunar valve closure.
extra: The onset-of-systole atrioventricular closure is being credited with the post-ejection sound.

front: Why is “Opening of the atrioventricular valves during ventricular filling” wrong here? A 67-year-old man with long-standing hypertension undergoes left heart catheterization with simultaneous phonocardiograp…
back: Atrioventricular valves open silently during diastole when atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure; the audible event after ejection is semilunar closure.
extra: A silent diastolic opening event is being substituted for an audible closure.

front: Which of the following equations defines cardiac output?
back: Heart rate multiplied by stroke volume
extra: Each beat ejects the stroke volume, and multiplying by heart rate gives total volume per minute — the definition of cardiac output.

front: Why is “Heart rate divided by stroke volume” wrong here? Which of the following equations defines cardiac output?
back: Cardiac output is the volume ejected per minute, so rate and stroke volume multiply; dividing would give beats per milliliter, not liters per minute.
extra: The product relationship is being inverted.

front: Why is “Stroke volume minus end-diastolic volume” wrong here? Which of the following equations defines cardiac output?
back: End-diastolic minus end-systolic volumes relate to stroke volume itself, not to the minute-by-minute output equation.
extra: A chamber volume difference is being substituted for minute output.

front: Why is “Mean arterial pressure divided by systemic vascular resistance” wrong here? Which of the following equations defines cardiac output?
back: That relationship links pressure, flow, and resistance; cardiac output is defined directly as heart rate times stroke volume.
extra: A hemodynamic rearrangement is being confused with the pump definition.

front:
A 68-year-old man with systolic heart failure has fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 25 percent. His resting heart rate is 88 beats per minute and stroke volume is 40 mL.

Which of the following values best approximates his resting cardiac output?
back: 3.5 L/min
extra: Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume: 88 × 40 mL = 3,520 mL/min ≈ 3.5 L/min, well below the normal resting average near 5.25 L/min in pump failure.

front: Why is “7.0 L/min” wrong here? A 68-year-old man with systolic heart failure has fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Echocardiography shows an ejection fra…
back: 7.0 L/min exceeds what 88 × 40 mL yields and is more typical of moderate exercise than decompensated resting failure.
extra: An exertional output is being reported at rest.

front: Why is “14.0 L/min” wrong here? A 68-year-old man with systolic heart failure has fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Echocardiography shows an ejection fra…
back: Outputs near 14–20 L/min occur in vigorous exercise; resting failure with low stroke volume gives about 3.5 L/min.
extra: Maximal exercise output is being chosen for a resting heart-failure patient.

front: Why is “1.8 L/min” wrong here? A 68-year-old man with systolic heart failure has fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Echocardiography shows an ejection fra…
back: 40 mL alone is not cardiac output; multiplying 88 beats per minute by 40 mL gives about 3.5 L/min.
extra: Heart rate is being omitted from the product.

front:
A 68-year-old man with a prior myocardial infarction presents with progressive dyspnea and orthopnea. Examination shows elevated jugular venous pressure and bilateral crackles. Echocardiography reveals a dilated left ventricle with a markedly depressed ejection fraction. Despite an elevated end-diastolic volume, his forward stroke volume remains low.

Which of the following best explains why the Frank–Starling mechanism fails to restore adequate output in this patient?
back: Reduced contractility flattens the stretch–force relationship
extra: Frank–Starling links greater stretch to stronger contraction only within limits and for a given inotropic state; after infarction, reduced contractility flattens that curve so elevated end-diastolic volume no longer yields adequate stroke volume.

front: Why is “Increased preload has abolished venous return to the heart” wrong here? A 68-year-old man with a prior myocardial infarction presents with progressive dyspnea and orthopnea. Examination shows …
back: Venous return and preload are elevated; the problem is that the damaged myocardium cannot convert that stretch into an adequate stroke volume.
extra: High filling is being treated as loss of venous return.

front: Why is “Decreased afterload prevents the ventricle from ejecting” wrong here? A 68-year-old man with a prior myocardial infarction presents with progressive dyspnea and orthopnea. Examination shows …
back: Lower afterload would favor ejection; in systolic failure the limiting factor is reduced contractility, often with elevated afterload from vasoconstriction.
extra: Low afterload is being blamed for low output.

front: Why is “Heart rate alone determines stroke volume in dilated ventricles” wrong here? A 68-year-old man with a prior myocardial infarction presents with progressive dyspnea and orthopnea. Examination shows …
back: Heart rate multiplies stroke volume to give cardiac output; it does not replace preload–contractility coupling as the per-beat mechanism.
extra: Rate is being substituted for the length–tension mechanism.

front: Mean arterial pressure is calculated by adding what fraction of the pulse pressure to the diastolic pressure?
back: One-third
extra: Mean arterial pressure equals diastolic pressure plus one-third of the difference between systolic and diastolic pressures.

front: Why is “Two-thirds” wrong here? Mean arterial pressure is calculated by adding what fraction of the pulse pressure to the diastolic pressure?
back: Adding two-thirds of the pulse pressure overweights systole; the correct weighting is one-third above diastolic.
extra: Systolic pressure is being overweighted relative to diastolic.

front: Why is “The full pulse pressure” wrong here? Mean arterial pressure is calculated by adding what fraction of the pulse pressure to the diastolic pressure?
back: Adding the full pulse pressure would approximate systolic pressure, not the time-averaged mean.
extra: The entire systolic-diastolic difference is being added to diastolic.

front: Why is “Zero — MAP equals diastolic pressure alone” wrong here? Mean arterial pressure is calculated by adding what fraction of the pulse pressure to the diastolic pressure?
back: Diastolic pressure alone ignores systolic flow during systole; one-third of the pulse pressure must be added.
extra: The contribution of systolic pressure during systole is being ignored entirely.

front:
A 74-year-old woman with urosepsis is brought to the emergency department lethargic and confused. Examination shows cool extremities, delayed capillary refill, and a blood pressure of 80/50 mm Hg with a heart rate of 118 beats per minute.

Which of the following values best approximates her mean arterial pressure?
back: 60 mm Hg
extra: Mean arterial pressure equals diastolic plus one-third of the pulse pressure: 50 + 30/3 = 60 mm Hg, consistent with hypotensive shock.

front: Why is “50 mm Hg” wrong here? A 74-year-old woman with urosepsis is brought to the emergency department lethargic and confused. Examination shows cool…
back: MAP adds one-third of the pulse pressure to diastolic; 50 mm Hg ignores the systolic contribution during the brief systolic phase.
extra: Diastolic pressure alone is being reported as the mean.

front: Why is “65 mm Hg” wrong here? A 74-year-old woman with urosepsis is brought to the emergency department lethargic and confused. Examination shows cool…
back: The simple midpoint of 80 and 50 is 65 mm Hg; MAP weights diastole more heavily and gives about 60 mm Hg.
extra: The arithmetic midpoint of systolic and diastolic is being used.

front: Why is “70 mm Hg” wrong here? A 74-year-old woman with urosepsis is brought to the emergency department lethargic and confused. Examination shows cool…
back: Adding two-thirds of the pulse pressure to diastolic overestimates MAP; the correct computation yields about 60 mm Hg.
extra: Two-thirds of the pulse pressure is being added instead of one-third.

front: According to Poiseuille's law, blood flow through a vessel is proportional to the vessel radius raised to which power?
back: Fourth power
extra: Poiseuille's equation includes r⁴ in the numerator, so even modest arteriolar constriction dramatically reduces flow.

front: Why is “First power (linear)” wrong here? According to Poiseuille's law, blood flow through a vessel is proportional to the vessel radius raised to which power?
back: A linear dependence would mean halving radius halves flow; Poiseuille's law uses a much stronger radius dependence.
extra: Flow is being assumed to vary directly with radius.

front: Why is “Second power (squared)” wrong here? According to Poiseuille's law, blood flow through a vessel is proportional to the vessel radius raised to which power?
back: Radius squared appears in cross-sectional area, but Poiseuille's law raises radius to the fourth power in the full flow equation.
extra: A squared relationship is being applied instead of the fourth-power term.

front: Why is “Third power (cubed)” wrong here? According to Poiseuille's law, blood flow through a vessel is proportional to the vessel radius raised to which power?
back: The radius term in Poiseuille's law is r⁴, not r³; small radius changes therefore have outsized effects on flow.
extra: A cubic exponent is being chosen.

front:
A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension undergoes research imaging that shows his renal arterioles have an average lumen radius 10 percent smaller than age-matched normotensive controls, while blood viscosity, vessel length, and driving pressure are similar.

Assuming Poiseuille's law applies, renal blood flow in his arterioles is expected to be which of the following fractions of normal?
back: About 66 percent of baseline flow
extra: Flow ∝ r⁴, so a 10 percent radius reduction yields (0.9)⁴ ≈ 0.66 of baseline flow — a disproportionately large drop from a small anatomic change.

front: Why is “About 90 percent of baseline flow” wrong here? A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension undergoes research imaging that shows his renal arterioles have an…
back: A 10 percent radius reduction is not a 10 percent flow reduction; Poiseuille's law raises radius to the fourth power.
extra: Flow is being assumed to track radius linearly.

front: Why is “About 81 percent of baseline flow” wrong here? A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension undergoes research imaging that shows his renal arterioles have an…
back: Radius squared would give ~0.81, not 0.66; the correct exponent is four.
extra: A squared relationship (0.9²) is being applied.

front: Why is “About 73 percent of baseline flow” wrong here? A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension undergoes research imaging that shows his renal arterioles have an…
back: 0.9³ ≈ 0.73; the Poiseuille exponent is four, giving (0.9)⁴ ≈ 0.66.
extra: A cubic approximation is being used.

front:
During a physiology laboratory, a 23-year-old medical student records an action potential from an isolated ventricular myocyte obtained from a 50-year-old donor heart. After a drug that selectively blocks slow calcium channels is applied, the rapid upstroke of the action potential is preserved, but the waveform that follows is markedly shortened.

Which of the following phases of the myocyte action potential is most directly dependent on the blocked channels?
back: Plateau phase (phase 2)
extra: The plateau phase is maintained largely by the opening of slow Ca2+ channels, allowing Ca2+ to enter the cell, so blocking these channels shortens the plateau while sparing the sodium-driven upstroke.

front: Why is “Rapid upstroke (phase 0)” wrong here? During a physiology laboratory, a 23-year-old medical student records an action potential from an isolated ventricular m…
back: A prepotential phase with a slow influx of Na+ is a feature of conductive cells, not of the contractile myocyte being recorded here.
extra: A pacemaker-cell feature is being assigned to a contractile myocyte.

front: Why is “Prepotential drift phase” wrong here? During a physiology laboratory, a 23-year-old medical student records an action potential from an isolated ventricular m…
back: The rapid upstroke is produced by a rapid influx of Na+, which raises the membrane potential to approximately +30 mV; it is preserved when slow calcium channels are blocked.
extra: The upstroke is being attributed to calcium influx rather than sodium influx.

front: Why is “Repolarization (phase 3)” wrong here? During a physiology laboratory, a 23-year-old medical student records an action potential from an isolated ventricular m…
back: Repolarization follows closure of Ca2+ channels with opening of K+ channels, allowing K+ to exit the cell; it is not driven by calcium influx.
extra: Repolarization is being attributed to calcium rather than potassium movement.

front:
During coronary angiography of a 58-year-old man with exertional chest pain, the interventional cardiologist engages the catheter tip in the anterior aortic sinus, just superior to the aortic valve cusps, and injects contrast medium.

Which of the following vessels is most directly opacified by this injection?
back: Right coronary artery
extra: The right coronary artery arises from the anterior aortic sinus, so contrast injected at that site fills the right coronary system first.

front: Why is “Left anterior descending artery” wrong here? During coronary angiography of a 58-year-old man with exertional chest pain, the interventional cardiologist engages the…
back: The left anterior descending artery is a branch of the left coronary artery, which arises from a different aortic sinus than the anterior site described.
extra: A branch of the left coronary system is being filled from the right-sided origin.

front: Why is “Circumflex artery” wrong here? During coronary angiography of a 58-year-old man with exertional chest pain, the interventional cardiologist engages the…
back: The circumflex artery branches from the left coronary artery; contrast in the anterior aortic sinus enters the right coronary artery instead.
extra: Another left-sided branch is being opacified from the anterior sinus.

front: Why is “Left main coronary artery” wrong here? During coronary angiography of a 58-year-old man with exertional chest pain, the interventional cardiologist engages the…
back: The left main coronary artery does not arise from the anterior aortic sinus; the anterior sinus gives rise to the right coronary artery.
extra: The left coronary origin is being placed in the anterior aortic sinus.

front:
In an experiment, an isolated skeletal muscle fiber from a 30-year-old donor is stimulated electrically, generating an action potential that propagates along the sarcolemma and into the T-tubules. The fiber is then bathed in a solution that chelates calcium ions, and contraction fails to occur despite a normal action potential.

Which of the following steps in excitation-contraction coupling is most directly interrupted by the chelator?
back: Exposure of myosin-binding sites on actin
extra: The action potential triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and in relaxed muscle the myosin-binding site on actin is blocked by tropomyosin; without calcium, that blockade is not lifted.

front: Why is “Propagation of the action potential along the sarcolemma” wrong here? In an experiment, an isolated skeletal muscle fiber from a 30-year-old donor is stimulated electrically, generating an a…
back: The action potential propagates normally in the chelating solution; the failure is downstream of the electrical signal, at the calcium-dependent regulatory step.
extra: The electrical step is being treated as calcium-dependent.

front: Why is “Binding of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction” wrong here? In an experiment, an isolated skeletal muscle fiber from a 30-year-old donor is stimulated electrically, generating an a…
back: The fiber is stimulated electrically, bypassing the neuromuscular junction; acetylcholine binding is not the step interrupted by calcium chelation.
extra: An upstream synaptic event is being blamed for a failure inside the fiber.

front: Why is “Hydrolysis of ATP by the myosin head” wrong here? In an experiment, an isolated skeletal muscle fiber from a 30-year-old donor is stimulated electrically, generating an a…
back: ATP hydrolysis powers the cross-bridge cycle but is not the calcium-dependent switch; the chelator blocks site exposure, not ATP use.
extra: The energy-supplying step is being confused with the regulatory trigger.

front: Which rhythm diagnosis best matches the R-R spacing and baseline pattern visible in this recorded tracing?
back: Atrial fibrillation
extra: The baseline lacks discrete P waves and the QRS complexes occur at unequal intervals, matching atrial fibrillation.

front: Why is “Normal sinus rhythm” wrong here? Which rhythm diagnosis best matches the R-R spacing and baseline pattern visible in this recorded tracing?
back: Sinus rhythm requires organized P waves preceding QRS complexes with a regular relationship, which is absent here.
extra: Irregular ventricular timing and absent organized P waves are being overlooked.

front: Why is “Second-degree AV block” wrong here? Which rhythm diagnosis best matches the R-R spacing and baseline pattern visible in this recorded tracing?
back: Second-degree block has identifiable regular P waves, some of which fail to conduct; this tracing has no discrete P waves.
extra: Intermittent failure of conduction is being inferred without discrete P waves.

front: Why is “Ventricular tachycardia” wrong here? Which rhythm diagnosis best matches the R-R spacing and baseline pattern visible in this recorded tracing?
back: The QRS complexes here are narrow and variably spaced rather than broad, rapid, and regularly repeated.
extra: An irregular narrow-complex rhythm is being confused with a regular broad-complex tachycardia.

front: The waveform marked X on this recorded rhythm strip corresponds most directly to which electrical event?
back: Ventricular depolarization
extra: The highlighted sharp QRS complex represents depolarization spreading through the ventricles.

front: Why is “Atrial depolarization” wrong here? The waveform marked X on this recorded rhythm strip corresponds most directly to which electrical event?
back: Atrial depolarization produces the smaller P wave that precedes the highlighted complex.
extra: The P wave is being confused with the larger ventricular complex.

front: Why is “Atrial repolarization” wrong here? The waveform marked X on this recorded rhythm strip corresponds most directly to which electrical event?
back: Atrial repolarization is normally obscured by ventricular depolarization rather than forming this prominent complex.
extra: A hidden atrial event is being assigned to the visible QRS complex.

front: Why is “Ventricular repolarization” wrong here? The waveform marked X on this recorded rhythm strip corresponds most directly to which electrical event?
back: Ventricular repolarization is represented by the broader T wave after the QRS complex.
extra: The QRS complex is being confused with the later T wave.

front: Which atrioventricular conduction pattern is visible in this rhythm strip?
back: Intermittent P-to-QRS conduction
extra: Regular P waves are present, but only one of every three atrial impulses is followed by a ventricular QRS complex.

front: Why is “Fixed one-to-one P-to-QRS conduction” wrong here? Which atrioventricular conduction pattern is visible in this rhythm strip?
back: Several P waves are followed by no QRS complex, so conduction is not one-to-one.
extra: The tracing is being read as one-to-one atrioventricular conduction.

front: Why is “Independent atrial and ventricular rhythms” wrong here? Which atrioventricular conduction pattern is visible in this rhythm strip?
back: The conducted beats retain a visible P-to-QRS relationship; complete independence would indicate third-degree block.
extra: Complete atrioventricular dissociation is being substituted for intermittent block.

front: Why is “Absent P waves with irregular QRS timing” wrong here? Which atrioventricular conduction pattern is visible in this rhythm strip?
back: This strip contains distinct regular P waves, unlike the disorganized atrial activity of atrial fibrillation.
extra: Atrial fibrillation is being substituted for regularly timed P waves.

front: Which atrioventricular relationship is visible in this rhythm strip?
back: Independent atrial and ventricular rhythms
extra: The P waves march through at one rate while the QRS complexes occur at a slower separate rate, with no fixed correlation.

front: Why is “Fixed one-to-one AV conduction” wrong here? Which atrioventricular relationship is visible in this rhythm strip?
back: The P waves do not maintain a fixed interval before the QRS complexes, so each atrial impulse is not conducting normally.
extra: One-to-one atrioventricular conduction is being inferred despite changing P-to-QRS positions.

front: Why is “Alternating two-to-one AV conduction” wrong here? Which atrioventricular relationship is visible in this rhythm strip?
back: There is no repeating conducted P-to-QRS relationship; the two rhythms move independently.
extra: A fixed partial block is being substituted for complete dissociation.

front: Why is “Absent P waves with irregular QRS timing” wrong here? Which atrioventricular relationship is visible in this rhythm strip?
back: Regular P waves remain visible, and the ventricular complexes also follow a regular slower rhythm.
extra: Atrial fibrillation is being substituted despite visible organized P waves.

front:
A model of the resting cardiac cycle receives 100 mL of filling volume per beat. For this experiment, 75 mL enters during passive filling and 25 mL during atrial contraction. The active atrial contribution is then abolished while the passive contribution is held fixed.

Which of the following filling volumes remains?
back: 75 mL per beat
extra: The removed contribution is the 25 mL supplied by atrial contraction. Because passive filling is explicitly preserved, its 75 mL remains available each beat.

front: Why is “25 mL per beat” wrong here? A model of the resting cardiac cycle receives 100 mL of filling volume per beat. For this experiment, 75 mL enters durin…
