front: Why is “Acinar cells that secrete digestive enzymes” wrong here? A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with 3 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss. Examinat…
back: Acinar destruction causes exocrine insufficiency, not the absolute insulin deficiency that drives ketoacidosis in type 1 diabetes.
extra: Exocrine pancreatic injury is being confused with endocrine insulin deficiency.

front:
A 35-year-old flight attendant flying across eight time zones struggles with daytime sleepiness for several days after arrival. Her symptoms reflect a pineal hormone whose secretion is entrained by light.

Retinal light exposure reduces this hormone's blood level by signaling through which of the following?
back: The suprachiasmatic nucleus, which relays the light signal to inhibit pineal melatonin
extra: Retinal photons send a nerve impulse to the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which relays through the cord to the pineal gland, inhibiting melatonin and promoting wakefulness; declining light lets melatonin rise, causing drowsiness.

front: Why is “The lateral geniculate nucleus, routing vision to the cortex” wrong here? A 35-year-old flight attendant flying across eight time zones struggles with daytime sleepiness for several days after a…
back: The geniculate pathway serves visual perception; circadian light information goes from the retina to the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which inhibits pineal melatonin.
extra: The image-forming visual relay is being confused with circadian entrainment.

front: Why is “The paraventricular nucleus, which releases oxytocin to suppress the pineal” wrong here? A 35-year-old flight attendant flying across eight time zones struggles with daytime sleepiness for several days after a…
back: Paraventricular nuclei make oxytocin; the light-dark signal for melatonin travels from retina to the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which regulates pineal output.
extra: A hypothalamic hormone nucleus is being substituted for the rhythm center.

front: Why is “The area postrema, sampling blood light levels outside the barrier” wrong here? A 35-year-old flight attendant flying across eight time zones struggles with daytime sleepiness for several days after a…
back: The area postrema detects blood-borne toxins for emesis; light information reaches the pineal gland via the retina and suprachiasmatic nucleus.
extra: A chemosensory circumventricular organ is being given a photic role.

front:
A 48-year-old man becomes dehydrated on a long hike, and his blood osmolarity climbs. Hypothalamic osmoreceptors trigger ADH release, his kidneys reabsorb more water, his osmolarity falls back toward normal, and ADH secretion then declines.

This pattern of endocrine control is best described as which of the following?
back: Negative feedback reversing a deviation from the set point
extra: Negative feedback reverses a deviation from the set point: high osmolarity provokes ADH, water retention lowers osmolarity, and the corrected signal then reduces ADH secretion — the primary mode of hormone regulation.

front: Why is “Upregulation of renal ADH receptors from chronic stimulation” wrong here? A 48-year-old man becomes dehydrated on a long hike, and his blood osmolarity climbs. Hypothalamic osmoreceptors trigger…
back: Upregulation raises receptor numbers when hormone is chronically low; the vignette describes the stimulus being reversed by the response, which defines negative feedback.
extra: A receptor-sensitivity change is being confused with the feedback pattern itself.

front: Why is “Positive feedback amplifying the original osmolar signal” wrong here? A 48-year-old man becomes dehydrated on a long hike, and his blood osmolarity climbs. Hypothalamic osmoreceptors trigger…
back: Positive feedback would drive osmolarity further from normal; here the output (water retention) corrects the stimulus and ADH secretion falls, which is negative feedback.
extra: A self-amplifying loop is being attributed to a response that shuts itself down.

front: Why is “A permissive interaction between two pituitary hormones” wrong here? A 48-year-old man becomes dehydrated on a long hike, and his blood osmolarity climbs. Hypothalamic osmoreceptors trigger…
back: Permissiveness means one hormone enables another's action; this vignette shows a hormone response that reverses its own triggering stimulus — negative feedback.
extra: A hormone-hormone interaction is being confused with stimulus-response regulation.

front:
A 55-year-old man develops persistent thirst and large volumes of dilute urine after a closed head injury, and he is diagnosed with central diabetes insipidus from deficient antidiuretic hormone (ADH). The posterior pituitary itself does not synthesize ADH.

In a healthy person, the ADH stored in the posterior pituitary is produced by which of the following?
back: Supraoptic nuclei of the hypothalamus
extra: The posterior pituitary only stores and secretes hypothalamic hormones; ADH is produced by the supraoptic nuclei and oxytocin by the paraventricular nuclei, both traveling along axons to the posterior lobe.

front: Why is “Juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney” wrong here? A 55-year-old man develops persistent thirst and large volumes of dilute urine after a closed head injury, and he is dia…
back: Juxtaglomerular cells release renin, not ADH; ADH is made by hypothalamic supraoptic neurons and released from their posterior pituitary axon terminals.
extra: A renal secretory cell responding to the same system is being named as the source.

front: Why is “Paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus” wrong here? A 55-year-old man develops persistent thirst and large volumes of dilute urine after a closed head injury, and he is dia…
back: The paraventricular nuclei produce oxytocin; ADH comes from the supraoptic nuclei, both hormones then traveling down axons for storage in the posterior pituitary.
extra: The two posterior-lobe hormones are being assigned to each other's nuclei.

front: Why is “Anterior pituitary endocrine cells” wrong here? A 55-year-old man develops persistent thirst and large volumes of dilute urine after a closed head injury, and he is dia…
back: The anterior lobe makes GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, and prolactin — not ADH, which is hypothalamic in origin and merely stored in the posterior lobe.
extra: The wrong pituitary lobe is being credited with ADH synthesis.

front:
A 62-year-old woman has a parathyroid adenoma producing excess parathyroid hormone (PTH). Her serum calcium is elevated and a wrist fracture follows minimal trauma.

The rise in her blood calcium is driven most directly by PTH doing which of the following?
back: Stimulating osteoclasts, which release calcium from bone into blood
extra: PTH stimulates osteoclast proliferation and activity, releasing calcium from bone into the circulation; it also promotes calcium reabsorption by kidney tubules, compounding the hypercalcemia.

front: Why is “Stimulating osteoblasts to secrete excess calcium-rich matrix” wrong here? A 62-year-old woman has a parathyroid adenoma producing excess parathyroid hormone (PTH). Her serum calcium is elevated …
back: Osteoblasts lay down new bone, which removes calcium from blood; PTH raises calcium by stimulating osteoclast-mediated resorption, not formation.
extra: The bone-forming cell is being credited with raising blood calcium.

front: Why is “Triggering calcitonin release from the thyroid gland” wrong here? A 62-year-old woman has a parathyroid adenoma producing excess parathyroid hormone (PTH). Her serum calcium is elevated …
back: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts and driving calcium uptake into bone; PTH and calcitonin act in opposition and are generally not secreted together.
extra: The opposing hormone is being cast as PTH's effector.

front: Why is “Blocking renal calcium reabsorption to protect the kidneys” wrong here? A 62-year-old woman has a parathyroid adenoma producing excess parathyroid hormone (PTH). Her serum calcium is elevated …
back: PTH promotes calcium reabsorption by the kidney tubules, which raises blood calcium; blocking reabsorption would lower it.
extra: One of PTH's renal actions is being inverted.

front: Which of the following hormones raises blood calcium by stimulating osteoclast activity?
back: Parathyroid hormone from parathyroid glands
extra: PTH stimulates osteoclast proliferation and activity, releasing calcium from bone into blood.

front: Why is “Calcitonin from thyroid C cells” wrong here? Which of the following hormones raises blood calcium by stimulating osteoclast activity?
back: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts; PTH raises calcium.
extra: The calcium-lowering hormone is being confused with the calcium-raising one.

front: Why is “Insulin from pancreatic beta cells” wrong here? Which of the following hormones raises blood calcium by stimulating osteoclast activity?
back: Insulin regulates glucose uptake; it does not raise blood calcium via osteoclasts.
extra: Glucose regulation is being confused with calcium regulation.

front: Why is “Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex” wrong here? Which of the following hormones raises blood calcium by stimulating osteoclast activity?
back: Aldosterone regulates sodium and potassium balance, not osteoclast-driven calcium release.
extra: Sodium/volume control is being confused with calcium control.

front: Serum calcium falls after a prolonged fast without dairy intake. Which hormone response most directly restores calcium toward normal?
back: Increased parathyroid hormone release
extra: Falling blood calcium stimulates PTH secretion, which raises calcium via bone resorption and renal reabsorption.

front: Why is “Increased calcitonin release from thyroid C cells” wrong here? Serum calcium falls after a prolonged fast without dairy intake. Which hormone response most directly restores calcium t…
back: Calcitonin lowers calcium; the corrective response to hypocalcemia is increased PTH.
extra: Further lowering calcium is being treated as the corrective response.

front: Why is “Decreased parathyroid hormone release” wrong here? Serum calcium falls after a prolonged fast without dairy intake. Which hormone response most directly restores calcium t…
back: Low calcium stimulates PTH release; decreasing PTH would worsen hypocalcemia.
extra: PTH is being assumed to fall when calcium is already low.

front: Why is “Increased aldosterone release” wrong here? Serum calcium falls after a prolonged fast without dairy intake. Which hormone response most directly restores calcium t…
back: Aldosterone responds to volume/potassium signals, not to low serum calcium.
extra: Mineralocorticoid volume signaling is being confused with calcium homeostasis.

front:
A 58-year-old woman reports several months of fatigue, constipation, and increased thirst with polyuria. Laboratory evaluation shows an elevated serum calcium concentration and a low serum phosphate concentration. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry demonstrates reduced bone mineral density at the lumbar spine and femoral neck.

Excess activity of which of the following hormones most directly accounts for both the electrolyte pattern and the densitometric findings?
back: The hormone secreted by the parathyroid glands
extra: Excess PTH stimulates osteoclast activity, releasing calcium from bone into blood and producing hypercalcemia with reduced bone density.

front: Why is “The hormone secreted by thyroid C cells” wrong here? A 58-year-old woman reports several months of fatigue, constipation, and increased thirst with polyuria. Laboratory eval…
back: Calcitonin inhibits osteoclasts and lowers calcium; excess calcitonin would not cause this picture.
extra: A calcium-lowering hormone is being blamed for hypercalcemia and bone loss.

front: Why is “The hormone secreted by pancreatic beta cells” wrong here? A 58-year-old woman reports several months of fatigue, constipation, and increased thirst with polyuria. Laboratory eval…
back: Insulin does not drive osteoclast-mediated bone resorption or this electrolyte pattern.
extra: Glucose metabolism is being confused with calcium-bone pathology.

front: Why is “The hormone secreted by the zona glomerulosa” wrong here? A 58-year-old woman reports several months of fatigue, constipation, and increased thirst with polyuria. Laboratory eval…
back: Aldosterone affects sodium and potassium handling, not osteoclast-driven hypercalcemia.
extra: Mineralocorticoid excess is being confused with PTH-driven bone resorption.

front:
A 60-year-old woman starts a corticosteroid for an inflammatory condition, and her physician explains that the drug's full cellular effects take hours to appear because it works by changing protein production.

Which of the following sequences correctly describes how a steroid hormone alters its target cell?
back: Diffuses in, binds a cytosolic receptor, and the complex activates gene transcription
extra: Steroid hormones diffuse through the cell membrane and bind cytosolic receptors; the receptor-hormone complex enters the nucleus, binds the target gene, and transcription produces mRNA that is translated into protein — a process taking time.

front: Why is “Binds a surface receptor, generating cAMP that phosphorylates existing proteins” wrong here? A 60-year-old woman starts a corticosteroid for an inflammatory condition, and her physician explains that the drug's fu…
back: Surface receptors with cAMP second messengers serve water-soluble hormones and act in seconds; steroids cross the membrane and work through gene transcription, which is why effects take hours.
extra: The water-soluble hormone pathway is being applied to a lipid-soluble hormone.

front: Why is “Opens a ligand-gated ion channel that depolarizes the cell” wrong here? A 60-year-old woman starts a corticosteroid for an inflammatory condition, and her physician explains that the drug's fu…
back: Ion channel effects are millisecond events at synapses; steroids diffuse into cells, bind cytosolic receptors, and alter gene transcription in the nucleus.
extra: A neurotransmitter mechanism is being assigned to a steroid.

front: Why is “Is endocytosed and degraded by lysosomes into active fragments” wrong here? A 60-year-old woman starts a corticosteroid for an inflammatory condition, and her physician explains that the drug's fu…
back: Steroids are not activated by degradation; they diffuse through the membrane, bind intracellular receptors, and direct transcription of target genes.
extra: A degradative pathway is being described as the signaling mechanism.

front: During thyroid hormone synthesis in the follicle colloid, iodine is first linked to which of the following amino acid residues in thyroglobulin?
back: Tyrosine residues
extra: In the colloid, peroxidase enzymes link iodine to tyrosine amino acids in thyroglobulin, forming intermediaries that couple to T3 and T4.

front: Why is “Tryptophan residues” wrong here? During thyroid hormone synthesis in the follicle colloid, iodine is first linked to which of the following amino acid re…
back: Tryptophan is a precursor for serotonin and melatonin; thyroid hormones are built from iodinated tyrosines in thyroglobulin.
extra: An amine-hormone precursor amino acid is being substituted for the thyroid substrate.

front: Why is “Phenylalanine residues” wrong here? During thyroid hormone synthesis in the follicle colloid, iodine is first linked to which of the following amino acid re…
back: Phenylalanine feeds catecholamine synthesis; thyroid hormones require iodinated tyrosines, not phenylalanines.
extra: A catecholamine precursor is being confused with the thyroid substrate.

front: Why is “Histidine residues” wrong here? During thyroid hormone synthesis in the follicle colloid, iodine is first linked to which of the following amino acid re…
back: Histidine is not the substrate for thyroid peroxidase; iodination occurs on tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin.
extra: An unrelated amino acid is being named as the iodination site.

front:
A 28-year-old woman who recently emigrated from an inland region without iodized salt presents with progressive neck swelling, fatigue, cold intolerance, and constipation. Examination shows dry skin and delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes. Thyroid palpation reveals a firm, symmetrically enlarged gland. Thyroid function tests show low free thyroxine and markedly elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone.

Which of the following best explains why her hormone output is low despite abundant thyroglobulin in follicle colloid?
back: Dietary iodine deficiency prevents iodination of thyroglobulin tyrosines
extra: Thyroid hormones require iodination of tyrosine residues in thyroglobulin; iodine deficiency blocks synthesis, causing low T4, high TSH, and compensatory goiter.

front: Why is “Excess iodine directly destroys follicle cells and abolishes thyroglobulin production” wrong here? A 28-year-old woman who recently emigrated from an inland region without iodized salt presents with progressive neck swe…
back: This patient lacks dietary iodine; the gland still produces thyroglobulin but cannot iodinate it to form hormone.
extra: The problem is iodine lack, not iodine excess.

front: Why is “Parafollicular cell hyperplasia suppresses follicle colloid storage” wrong here? A 28-year-old woman who recently emigrated from an inland region without iodized salt presents with progressive neck swe…
back: Parafollicular cells secrete calcitonin for calcium homeostasis; hypothyroidism here reflects failed iodination in follicle colloid.
extra: Calcitonin-secreting cells are being blamed for hypothyroidism.

front: Why is “Thyroglobulin is assembled in the bloodstream rather than the colloid” wrong here? A 28-year-old woman who recently emigrated from an inland region without iodized salt presents with progressive neck swe…
back: Thyroglobulin is produced and iodinated in follicle colloid; the defect is missing iodine substrate, not mislocalized assembly.
extra: The anatomic site of synthesis is misidentified.

front:
A 30-year-old woman from a region without iodized salt presents with an enlarged thyroid. Her follicle cells still produce their usual storage protein, but hormone output is low because a critical element is missing.

In the normal gland, thyroxine (T4) is assembled when iodine is first linked to which of the following?
back: Tyrosine residues within thyroglobulin in the colloid
extra: In the colloid, peroxidase links iodine to tyrosine amino acids in thyroglobulin; one- and two-iodine intermediaries then couple to form T3, and two two-iodine intermediaries form T4.

front: Why is “Tryptophan residues within the follicle cell cytosol” wrong here? A 30-year-old woman from a region without iodized salt presents with an enlarged thyroid. Her follicle cells still produ…
back: Amine hormones from tryptophan include melatonin; thyroid hormones are built by iodinating the tyrosines of thyroglobulin within the follicle colloid.
extra: The wrong amino acid substrate is being chosen for thyroid hormone.

front: Why is “Free thyroid hormone already circulating in the blood” wrong here? A 30-year-old woman from a region without iodized salt presents with an enlarged thyroid. Her follicle cells still produ…
back: T3 and T4 are synthesized in the colloid by iodinating thyroglobulin tyrosines, then stored until TSH triggers their release; circulating hormone is the endpoint, not the substrate.
extra: A downstream product is being named as the synthetic substrate.

front: Why is “Cholesterol side chains in the follicle cell membrane” wrong here? A 30-year-old woman from a region without iodized salt presents with an enlarged thyroid. Her follicle cells still produ…
back: Steroid hormones derive from cholesterol; T3 and T4 are amino acid-derived hormones assembled by iodinating tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin in the colloid.
extra: The steroid hormone precursor is being applied to an amino acid-derived hormone.

front:
An isolated liver preparation exposed to growth hormone shows increased breakdown of stored glycogen. Uptake of glucose from the perfusion fluid and other sources of glucose are held constant.

Which of the following findings would be most consistent with the measured glycogen change?
back: More glucose leaves the liver as glycogen is broken down
extra: Hepatic glycogen breakdown supplies glucose for release. With competing inputs held constant, increased glucose output is consistent with the observed change.

front: Why is “Less glucose leaves the liver as glycogen breakdown increases” wrong here? An isolated liver preparation exposed to growth hormone shows increased breakdown of stored glycogen. Uptake of glucose …
back: Breaking down hepatic glycogen provides glucose for release. A lower output would require an additional change not supplied in this controlled experiment.
extra: Reverses the glucose-output consequence of hepatic glycogen breakdown.

front: Why is “Glucose output is unrelated to breakdown of hepatic glycogen” wrong here? An isolated liver preparation exposed to growth hormone shows increased breakdown of stored glycogen. Uptake of glucose …
back: Hepatic glycogen breakdown supplies glucose for release. The controlled preparation therefore links the loss of stored glycogen with glucose output rather than treating them as unrelated measurements.
extra: Disconnects released glucose from its hepatic glycogen source.

front: Why is “Hepatic glycogen increases while glucose release falls” wrong here? An isolated liver preparation exposed to growth hormone shows increased breakdown of stored glycogen. Uptake of glucose …
back: This reverses both the observed storage change and the expected direction of output from glycogen breakdown.
extra: Reverses both glycogen depletion and the predicted glucose output.

front:
A hormone normally raises cellular cyclic AMP and increases phosphorylation of cytoplasmic proteins. After an inhibitor is added, receptor binding and the cyclic AMP rise are preserved, but protein phosphorylation falls.

Which of the following sites best accounts for this pattern?
back: A protein kinase acting downstream of cyclic AMP
extra: Preserved cyclic AMP with reduced phosphorylation places the defect after second-messenger production, at the kinase-dependent response.

front: Why is “The surface receptor that initially binds the hormone” wrong here? A hormone normally raises cellular cyclic AMP and increases phosphorylation of cytoplasmic proteins. After an inhibitor …
back: Blocking initial receptor binding would undermine the preserved upstream response. The stem explicitly reports that binding remains intact.
extra: Attributes the defect to receptor binding despite preserved binding.

front: Why is “The G protein that activates adenylyl cyclase” wrong here? A hormone normally raises cellular cyclic AMP and increases phosphorylation of cytoplasmic proteins. After an inhibitor …
back: A failure before cyclase activation would not best explain a normal cyclic AMP increase followed by reduced phosphorylation.
extra: Places the block upstream of cyclase despite normal cAMP generation.

front: Why is “The cyclase responsible for producing cyclic AMP” wrong here? A hormone normally raises cellular cyclic AMP and increases phosphorylation of cytoplasmic proteins. After an inhibitor …
back: Inhibiting cyclic AMP production contradicts the observed rise. The interruption is downstream of that measured intermediate.
extra: Attributes normal cAMP generation to failure of its producing enzyme.

front:
A steroid enters a cell, binds its receptor, and the complex reaches the nucleus. An experimental inhibitor then prevents transcription of the target gene.

Which of the following downstream outcomes is most directly expected?
back: Reduced target messenger RNA with reduced new protein production
extra: The receptor complex normally promotes target-gene transcription. Blocking that step reduces the messenger RNA available for subsequent production of the target protein.

front: Why is “Reduced steroid entry with preserved target messenger RNA” wrong here? A steroid enters a cell, binds its receptor, and the complex reaches the nucleus. An experimental inhibitor then prevent…
back: Entry already occurred and does not depend on the later transcription step described in the experiment.
extra: Moves a nuclear transcription defect backward to completed steroid entry.

front: Why is “Increased target messenger RNA with reduced steroid entry” wrong here? A steroid enters a cell, binds its receptor, and the complex reaches the nucleus. An experimental inhibitor then prevent…
back: The intervention prevents transcription rather than increasing it. Earlier steroid entry is not the limiting step.
extra: Reverses the effect of transcription blockade on target mRNA.

front: Why is “Preserved new protein production despite absent target RNA” wrong here? A steroid enters a cell, binds its receptor, and the complex reaches the nucleus. An experimental inhibitor then prevent…
back: New production of the target protein depends on the corresponding messenger RNA. Existing protein may remain, but that does not preserve new synthesis.
extra: Confuses persistence of existing protein with continued new synthesis.

front:
A 34-year-old woman has progressive fatigue, weight loss, orthostatic hypotension, a serum sodium concentration of 128 mEq/L, and a serum potassium concentration of 5.9 mEq/L. Autoimmune destruction of both adrenal glands is suspected.

Deficiency of which hormone most directly accounts for the paired electrolyte abnormalities?
back: Reduced aldosterone secretion
extra: Aldosterone deficiency reduces renal return of sodium to blood and renal elimination of potassium, favoring hyponatremia and hyperkalemia.

front: Why is “Reduced cortisol secretion” wrong here? A 34-year-old woman has progressive fatigue, weight loss, orthostatic hypotension, a serum sodium concentration of 128 m…
back: Low cortisol contributes to hypotension and impaired stress responses; aldosterone loss is the direct renal mechanism here.
extra: Cortisol deficiency is central to adrenal insufficiency but does not directly explain both electrolyte changes.

front: Why is “Reduced ACTH secretion” wrong here? A 34-year-old woman has progressive fatigue, weight loss, orthostatic hypotension, a serum sodium concentration of 128 m…
back: Low ACTH suggests central adrenal insufficiency, in which mineralocorticoid production is generally preserved.
extra: Primary adrenal destruction removes negative feedback and usually raises, rather than lowers, ACTH.

front: Why is “Reduced epinephrine secretion” wrong here? A 34-year-old woman has progressive fatigue, weight loss, orthostatic hypotension, a serum sodium concentration of 128 m…
back: Epinephrine does not directly maintain sodium retention or renal potassium excretion.
extra: Adrenal medullary output is being confused with mineralocorticoid control of the distal nephron.

front:
A 46-year-old man develops fatigue and fasting hypoglycemia several months after pituitary surgery. Secondary adrenal insufficiency is suspected.

Which hormone pattern is most consistent with this diagnosis?
back: Low ACTH with low cortisol
extra: Damage to the pituitary can lower ACTH, so the adrenal cortex receives less stimulation to produce cortisol.

front: Why is “Normal ACTH with high cortisol” wrong here? A 46-year-old man develops fatigue and fasting hypoglycemia several months after pituitary surgery. Secondary adrenal in…
back: The expected central-deficiency pattern is low ACTH accompanied by low cortisol.
extra: A normal ACTH value can be inappropriate in context, but high cortisol rules out this deficiency pattern.

front: Why is “High ACTH with low cortisol” wrong here? A 46-year-old man develops fatigue and fasting hypoglycemia several months after pituitary surgery. Secondary adrenal in…
back: When the adrenal gland itself fails, low cortisol removes feedback and ACTH rises.
extra: This is the loss-of-feedback pattern of primary adrenal failure.

front: Why is “Low ACTH with high cortisol” wrong here? A 46-year-old man develops fatigue and fasting hypoglycemia several months after pituitary surgery. Secondary adrenal in…
back: High cortisol would be inconsistent with the suspected cortisol-deficient state.
extra: This pattern implies cortisol excess suppressing ACTH, not adrenal insufficiency.

front:
A 58-year-old woman abruptly stops prednisone after taking a high daily dose for eight months. She subsequently develops weakness, nausea, and hypotension.

Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?
back: Tertiary adrenal insufficiency
extra: Abrupt withdrawal after prolonged glucocorticoid exposure can reveal a suppressed hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.

front: Why is “Primary hyperaldosteronism” wrong here? A 58-year-old woman abruptly stops prednisone after taking a high daily dose for eight months. She subsequently develops…
back: The symptoms began after glucocorticoid withdrawal and fit cortisol deficiency, not aldosterone excess.
extra: Hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalemia rather than this withdrawal syndrome.

front: Why is “Pheochromocytoma syndrome” wrong here? A 58-year-old woman abruptly stops prednisone after taking a high daily dose for eight months. She subsequently develops…
back: Pheochromocytoma does not follow abrupt cessation of chronic glucocorticoid therapy.
extra: Catecholamine excess more often causes episodic hypertension, palpitations, and diaphoresis.

front: Why is “Syndrome of inappropriate ADH” wrong here? A 58-year-old woman abruptly stops prednisone after taking a high daily dose for eight months. She subsequently develops…
back: The medication history directly identifies suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.
extra: SIADH can cause nausea and hyponatremia but does not explain the steroid-withdrawal timing.

front: A 13-year-old boy has polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, hyperglycemia, and circulating islet autoantibodies. Immune destruction of which pancreatic cell type is central to this disease?
back: Beta cells that secrete insulin
extra: Pancreatic beta cells synthesize insulin, and their immune-mediated loss causes type 1 diabetes.

front: Why is “Alpha cells that secrete glucagon” wrong here? A 13-year-old boy has polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, hyperglycemia, and circulating islet autoantibodies. Immune des…
back: Alpha cells produce glucagon; they are not the principal autoimmune target in type 1 diabetes.
extra: Glucagon-producing alpha cells are being confused with insulin-producing beta cells.

front: Why is “Acinar cells that secrete enzymes” wrong here? A 13-year-old boy has polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, hyperglycemia, and circulating islet autoantibodies. Immune des…
back: Acinar cells make digestive enzymes and do not account for absolute insulin deficiency.
extra: Exocrine pancreatic cells are being confused with endocrine islet cells.

front: Why is “Delta cells that secrete somatostatin” wrong here? A 13-year-old boy has polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, hyperglycemia, and circulating islet autoantibodies. Immune des…
back: Delta cells produce somatostatin, whereas beta cells provide insulin.
extra: A regulatory islet cell is being mistaken for the source of insulin.

front: The attributable proportion (attributable risk percent) is primarily a measure of what?
back: Public health impact of a causative factor
extra: CDC defines the attributable proportion, also called the attributable risk percent, as a measure of the public health impact of a causative factor.

front: Why is “Strength of association between an exposure and a disease” wrong here? The attributable proportion (attributable risk percent) is primarily a measure of what?
back: Strength of association is what the risk ratio or odds ratio quantifies; the attributable proportion instead places an association in a public health context.
extra: Confuses a measure of public health impact with a measure of association such as the risk ratio.

front: Why is “Frequency of new cases in a population over time” wrong here? The attributable proportion (attributable risk percent) is primarily a measure of what?
back: The frequency of new cases over a period is incidence, a measure of disease occurrence rather than of an exposure's impact.
extra: Confuses an impact measure with incidence, a measure of new-case frequency.

front: Why is “Proportion of cases who die from the condition” wrong here? The attributable proportion (attributable risk percent) is primarily a measure of what?
back: The proportion of cases who die from a condition is the case-fatality rate, which describes how severe a disease is, not an exposure's impact.
extra: Confuses an exposure-impact measure with case-fatality, a measure of severity.

front: A health department reports the case-fatality rate for an infectious disease. Which of the following does this measure express?
back: Proportion of people with the disease who die of it
extra: CDC defines the case-fatality rate as the proportion of persons with a particular condition (cases) who die from that condition.

front: Why is “Deaths from the disease per total population at risk” wrong here? A health department reports the case-fatality rate for an infectious disease. Which of the following does this measure e…
back: Deaths from a disease divided by the whole population at risk is the cause-specific mortality rate; its denominator is the population, not the cases.
extra: Uses the whole population as denominator, which gives the cause-specific mortality rate.

front: Why is “New cases of the disease per population over a period” wrong here? A health department reports the case-fatality rate for an infectious disease. Which of the following does this measure e…
back: New cases per population over a period is incidence, which counts disease occurrence rather than deaths among cases.
extra: Confuses deaths among cases with incidence of new cases.

front: Why is “Proportion of the population that has the disease now” wrong here? A health department reports the case-fatality rate for an infectious disease. Which of the following does this measure e…
back: The share of a population that currently has a disease is prevalence, which says nothing about how many cases die.
extra: Confuses a measure of fatality with prevalence of existing disease.

front: Confounding describes which problem when interpreting a study?
back: Inability to separate the effects of multiple factors on a response
extra: Confounding occurs when the effects of multiple factors on a response cannot be separated, making valid conclusions about each factor difficult or impossible.

front: Why is “Systematic error in how participants are selected for the study” wrong here? Confounding describes which problem when interpreting a study?
back: Selection bias is systematic error from how participants are chosen or retained, not a mixing of the effects of several factors.
extra: Confuses confounding with selection bias from how participants are chosen.

front: Why is “Random sampling variation between a sample estimate and the truth” wrong here? Confounding describes which problem when interpreting a study?
back: Random sampling error is chance variation that shrinks with larger samples; confounding is a mixing of effects that sample size does not fix.
extra: Confuses a systematic mixing of effects with random sampling error.

front: Why is “Systematic error in measuring the exposure or the outcome” wrong here? Confounding describes which problem when interpreting a study?
back: Information bias comes from inaccurate measurement of exposure or outcome, not from factors whose effects are intertwined.
extra: Confuses confounding with measurement (information) bias.

front: Incidence refers to which epidemiologic quantity?
back: New cases in a population over a defined period
extra: Incidence refers to the occurrence of new cases of disease or injury in a population over a specified period of time.

front: Why is “All existing cases in a population at one point in time” wrong here? Incidence refers to which epidemiologic quantity?
back: Existing cases at one point in time define point prevalence, which counts long-standing and new cases alike rather than only new ones.
extra: Confuses incidence (new cases) with prevalence (all existing cases).

front: Why is “Deaths in a population over a defined period” wrong here? Incidence refers to which epidemiologic quantity?
back: Deaths in a population over a defined period give the mortality rate, which measures dying rather than developing disease.
extra: Confuses the occurrence of new disease with the occurrence of death.

front: Why is “Deaths from the disease among all people who have it” wrong here? Incidence refers to which epidemiologic quantity?
back: Deaths from a disease among all people who have it is the case-fatality rate, a measure of disease severity.
extra: Confuses incidence with case-fatality, which uses cases as its denominator.

front: A mortality rate measures which epidemiologic quantity about deaths?
back: Frequency of death in a defined population over an interval
extra: CDC defines a mortality rate as the frequency of occurrence of death in a defined population during a specified interval.

front: Why is “Proportion of people with a disease who die from it” wrong here? A mortality rate measures which epidemiologic quantity about deaths?
back: Deaths among people who have a disease, divided by those cases, is the case-fatality rate; its denominator is cases, not the population.
extra: Confuses a population mortality rate with case-fatality, which is restricted to cases.

front: Why is “Proportion of all deaths that are due to one cause” wrong here? A mortality rate measures which epidemiologic quantity about deaths?
back: The share of all deaths due to one cause is proportionate mortality; its denominator is deaths, so it is not a rate of death in a population.
extra: Confuses a mortality rate with proportionate mortality, whose denominator is total deaths.

front: Why is “Years of potential life lost before a reference age” wrong here? A mortality rate measures which epidemiologic quantity about deaths?
back: Years of potential life lost weights each death by how early it occurs, measuring premature mortality rather than how often death occurs.
extra: Confuses death frequency with years of potential life lost, a premature-death burden measure.

front: An odds ratio is described by CDC as which kind of epidemiologic quantity?
back: Association of a binary exposure with an outcome
extra: CDC: OR quantifies relationship between exposure and health outcome.

front: Why is “A synonym used only for median lethal dose values” wrong here? An odds ratio is described by CDC as which kind of epidemiologic quantity?
back: Wrong concept; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Virulence distractor.

front: Why is “A formula for net ATP yield from glycolysis alone” wrong here? An odds ratio is described by CDC as which kind of epidemiologic quantity?
back: Wrong domain; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Biochem distractor — does not match the cited teaching point.

front: Why is “A synonym used only for polysaccharide capsules” wrong here? An odds ratio is described by CDC as which kind of epidemiologic quantity?
back: Wrong concept; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Micro distractor — does not match the cited teaching point.

front: For a given condition in a population, which of the following correctly distinguishes prevalence from incidence?
back: Prevalence: persons who have it; incidence: persons who develop it
extra: CDC: prevalence is the proportion of persons who have a condition at or during a period; incidence is the proportion or rate who develop it.

front: Why is “Prevalence: persons who develop it; incidence: persons who have it” wrong here? For a given condition in a population, which of the following correctly distinguishes prevalence from incidence?
back: This reverses the two measures: incidence counts persons who develop a condition, and prevalence counts persons who have it.
extra: Reverses the definitions of prevalence and incidence.

front: Why is “Prevalence: persons who develop it; incidence: persons who die of it” wrong here? For a given condition in a population, which of the following correctly distinguishes prevalence from incidence?
back: Prevalence counts persons who have a condition, not those who develop it, and deaths are counted by mortality measures, not incidence.
extra: Assigns new cases to prevalence and deaths to incidence.

front: Why is “Prevalence: persons who die of it; incidence: persons who have it” wrong here? For a given condition in a population, which of the following correctly distinguishes prevalence from incidence?
back: Deaths are counted by mortality measures, not prevalence, and persons who have a condition are counted by prevalence, not incidence.
extra: Assigns deaths to prevalence and existing cases to incidence.

front: A risk ratio (relative risk) compares what between two groups?
back: Risk of a health event in one group versus another
extra: CDC: a risk ratio, also called relative risk, compares the risk of a health event among one group with the risk among another group.

front: Why is “Odds of prior exposure among cases versus among controls” wrong here? A risk ratio (relative risk) compares what between two groups?
back: Comparing the odds of prior exposure in cases and controls gives the odds ratio, the measure of association used in case-control studies.
extra: Confuses the risk ratio with the odds ratio from a case-control study.

front: Why is “Risk of the health event within a single group” wrong here? A risk ratio (relative risk) compares what between two groups?
back: The risk of an event within a single group is an incidence proportion; a risk ratio needs a second group's risk to compare against.
extra: Confuses a single group's risk (incidence proportion) with a ratio comparing two groups.

front: Why is “Baseline characteristics of participants in the two groups” wrong here? A risk ratio (relative risk) compares what between two groups?
back: Baseline characteristics are compared to check that groups are similar at the start; this describes the groups, not their risk of an outcome.
extra: Confuses a measure of association with a check of baseline comparability.

front:
An outbreak affects 200 residents in a closed population of 10,000. By the end of complete follow-up, 10 affected residents have died from the disease and the remaining cases have recovered.

Which of the following is the case-fatality proportion for this outbreak?
back: 10/200, corresponding to 5%
extra: Case fatality is the proportion of people with the condition who die from it. Ten deaths among 200 cases gives 10/200, or 5%, with complete outcome follow-up.

front: Why is “10/10,000, corresponding to 0.1%” wrong here? An outbreak affects 200 residents in a closed population of 10,000. By the end of complete follow-up, 10 affected reside…
back: This calculation relates disease deaths to the entire population and describes disease-specific mortality over the observation period. Case fatality instead uses the people with the disease as its denominator.
extra: Uses the population mortality denominator for case fatality.

front: Why is “200/10,000, corresponding to 2%” wrong here? An outbreak affects 200 residents in a closed population of 10,000. By the end of complete follow-up, 10 affected reside…
back: This calculation describes the fraction of residents affected during the outbreak. It counts cases rather than deaths and therefore does not measure fatal outcomes among affected people.
extra: Counts outbreak cases rather than fatal outcomes among cases.

front: Why is “190/200, corresponding to 95%” wrong here? An outbreak affects 200 residents in a closed population of 10,000. By the end of complete follow-up, 10 affected reside…
back: This calculation gives the proportion of cases that survived and recovered. Case fatality uses the ten deaths, rather than the 190 survivors, in the numerator.
extra: Uses recovered survivors rather than deaths in the fatality numerator.

front:
In a closed population of 1,000 people, 100 have a condition on January 1. During the year, 45 initially unaffected people develop the condition, and 20 of the original cases recover. These are the only recoveries; no one dies or leaves.

Which of the following gives the year-end point-prevalence numerator and the number of incident cases during the year?
back: Point-prevalence numerator 125; incident cases 45
extra: Year-end existing cases are 100 original cases minus 20 recoveries plus 45 new cases, giving 125. Incident cases count the 45 new occurrences during the specified year.

front: Why is “Point-prevalence numerator 145; incident cases 45” wrong here? In a closed population of 1,000 people, 100 have a condition on January 1. During the year, 45 initially unaffected peop…
back: Adding the original and new cases gives 145 people who had the condition at some time during the year. Point prevalence at year end excludes the 20 who have recovered.
extra: Includes recovered people in the year-end point-prevalence count.

front: Why is “Point-prevalence numerator 125; incident cases 125” wrong here? In a closed population of 1,000 people, 100 have a condition on January 1. During the year, 45 initially unaffected peop…
back: The point-prevalence numerator is correct, but incident cases exclude people who already had the condition at the start. Only the 45 newly affected people contribute to incidence.
extra: Treats all year-end existing cases as new cases during the year.

front: Why is “Point-prevalence numerator 100; incident cases 25” wrong here? In a closed population of 1,000 people, 100 have a condition on January 1. During the year, 45 initially unaffected peop…
back: Year-end point prevalence must reflect both new cases and recoveries rather than retain the original count. Incident cases count new disease occurrences, so recoveries are not subtracted from the 45.
extra: Ignores prevalence changes and incorrectly subtracts recoveries from incidence.

front:
Two towns each have 10,000 residents and complete outcome follow-up for the same outbreak period. Town A has 100 cases and 10 disease-related deaths. Town B has 500 cases and 10 disease-related deaths.

Which of the following comparisons is supported by these counts?
back: A has higher case fatality and equal disease-specific mortality
extra: Case fatality is 10% in A and 2% in B, so it is higher in A. Disease-specific mortality is 10/10,000 in each town over the same interval.

front: Why is “A has higher case fatality and higher disease-specific mortality” wrong here? Two towns each have 10,000 residents and complete outcome follow-up for the same outbreak period. Town A has 100 cases a…
back: Case fatality is higher in A because ten deaths occur among fewer cases. Population mortality is equal, however, because both towns have ten disease deaths among 10,000 residents.
extra: Infers greater population mortality from greater fatality among cases.

front: Why is “A has lower case fatality and equal disease-specific mortality” wrong here? Two towns each have 10,000 residents and complete outcome follow-up for the same outbreak period. Town A has 100 cases a…
back: The mortality comparison is correct, but case fatality is 10/100 in A and 10/500 in B. A therefore has the higher fatality proportion among affected people.
extra: Reverses the fatality comparison despite fewer cases per death in A.

front: Why is “A has equal case fatality and lower disease-specific mortality” wrong here? Two towns each have 10,000 residents and complete outcome follow-up for the same outbreak period. Town A has 100 cases a…
back: Equal death counts do not imply equal case fatality when case counts differ. Both population size and disease deaths are equal, so the disease-specific mortality comparison is also incorrect.
extra: Ignores unequal case denominators and misreads equal population mortality.

front:
In a study with complete follow-up, 40 of 200 participants in group X and 20 of 400 participants in group Y develop the same outcome.

A report originally compares X with Y, but the investigator now wants Y compared with X. Which of the following pairs uses the requested reference group?
back: Risk ratio 0.25; Y has one-quarter the outcome risk of X
extra: Group Y has risk 20/400, or 5%, and group X has risk 40/200, or 20%. Comparing Y with X gives 0.05/0.20 = 0.25, one-quarter the risk.

front: Why is “Risk ratio 0.5; Y has half the outcome risk of X” wrong here? In a study with complete follow-up, 40 of 200 participants in group X and 20 of 400 participants in group Y develop the …
back: Dividing the case counts alone gives 20/40 but ignores the different group sizes. The requested ratio compares risks of 20/400 and 40/200, rather than the numbers of cases.
extra: Compares raw case counts without adjusting for unequal group sizes.

front: Why is “Risk ratio 2.0; Y has twice the outcome risk of X” wrong here? In a study with complete follow-up, 40 of 200 participants in group X and 20 of 400 participants in group Y develop the …
back: Two is the ratio of the raw case counts in the opposite direction. Both the specified direction and the different group sizes must be reflected in the risk calculation.
extra: Reverses the requested direction and compares case counts instead of risks.

front: Why is “Risk ratio 4.0; Y has four times the outcome risk of X” wrong here? In a study with complete follow-up, 40 of 200 participants in group X and 20 of 400 participants in group Y develop the …
back: Four is the risk ratio for X compared with Y. Reversing the comparison makes X the denominator, so the requested ratio is the reciprocal, 0.25.
extra: Reports the X-to-Y ratio when the requested numerator is group Y.

front:
A clinic reviews a closed cohort at the end of June. Person X developed a condition in April and recovered in May. Person Y developed it in the previous December and still has it. Person Z developed it in May and still has it.

Which of the following classifications identifies the people contributing to incident cases from January through June and to point prevalence on June 30?
back: Incident cases: X and Z; point prevalence: Y and Z
extra: X and Z developed the condition during January through June, so both are incident cases. Y and Z still have the condition on June 30, so they contribute to point prevalence.

front: Why is “Incident cases: Y and Z; point prevalence: X and Z” wrong here? A clinic reviews a closed cohort at the end of June. Person X developed a condition in April and recovered in May. Perso…
back: Person Y already had the condition before January, so does not contribute to new cases in this interval. Person X recovered before June 30 and is excluded from point prevalence on that date.
extra: Counts a pre-existing case as incident and a recovered case as prevalent.

front: Why is “Incident cases: X and Y; point prevalence: X and Z” wrong here? A clinic reviews a closed cohort at the end of June. Person X developed a condition in April and recovered in May. Perso…
back: Person X is incident, but person Y developed the condition before the interval. The June 30 point-prevalence set includes ongoing cases Y and Z, excluding X after recovery.
extra: Includes an old onset in incidence and a recovered person in current prevalence.

front: Why is “Incident cases: X and Z; point prevalence: X and Y” wrong here? A clinic reviews a closed cohort at the end of June. Person X developed a condition in April and recovered in May. Perso…
back: The incident-case set is correct because X and Z developed the condition during the interval. Point prevalence on June 30 excludes recovered person X and includes ongoing case Z.
extra: Includes recovered X and omits ongoing Z from point prevalence.

front:
A closed cohort includes 300 exposed and 600 unexposed participants, all initially free of a condition. Complete follow-up over one year identifies 60 new cases in the exposed group and 60 in the unexposed group.

Which of the following is the risk ratio for exposed compared with unexposed participants?
extra: The exposed risk is 60/300 = 20%, and the unexposed risk is 60/600 = 10%. Dividing 0.20 by 0.10 gives 2.0.

front: Why is “0.50” wrong here? A closed cohort includes 300 exposed and 600 unexposed participants, all initially free of a condition. Complete follow-…
back: This reverses the comparison, dividing the unexposed risk of 10% by the exposed risk of 20%. The requested numerator is the exposed risk.
extra: Reverses the exposed-to-unexposed risk ratio.

front: Why is “1.00” wrong here? A closed cohort includes 300 exposed and 600 unexposed participants, all initially free of a condition. Complete follow-…
back: Equal case counts do not imply equal risks with unequal group sizes. Sixty of 300 is a larger risk than sixty of 600.
extra: Assumes equal case counts imply equal risks despite unequal group sizes.

front: Why is “0.20” wrong here? A closed cohort includes 300 exposed and 600 unexposed participants, all initially free of a condition. Complete follow-…
back: This is the exposed group risk alone. A risk ratio requires dividing that risk by the unexposed group risk.
extra: Reports the exposed-group risk without forming a comparison.

front:
An investigator collects a chief-cell secretion containing an inactive protein-digesting precursor. Adding a second aliquot of the same secretion does not restore digestion. Acidification permits activation, after which protein cleavage is detected.

Which of the following steps was limiting before acidification?
back: Failure to activate the precursor already present in secretion
extra: The available precursor becomes functional when acidification permits activation. This distinguishes an activation defect from failed secretion or insufficient precursor.

front: Why is “Loss of the precursor during collection of the secretion” wrong here? An investigator collects a chief-cell secretion containing an inactive protein-digesting precursor. Adding a second aliq…
back: The experiment establishes that inactive precursor remains in the sample. A loss during collection does not explain why acidification rescues that stored material.
extra: Assumes precursor loss despite its demonstrated presence in the sample.

front: Why is “Insufficient precursor abundance in the collected gastric secretion” wrong here? An investigator collects a chief-cell secretion containing an inactive protein-digesting precursor. Adding a second aliq…
back: Adding another aliquot does not restore digestion. The successful acidification step identifies an activation condition rather than inadequate precursor abundance.
extra: Mistakes a missing activation condition for insufficient precursor quantity.

front: Why is “Failure to release the precursor from the gastric cells” wrong here? An investigator collects a chief-cell secretion containing an inactive protein-digesting precursor. Adding a second aliq…
back: The secretion contains the precursor, so release has already occurred. The defect lies between the presence of precursor and detectable digestive activity.
extra: Places the defect at secretion even though precursor was collected.

front:
A gastric mucosal preparation retains its mucus layer and intact epithelial tight junctions. A selective intervention removes bicarbonate from the mucus without changing acid secretion into the lumen.

Which of the following protective functions is most directly reduced?
back: Neutralization of acid in the mucus near the epithelial surface
extra: Bicarbonate neutralizes acid within the mucus. Removing it reduces chemical protection even when mucus thickness and epithelial junctions are preserved.

front: Why is “Exclusion of gastric fluid by intact epithelial tight junctions” wrong here? A gastric mucosal preparation retains its mucus layer and intact epithelial tight junctions. A selective intervention re…
back: Tight junctions provide an intercellular seal and remain intact in this preparation. The selective loss is in chemical buffering, not that seal.
extra: Confuses loss of chemical buffering with a junctional seal defect.

front: Why is “Shielding of the epithelial surface by the physical mucus layer” wrong here? A gastric mucosal preparation retains its mucus layer and intact epithelial tight junctions. A selective intervention re…
back: The physical mucus coating is preserved. Its presence does not replace the neutralizing action of the bicarbonate removed from it.
extra: Treats preserved physical mucus as equivalent to bicarbonate buffering.

front: Why is “Reduction of acid delivery through decreased luminal acid secretion” wrong here? A gastric mucosal preparation retains its mucus layer and intact epithelial tight junctions. A selective intervention re…
back: The stem fixes luminal acid secretion. Bicarbonate acts on acid locally within mucus rather than explaining the result by changing acid delivery.
extra: Attributes reduced local protection to an acid-secretion change excluded by the model.

front:
Two gastric epithelial preparations have comparable mucus and bicarbonate. In one, an intervention disrupts the seals between adjacent cells. A marker placed in the gastric fluid then appears between those cells and in underlying tissue.

Which of the following best explains the new pathway?
back: Failure of tight junctions permits passage along intercellular spaces
extra: The marker travels along the boundaries of adjacent cells after their seals are disrupted. That path localizes the defect to tight junctions rather than uptake through cell interiors.

front: Why is “Loss of surface mucus exposes the epithelial apical membranes” wrong here? Two gastric epithelial preparations have comparable mucus and bicarbonate. In one, an intervention disrupts the seals be…
back: The preparations have comparable mucus, and the marker follows intercellular borders. Loss of physical surface coating does not match either observation.
extra: Attributes an intercellular leak to mucus loss despite comparable coating.

front: Why is “Loss of mucus bicarbonate removes local protection against acid” wrong here? Two gastric epithelial preparations have comparable mucus and bicarbonate. In one, an intervention disrupts the seals be…
back: Bicarbonate is comparable in both preparations. Loss of chemical buffering would not identify the observed pathway through disrupted intercellular seals.
extra: Confuses chemical buffering with the route through disrupted cell junctions.

front: Why is “Enhanced cellular uptake carries the marker through epithelial cytoplasm” wrong here? Two gastric epithelial preparations have comparable mucus and bicarbonate. In one, an intervention disrupts the seals be…
back: This describes a route through cell interiors. The observed marker lies between cells, matching a failure of their junctional seal instead.
extra: Mistakes passage between cells for uptake through their cytoplasm.

front:
A 43-year-old patient has obstruction of intestinal lymphatic drainage. Intestinal epithelial cells still take up glucose and assemble absorbed fatty acids into triglycerides.

Which of the following nutrient-transport findings best follows from the obstruction?
back: Triglyceride export is impaired while glucose reaches portal blood
extra: Reassembled intestinal triglycerides leave through lacteals, while absorbed glucose enters capillary blood and the hepatic portal route. The routes explain the selective effect.

front: Why is “Both nutrients are retained because both leave through lacteals” wrong here? A 43-year-old patient has obstruction of intestinal lymphatic drainage. Intestinal epithelial cells still take up glucos…
back: Glucose normally enters villus capillary blood rather than lymph. A lymphatic obstruction does not block both routes equally.
extra: Incorrectly assigns glucose and triglycerides to the same lymphatic exit.

front: Why is “Glucose export is impaired while triglycerides reach portal blood” wrong here? A 43-year-old patient has obstruction of intestinal lymphatic drainage. Intestinal epithelial cells still take up glucos…
back: This assigns the nutrients to the wrong exits. Glucose enters blood; intestinal triglyceride transport depends on lymphatic drainage.
extra: Reverses the blood and lymph exit routes of glucose and triglycerides.

front: Why is “Both nutrients reach portal blood through the same capillary route” wrong here? A 43-year-old patient has obstruction of intestinal lymphatic drainage. Intestinal epithelial cells still take up glucos…
back: The shared portal route applies to absorbed carbohydrates, not to the reassembled intestinal triglycerides described in this case.
extra: Extends the carbohydrate portal route to intestinal triglyceride packages.

front:
A preparation of small intestine preserves forward-moving waves but loses its alternating local contractions. Luminal nutrients move onward with less repeated exposure to nearby mucosal surfaces.

Which of the following functions has been selectively impaired?
back: Mixing of chyme against the surface of the intestinal mucosa
extra: Segmentation mixes chyme with digestive juices and repeatedly brings particles to the mucosa. Its loss reduces local contact even when peristalsis continues.

front: Why is “Propulsion of food along the length of the intestinal lumen” wrong here? A preparation of small intestine preserves forward-moving waves but loses its alternating local contractions. Luminal nu…
back: Forward-moving waves and onward movement are preserved. The abnormality is local mixing rather than the movement of food along the tract.
extra: Confuses preserved forward propulsion with the lost local mixing function.

front: Why is “Entry of glucose across the luminal intestinal epithelial membrane” wrong here? A preparation of small intestine preserves forward-moving waves but loses its alternating local contractions. Luminal nu…
back: Glucose entry uses a membrane transport mechanism. The direct observation of lost alternating contractions localizes the deficit to motility before epithelial uptake.
extra: Places an observed motility defect at the epithelial glucose transporter.

front: Why is “Export of triglyceride-rich particles into the intestinal villus lacteals” wrong here? A preparation of small intestine preserves forward-moving waves but loses its alternating local contractions. Luminal nu…
back: Lacteal export follows lipid uptake and packaging in enterocytes. The observed loss of local luminal contractions does not demonstrate a defect in that later export route.
extra: Attributes lost luminal contractions to a later lymphatic export step.

front:
Pressure sensors along the small intestine record contractions during a fasting study. A motilin stimulus is followed by a coordinated sequence that travels along the intestine.

Which of the following observations best identifies the resulting motility pattern?
back: A migrating contraction complex moves contents along the intestine
extra: Motilin stimulates a migrating motility complex. A traveling sequence distinguishes this response from stationary mixing contractions.

front: Why is “Repeated local mixing keeps the contents within one short segment” wrong here? Pressure sensors along the small intestine record contractions during a fasting study. A motilin stimulus is followed by…
back: Local mixing without net propulsion describes segmentation. It does not match the coordinated migrating response to motilin.
extra: Substitutes stationary segmentation for the migrating motility response.

front: Why is “A stationary contraction blocks movement throughout the intestine” wrong here? Pressure sensors along the small intestine record contractions during a fasting study. A motilin stimulus is followed by…
back: A persistent stationary block is not a migrating complex and would not explain the sequential pressure changes.
extra: Mistakes a traveling contraction sequence for a stationary obstruction.

front: Why is “A fall in all contractions increases contact with the mucosal surface” wrong here? Pressure sensors along the small intestine record contractions during a fasting study. A motilin stimulus is followed by…
back: Reduced contractile activity is the opposite of the observed coordinated contraction sequence. It does not establish enhanced mixing.
extra: Reverses the observed contractile response and assumes improved mixing.

front:
A researcher measures sugar entry across the luminal membrane of intestinal epithelial cells. Sodium is then removed from the luminal solution, while sugar concentrations, cell viability, and the other transport conditions remain unchanged.

Which of the following changes is expected?
back: Glucose entry falls; fructose entry is preserved
extra: Glucose uptake depends on sodium cotransport, whereas fructose uses facilitated diffusion. Removing sodium therefore separates the two transport mechanisms.

front: Why is “Glucose entry is preserved; fructose entry falls” wrong here? A researcher measures sugar entry across the luminal membrane of intestinal epithelial cells. Sodium is then removed fro…
back: This reverses the dependence: glucose, rather than fructose, uses sodium cotransport at the luminal membrane.
extra: Assigns sodium dependence to fructose instead of glucose uptake.

front: Why is “Entry of both sugars increases to a similar extent” wrong here? A researcher measures sugar entry across the luminal membrane of intestinal epithelial cells. Sodium is then removed fro…
back: Removing a required cotransport ion cannot increase glucose entry. Fructose transport has no corresponding sodium requirement in this experiment.
extra: Assumes removal of a required cotransport ion improves glucose entry.

front: Why is “Entry of both sugars stops to a similar extent” wrong here? A researcher measures sugar entry across the luminal membrane of intestinal epithelial cells. Sodium is then removed fro…
back: Only glucose entry directly depends on sodium cotransport. Preserved fructose transport is the internal comparison that makes the experiment informative.
extra: Extends glucose sodium dependence to the separate fructose transporter.

front: Bile, an alkaline fluid that emulsifies dietary lipids, is produced by which of the following cell types?
back: Hepatocytes in the liver
extra: The digestive role of the liver is to produce bile and export it to the duodenum; hepatocytes in the liver lobules are the source.

front: Why is “Epithelial cells of the gallbladder” wrong here? Bile, an alkaline fluid that emulsifies dietary lipids, is produced by which of the following cell types?
back: The gallbladder stores, concentrates, and releases bile made by the liver; it does not synthesize bile.
extra: The storage organ is being cast as the producer.

front: Why is “Acinar cells of the pancreas” wrong here? Bile, an alkaline fluid that emulsifies dietary lipids, is produced by which of the following cell types?
back: Pancreatic acini secrete enzyme-rich juice; bile is a hepatic product.
extra: A digestive enzyme source is being confused with bile production.

front: Why is “Goblet cells of the duodenal mucosa” wrong here? Bile, an alkaline fluid that emulsifies dietary lipids, is produced by which of the following cell types?
back: Goblet cells secrete protective mucus; bile arrives from the liver via the biliary tree.
extra: A mucus-secreting cell is being assigned bile synthesis.

front:
A 58-year-old woman with progressive pruritus and dark urine has scleral icterus and elevated direct bilirubin. Right-upper-quadrant ultrasound shows dilated intrahepatic bile ducts but a normal gallbladder.

Which of the following best explains why her hepatocytes continue to produce bile despite impaired delivery to the duodenum?
back: Bile synthesis is a continuous hepatic function independent of downstream duct patency
extra: Hepatocytes continuously produce and conjugate bile; obstruction prevents delivery to the duodenum but not hepatic synthesis, so direct bilirubin rises and backs up into blood.

front: Why is “The gallbladder compensates by synthesizing additional bile salts” wrong here? A 58-year-old woman with progressive pruritus and dark urine has scleral icterus and elevated direct bilirubin. Right-up…
back: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile made by the liver; it cannot synthesize bile salts de novo.
extra: The storage organ is being credited with hepatic synthetic capacity.

front: Why is “Pancreatic acinar cells secrete bile when the common bile duct is blocked” wrong here? A 58-year-old woman with progressive pruritus and dark urine has scleral icterus and elevated direct bilirubin. Right-up…
back: The pancreas secretes enzymatic juice, not bile; continued bile production in cholestasis reflects ongoing hepatic synthesis.
extra: An alternate digestive gland is being assigned a hepatic function.

front: Why is “Duodenal CCK stimulation stops all hepatic bile production until ducts reopen” wrong here? A 58-year-old woman with progressive pruritus and dark urine has scleral icterus and elevated direct bilirubin. Right-up…
back: CCK mainly stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic secretion; hepatic bile production continues despite outflow obstruction.
extra: Hormonal regulation is being cast as a complete shutoff of synthesis.

front: Three years after a cholecystectomy for gallstones, a 44-year-old woman digests fatty meals without difficulty. In this patient, bile is produced by which of the following structures?
back: Hepatocytes in the liver lobules
extra: The digestive role of the liver is to produce bile and export it to the duodenum; bile emulsifies lipids, and its production is unaffected by gallbladder removal.

front: Why is “Epithelial cells of the gallbladder” wrong here? Three years after a cholecystectomy for gallstones, a 44-year-old woman digests fatty meals without difficulty. In this …
back: The gallbladder primarily stores, concentrates, and releases bile made by the liver; it does not synthesize bile, and this patient no longer has one.
extra: The storage organ is being cast as the producer, and it is absent here.

front: Why is “Acinar cells of the pancreas” wrong here? Three years after a cholecystectomy for gallstones, a 44-year-old woman digests fatty meals without difficulty. In this …
back: Pancreatic acini secrete enzyme-rich juice in response to CCK; bile is an alkaline, lipid-emulsifying solution produced by the liver.
extra: A digestive gland is being credited with a hepatic product.

front: Why is “Mucosal cells of the duodenum” wrong here? Three years after a cholecystectomy for gallstones, a 44-year-old woman digests fatty meals without difficulty. In this …
back: The duodenal mucosa secretes hormones such as secretin, CCK, and motilin that regulate digestion; bile itself arrives from the liver.
extra: The hormone-secreting mucosa is being cast as the bile source.

front: A 40-year-old man has autoimmune gastritis that destroys the glands of his gastric body. Loss of his chief-cell secretion most directly reduces the initial digestion of which of the following?
back: Proteins
extra: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, which acid converts to pepsin; pepsin starts the enzymatic digestion of proteins, so losing chief cells removes this first step.

front: Why is “Starches” wrong here? A 40-year-old man has autoimmune gastritis that destroys the glands of his gastric body. Loss of his chief-cell secretio…
back: Starch digestion begins in the mouth with salivary amylase and is completed by pancreatic amylase and brush-border enzymes, not by pepsin.
extra: Starch digestion is being assigned to the stomach.

front: Why is “Nucleic acids” wrong here? A 40-year-old man has autoimmune gastritis that destroys the glands of his gastric body. Loss of his chief-cell secretio…
back: Nucleic acids are digested by pancreatic nucleases and brush-border enzymes in the small intestine, well downstream of pepsin's action.
extra: Nucleic-acid breakdown is being assigned to the stomach.

front: Why is “Triglycerides” wrong here? A 40-year-old man has autoimmune gastritis that destroys the glands of his gastric body. Loss of his chief-cell secretio…
back: Triglyceride digestion depends mainly on pancreatic lipase with bile-salt emulsification in the small intestine; pepsin does not act on lipids.
extra: Fat digestion is being assigned to a gastric protease.

front: A 70-year-old man has a brainstem stroke and food repeatedly enters his airway while eating. Failure of the epiglottis to fold over the glottis disrupts which of the following phases of swallowing?
back: The pharyngeal phase
extra: During the involuntary pharyngeal phase, the soft palate rises to close the nasopharynx, the larynx elevates, and the epiglottis folds over the glottis so the bolus enters the esophagus rather than the airway.

front: Why is “The esophageal phase” wrong here? A 70-year-old man has a brainstem stroke and food repeatedly enters his airway while eating. Failure of the epiglottis t…
back: The esophageal phase moves the bolus down the esophagus by peristalsis after the airway has already been sealed; it cannot guard the glottis.
extra: A phase downstream of airway closure is being blamed for the aspiration.

front: Why is “The voluntary oral phase” wrong here? A 70-year-old man has a brainstem stroke and food repeatedly enters his airway while eating. Failure of the epiglottis t…
back: The voluntary phase covers chewing and forming a bolus under conscious control; airway protection by the epiglottis occurs later, in the pharyngeal phase.
extra: The conscious phase is being blamed for a reflex failure.

front: Why is “The cephalic phase” wrong here? A 70-year-old man has a brainstem stroke and food repeatedly enters his airway while eating. Failure of the epiglottis t…
back: The cephalic phase describes gastric secretion triggered by the sight or smell of food; it is not a stage of deglutition.
extra: A gastric secretory phase is being conflated with swallowing.

front: After a meal, parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid into the gastric lumen. This low pH is required for which of the following enzymatic conversions?
back: Conversion of pepsinogen to active pepsin
extra: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen; HCl from parietal cells is necessary for the conversion of pepsinogen to pepsin, which begins protein digestion.

front: Why is “Conversion of trypsinogen to trypsin in the duodenum” wrong here? After a meal, parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid into the gastric lumen. This low pH is required for which of the …
back: Trypsinogen activation occurs in the duodenum via enterokinase; it is not an HCl-dependent gastric conversion.
extra: A pancreatic protease activation step is being placed in the stomach.

front: Why is “Conversion of chymotrypsinogen to chymotrypsin” wrong here? After a meal, parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid into the gastric lumen. This low pH is required for which of the …
back: Chymotrypsinogen is activated by trypsin in the small intestine, not by gastric HCl.
extra: A downstream pancreatic protease is being assigned to gastric acid.

front: Why is “Emulsification of dietary triglycerides by bile salts” wrong here? After a meal, parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid into the gastric lumen. This low pH is required for which of the …
back: Triglyceride emulsification depends on bile salts in the duodenum; gastric HCl does not activate lipases this way.
extra: A lipid-digestion step in the duodenum is being confused with gastric protease activation.

front:
A 48-year-old man presents with recurrent duodenal ulcers refractory to proton-pump inhibitor therapy. He reports daily watery diarrhea and epigastric pain. Fasting serum gastrin is markedly elevated, and secretin administration fails to suppress gastrin levels. Abdominal imaging shows a 2-cm mass in the wall of the duodenum.

Which of the following mechanisms best explains his hypersecretory gastric acid state?
back: Excess hormone from the tumor directly stimulates parietal cells to secrete hydrochloric acid
extra: Gastrin is the principal stimulatory hormone for parietal cells; a gastrin-secreting tumor causes excess HCl production, recurrent ulcers, and often diarrhea.

front: Why is “Chief-cell hyperplasia alone increases acid without parietal-cell stimulation” wrong here? A 48-year-old man presents with recurrent duodenal ulcers refractory to proton-pump inhibitor therapy. He reports daily …
back: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, not acid; hyperacidity in gastrinoma reflects gastrin-driven parietal-cell stimulation.
extra: The enzyme-secreting cell is being cast as the acid source.

front: Why is “Antral G cells secrete excess gastrin that is blocked from reaching parietal cells” wrong here? A 48-year-old man presents with recurrent duodenal ulcers refractory to proton-pump inhibitor therapy. He reports daily …
back: Antral cells secrete mucus and gastrin; they do not produce hydrochloric acid, which comes from parietal cells in the gastric body.
extra: Antral mucus cells are being mistaken for acid-secreting cells.

front: Why is “Pancreatic duct cells secrete acid to compensate for bicarbonate loss” wrong here? A 48-year-old man presents with recurrent duodenal ulcers refractory to proton-pump inhibitor therapy. He reports daily …
back: Pancreatic duct cells secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid to neutralize gastric acid in the duodenum; they do not cause gastric hypersecretion.
extra: A bicarbonate-secreting cell is being inverted to an acid source.

front:
In a gastric-emptying study, a healthy 32-year-old volunteer eats three different solid test meals on separate days, and the time to empty the stomach is measured.

Which of the following meals would be expected to remain in the stomach the longest?
back: A meal high in triglycerides
extra: Stomach contents normally empty within 2 to 4 hours; carbohydrate-heavy meals empty fastest, protein-rich meals next, and meals with high triglyceride content remain in the stomach the longest.

front: Why is “A meal high in carbohydrates” wrong here? In a gastric-emptying study, a healthy 32-year-old volunteer eats three different solid test meals on separate days, and…
back: Foods heavy in carbohydrates empty fastest from the stomach; triglyceride-rich meals empty most slowly.
extra: The fastest-emptying meal is being cast as the slowest.

front: Why is “A meal high in protein” wrong here? In a gastric-emptying study, a healthy 32-year-old volunteer eats three different solid test meals on separate days, and…
back: High-protein foods empty after carbohydrates but before fatty meals; triglyceride content keeps chyme in the stomach longest.
extra: The intermediate meal is being cast as the slowest.

front: Why is “A mixed meal low in fat” wrong here? In a gastric-emptying study, a healthy 32-year-old volunteer eats three different solid test meals on separate days, and…
back: A low-fat meal lacks the triglyceride content that most delays emptying, so it would leave the stomach sooner than a fatty meal.
extra: Removing the delaying nutrient is being cast as prolonging emptying.

front:
A 25-year-old student notices hunger pangs and increased gastric secretion while smelling bread baking, before she has eaten anything.

Which of the following phases of gastric secretion does this illustrate?
back: The cephalic phase
