extra: The cephalic (reflex) phase of gastric secretion takes place before food enters the stomach and is triggered by the smell, taste, sight, or thought of food.

front: Why is “The gastric phase” wrong here? A 25-year-old student notices hunger pangs and increased gastric secretion while smelling bread baking, before she has e…
back: The gastric phase is set in motion by the entry of food into the stomach, which triggers local neural and hormonal mechanisms; here no food has been swallowed.
extra: A food-in-stomach phase is being applied before any food has been eaten.

front: Why is “The intestinal phase” wrong here? A 25-year-old student notices hunger pangs and increased gastric secretion while smelling bread baking, before she has e…
back: The intestinal phase begins when chyme reaches the duodenum and modulates further gastric activity; it cannot be triggered by the smell of food.
extra: A downstream phase is being applied to a pre-ingestion stimulus.

front: Why is “The migrating motility phase” wrong here? A 25-year-old student notices hunger pangs and increased gastric secretion while smelling bread baking, before she has e…
back: The migrating motility complex is a pattern of peristalsis that sweeps the empty gut between meals, initiated by motilin; it is not a secretory response to food cues.
extra: An inter-digestive motility pattern is being cast as a secretory phase.

front: Gastrin stimulates hydrochloric acid secretion primarily from which of the following gastric cell types?
back: Parietal cells of the gastric body
extra: Parietal cells produce both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, and gastrin is their principal stimulatory hormone, so a gastrinoma drives excess acid production.

front: Why is “Mucous cells of the pyloric antrum” wrong here? Gastrin stimulates hydrochloric acid secretion primarily from which of the following gastric cell types?
back: Cells of the pyloric antrum secrete mucus and hormones, including most of the stomach's gastrin; the antrum is the source of the hormone, not its acid-producing target.
extra: The antrum is being cast as the acid-producing region.

front: Why is “Chief cells of the gastric fundus” wrong here? Gastrin stimulates hydrochloric acid secretion primarily from which of the following gastric cell types?
back: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, the inactive precursor of pepsin; they sit beside parietal cells but do not themselves secrete acid in response to gastrin.
extra: The enzyme-secreting cell is being cast as the acid source.

front: Why is “Duct cells of the pancreas” wrong here? Gastrin stimulates hydrochloric acid secretion primarily from which of the following gastric cell types?
back: Pancreatic duct cells secrete bicarbonate-rich juice in response to secretin; they neutralize acid entering the duodenum rather than produce it.
extra: A neighboring gland's cells are being cast as gastrin's target.

front:
A 24-year-old man with cholera is given an oral rehydration solution containing glucose and sodium.

Intestinal uptake of the glucose is enhanced because it crosses the apical enterocyte membrane by which of the following mechanisms?
back: Cotransport of glucose with sodium ions
extra: Glucose is absorbed by cotransport with sodium ions across the apical membrane into the villus capillary blood, which is why rehydration solutions pair glucose with salt.

front:
Why is “Facilitated diffusion independent of sodium” wrong here? A 24-year-old man with cholera is given an oral rehydration solution containing glucose and sodium.

Intestinal uptake o…
back: Fructose enters by facilitated diffusion, but glucose and galactose are absorbed by sodium cotransport; removing sodium abolishes their uptake.
extra: Fructose's mechanism is being assigned to glucose.

front:
Why is “Simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer” wrong here? A 24-year-old man with cholera is given an oral rehydration solution containing glucose and sodium.

Intestinal uptake o…
back: Glucose is hydrophilic and cannot cross the lipid bilayer unaided; it requires a carrier coupled to sodium.
extra: A polar sugar is being treated as membrane-permeant.

front:
Why is “Primary active transport driven by ATP” wrong here? A 24-year-old man with cholera is given an oral rehydration solution containing glucose and sodium.

Intestinal uptake o…
back: The apical carrier uses the sodium gradient (secondary active transport); ATP powers the basolateral sodium pump that maintains that gradient, not the apical entry step itself.
extra: The apical step is being cast as directly ATP-driven.

front: Intrinsic factor, secreted by gastric parietal cells, is required for absorption of which of the following in the terminal ileum?
back: Vitamin B12
extra: Intrinsic factor binds vitamin B12, allowing its absorption in the terminal ileum; without it, B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anemia and neurological dysfunction.

front: Why is “Iron” wrong here? Intrinsic factor, secreted by gastric parietal cells, is required for absorption of which of the following in the termin…
back: Iron is absorbed in the duodenum and does not require intrinsic factor; its deficiency causes microcytic anemia.
extra: A microcytic-anemia mineral is being confused with the intrinsic-factor-dependent vitamin.

front: Why is “Folate” wrong here? Intrinsic factor, secreted by gastric parietal cells, is required for absorption of which of the following in the termin…
back: Folate is absorbed proximally in the jejunum without intrinsic factor; B12 is the ileal, intrinsic-factor-dependent vitamin.
extra: Another macrocytic vitamin is being selected, but it does not need intrinsic factor.

front: Why is “Vitamin D” wrong here? Intrinsic factor, secreted by gastric parietal cells, is required for absorption of which of the following in the termin…
back: Vitamin D is absorbed with dietary fat throughout the small intestine and does not require intrinsic factor.
extra: A fat-soluble vitamin absorbed with bile is being confused with B12.

front: Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells eliminates a product required for terminal ileal absorption of vitamin B12. Loss of which of the following gastric secretions most directly causes the resulting macrocytic anemia?
back: Intrinsic factor
extra: Parietal cells secrete both HCl and intrinsic factor; loss of intrinsic factor prevents ileal B12 absorption, causing macrocytic anemia and, over time, neurological deficits.

front: Why is “Pepsinogen” wrong here? Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells eliminates a product required for terminal ileal absorption of vitamin …
back: Pepsinogen is activated to pepsin for protein digestion; it is not required for B12 absorption.
extra: A protease precursor is being substituted for the B12 carrier.

front: Why is “Gastrin” wrong here? Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells eliminates a product required for terminal ileal absorption of vitamin …
back: Gastrin stimulates acid secretion but is not the product without which B12 absorption fails.
extra: A regulatory hormone is being cast as the indispensable ileal cofactor.

front: Why is “Mucus from surface mucous cells” wrong here? Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells eliminates a product required for terminal ileal absorption of vitamin …
back: Mucus protects the gastric lining; macrocytic anemia from parietal-cell loss reflects intrinsic factor deficiency, not mucus loss.
extra: A protective secretion is being confused with the B12 absorption cofactor.

front:
A 60-year-old man develops progressive fatigue, glossitis, and a wide-based unsteady gait two years after total gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma. Examination shows loss of vibration sense in the lower limbs. His blood smear shows macrocytic anemia and serum vitamin B12 is low.

The anemia developed because gastrectomy eliminated a gastric product required for which of the following?
back: Vitamin B12 uptake in the terminal ileum
extra: Parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor, without which vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed in the terminal ileum; B12 is needed for mature red-cell production and normal neurological function.

front: Why is “Iron uptake in the proximal duodenum” wrong here? A 60-year-old man develops progressive fatigue, glossitis, and a wide-based unsteady gait two years after total gastrect…
back: Iron deficiency produces a microcytic anemia and does not require intrinsic factor; the macrocytosis and gait findings point to B12 malabsorption.
extra: An iron-deficiency mechanism is being applied to a macrocytic anemia.

front: Why is “Folate uptake in the proximal jejunum” wrong here? A 60-year-old man develops progressive fatigue, glossitis, and a wide-based unsteady gait two years after total gastrect…
back: Folate deficiency also causes macrocytosis, but folate absorption does not depend on intrinsic factor; it lacks the neurological signs of B12 deficiency.
extra: Another macrocytic cause is being chosen, but its uptake does not need a gastric product.

front: Why is “Calcium uptake in the proximal duodenum” wrong here? A 60-year-old man develops progressive fatigue, glossitis, and a wide-based unsteady gait two years after total gastrect…
back: Calcium absorption is vitamin-D dependent and unrelated to intrinsic factor; hypocalcemia does not produce macrocytic anemia.
extra: A mineral is being cast as the cause of the anemia.

front: Which of the following diagnoses describes a bowel blockage in which one segment folds into itself like a telescope?
back: Intussusception
extra: The CDC passage defines intussusception as a bowel blockage produced when the bowel folds into itself like a telescope.

front: Why is “Small-bowel volvulus” wrong here? Which of the following diagnoses describes a bowel blockage in which one segment folds into itself like a telescope?
back: The cited passage assigns bowel folding into itself like a telescope to intussusception, not small-bowel volvulus.
extra: Generic bowel obstruction is recognized, but the source's defining telescope-folding process is missed.

front: Why is “Meconium ileus” wrong here? Which of the following diagnoses describes a bowel blockage in which one segment folds into itself like a telescope?
back: A bowel blockage alone is not the complete cue; the passage identifies the telescope-like folding process as intussusception.
extra: The blockage cue is used without matching the mechanism explicitly named in the citation.

front: Why is “Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis” wrong here? Which of the following diagnoses describes a bowel blockage in which one segment folds into itself like a telescope?
back: The evidence names intussusception when bowel folds into itself like a telescope; it does not attach that definition to pyloric stenosis.
extra: Another obstructive diagnosis is substituted for the cited folding-into-itself definition.

front: A 65-year-old man undergoes a total colectomy for ulcerative colitis, with his ileum connected to a stoma. Which of the following functions of the removed organ is most directly lost in this patient?
back: Absorption of water and formation of the feces
extra: The large intestine absorbs water and forms feces, and houses bacterial flora that break down additional carbohydrate residue and synthesize certain vitamins.

front: Why is “Final digestion of dietary protein by enzymes” wrong here? A 65-year-old man undergoes a total colectomy for ulcerative colitis, with his ileum connected to a stoma. Which of the …
back: Protein digestion is completed by pancreatic proteases and brush-border enzymes upstream in the small intestine; the colon has no significant enzymatic digestion.
extra: A small-intestinal task is being assigned to the colon.

front: Why is “Absorption of glucose into the portal blood” wrong here? A 65-year-old man undergoes a total colectomy for ulcerative colitis, with his ileum connected to a stoma. Which of the …
back: Glucose is absorbed by sodium cotransport into the capillary blood of small-intestinal villi, well before residue reaches the colon.
extra: A small-intestinal absorptive task is being assigned to the colon.

front: Why is “Production of bile for delivery to the duodenum” wrong here? A 65-year-old man undergoes a total colectomy for ulcerative colitis, with his ileum connected to a stoma. Which of the …
back: Bile is produced by hepatocytes and delivered to the duodenum; the colon neither makes nor handles bile production.
extra: A hepatic product is being assigned to the colon.

front: A 58-year-old woman with cirrhosis develops yellowing of her skin and eyes. In the healthy liver, bilirubin is processed by hepatocytes and excreted into which of the following structures?
back: The bile canaliculi
extra: Hepatocytes process nutrients, toxins, and waste materials carried by the blood, and materials such as bilirubin are processed and excreted into the bile canaliculi.

front: Why is “The hepatic sinusoids” wrong here? A 58-year-old woman with cirrhosis develops yellowing of her skin and eyes. In the healthy liver, bilirubin is processed…
back: Sinusoids deliver blood to the hepatocytes and contain phagocytic Kupffer cells; excretion of bilirubin runs in the opposite direction, into the bile canaliculi.
extra: The blood-supply channel is being cast as the excretion route.

front: Why is “Branches of the portal vein” wrong here? A 58-year-old woman with cirrhosis develops yellowing of her skin and eyes. In the healthy liver, bilirubin is processed…
back: The portal vein brings nutrient-rich blood to the liver; bilirubin leaves the hepatocyte through the biliary tree, not back into the venous inflow.
extra: The inflow vessel is being cast as the excretion route.

front: Why is “The spaces of Disse” wrong here? A 58-year-old woman with cirrhosis develops yellowing of her skin and eyes. In the healthy liver, bilirubin is processed…
back: The spaces of Disse lie between sinusoid lining and hepatocytes and mediate exchange with blood; bile, carrying bilirubin, drains into canaliculi on the opposite pole of the cell.
extra: The exchange space is being cast as the excretion route.

front:
After a fatty meal, long-chain fatty acids are absorbed into enterocytes, reassembled into triglycerides, and packaged for export.

In a healthy 26-year-old woman, these packages leave the enterocyte and first enter which of the following?
back: Intestinal lacteals draining into the lymphatics
extra: Absorbed fatty acids are re-esterified to triglycerides, coated with phospholipid, cholesterol, and protein to form chylomicrons, which exit the cell and enter the lacteals of the villi for transport by lymphatic vessels to the systemic circulation via the thoracic duct.

front: Why is “Bile canaliculi lying between adjacent hepatocytes” wrong here? After a fatty meal, long-chain fatty acids are absorbed into enterocytes, reassembled into triglycerides, and packaged f…
back: Bile canaliculi carry bile out of hepatocytes toward the duodenum; absorbed lipids reach the liver secondhand through the circulation, never through canaliculi.
extra: The bile-excretion route is being reversed into an absorption route.

front: Why is “Mucosal capillaries draining into the thoracic duct” wrong here? After a fatty meal, long-chain fatty acids are absorbed into enterocytes, reassembled into triglycerides, and packaged f…
back: The thoracic duct is a lymphatic vessel fed by the lacteals; mucosal blood capillaries drain into the portal venous system, not the lymph.
extra: Blood and lymph vessels are being conflated.

front: Why is “Capillaries draining into the hepatic portal vein” wrong here? After a fatty meal, long-chain fatty acids are absorbed into enterocytes, reassembled into triglycerides, and packaged f…
back: Monosaccharides and amino acids enter villus capillary blood for the hepatic portal vein; bulky chylomicrons cannot enter these capillaries and use the lymphatics instead.
extra: The water-soluble nutrient route is being applied to large lipid packages.

front: A 28-year-old athlete takes ibuprofen daily for knee pain and develops a gastric ulcer. Which of the following normally prevents the acidic gastric contents from digesting the stomach wall itself?
back: A bicarbonate-rich mucus layer over tight-junctioned epithelium
extra: The stomach wall is coated by bicarbonate-rich mucus that physically shields it and neutralizes acid, while tight junctions between epithelial cells block gastric juice from reaching deeper tissue.

front: Why is “Neutralization of the luminal acid by secreted gastric lipase” wrong here? A 28-year-old athlete takes ibuprofen daily for knee pain and develops a gastric ulcer. Which of the following normally …
back: Gastric lipase digests lipid; it does not neutralize acid. Neutralization at the wall is performed by bicarbonate secreted into the mucus layer.
extra: An enzyme is being cast as an acid buffer.

front: Why is “Rapid emptying of the acid into the duodenum after meals” wrong here? A 28-year-old athlete takes ibuprofen daily for knee pain and develops a gastric ulcer. Which of the following normally …
back: Chyme normally remains in the stomach for hours, so the wall needs a standing barrier; emptying speed does not protect the mucosa from acid.
extra: Reduced exposure time is being cast as the protective mechanism.

front: Why is “Dilution of the gastric juice by large volumes of saliva” wrong here? A 28-year-old athlete takes ibuprofen daily for knee pain and develops a gastric ulcer. Which of the following normally …
back: Saliva contributes little volume to the stomach and cannot meaningfully dilute its strongly acidic contents; the mucus-bicarbonate barrier is the protective layer.
extra: Dilution is being cast as meaningful protection against a pH of 1.5-3.5.

front:
A 19-year-old man with cystic fibrosis has pancreatic exocrine insufficiency and loses weight despite eating well.

Enzyme replacement improves his protein digestion mainly by supplying which of the following?
back: Trypsin, chymotrypsin, and elastase
extra: The pancreas releases most of the digestive enzymes, including the proteases trypsin, chymotrypsin, and elastase, which cleave specific bonds in amino-acid sequences.

front:
Why is “Pepsin, gastrin, and mucus” wrong here? A 19-year-old man with cystic fibrosis has pancreatic exocrine insufficiency and loses weight despite eating well.

Enzy…
back: Pepsin begins gastric protein digestion and gastrin is a hormone; neither is supplied by pancreatic extracts, and gastric protein digestion is intact in this patient.
extra: Gastric products are being cast as pancreatic enzymes.

front:
Why is “Amylase, lactase, and sucrase” wrong here? A 19-year-old man with cystic fibrosis has pancreatic exocrine insufficiency and loses weight despite eating well.

Enzy…
back: Amylase digests starch and lactase and sucrase are brush-border disaccharidases; none of them acts on proteins.
extra: Carbohydrate-digesting enzymes are being used to fix protein digestion.

front:
Why is “Bile salts, lecithin, and cholesterol” wrong here? A 19-year-old man with cystic fibrosis has pancreatic exocrine insufficiency and loses weight despite eating well.

Enzy…
back: Bile components emulsify lipids into micelles for absorption; they have no enzymatic activity and do not digest protein.
extra: Fat-emulsifying agents are being cast as proteases.

front: Acidic chyme entering the duodenum stimulates secretion of which of the following hormones?
back: Secretin from duodenal mucosa
extra: Secretin is released when acidic chyme reaches the duodenum and drives bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice to neutralize the acid.

front: Why is “Gastrin from antral G cells” wrong here? Acidic chyme entering the duodenum stimulates secretion of which of the following hormones?
back: Gastrin is released when food enters the stomach; acidic chyme in the duodenum triggers secretin, not gastrin.
extra: The gastric acid stimulator is being assigned to the duodenal acid signal.

front: Why is “Cholecystokinin from gastric parietal cells” wrong here? Acidic chyme entering the duodenum stimulates secretion of which of the following hormones?
back: CCK responds to protein and fat in the duodenum, not to acid alone, and it is not secreted by parietal cells.
extra: Both the hormone and its source are wrong for an acid stimulus.

front: Why is “Motilin from the ileocecal valve” wrong here? Acidic chyme entering the duodenum stimulates secretion of which of the following hormones?
back: Motilin initiates migrating motor complexes; acidic chyme triggers secretin for bicarbonate secretion.
extra: A motility hormone is being substituted for the acid-neutralizing hormone.

front:
A 47-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis has steatorrhea and postprandial bloating. After a fatty meal, duodenal pH falls briefly then normalizes, but his fecal fat remains elevated. Secretin secretion and bicarbonate-rich duct flow are intact on stimulation testing.

Failure of which of the following hormone–product pairings most directly explains persistent fat malabsorption despite acid neutralization?
back: CCK failing to trigger enzyme-rich acinar secretion
extra: Protein and fat in the duodenum stimulate CCK, which drives enzyme-rich juice from pancreatic acini; chronic pancreatitis destroys acini, so CCK cannot restore lipase/protease delivery despite secretin-normalizing pH.

front: Why is “Secretin failing to release bicarbonate-rich juice” wrong here? A 47-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis has steatorrhea and postprandial bloating. After a fatty meal, duodenal pH f…
back: The stem specifies intact secretin-driven bicarbonate; steatorrhea with normal acid neutralization implicates deficient enzyme-rich juice instead.
extra: The acid-neutralizing arm is being blamed though the vignette states it is intact.

front: Why is “Gastrin failing to stimulate parietal-cell acid secretion” wrong here? A 47-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis has steatorrhea and postprandial bloating. After a fatty meal, duodenal pH f…
back: Gastrin regulates gastric acid; steatorrhea after a fatty meal implicates inadequate pancreatic enzymes, the CCK-dependent product.
extra: Gastric acid drive is being treated as the fat-malabsorption mechanism.

front: Why is “Motilin failing to initiate migrating motor complexes” wrong here? A 47-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis has steatorrhea and postprandial bloating. After a fatty meal, duodenal pH f…
back: Motilin governs fasting motility patterns; postprandial fat digestion depends on CCK-driven enzyme release.
extra: Interdigestive motility is being substituted for nutrient-stimulated enzyme secretion.

front: A 52-year-old woman eats a dinner rich in protein and fat. As the chyme reaches her duodenum, which of the following sequences correctly couples the stimulus to her pancreatic secretion?
back: Protein and fat stimulate CCK, releasing enzyme-rich juice
extra: Proteins and fats in the duodenum stimulate CCK secretion, and CCK causes the pancreatic acini to secrete enzyme-rich juice while enhancing secretin's effect.

front: Why is “Protein and fat stimulate motilin, releasing bicarbonate-rich juice” wrong here? A 52-year-old woman eats a dinner rich in protein and fat. As the chyme reaches her duodenum, which of the following seq…
back: Motilin from the duodenal mucosa initiates peristalsis as a migrating motility complex; it does not couple nutrient detection to pancreatic enzyme secretion.
extra: A motility hormone is being cast as a secretion hormone.

front: Why is “Acidic chyme stimulates gastrin, releasing bicarbonate-rich juice” wrong here? A 52-year-old woman eats a dinner rich in protein and fat. As the chyme reaches her duodenum, which of the following seq…
back: Acidic chyme triggers secretin, not gastrin; secretin then causes pancreatic duct cells to release bicarbonate-rich juice that neutralizes the acid.
extra: The acid-neutralizing response is being attributed to the wrong hormone.

front: Why is “Acidic chyme stimulates secretin, releasing enzyme-rich juice” wrong here? A 52-year-old woman eats a dinner rich in protein and fat. As the chyme reaches her duodenum, which of the following seq…
back: Acidic chyme does trigger secretin, but secretin drives bicarbonate-rich fluid from duct cells; enzyme-rich juice from acini is CCK's domain.
extra: Secretin's product is being swapped with CCK's product.

front:
During a physiology demonstration, a healthy 22-year-old volunteer's small intestine shows contractions that churn and mix chyme with digestive juices but produce no net forward movement of the contents.

Which of the following terms describes this motility pattern?
back: Segmentation
extra: Segmentation does not force chyme through the tract; it combines chyme with digestive juices and pushes food particles against the mucosa to be absorbed.

front: Why is “Peristalsis” wrong here? During a physiology demonstration, a healthy 22-year-old volunteer's small intestine shows contractions that churn and m…
back: Peristalsis consists of sequential, alternating waves of contraction and relaxation that propel food along the tract, the opposite of the stationary mixing described.
extra: The propulsive pattern is being chosen for a non-propulsive one.

front: Why is “Mass movement” wrong here? During a physiology demonstration, a healthy 22-year-old volunteer's small intestine shows contractions that churn and m…
back: Mass movements are strong waves that start midway through the transverse colon and force contents toward the rectum; they do not occur in the small intestine.
extra: A colonic pattern is being assigned to the small intestine.

front: Why is “Haustration” wrong here? During a physiology demonstration, a healthy 22-year-old volunteer's small intestine shows contractions that churn and m…
back: Haustra are the pouches of the colon, whose slow churning aids water absorption; the pattern described is small-intestinal segmentation.
extra: A large-intestinal pattern is being assigned to the small intestine.

front: A 30-year-old woman with chronic diarrhea and weight loss has a duodenal biopsy showing complete loss of villi. Her malabsorption results mainly from loss of which of the following?
back: A 600-fold amplification of absorptive surface area
extra: Circular folds, villi, and microvilli increase the small-intestinal mucosal surface area by 600-fold, with about 200 million microvilli per square millimeter; losing villi collapses this absorptive capacity.

front: Why is “The mucosal cells that secrete the hormone secretin” wrong here? A 30-year-old woman with chronic diarrhea and weight loss has a duodenal biopsy showing complete loss of villi. Her mala…
back: Secretin regulates pancreatic bicarbonate release; its loss would impair acid neutralization, not the absorptive surface needed for nutrients.
extra: A hormone deficiency is being cast as the cause of generalized malabsorption.

front: Why is “Gut-associated lymphoid tissue within the mucosa” wrong here? A 30-year-old woman with chronic diarrhea and weight loss has a duodenal biopsy showing complete loss of villi. Her mala…
back: Mucosal lymphoid tissue defends against pathogens; it plays no direct role in absorbing nutrients from chyme.
extra: Immune tissue is being cast as an absorptive structure.

front: Why is “The pacemaker cells that set the intestinal rhythm” wrong here? A 30-year-old woman with chronic diarrhea and weight loss has a duodenal biopsy showing complete loss of villi. Her mala…
back: Pacemaker activity drives segmentation and peristalsis; disordered motility alters transit but does not remove the surface area across which absorption occurs.
extra: A motility defect is being cast as the cause of the malabsorption.

front: Two unaffected parents are each known carriers of the same pathogenic variant for an autosomal recessive disorder. What is the probability that their next child will inherit the disorder?
back: 25% for each pregnancy
extra: An Aa by Aa cross yields AA, Aa, Aa, and aa in equal quarter-probabilities; only aa is affected.

front: Why is “50% for each pregnancy” wrong here? Two unaffected parents are each known carriers of the same pathogenic variant for an autosomal recessive disorder. What …
back: Half of children are expected to be carriers, while one quarter are expected to be affected.
extra: Carrier probability is being confused with affected-child probability.

front: Why is “100% for each pregnancy” wrong here? Two unaffected parents are each known carriers of the same pathogenic variant for an autosomal recessive disorder. What …
back: Each parent transmits either allele independently, so affected inheritance is not certain.
extra: Carrier parents are being treated as if both always transmit the pathogenic allele.

front: Why is “0% for each pregnancy” wrong here? Two unaffected parents are each known carriers of the same pathogenic variant for an autosomal recessive disorder. What …
back: Unaffected carriers can each transmit the pathogenic allele, creating a one-in-four affected risk.
extra: The parents' unaffected status is being mistaken for absence of transmissible variants.

front:
A child has a completely penetrant autosomal recessive disorder. Sequencing identifies two distinct pathogenic variants in the same gene. One was inherited from the mother and one from the father. Neither parent is affected.

Which of the following best describes the child's genotype?
back: Different pathogenic alleles in the two gene copies
extra: Each parent contributed a different pathogenic allele at the same locus. Both copies are affected, satisfying the recessive model through compound heterozygosity rather than identical variants.

front: Why is “The same pathogenic allele in the two gene copies” wrong here? A child has a completely penetrant autosomal recessive disorder. Sequencing identifies two distinct pathogenic variants …
back: Two identical pathogenic alleles would describe homozygosity. Sequencing explicitly distinguishes the maternal variant from the paternal variant, favoring compound heterozygosity in this child.
extra: Treats two distinct pathogenic variants as the same allele and confuses compound heterozygosity with homozygosity.

front: Why is “Two normal alleles despite the clinical phenotype” wrong here? A child has a completely penetrant autosomal recessive disorder. Sequencing identifies two distinct pathogenic variants …
back: Both gene copies are reported to contain pathogenic variants. Reclassifying them as normal would contradict the supplied sequence results rather than explain the disease.
extra: Discards the pathogenic sequence findings by assuming both gene copies are normal.

front: Why is “Two pathogenic variants confined to one gene copy” wrong here? A child has a completely penetrant autosomal recessive disorder. Sequencing identifies two distinct pathogenic variants …
back: The variants were inherited from different parents and occupy the two copies at one locus. Placing both on one copy discards the parental-origin information.
extra: Places both variants on one copy despite evidence that different parents contributed them.

front:
A hypothetical autosomal dominant condition has 80% penetrance among people who inherit its pathogenic allele. A 27-year-old man is heterozygous; his partner has no copy of that allele. Assume penetrance is independent of which parent transmits it.

Which of the following is the probability that their next child will inherit the allele and express the condition?
back: 40% for the next child
extra: The child must first inherit the allele and then express it. Multiplying the one-half transmission probability by the stated 80% penetrance gives 40%.

front: Why is “90% for the next child” wrong here? A hypothetical autosomal dominant condition has 80% penetrance among people who inherit its pathogenic allele. A 27-year…
back: Adding event probabilities does not calculate the chance that both occur. The child must pass the inheritance and expression steps, requiring multiplication here.
extra: Combines inheritance and expression by addition instead of calculating their joint probability.

front: Why is “20% for the next child” wrong here? A hypothetical autosomal dominant condition has 80% penetrance among people who inherit its pathogenic allele. A 27-year…
back: This treats transmission as a one-quarter event, as in a carrier-pair recessive calculation. A heterozygous parent transmits a dominant allele with probability one half.
extra: Uses a one-quarter recessive affected-child probability for transmission from one heterozygous parent.

front: Why is “50% for the next child” wrong here? A hypothetical autosomal dominant condition has 80% penetrance among people who inherit its pathogenic allele. A 27-year…
back: This is the probability of inheriting the allele. It does not incorporate the additional requirement that an inheriting child express this incompletely penetrant condition.
extra: Equates inheriting the allele with expressing it and omits incomplete penetrance.

front:
A 32-year-old woman has a pathogenic allele associated with an autosomal dominant disorder but has no manifestations. Her father and daughter carry the same allele and are affected. Testing is reliable, and the family has the same disease-causing variant. In this hypothetical condition, anyone who expresses the phenotype would have developed manifestations by her age.

Which of the following best explains the woman's findings?
back: Incomplete expression of the pathogenic genotype
extra: The woman carries the familial allele despite lacking manifestations. Incomplete penetrance separates genotype from phenotype and permits an unaffected person within an affected pedigree.

front: Why is “Recessive expression requiring two altered alleles” wrong here? A 32-year-old woman has a pathogenic allele associated with an autosomal dominant disorder but has no manifestations. He…
back: A recessive model requires two pathogenic alleles. This family is explicitly described as having a dominant disorder, so that requirement does not explain the observed pattern.
extra: Applies the two-pathogenic-copy requirement of recessive inheritance to a stated dominant disorder.

front: Why is “Complete expression of the pathogenic genotype” wrong here? A 32-year-old woman has a pathogenic allele associated with an autosomal dominant disorder but has no manifestations. He…
back: Complete penetrance means the disease-associated genotype is expressed in each carrier. Her confirmed genotype without manifestations directly conflicts with that proposed explanation.
extra: Assumes every carrier must express the phenotype despite the confirmed unaffected carrier.

front: Why is “Failure to inherit the disease-associated allele” wrong here? A 32-year-old woman has a pathogenic allele associated with an autosomal dominant disorder but has no manifestations. He…
back: The sequencing result establishes that she inherited the relevant allele. Interpreting her phenotype as proof of a normal genotype discards the decisive laboratory observation.
extra: Treats an unaffected phenotype as proof that the pathogenic allele was not inherited.

front:
In a hypothetical lineage study, a sperm carrying variant X fertilizes an egg. A different variant Y is confined to the father’s skin cells and is absent from both gametes. Assume no later mutation or loss of either sequence.

Which of the following distributions is expected in the resulting child?
back: Variant X throughout the child; variant Y absent
extra: Variant X enters the founding cell through the sperm and follows the resulting cellular lineage. The skin-confined variant Y lacks a route through either gamete.

front: Why is “Variant X and variant Y absent from the child” wrong here? In a hypothetical lineage study, a sperm carrying variant X fertilizes an egg. A different variant Y is confined to the …
back: The fertilizing sperm is specifically stated to contain X. Under the assumption of no subsequent sequence loss, excluding both variants discards that direct transmission route.
extra: Ignores the variant carried by the fertilizing sperm despite the stated absence of later sequence loss.

front: Why is “Variant X confined to skin; variant Y absent” wrong here? In a hypothetical lineage study, a sperm carrying variant X fertilizes an egg. A different variant Y is confined to the …
back: The transmitted variant entered through a gamete rather than arising later in a skin cell. Restricting it to skin misapplies the parental somatic-lineage example.
extra: Applies a skin-cell lineage restriction to a variant introduced through the fertilizing gamete.

front: Why is “Variant X absent throughout; variant Y present” wrong here? In a hypothetical lineage study, a sperm carrying variant X fertilizes an egg. A different variant Y is confined to the …
back: This reverses the supplied routes. The fertilizing sperm carries X, while neither gamete carries Y, so the proposed inheritance pattern contradicts the lineage observations.
extra: Reverses the inheritance routes of the gametic variant and the skin-confined variant.

front:
A hypothetical pedigree study compares five markers on the same chromosome as a disease-associated allele. Their separations from that allele are 1, 8, 20, 35, and 50 arbitrary distance units. Assume the stated separations accurately rank physical proximity and no other factor differs.

Which marker should most reliably remain associated with the allele through meiosis?
back: The marker separated by 1 distance unit
extra: This marker is the closest under the stated assumptions. Closely linked loci are less often separated by recombination and therefore more reliably travel together through meiosis.

front: Why is “The marker separated by 35 distance units” wrong here? A hypothetical pedigree study compares five markers on the same chromosome as a disease-associated allele. Their separat…
back: This marker is farther from the allele than several alternatives. Greater separation provides less reliable tracking when the comparison depends on the chance of meiotic recombination.
extra: Chooses a relatively distant marker despite nearer alternatives in a proximity-controlled comparison.

front: Why is “The marker separated by 50 distance units” wrong here? A hypothetical pedigree study compares five markers on the same chromosome as a disease-associated allele. Their separat…
back: This is the largest stated separation. Choosing it reverses the relationship between chromosomal proximity and co-inheritance rather than selecting the most tightly linked marker.
extra: Assumes the greatest chromosomal separation produces the strongest co-inheritance.

front: Why is “The marker separated by 8 distance units” wrong here? A hypothetical pedigree study compares five markers on the same chromosome as a disease-associated allele. Their separat…
back: This marker is relatively close, but another marker has a smaller stated separation. The smallest separation provides the strongest expected co-inheritance in this controlled comparison.
extra: Treats a nearby marker as optimal without comparing it with the still closer alternative.

front:
A laboratory changes one nucleotide in a hypothetical coding sequence. The resulting protein has one substituted amino acid, its original length, and unchanged activity in the specified assay.

Which of the following best characterizes this result?
back: Missense change with preserved measured protein activity
extra: An amino-acid substitution identifies a missense change. The unchanged assay result shows that classification alone does not establish functional impairment in the tested setting.

front: Why is “Nonsense change with preserved measured protein activity” wrong here? A laboratory changes one nucleotide in a hypothetical coding sequence. The resulting protein has one substituted amino a…
back: A nonsense change introduces a premature stop. Here the protein retains its original length and has a substituted residue, supporting a missense classification instead.
extra: Classifies a residue substitution as premature termination despite preserved protein length.

front: Why is “Frameshift change with demonstrated loss of protein activity” wrong here? A laboratory changes one nucleotide in a hypothetical coding sequence. The resulting protein has one substituted amino a…
back: The experiment reports a nucleotide substitution and one amino-acid replacement, not a nontriplet insertion or deletion. It also explicitly reports preserved measured activity.
extra: Infers both a frameshift and functional loss from observations showing a substitution with preserved activity.

front: Why is “Nonsense change with demonstrated shortening of the protein” wrong here? A laboratory changes one nucleotide in a hypothetical coding sequence. The resulting protein has one substituted amino a…
back: The protein length is unchanged. A result involving premature termination and shortening would require different sequence and protein observations from those supplied here.
extra: Assumes premature termination and shortening even though the measured protein remains full length.

front:
In a hypothetical coding-sequence experiment, investigators remove two nucleotides from the middle of a gene. A second construct instead removes three nucleotides at that position. Translation begins upstream of either deletion.

Which of the following best compares the downstream grouping of nucleotides?
back: Changed after the two-base deletion; preserved after the three-base deletion
extra: Codons use three nucleotides. Removing two changes the alignment of downstream triplets, whereas removing a complete triplet preserves the reading frame after the deletion.

front: Why is “Unchanged before either deletion; undetermined after either deletion” wrong here? In a hypothetical coding-sequence experiment, investigators remove two nucleotides from the middle of a gene. A second c…
back: The position of each deletion is known, and codon length is specified by the genetic code. Those facts determine whether downstream triplet grouping changes.
extra: Treats downstream triplet grouping as indeterminate despite knowing both deletion lengths.

front: Why is “Preserved after the two-base deletion; changed after the three-base deletion” wrong here? In a hypothetical coding-sequence experiment, investigators remove two nucleotides from the middle of a gene. A second c…
back: This reverses the effect of deletion size. The nontriplet deletion changes downstream grouping, while deletion of three nucleotides leaves subsequent triplets in the original frame.
extra: Reverses the distinction between deletion lengths divisible and not divisible by three.

front: Why is “Changed after the two-base deletion; changed after the three-base deletion” wrong here? In a hypothetical coding-sequence experiment, investigators remove two nucleotides from the middle of a gene. A second c…
back: Both constructs lose sequence, but sequence loss is distinct from a frame shift. Removing an entire triplet does not change the downstream reading frame.
extra: Assumes every deletion shifts the reading frame, including loss of a complete triplet.

front:
A hypothetical coding sequence undergoes a one-nucleotide insertion followed farther downstream by a one-nucleotide deletion. Both changes occur within the translated region. Assume no premature stop is encountered between them.

Which of the following best describes the reading frame across the three regions?
back: Original before insertion, shifted between sites, restored after deletion
extra: The insertion offsets triplet grouping by one nucleotide. The later deletion removes that offset, restoring the downstream frame while leaving the intervening region read differently.

front: Why is “Shifted before insertion, shifted between sites, restored after deletion” wrong here? A hypothetical coding sequence undergoes a one-nucleotide insertion followed farther downstream by a one-nucleotide dele…
back: Translation begins upstream in the original frame. A downstream insertion cannot alter the already specified grouping of nucleotides before its own position in the sequence.
extra: Assumes a downstream sequence alteration changes codon grouping before its own position.

front: Why is “Original before insertion, restored between sites, shifted after deletion” wrong here? A hypothetical coding sequence undergoes a one-nucleotide insertion followed farther downstream by a one-nucleotide dele…
back: The first alteration creates an offset rather than restoring one. Restoration occurs after the later compensating deletion, not within the interval separating the two changes.
extra: Places frame restoration between the changes rather than after the compensating deletion.

front: Why is “Original before insertion, original between sites, original after deletion” wrong here? A hypothetical coding sequence undergoes a one-nucleotide insertion followed farther downstream by a one-nucleotide dele…
back: The net length change is zero, but the changes occur at different positions. Codon grouping is disrupted between them before the compensating deletion is reached.
extra: Uses zero net length change to conclude that the interval between the two changes is unaffected.

front:
Two unaffected parents each carry one normal allele and one pathogenic allele at the same autosomal locus. Their hypothetical disorder has complete penetrance when both copies are pathogenic. Their adult son is unaffected, and his genotype has not been measured.

Which of the following is his probability of carrying one pathogenic allele?
back: Two thirds of the remaining outcomes
extra: The four equally likely parental allele combinations include one affected genotype. Excluding it leaves two carrier combinations and one noncarrier combination, giving two thirds.

front: Why is “One half of the remaining outcomes” wrong here? Two unaffected parents each carry one normal allele and one pathogenic allele at the same autosomal locus. Their hypothe…
back: One half is the unconditional carrier probability before considering the son's phenotype. Conditioning on his being unaffected removes the affected genotype from the denominator.
extra: Uses the unconditional carrier probability after the unaffected phenotype has excluded one outcome.

front: Why is “Three quarters of the remaining outcomes” wrong here? Two unaffected parents each carry one normal allele and one pathogenic allele at the same autosomal locus. Their hypothe…
back: Three quarters is the probability of an unaffected child before conditioning. It is not the fraction of unaffected offspring who retain one pathogenic allele.
extra: Confuses the probability of being unaffected with carrier probability among unaffected offspring.

front: Why is “One quarter of the remaining outcomes” wrong here? Two unaffected parents each carry one normal allele and one pathogenic allele at the same autosomal locus. Their hypothe…
back: One quarter is the unconditional affected-child probability for this parental cross. The question instead asks about carrier status after the affected outcome has been excluded.
extra: Substitutes the unconditional affected-child probability for conditional carrier probability.

front:
A hypothetical pair of homologous chromosomes has markers arranged A-B-C and a-b-c at matching gene locations. A single reciprocal exchange produces A-b-c and a-B-C. Marker order is preserved, and no sequence change occurs outside the exchanged segments.

Which of the following best locates the exchange?
back: Between the first and second marker loci
extra: The first marker retains its original association, while the second and third come from the other chromosome. That transition places the exchange between the first two loci.

front: Why is “Before the first of the three marker loci” wrong here? A hypothetical pair of homologous chromosomes has markers arranged A-B-C and a-b-c at matching gene locations. A single …
back: Exchanging the entire marked segment would preserve the three markers together as a block. It would not create the observed separation of the first marker from the others.
extra: Places the exchange before the entire marker block even though the first marker separates from the others.

front: Why is “After the third of the three marker loci” wrong here? A hypothetical pair of homologous chromosomes has markers arranged A-B-C and a-b-c at matching gene locations. A single …
back: An exchange beyond the marked region would leave these three-marker combinations intact. It cannot explain the observed mixing of parental origin within the displayed segment.
extra: Places the exchange outside the marker block despite the observed change within it.

front: Why is “Within another chromosome lacking these loci” wrong here? A hypothetical pair of homologous chromosomes has markers arranged A-B-C and a-b-c at matching gene locations. A single …
back: The altered combinations occur at the displayed matched loci. Exchanging a different chromosome would not account for the reciprocal change within this specified marker series.
extra: Attributes a change in these marker combinations to an exchange on a different chromosome.

front:
In a hypothetical lineage-tracing study, a DNA sequence change first appears in one skin cell after birth. It is subsequently found in that cell's descendants. The reproductive-cell lineage does not contain the change.

Which of the following best describes its distribution?
back: Restricted to descendants of the altered body cell
extra: The alteration arose in a body cell and follows that cell's descendants. The explicitly unaffected reproductive lineage supports somatic distribution rather than transmission through gametes.

front: Why is “Distributed through offspring by the unaltered gametes” wrong here? In a hypothetical lineage-tracing study, a DNA sequence change first appears in one skin cell after birth. It is subsequ…
back: The gametes are stated to lack this change. Its expansion within skin-cell descendants therefore does not supply a route for transmission through those reproductive cells.
extra: Assumes a skin-cell alteration can be transmitted through gametes that do not contain it.

front: Why is “Present in the parental gamete before fertilization” wrong here? In a hypothetical lineage-tracing study, a DNA sequence change first appears in one skin cell after birth. It is subsequ…
back: The study locates the change after birth in a skin cell. An origin before fertilization contradicts the observed timing and lineage of the event.
extra: Moves an observed postnatal skin-cell event back to a parental gamete before fertilization.

front: Why is “Restricted to reproductive cells rather than skin cells” wrong here? In a hypothetical lineage-tracing study, a DNA sequence change first appears in one skin cell after birth. It is subsequ…
back: This reverses the directly measured distribution. The changed sequence is present in the skin-cell lineage and absent from the reproductive lineage in the study.
extra: Reverses the measured presence in skin descendants and absence from reproductive cells.

front:
Two hypothetical variants are studied. Variant X produces a shortened protein ending at a newly introduced stop signal. Variant Y produces a full-length protein with one changed amino acid. Both proteins have reduced activity in the same assay.

Which of the following best explains why the variants receive different sequence classifications?
back: X terminates translation early; Y replaces an amino acid
extra: Premature termination classifies X as nonsense, while residue substitution classifies Y as missense. Their shared reduction in measured activity does not erase that sequence-level distinction.

front: Why is “X replaces an amino acid; Y terminates translation early” wrong here? Two hypothetical variants are studied. Variant X produces a shortened protein ending at a newly introduced stop signal. …
back: This reverses the observations. X is shortened at a new stop, whereas Y retains its length and contains an amino-acid substitution in the protein.
extra: Reverses which variant creates a stop signal and which substitutes an amino acid.

front: Why is “X and Y terminate translation at an earlier stop signal” wrong here? Two hypothetical variants are studied. Variant X produces a shortened protein ending at a newly introduced stop signal. …
back: Only X is reported to end at a new stop. Y remains full length, so its reduced activity should not be attributed to premature termination.
extra: Attributes both activity defects to premature termination even though one protein remains full length.

front: Why is “X and Y replace a residue without changing protein length” wrong here? Two hypothetical variants are studied. Variant X produces a shortened protein ending at a newly introduced stop signal. …
back: X is explicitly shortened, so a preserved-length substitution cannot explain its result. Y alone has the stated full-length protein with one altered amino acid.
extra: Treats both changes as full-length substitutions despite the measured truncation of one protein.

front:
In a hypothetical cell model, an X-linked gene has one pathogenic copy and one normal copy. The normal copy contributes measurable protective function. Investigators selectively disable that copy while preserving the pathogenic copy and the remaining experimental conditions.

Which of the following paired results best supports protection from the nonmutated copy?
back: Greater phenotype severity; unchanged pathogenic-copy number
extra: Disabling the normal copy removes its protective contribution while leaving the pathogenic copy unchanged. Greater severity without additional pathogenic copies supports the proposed functional contribution.

front: Why is “Lower phenotype severity; unchanged pathogenic-copy number” wrong here? In a hypothetical cell model, an X-linked gene has one pathogenic copy and one normal copy. The normal copy contributes …
back: The copy number matches the controlled intervention, but the severity direction opposes the stated protective role. Removing protection would not explain an improvement through this mechanism.
extra: Predicts improvement from removing a contribution explicitly shown to be protective.

front: Why is “Greater phenotype severity; increased pathogenic-copy number” wrong here? In a hypothetical cell model, an X-linked gene has one pathogenic copy and one normal copy. The normal copy contributes …
back: Greater severity could follow another change, but increased pathogenic-copy number violates the controlled design. The experiment isolates loss of normal-copy function rather than adding pathogenic copies.
extra: Attributes the outcome to extra pathogenic copies even though their number is held constant.

front: Why is “Lower phenotype severity; increased pathogenic-copy number” wrong here? In a hypothetical cell model, an X-linked gene has one pathogenic copy and one normal copy. The normal copy contributes …
back: Both the additional pathogenic copies and improved severity fall outside the proposed controlled mechanism. The design changes normal-copy function while preserving the pathogenic-copy count.
extra: Combines an unperformed copy-number change with a severity direction opposite to loss of protection.

front:
A family carries a pathogenic variant in an X-linked gene. A boy with an XY chromosome complement has manifestations, while his XX sister has the variant on one X chromosome and a normal copy on the other. Her manifestations are milder.

Which of the following best accounts for this difference?
back: A second normal copy reduces expression in the sister
extra: The sister has a nonmutated copy at the X-linked locus, whereas the brother has one X chromosome. This can reduce expression without guaranteeing an absent phenotype.

front: Why is “A second normal copy reduces expression in the brother” wrong here? A family carries a pathogenic variant in an X-linked gene. A boy with an XY chromosome complement has manifestations, wh…
back: The boy's stated chromosome complement contains one X chromosome. At this X-linked locus, the additional normal X copy belongs to his sister rather than him.
extra: Assigns the additional normal X-linked copy to the sibling who has only one X chromosome.

front: Why is “Two pathogenic copies are required in the brother” wrong here? A family carries a pathogenic variant in an X-linked gene. A boy with an XY chromosome complement has manifestations, wh…
back: A boy with one X chromosome can express an X-linked pathogenic allele without a second X-linked copy. Requiring two copies misapplies a recessive autosomal model.
extra: Applies a two-copy autosomal requirement to a boy with one copy of the X-linked locus.

front: Why is “The variant lies on a nonsex chromosome in the sister” wrong here? A family carries a pathogenic variant in an X-linked gene. A boy with an XY chromosome complement has manifestations, wh…
back: The gene is explicitly X-linked in both siblings. Moving it to an autosome in one sibling does not follow from their different levels of expression.
extra: Treats different phenotype severity as evidence that the gene changes chromosome location.

front: In meiosis, homologous chromosomes are best described as which of the following?
back: Matched pairs sharing the same gene loci
extra: OpenStax: homologous chromosomes are matched pairs containing the same genes in identical locations.

front: Why is “Random DNA fragments absorbed from food” wrong here? In meiosis, homologous chromosomes are best described as which of the following?
back: They are chromosomal pairs.
extra: Nonsense — does not match the cited teaching point.

front: Why is “Only mitochondrial plasmids in the matrix” wrong here? In meiosis, homologous chromosomes are best described as which of the following?
back: Nuclear homologs; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Mitochondria are separate.

front: Why is “Extracellular matrix collagen fiber bundles” wrong here? In meiosis, homologous chromosomes are best described as which of the following?
back: Chromosomes are DNA; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Wrong polymer — does not match the cited teaching point.

front: Mendel's law of independent assortment concerns which genetic idea?
back: Different gene pairs segregating independently in gametes
extra: OpenStax Biology: independent assortment of different gene pairs.

front: Why is “Sensitivity equaling true positives over diseased only” wrong here? Mendel's law of independent assortment concerns which genetic idea?
back: Wrong domain; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Biostats distractor — does not match the cited teaching point.

front: Why is “Aspirin irreversibly activating ACE in vessels” wrong here? Mendel's law of independent assortment concerns which genetic idea?
back: Wrong domain; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Pharm distractor — does not match the cited teaching point.

front: Why is “Complement destroying only self antigens in blood” wrong here? Mendel's law of independent assortment concerns which genetic idea?
back: Wrong domain; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Immuno distractor — does not match the cited teaching point.

front:
A pathogenic mitochondrial DNA variant is present in a woman and in each of her children. Her affected brother has children, but none inherited the variant from him.

Which inheritance pattern best explains this pedigree?
back: Maternal cytoplasmic transmission
extra: Affected mothers can transmit mitochondrial DNA variants, whereas affected fathers do not transmit their mitochondria to offspring.

front: Why is “Y-linked paternal transmission” wrong here? A pathogenic mitochondrial DNA variant is present in a woman and in each of her children. Her affected brother has child…
back: Y-linked variants pass from fathers to sons, unlike the maternal pattern shown here.
extra: The direction of transmission is reversed and female transmission would be impossible.

front: Why is “Autosomal dominant transmission” wrong here? A pathogenic mitochondrial DNA variant is present in a woman and in each of her children. Her affected brother has child…
back: Autosomal dominant alleles can be transmitted by either an affected mother or an affected father.
extra: Vertical transmission is being recognized without accounting for the parent-of-origin restriction.

front: Why is “Autosomal recessive transmission” wrong here? A pathogenic mitochondrial DNA variant is present in a woman and in each of her children. Her affected brother has child…
back: Autosomal recessive transmission does not predict that only mothers pass the variant onward.
extra: A carrier-pair pattern is being substituted for uniparental organelle inheritance.

front:
Two hypothetical anemia models are compared. In model X, erythrocyte destruction is measured to exceed replacement. In model Y, the marrow fails to produce adequate blood cells.

Which of the following best distinguishes the primary mechanisms?
back: X has a destruction imbalance; Y has marrow production failure
extra: X matches the definition of hemolytic anemia: destruction exceeds replacement. Y identifies the production failure described by aplastic anemia, separating the two mechanisms despite their shared outcome.

front: Why is “Both models have marrow failure without increased erythrocyte destruction” wrong here? Two hypothetical anemia models are compared. In model X, erythrocyte destruction is measured to exceed replacement. In m…
back: The first model directly measures destruction exceeding replacement. A uniform production-failure explanation therefore omits its defining loss-side abnormality in the stated experiment.
extra: Assigns production failure to both models despite direct evidence of a destruction imbalance in the first.

front: Why is “Neither model changes the balance of circulating blood-cell numbers” wrong here? Two hypothetical anemia models are compared. In model X, erythrocyte destruction is measured to exceed replacement. In m…
back: Both models identify a process that can lower circulating cells. Excess destruction and deficient production are different ways of shifting the balance away from maintenance.
extra: Assumes excess destruction and inadequate production cannot alter circulating cell numbers.

front: Why is “X has marrow production failure; Y has a destruction imbalance” wrong here? Two hypothetical anemia models are compared. In model X, erythrocyte destruction is measured to exceed replacement. In m…
back: This reverses the measured mechanisms. X is defined by excess destruction, whereas Y directly identifies failure of the marrow production compartment in the comparison.
extra: Reverses which model directly measures excess destruction and which identifies inadequate production.

front:
A hypothetical intestinal transport experiment supplies adequate vitamin B12 and functional intrinsic factor directly to the intestinal contents. Uptake remains markedly reduced after a specific distal small-intestinal segment is removed. There is no vitamin breakdown or alternative transport defect.

Which of the following localizations best explains the persistent uptake failure?
back: Loss of the terminal ileal absorption compartment
extra: B12 absorption occurs in the terminal ileum. Adequate vitamin and functional intrinsic factor cannot restore uptake when the relevant intestinal compartment itself has been removed.

front: Why is “Failure to supply the vitamin to the intestinal contents” wrong here? A hypothetical intestinal transport experiment supplies adequate vitamin B12 and functional intrinsic factor directly to…
back: Adequate B12 is directly provided. The persistent failure must therefore be interpreted despite substrate availability rather than attributed to a deficiency of vitamin input.
extra: Attributes failed uptake to inadequate vitamin supply even though the experiment directly supplies it.

front: Why is “Accelerated destruction of the vitamin before absorption” wrong here? A hypothetical intestinal transport experiment supplies adequate vitamin B12 and functional intrinsic factor directly to…
back: The experimental conditions exclude vitamin breakdown. Introducing that mechanism would contradict the control intended to isolate the effect of losing a specific intestinal segment.
extra: Introduces vitamin destruction despite an experimental condition that explicitly excludes it.

front: Why is “Replacement of the absent segment by an intact gastric factor” wrong here? A hypothetical intestinal transport experiment supplies adequate vitamin B12 and functional intrinsic factor directly to…
back: Intrinsic factor supports absorption but is not a substitute for the absorbing tissue. Supplying it does not recreate the removed terminal ileal compartment in this experiment.
extra: Assumes a soluble absorption factor can replace the removed tissue where uptake occurs.

front:
A hypothetical erythrocyte pool initially contains 100 units. During a fixed observation interval, 14 units are destroyed and 9 units are replaced. Assume no bleeding, transfer, or other source of change.

Which of the following interpretations best describes the pool at the end of the interval?
back: 95 units remain because destruction exceeds replacement
extra: The pool loses 14 units and gains 9, leaving a net loss of 5. Destruction exceeds replacement even though production continues during the interval.

front: Why is “109 units remain because destruction cannot change the pool” wrong here? A hypothetical erythrocyte pool initially contains 100 units. During a fixed observation interval, 14 units are destroye…
back: This adds replacement while discarding the measured destruction. The final count requires both the gain and the loss, not the production-side contribution alone.
extra: Adds replacement to the starting pool while ignoring the measured destruction.

front: Why is “105 units remain because replacement exceeds destruction” wrong here? A hypothetical erythrocyte pool initially contains 100 units. During a fixed observation interval, 14 units are destroye…
back: This reverses the two measured flows. Replacement is 9 units, below destruction at 14, so the pool contracts rather than growing by five units.
extra: Reverses the measured destruction and replacement quantities and therefore the direction of net change.

front: Why is “100 units remain because some replacement is maintained” wrong here? A hypothetical erythrocyte pool initially contains 100 units. During a fixed observation interval, 14 units are destroye…
back: Continued replacement does not guarantee balance. Its rate must equal destruction to preserve the pool, and the given replacement is insufficient in this interval.
extra: Assumes any continued replacement is sufficient to maintain the pool regardless of the greater loss.

front:
A 22-year-old patient develops petechiae, purpura, and mucosal bleeding after an infection. Platelet counts are low, while other circulating cell counts and marrow cellularity are preserved. In an experimental assay, the patient’s immune components accelerate platelet destruction.

Which mechanism best integrates the findings?
back: Immune destruction of circulating platelets
extra: The low platelet count and bleeding pattern fit platelet depletion. Preserved other counts and marrow cellularity, together with the immune assay, support selective immune platelet destruction.

front: Why is “Immune destruction of circulating erythrocytes” wrong here? A 22-year-old patient develops petechiae, purpura, and mucosal bleeding after an infection. Platelet counts are low, whi…
back: A red-cell destruction process does not explain the selective platelet reduction and platelet-directed assay. The observed bleeding manifestations are linked to the depleted platelet pool.
extra: Assigns immune destruction to red cells despite selective platelet loss and a platelet-directed assay.

front: Why is “Impaired absorption of intestinal vitamin B12” wrong here? A 22-year-old patient develops petechiae, purpura, and mucosal bleeding after an infection. Platelet counts are low, whi…
back: B12-related absorption failure affects blood-cell formation through a different pathway. It does not account for the directly measured immune acceleration of platelet destruction in this case.
extra: Substitutes nutrient malabsorption for the directly measured immune acceleration of platelet destruction.

front: Why is “Malaria-associated infection of erythrocytes” wrong here? A 22-year-old patient develops petechiae, purpura, and mucosal bleeding after an infection. Platelet counts are low, whi…
back: Malaria can accompany low platelets, but the case provides a platelet-directed immune assay and preserved other counts. No demonstrated erythrocytic infection explains the findings as directly.
extra: Uses a possible malaria-associated pattern instead of the demonstrated platelet-directed mechanism in this case.

front:
A 31-year-old patient with immune thrombocytopenia receives corticosteroid treatment and the platelet count rises. In a hypothetical model, the treatment suppresses the platelet-directed immune process without directly changing platelet production.

Which of the following paired changes best explains the response?
back: Longer platelet survival; unchanged platelet production
extra: Suppressing immune-mediated platelet destruction allows platelets to remain available longer. With production fixed by the model, increased survival explains the rise in the circulating count.

front: Why is “Shorter platelet survival; unchanged platelet production” wrong here? A 31-year-old patient with immune thrombocytopenia receives corticosteroid treatment and the platelet count rises. In a …
back: Shortening survival would increase loss from the pool while production remains fixed. That combination would oppose, rather than explain, the observed increase in platelet count.
extra: Predicts count recovery from shorter platelet survival while holding production fixed.

front: Why is “Longer platelet survival; reduced platelet production” wrong here? A 31-year-old patient with immune thrombocytopenia receives corticosteroid treatment and the platelet count rises. In a …
back: Longer survival fits reduced destruction, but lower production is not part of the stated selective effect. The model explicitly isolates immune suppression without changing platelet production.
extra: Adds reduced production to a model that changes immune destruction without changing platelet production.

front: Why is “Shorter platelet survival; increased platelet production” wrong here? A 31-year-old patient with immune thrombocytopenia receives corticosteroid treatment and the platelet count rises. In a …
back: Increased production could introduce a separate explanation for count recovery, but it violates the controlled model. The specified intervention instead reduces immune-mediated platelet loss.
extra: Introduces increased production and shorter survival instead of the stated selective reduction in immune loss.

front:
A 47-year-old patient reports fatigue, infections that persist, and easy bruising. Blood testing shows reduced counts in multiple cell groups. A marrow specimen has markedly reduced cellularity.

Which of the following best unifies these findings?
back: Failure of blood-cell production within the marrow
extra: Reduced marrow cellularity and low counts across cell groups support a production defect. Aplastic anemia connects that finding with fatigue, prolonged infections and easy bruising.

front: Why is “Increased production of circulating blood cells” wrong here? A 47-year-old patient reports fatigue, infections that persist, and easy bruising. Blood testing shows reduced counts in…
back: Increased production does not account for the low marrow cellularity and reduced circulating counts. The observed pattern instead points toward failure of the production compartment.
extra: Uses increased production to explain both reduced circulating counts and low marrow cellularity.

front: Why is “Preserved marrow production with isolated platelet loss” wrong here? A 47-year-old patient reports fatigue, infections that persist, and easy bruising. Blood testing shows reduced counts in…
back: The case describes reduced counts in multiple cell groups and a poorly cellular marrow. Restricting the problem to platelets misses both the broader blood findings and the tissue result.
extra: Reduces a multilineage production pattern to isolated platelet loss while assuming the marrow is preserved.

front: Why is “Preserved marrow production with isolated red-cell loss” wrong here? A 47-year-old patient reports fatigue, infections that persist, and easy bruising. Blood testing shows reduced counts in…
back: An isolated red-cell process does not unify prolonged infections, bruising, multilineage count reductions and low marrow cellularity. The production-side abnormality is the more comprehensive explanation.
extra: Reduces a multilineage production pattern to isolated red-cell loss while overlooking the abnormal marrow.

front:
A 39-year-old patient develops low blood-cell counts after chemotherapy. Marrow examination identifies stem-cell damage and low cellularity.

Which of the following best explains why the resulting problem can involve several circulating cell groups?
back: Damage to the compartment responsible for blood-cell production
extra: The observed stem-cell damage and low cellularity identify the marrow production compartment. Injury there explains low output across cell groups in the supplied aplastic-anemia model.

front: Why is “Enhanced replacement of the injured marrow stem-cell population” wrong here? A 39-year-old patient develops low blood-cell counts after chemotherapy. Marrow examination identifies stem-cell damage …
back: Successful replacement would oppose the measured low cellularity and production failure. It does not explain the continuing reduction in circulating cell counts after the documented injury.
extra: Treats successful stem-cell replacement as an explanation for persistent low cellularity and low output.

front: Why is “Preserved marrow output despite the observed stem-cell damage” wrong here? A 39-year-old patient develops low blood-cell counts after chemotherapy. Marrow examination identifies stem-cell damage …
back: This separates output from the production lesion without support. The supplied mechanism links marrow stem-cell damage to blood-cell failure and explains the measured low counts.
extra: Assumes output remains preserved despite the documented injury and reduced circulating counts.

front: Why is “Increased destruction restricted to circulating platelets” wrong here? A 39-year-old patient develops low blood-cell counts after chemotherapy. Marrow examination identifies stem-cell damage …
back: An isolated platelet process would not explain why several cell groups fall alongside demonstrated marrow stem-cell damage. It overlooks the directly examined site of the injury.
extra: Uses platelet-specific destruction to explain broad count reductions alongside directly observed marrow injury.

front:
A 55-year-old patient has anemia, tingling in the feet, and increasing difficulty walking. Investigation identifies deficiency of a stomach-derived factor needed for intestinal absorption of an essential nutrient.

Which of the following diagnoses best integrates the hematologic and neurologic findings with that absorption defect?
back: Anemia resulting from a lack of vitamin B12
extra: B12 deficiency can produce anemia together with paresthesias and walking difficulty. Deficiency of gastric intrinsic factor links the intestinal absorption defect to this combined pattern.

front: Why is “Bleeding from immune destruction of platelets” wrong here? A 55-year-old patient has anemia, tingling in the feet, and increasing difficulty walking. Investigation identifies defi…
back: Immune platelet destruction explains low platelets and bleeding manifestations. It does not explain the identified vitamin absorption mechanism linking anemia with paresthesias and difficulty walking.
extra: Explains the presentation through platelet loss while leaving the demonstrated nutrient-absorption defect unexplained.

front: Why is “Anemia from malaria activity within erythrocytes” wrong here? A 55-year-old patient has anemia, tingling in the feet, and increasing difficulty walking. Investigation identifies defi…
back: Blood-stage malaria can produce anemia, but no parasite observation is supplied. More importantly, that explanation does not account for the demonstrated gastric-factor-dependent absorption defect.
extra: Attributes anemia to erythrocytic infection without accounting for the measured gastric-factor-dependent absorption defect.

front: Why is “Anemia from marrow stem-cell production failure” wrong here? A 55-year-old patient has anemia, tingling in the feet, and increasing difficulty walking. Investigation identifies defi…
back: Aplastic marrow failure explains reduced blood-cell production, but it does not account for the specified intrinsic-factor-dependent vitamin absorption defect and accompanying B12-pattern neurologic findings.
extra: Uses marrow production failure without explaining the specific absorption defect that unifies this pattern.

front: A 30-year-old woman with blood group AB is scheduled for elective surgery. Which of the following best explains why she can receive packed red cells from donors of any ABO group?
back: Her plasma lacks preformed anti-A and anti-B antibodies
extra: AB recipients have A and B antigens on their own red cells and therefore do not make anti-A or anti-B; donor red cells of any ABO group are not attacked by her plasma.

front: Why is “Her erythrocytes lack A and B antigens entirely” wrong here? A 30-year-old woman with blood group AB is scheduled for elective surgery. Which of the following best explains why she …
back: Group AB erythrocytes express both A and B antigens; what she lacks are anti-A and anti-B antibodies in plasma.
extra: Group O red-cell phenotype is being ascribed to group AB.

front: Why is “Her plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies” wrong here? A 30-year-old woman with blood group AB is scheduled for elective surgery. Which of the following best explains why she …
back: Anti-A and anti-B define group O plasma (universal plasma donor risk to recipients); AB plasma lacks those antibodies.
extra: The group O plasma pattern is being applied to group AB.

front: Why is “Her Rh status alone determines ABO compatibility” wrong here? A 30-year-old woman with blood group AB is scheduled for elective surgery. Which of the following best explains why she …
back: Rh compatibility is separate; ABO compatibility for red cells depends on whether recipient plasma has anti-A/B against donor antigens.
extra: Rh and ABO systems are being conflated.

front:
A 28-year-old man arrives in hemorrhagic shock after a motor vehicle collision. There is no time to type and cross-match his blood before transfusion.

Which of the following donor blood types is most appropriate for this emergency transfusion?
back: Type O negative
extra: In emergencies without time for cross-matching, blood from a universal donor — an individual with type O negative blood — may be transfused because its cells lack the antigens that trigger recipient antibody attack.
