back: This assigns production to a different compartment without explaining intestinal spore colonization. The ongoing toxin source specified for infant botulism is the colonized large intestine.
extra: Relocates ongoing toxin production from the colonized intestine to circulating blood cells.

front: Why is “Colonization followed by toxin production within the cerebral cortex” wrong here? A 4-month-old infant has constipation, poor feeding, a weak cry, and diminished suck. Infant botulism is confirmed. The …
back: The illness's motor manifestations do not relocate toxin production to the brain. Intestinal colonization, followed by toxin action at cholinergic terminals, explains the sustained exposure.
extra: Infers a brain production site from motor manifestations rather than the known intestinal colonization.

front:
A 25-year-old patient has malaria confirmed by blood microscopy. Testing shows anemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated bilirubin. In a hypothetical observation of infected red cells, investigators record a burst of merozoites and hemozoin into the surrounding fluid.

Which of the following events most directly explains that burst?
back: Rupture of infected erythrocytes into extracellular fluid
extra: Lysis of infected erythrocytes releases merozoites and hemozoin. This directly matches both the observed cellular compartment and the simultaneous appearance of these materials outside it.

front: Why is “Attachment of intact erythrocytes to vascular lining” wrong here? A 25-year-old patient has malaria confirmed by blood microscopy. Testing shows anemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated bi…
back: Endothelial adherence is relevant to falciparum sequestration, but attachment of intact cells does not itself explain the observed burst of material from within infected erythrocytes.
extra: Confuses adherence of an intact infected cell with release of material from inside it.

front: Why is “Retention of parasite products within intact red cells” wrong here? A 25-year-old patient has malaria confirmed by blood microscopy. Testing shows anemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated bi…
back: Retention would keep the measured products inside the cell. The experiment instead observes their sudden appearance in surrounding fluid, requiring a release event.
extra: Uses intracellular retention to explain products observed outside the infected cells.

front: Why is “Transfer of extracellular products into uninfected red cells” wrong here? A 25-year-old patient has malaria confirmed by blood microscopy. Testing shows anemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated bi…
back: This describes movement into cells rather than the observed movement out of infected cells. It therefore reverses the direction of the measured release event.
extra: Reverses the measured direction of movement by describing entry into cells rather than release.

front:
A hypothetical intervention eliminates parasites from erythrocytes but has no effect on dormant hepatic forms. It is applied after Plasmodium ovale malaria, and the blood stage becomes undetectable. No new infection occurs.

Which of the following later sequences remains compatible with the intervention's stated limits?
back: Hepatic reactivation followed by renewed erythrocyte infection
extra: The intervention leaves hepatic hypnozoites intact. Their later reactivation can seed a new blood stage even after the original erythrocyte infection became undetectable.

front: Why is “Renewed blood infection without any residual parasite reservoir” wrong here? A hypothetical intervention eliminates parasites from erythrocytes but has no effect on dormant hepatic forms. It is app…
back: New infection is excluded, so recurrence requires persistence from the earlier episode. The surviving hepatic forms provide that reservoir rather than recurrence without retained parasites.
extra: Allows recurrence without either a persistent parasite reservoir or a new infection.

front: Why is “Immediate disappearance of dormant forms from both compartments” wrong here? A hypothetical intervention eliminates parasites from erythrocytes but has no effect on dormant hepatic forms. It is app…
back: Dormant forms are localized to the liver in this pathway, and the intervention leaves them intact. Simultaneous disappearance is inconsistent with the stipulated stage selectivity.
extra: Assumes a blood-stage intervention also removes dormant forms it explicitly leaves intact.

front: Why is “Continued symptoms without subsequent blood-stage parasite activity” wrong here? A hypothetical intervention eliminates parasites from erythrocytes but has no effect on dormant hepatic forms. It is app…
back: Malaria symptoms are linked to activity in the blood stage. It does not support symptomatic relapse while denying the subsequent erythrocyte infection in this scenario.
extra: Disconnects symptomatic malaria relapse from subsequent activity in the blood stage.

front:
A 41-year-old patient has latent TB infection with macrophage containment in granulomas. TNF-antagonist therapy is being considered for another condition.

Which of the following consequences is most relevant when reviewing the infection before treatment?
back: Greater risk of active disease from the existing infection
extra: TNF-antagonist therapy increases the risk of active TB in a person already infected. The relevant concern is progression from the contained state rather than proof of a new exposure.

front: Why is “Greater risk of transmission while the infection stays latent” wrong here? A 41-year-old patient has latent TB infection with macrophage containment in granulomas. TNF-antagonist therapy is being…
back: Latent infection is not the transmitting state. The treatment-associated concern is progression to active disease, not a change in contagiousness while the patient remains in the same latent state.
extra: Treats latent infection itself as a transmitting state instead of distinguishing progression to active disease.

front: Why is “Lower risk of active disease despite the immune intervention” wrong here? A 41-year-old patient has latent TB infection with macrophage containment in granulomas. TNF-antagonist therapy is being…
back: This reverses the stated risk association. TNF-antagonist therapy is identified as a factor increasing progression risk in infected patients rather than as protection from active disease.
extra: Reverses the association between TNF-antagonist therapy and risk of active TB.

front: Why is “Unchanged risk of disease because the bacilli are contained” wrong here? A 41-year-old patient has latent TB infection with macrophage containment in granulomas. TNF-antagonist therapy is being…
back: Current containment does not eliminate future progression risk. The proposed therapy changes the risk assessment even though the patient’s infection is presently classified as latent.
extra: Assumes present containment guarantees unchanged future risk despite the proposed immune intervention.

front:
A 29-year-old adult has a positive TB immune test. Evaluation finds no symptoms, a normal chest radiograph, and negative sputum smears and cultures obtained during the assessment. The clinician diagnoses latent infection after reviewing the combined evidence.

Which of the following interpretations best explains the role of the initial result?
back: It supports infection but does not determine disease activity
extra: A positive immune result supports evaluation for TB infection, but false-positive results remain possible. It does not determine active disease; the combined clinical assessment establishes the classification.

front: Why is “It establishes active disease without clinical assessment” wrong here? A 29-year-old adult has a positive TB immune test. Evaluation finds no symptoms, a normal chest radiograph, and negative…
back: An infection-directed immune assay does not independently establish active TB. This interpretation omits the disease evaluation needed to distinguish a contained infection from active disease.
extra: Equates a positive infection-directed immune result with an established diagnosis of active disease.

front: Why is “It excludes infection when chest imaging appears normal” wrong here? A 29-year-old adult has a positive TB immune test. Evaluation finds no symptoms, a normal chest radiograph, and negative…
back: Normal chest imaging is compatible with latent infection. Treating it as exclusion of infection confuses the role of structural disease assessment with an infection-directed immune response.
extra: Uses normal structural imaging to exclude an infection that may remain latent.

front: Why is “It directly counts organisms in the sampled sputum” wrong here? A 29-year-old adult has a positive TB immune test. Evaluation finds no symptoms, a normal chest radiograph, and negative…
back: The initial result comes from an immune test rather than sputum organism measurement. These are separate investigations with different readouts and roles in the combined assessment.
extra: Confuses an immune assay readout with direct organism measurement in a sputum specimen.

front:
A 38-year-old patient previously recovered from Plasmodium vivax malaria. Many months later, malaria recurs. For this case, new infection is excluded and dormant forms from the earlier episode are demonstrated.

Which of the following compartments contains the forms responsible for this recurrence?
back: Dormant parasites retained in the liver
extra: Vivax hypnozoites persist in the liver and can reactivate after a long symptom-free interval. Reactivation can then establish renewed infection of circulating erythrocytes.

front: Why is “Dormant parasites retained in neutrophils” wrong here? A 38-year-old patient previously recovered from Plasmodium vivax malaria. Many months later, malaria recurs. For this ca…
back: This assigns persistence to an unsupported circulating-cell compartment. The relapse sequence begins with hepatic hypnozoites before the parasite reestablishes activity in erythrocytes.
extra: Places the dormant relapse reservoir in circulating neutrophils rather than the hepatic compartment.

front: Why is “Dormant parasites retained in the intestine” wrong here? A 38-year-old patient previously recovered from Plasmodium vivax malaria. Many months later, malaria recurs. For this ca…
back: Intestinal persistence does not match the established vivax hypnozoite reservoir. The case excludes new infection and identifies reactivation of forms retained in the liver.
extra: Assigns the dormant relapse reservoir to the intestine instead of the liver.

front: Why is “Dormant parasites retained in erythrocytes” wrong here? A 38-year-old patient previously recovered from Plasmodium vivax malaria. Many months later, malaria recurs. For this ca…
back: Erythrocytic parasites account for the symptomatic blood stage. The persistent dormant reservoir responsible for the stipulated vivax relapse is hepatic rather than erythrocytic.
extra: Confuses the symptomatic erythrocyte stage with the dormant hepatic reservoir for relapse.

front:
A 27-year-old man develops malaise, jaundice, and elevated aminotransferases 12 weeks after a needlestick exposure. Hepatitis B surface antigen is detected.

Which of the following additional serologic markers most specifically supports recent acute hepatitis B infection?
back: Immunoglobulin M antibody to hepatitis B core antigen
extra: IgM directed against hepatitis B core antigen appears near clinical onset and supports a recent acute infection.

front: Why is “Antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen” wrong here? A 27-year-old man develops malaise, jaundice, and elevated aminotransferases 12 weeks after a needlestick exposure. Hepa…
back: Surface antibody is associated with immunity and does not identify the recent acute phase described in this patient.
extra: Uses surface antibody as the defining marker of a recent acute infection.

front: Why is “Hepatitis B e antigen” wrong here? A 27-year-old man develops malaise, jaundice, and elevated aminotransferases 12 weeks after a needlestick exposure. Hepa…
back: HBeAg can accompany active replication, but it does not date the infection as specifically as core-specific IgM.
extra: Uses a marker of active viral replication and infectivity as the most specific marker of recent acute infection.

front: Why is “Antibody to hepatitis B e antigen” wrong here? A 27-year-old man develops malaise, jaundice, and elevated aminotransferases 12 weeks after a needlestick exposure. Hepa…
back: Anti-HBe may appear as viral replication declines, but it is not the defining serologic evidence of recent acute infection.
extra: Uses a marker associated with declining replication rather than the standard recent-infection marker.

front:
A 29-year-old pregnant patient tests positive for hepatitis B surface antigen. The care team evaluates additional markers while counseling her about transmission risk.

Which of the following additional serologic findings is associated with a greater circulating burden of infectious hepatitis B particles?
back: HBeAg detected in serum
extra: Detection of hepatitis B e antigen is associated with more infectious viral particles in serum and a greater likelihood of transmission.

front: Why is “Anti-HBs detected in serum” wrong here? A 29-year-old pregnant patient tests positive for hepatitis B surface antigen. The care team evaluates additional marker…
back: Antibody to surface antigen indicates an immune response rather than a larger burden of infectious particles.
extra: Equates an immunity marker with increased viral infectivity.

front: Why is “Anti-HBe detected in serum” wrong here? A 29-year-old pregnant patient tests positive for hepatitis B surface antigen. The care team evaluates additional marker…
back: The association with a high concentration of infectious particles is made with detectable e antigen, not e antibody.
extra: Selects antibody to the e antigen instead of the antigen itself.

front: Why is “IgG anti-HBc detected in serum” wrong here? A 29-year-old pregnant patient tests positive for hepatitis B surface antigen. The care team evaluates additional marker…
back: Core-specific IgG can persist after prior exposure and does not by itself identify the high-infectivity state asked about here.
extra: Uses evidence of core exposure as a direct measure of current infectivity.

front:
A 45-year-old woman had documented hepatitis B infection 12 years ago and recovered without antiviral treatment. She is now asymptomatic, and hepatitis B surface antigen is undetectable.

Which of the following antibody combinations most strongly supports immunity after natural infection rather than vaccination alone?
back: Anti-HBs positive; total anti-HBc positive
extra: Recovery from natural infection commonly leaves both antibody to the surface antigen and antibody to the core antigen. Core antibody distinguishes this history from vaccination alone.

front: Why is “Anti-HBs positive; total anti-HBc negative” wrong here? A 45-year-old woman had documented hepatitis B infection 12 years ago and recovered without antiviral treatment. She is …
back: Surface antibody without core antibody is expected after vaccination but does not document previous natural infection.
extra: Chooses the pattern of vaccine-only immunity.

front: Why is “Anti-HBs negative; total anti-HBc positive” wrong here? A 45-year-old woman had documented hepatitis B infection 12 years ago and recovered without antiviral treatment. She is …
back: Core antibody alone does not provide the typical combined antibody pattern described after recovery from natural hepatitis B infection.
extra: Recognizes prior core exposure but omits the surface antibody expected after recovery.

front: Why is “Anti-HBs negative; total anti-HBc negative” wrong here? A 45-year-old woman had documented hepatitis B infection 12 years ago and recovered without antiviral treatment. She is …
back: The absence of both antibodies would not support either recovered natural infection or a successful vaccine response.
extra: Selects a pattern with no serologic evidence of immunity or prior infection.

front:
A 31-year-old health care worker completed hepatitis B vaccination and has no history of hepatitis or known exposure. Postvaccination testing confirms an immune response.

Which of the following serologic profiles is most consistent with immunity produced by vaccination alone?
back: HBsAg negative; anti-HBc negative; anti-HBs positive
extra: A person who responds to hepatitis B vaccination has antibody to the surface antigen without core antibody, because vaccination does not represent natural viral infection.

front: Why is “HBsAg positive; anti-HBc negative; anti-HBs negative” wrong here? A 31-year-old health care worker completed hepatitis B vaccination and has no history of hepatitis or known exposure. Po…
back: The expected response to vaccination is antibody to surface antigen, not persistent detection of surface antigen itself.
extra: Treats circulating surface antigen as evidence of successful vaccine immunity.

front: Why is “HBsAg negative; anti-HBc positive; anti-HBs negative” wrong here? A 31-year-old health care worker completed hepatitis B vaccination and has no history of hepatitis or known exposure. Po…
back: A successful vaccine response should include surface antibody and should not create antibody to the viral core.
extra: Selects an isolated core-antibody pattern instead of a vaccine response.

front: Why is “HBsAg negative; anti-HBc positive; anti-HBs positive” wrong here? A 31-year-old health care worker completed hepatitis B vaccination and has no history of hepatitis or known exposure. Po…
back: Core antibody indicates exposure to viral core antigen and therefore does not fit a response generated solely by vaccination.
extra: Confuses vaccine-only immunity with immunity after natural infection.

front:
Influenza surveillance across several successive seasons shows gradual accumulation of minor viral gene changes. The resulting viruses have modest alterations in their surface proteins compared with strains from prior years.

Which of the following processes best describes this pattern?
back: Antigenic drift
extra: Antigenic drift is the cumulative effect of small genetic changes that modestly alter influenza surface proteins over time.

front: Why is “Antigenic shift” wrong here? Influenza surveillance across several successive seasons shows gradual accumulation of minor viral gene changes. The res…
back: Antigenic shift is an abrupt large change in influenza A surface antigens, not the stepwise accumulation described here.
extra: Uses the term for a sudden major antigenic change to describe gradual variation.

front: Why is “Lysogenic conversion” wrong here? Influenza surveillance across several successive seasons shows gradual accumulation of minor viral gene changes. The res…
back: Lysogenic conversion changes bacterial traits through an integrated phage and does not name this influenza pattern.
extra: Applies a bacteriophage-mediated bacterial mechanism to influenza evolution.

front: Why is “Phenotypic mixing” wrong here? Influenza surveillance across several successive seasons shows gradual accumulation of minor viral gene changes. The res…
back: Phenotypic mixing does not describe the progressive, heritable alterations in influenza genes and surface proteins seen over seasons.
extra: Confuses a transient packaging phenomenon with inherited gene changes.

front:
Public health laboratories identify an influenza A virus whose hemagglutinin profile differs substantially from previously circulating strains. The new profile appeared abruptly rather than through a series of minor seasonal changes.

Which of the following processes best describes this event?
back: Antigenic shift
extra: Antigenic shift is a sudden major change in influenza A that yields a new hemagglutinin, with or without a new neuraminidase.

front: Why is “Antigenic drift” wrong here? Public health laboratories identify an influenza A virus whose hemagglutinin profile differs substantially from previous…
back: Antigenic drift produces gradual variation through minor mutations and does not fit the abrupt new surface-antigen profile described.
extra: Applies the term for small cumulative changes to a sudden major change.

front: Why is “Phenotypic mixing” wrong here? Public health laboratories identify an influenza A virus whose hemagglutinin profile differs substantially from previous…
back: Phenotypic mixing does not name the abrupt emergence of new influenza A hemagglutinin or neuraminidase antigens.
extra: Confuses a temporary virion phenotype with a stable major antigenic change.

front: Why is “Lysogenic conversion” wrong here? Public health laboratories identify an influenza A virus whose hemagglutinin profile differs substantially from previous…
back: Lysogenic conversion concerns bacterial characteristics encoded by an integrated phage and does not describe influenza surface-antigen change.
extra: Transfers a bacteriophage concept to an influenza A antigenic event.

front: Bacterial capsules aid immune evasion mainly by interfering with which host process?
back: Phagocyte ingestion of the bacterium
extra: OpenStax: capsules prevent ingestion by phagocytes.

front: Why is “Short-term memory encoding alone” wrong here? Bacterial capsules aid immune evasion mainly by interfering with which host process?
back: Wrong process; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Psych domain — does not match the cited teaching point.

front: Why is “Hepatic cholesterol synthesis alone” wrong here? Bacterial capsules aid immune evasion mainly by interfering with which host process?
back: Wrong process; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Statin domain — does not match the cited teaching point.

front: Why is “Renal sodium reabsorption alone” wrong here? Bacterial capsules aid immune evasion mainly by interfering with which host process?
back: Wrong process; see the cited source passage for detail.
extra: Diuretic domain — does not match the cited teaching point.

front: A newborn has deafness, an eye abnormality, and congenital heart disease. Which of the following diagnoses best unifies this combination?
back: Congenital rubella syndrome
extra: CDC lists deafness, eye abnormalities, and congenital heart disease as features of congenital rubella syndrome. The three findings together provide the recognition pattern.

front: Why is “Congenital cytomegalovirus infection” wrong here? A newborn has deafness, an eye abnormality, and congenital heart disease. Which of the following diagnoses best unifies …
back: The cited passage groups deafness, eye abnormalities, and congenital heart disease under congenital rubella syndrome, not cytomegalovirus infection.
extra: Congenital infection is recognized broadly, but the exact CDC feature cluster is not mapped to its named syndrome.

front: Why is “Congenital toxoplasmosis” wrong here? A newborn has deafness, an eye abnormality, and congenital heart disease. Which of the following diagnoses best unifies …
back: The evidence specifically identifies the combined hearing, eye, and congenital heart findings as features of congenital rubella syndrome.
extra: The congenital presentation is noticed without using all three source-defined features together.

front: Why is “Congenital syphilis” wrong here? A newborn has deafness, an eye abnormality, and congenital heart disease. Which of the following diagnoses best unifies …
back: The source-bounded triad in this stem is attached to congenital rubella syndrome rather than congenital syphilis.
extra: A congenital infection label is selected while the passage's full syndrome pattern is underweighted.

front: Besides myocarditis, which of the following sets of complications is associated with diphtheria?
back: Polyneuropathies, nephritis, and thrombocytopenia
extra: CDC lists myocarditis, polyneuropathies, nephritis, and thrombocytopenia among the complications of diphtheria.

front: Why is “Orchitis, pancreatitis, and aseptic meningitis” wrong here? Besides myocarditis, which of the following sets of complications is associated with diphtheria?
back: Orchitis, pancreatitis, and aseptic meningitis are classic complications of mumps, a paramyxovirus infection, not diphtheria.
extra: Confuses diphtheria with mumps, whose complications include orchitis and pancreatitis.

front: Why is “Cataracts, deafness, and patent ductus arteriosus” wrong here? Besides myocarditis, which of the following sets of complications is associated with diphtheria?
back: Cataracts, deafness, and patent ductus arteriosus make up congenital rubella syndrome after maternal rubella infection in pregnancy.
extra: Confuses diphtheria with congenital rubella syndrome.

front: Why is “Trismus, opisthotonos, and generalized muscle spasms” wrong here? Besides myocarditis, which of the following sets of complications is associated with diphtheria?
back: Trismus, opisthotonos, and muscle spasms are tetanus features: tetanospasmin blocks inhibitory neurotransmitter release in the spinal cord.
extra: Confuses diphtheria with tetanus, another toxin-mediated vaccine-preventable disease.

front: Diphtheria is caused by which of the following?
back: Toxin-producing strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae
extra: CDC attributes diphtheria to toxin-producing strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae, so toxin production, not the species alone, defines the cause.

front: Why is “Nontoxigenic strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae” wrong here? Diphtheria is caused by which of the following?
back: Nontoxigenic C. diphtheriae strains can cause sore throat or invasive infection, but diphtheria itself requires a toxin-producing strain.
extra: Overlooks that only toxin-producing strains cause diphtheria.

front: Why is “Beta-hemolytic strains of Streptococcus pyogenes” wrong here? Diphtheria is caused by which of the following?
back: Beta-hemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes causes pharyngitis and scarlet fever, not diphtheria, though both can present with sore throat.
extra: Confuses diphtheria with streptococcal pharyngitis or scarlet fever.

front: Why is “Encapsulated strains of Haemophilus influenzae” wrong here? Diphtheria is caused by which of the following?
back: Encapsulated Haemophilus influenzae, especially type b, causes meningitis and epiglottitis; it does not produce diphtheria toxin.
extra: Confuses diphtheria with Hib epiglottitis, another cause of airway disease.

front: Which of the following causes both the local and the systemic manifestations of diphtheria?
back: Toxin produced by the infecting bacterium
extra: CDC states that diphtheria toxin, made by toxin-producing strains, causes both the local and the systemic manifestations of diphtheria.

front: Why is “Bloodstream invasion by the infecting bacterium” wrong here? Which of the following causes both the local and the systemic manifestations of diphtheria?
back: In respiratory diphtheria the bacteria stay at the site of infection; distant effects come from absorbed toxin, not bloodstream invasion.
extra: Assumes systemic signs need bacteremia rather than a circulating exotoxin.

front: Why is “Lipoteichoic acid of the infecting bacterium” wrong here? Which of the following causes both the local and the systemic manifestations of diphtheria?
back: Lipoteichoic acid is a gram-positive cell-wall component that triggers inflammation; it does not account for diphtheria's systemic toxicity.
extra: Attributes a toxin-mediated disease to a cell-wall component.

front: Why is “Immune complexes formed against the infecting bacterium” wrong here? Which of the following causes both the local and the systemic manifestations of diphtheria?
back: Immune complexes cause type III disease such as serum sickness or poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, not the manifestations of diphtheria.
extra: Attributes a toxin-mediated disease to immune complex (type III) injury.

front: In microbiology, which of the following defines disease?
back: Damage or impairment of normal structure or function
extra: OpenStax defines disease as any condition in which the normal structure or functions of the body are damaged or impaired.

front: Why is “Presence of microbes living on or in the body” wrong here? In microbiology, which of the following defines disease?
back: Microbes on or in the body may be normal microbiota, colonization or infection; disease requires damage or impairment of structure or function, not mere presence.
extra: Equates the presence of microbes (colonization or infection) with disease.

front: Why is “Presence of antibodies against a specific microbe” wrong here? In microbiology, which of the following defines disease?
back: Antibodies against a microbe show past or present exposure; they do not by themselves mean body structure or function is impaired.
extra: Equates serologic evidence of exposure with disease.

front: Why is “Subjective symptoms reported by the patient” wrong here? In microbiology, which of the following defines disease?
back: Symptoms are subjective indicators a patient notices; disease is defined by damaged structure or function, which can occur with no symptoms.
extra: Equates disease with symptoms, missing asymptomatic structural or functional damage.

front: A 24-year-old develops an abrupt illness with fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, and jaundice. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
back: Acute hepatitis A
extra: The cited passage describes hepatitis A as an abrupt illness with fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, and jaundice.

front: Why is “Viral gastroenteritis” wrong here? A 24-year-old develops an abrupt illness with fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, and ja…
back: The complete pattern, including dark urine and jaundice, is the passage-grounded presentation of acute hepatitis A.
extra: Nausea and abdominal discomfort are over-weighted while dark urine and jaundice are ignored.

front: Why is “Acute appendicitis” wrong here? A 24-year-old develops an abrupt illness with fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, and ja…
back: The cited feature set is broader than isolated abdominal symptoms and specifically describes acute hepatitis A.
extra: Abdominal discomfort and nausea are considered without integrating anorexia, dark urine, and jaundice.

front: Why is “Meningococcal septicemia” wrong here? A 24-year-old develops an abrupt illness with fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, and ja…
back: Fever occurs within the cited hepatitis A cluster of malaise, anorexia, nausea, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, and jaundice.
extra: Abrupt fever is over-weighted while the paired dark urine and jaundice are not incorporated.

front: Hepatitis A virus transmission is classically listed as which route?
back: Fecal-oral spread through ingestion
extra: HAV is typically acquired through ingestion by fecal-oral transmission and then replicates in the liver.

front: Why is “Bite of an infected mosquito” wrong here? Hepatitis A virus transmission is classically listed as which route?
back: Mosquito bites transmit arboviruses such as dengue, West Nile, and yellow fever; hepatitis A is not vector-borne.
extra: Confuses hepatitis A with mosquito-borne viral infections.

front: Why is “Inhalation of airborne droplet nuclei” wrong here? Hepatitis A virus transmission is classically listed as which route?
back: Airborne droplet nuclei spread measles, varicella, and tuberculosis; hepatitis A virus is acquired by ingestion, not inhalation.
extra: Confuses hepatitis A with airborne viruses such as measles.

front: Why is “Direct contact with infected skin lesions” wrong here? Hepatitis A virus transmission is classically listed as which route?
back: Contact with skin lesions spreads agents such as herpes simplex virus or impetigo bacteria, not hepatitis A.
extra: Confuses hepatitis A with pathogens spread by lesion contact.

front: Acute HAV infection is confirmed in the acute or early convalescent phase by which serum finding?
back: IgM anti-HAV in serum
extra: Acute HAV infection is confirmed during the acute or early convalescent phase by the presence of IgM anti-HAV in serum.

front: Why is “IgG anti-HAV in serum” wrong here? Acute HAV infection is confirmed in the acute or early convalescent phase by which serum finding?
back: IgG anti-HAV persists after infection or vaccination, so it marks immunity and cannot by itself confirm acute infection.
extra: Confuses the lasting IgG marker of immunity with the IgM marker of acute infection.

front: Why is “Total anti-HAV in serum” wrong here? Acute HAV infection is confirmed in the acute or early convalescent phase by which serum finding?
back: Total anti-HAV measures IgM and IgG together, so it is positive after past infection or vaccination and cannot by itself confirm acute infection.
extra: Assumes a total antibody test distinguishes acute from past hepatitis A.

front: Why is “Elevated aminotransferases in serum” wrong here? Acute HAV infection is confirmed in the acute or early convalescent phase by which serum finding?
back: Raised aminotransferases show hepatocellular injury from any cause, such as other viral hepatitis or drugs; they do not identify hepatitis A.
extra: Treats a nonspecific marker of liver injury as virus-specific confirmation.

front: People get hepatitis C through which exposure?
back: Contact with blood from an infected person
extra: NIDDK states that people get hepatitis C through contact with an infected person's blood.

front: Why is “Hugging or shaking hands with an infected person” wrong here? People get hepatitis C through which exposure?
back: Hepatitis C virus is not spread by casual contact such as hugging or shaking hands, because no blood is exchanged.
extra: Assumes casual contact can spread a bloodborne virus.

front: Why is “Inhaling droplets from an infected person's cough” wrong here? People get hepatitis C through which exposure?
back: Respiratory droplets spread viruses such as influenza; hepatitis C virus is bloodborne and is not transmitted by coughing.
extra: Confuses a bloodborne virus with respiratory transmission.

front: Why is “Eating food prepared by an infected person” wrong here? People get hepatitis C through which exposure?
back: Food prepared by an infected person spreads fecal-oral viruses such as hepatitis A, not bloodborne hepatitis C.
extra: Confuses hepatitis C with fecal-oral hepatitis A.

front: Among people with acute hepatitis C, what proportion will develop chronic hepatitis C?
back: More than 50%
extra: NIDDK states that more than half of people with acute hepatitis C will develop chronic hepatitis C, in which the virus stays in the body.

front: Why is “Fewer than 1%” wrong here? Among people with acute hepatitis C, what proportion will develop chronic hepatitis C?
back: Chronic infection is the common outcome of hepatitis C, not a rarity; more than half of acute infections persist.
extra: Treats chronic hepatitis C as rare when it is the usual outcome.

front: Why is “About 5%” wrong here? Among people with acute hepatitis C, what proportion will develop chronic hepatitis C?
back: Roughly 5% or less is the rate at which adult-acquired hepatitis B becomes chronic; hepatitis C persists in more than half of acute cases.
extra: Applies the low adult hepatitis B chronicity rate to hepatitis C.

front: Why is “About 20%” wrong here? Among people with acute hepatitis C, what proportion will develop chronic hepatitis C?
back: One in five understates it; most people with acute hepatitis C do not clear the virus, and more than half develop chronic infection.
extra: Underestimates how often acute hepatitis C becomes chronic.

front: Hepatitis C is described as which kind of process affecting the liver?
back: Liver inflammation and damage caused by a viral infection
extra: NIDDK defines hepatitis C as a viral infection that causes liver inflammation and damage.

front: Why is “Liver inflammation and damage caused by autoimmune attack on hepatocytes” wrong here? Hepatitis C is described as which kind of process affecting the liver?
back: Autoimmune hepatitis is inflammation from an immune attack on the body's own hepatocytes; hepatitis C is caused by a virus.
extra: Confuses viral hepatitis with autoimmune hepatitis.

front: Why is “Liver inflammation and damage caused by chronic heavy alcohol use” wrong here? Hepatitis C is described as which kind of process affecting the liver?
back: Alcoholic hepatitis results from heavy alcohol use; hepatitis C is an infection with a virus, not a toxic effect of ethanol.
extra: Confuses viral hepatitis with alcoholic hepatitis.

front: Why is “Liver inflammation and damage caused by a toxic drug reaction” wrong here? Hepatitis C is described as which kind of process affecting the liver?
back: Drug-induced hepatitis, such as from acetaminophen or isoniazid, is a toxic reaction; hepatitis C is a viral infection.
extra: Confuses viral hepatitis with drug-induced liver injury.

front: Encapsulated Haemophilus influenzae strains are classified into how many polysaccharide capsule serotypes?
back: Six serotypes, a through f
extra: CDC: H. influenzae has six different polysaccharide capsule serotypes (a-f); type b caused 95% of invasive disease before vaccines.

front: Why is “Two serotypes, a and b” wrong here? Encapsulated Haemophilus influenzae strains are classified into how many polysaccharide capsule serotypes?
back: H. influenzae splits into encapsulated (typeable) and nontypeable strains, but the capsule itself comes in six serotypes, a through f.
extra: Confuses the typeable-versus-nontypeable split with the number of capsular serotypes.

front: Why is “Four serotypes, a through d” wrong here? Encapsulated Haemophilus influenzae strains are classified into how many polysaccharide capsule serotypes?
back: Four matches no H. influenzae classification; the polysaccharide capsule has six serotypes, designated a through f.
extra: Undercounts the capsular serotypes of H. influenzae.

front: Why is “Five serotypes, a through e” wrong here? Encapsulated Haemophilus influenzae strains are classified into how many polysaccharide capsule serotypes?
back: Five omits one type; the six capsular serotypes run a through f, and type b caused most invasive disease before vaccination.
extra: Undercounts the serotypes by one; there are six, a through f.

front: In the prevaccine era, meningitis accounted for about what share of invasive Hib disease cases?
back: About 50% to 65% of cases
extra: CDC reports that in the prevaccine era meningitis accounted for 50% to 65% of invasive Hib cases, with a fatality ratio of 3% to 6%.

front: Why is “About 3% to 6% of cases” wrong here? In the prevaccine era, meningitis accounted for about what share of invasive Hib disease cases?
back: Three to six percent was the fatality ratio of Hib meningitis, not the share of invasive cases that were meningitis.
extra: Confuses the proportion of cases with the fatality ratio of 3% to 6%.

front: Why is “About 10% to 15% of cases” wrong here? In the prevaccine era, meningitis accounted for about what share of invasive Hib disease cases?
back: Ten to fifteen percent understates meningitis, which made up more than half of invasive Hib cases before vaccination.
extra: Underestimates how dominant meningitis was among invasive Hib cases.

front: Why is “About 25% to 35% of cases” wrong here? In the prevaccine era, meningitis accounted for about what share of invasive Hib disease cases?
back: A quarter to a third understates it; meningitis accounted for 50% to 65% of invasive Hib disease before vaccination.
extra: Underestimates meningitis, which accounted for over half of invasive Hib cases.

front: High-risk HPV types such as 16 and 18 can cause which of the following?
back: Cervical cell abnormalities that are precursors to cancer
extra: CDC: high-risk HPV types, including 16 and 18, cause cervical cell abnormalities that are precursors to cancer, and anogenital cancers.

front: Why is “Hepatocellular carcinoma following chronic liver infection” wrong here? High-risk HPV types such as 16 and 18 can cause which of the following?
back: Hepatocellular carcinoma after chronic liver infection is linked to hepatitis B and C viruses, not HPV.
extra: Confuses HPV with the hepatitis viruses that cause liver cancer.

front: Why is “Kaposi sarcoma in immunosuppressed patients” wrong here? High-risk HPV types such as 16 and 18 can cause which of the following?
back: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by human herpesvirus 8, mainly in people with HIV or other immunosuppression.
extra: Confuses HPV with HHV-8, the cause of Kaposi sarcoma.

front: Why is “Adult T-cell leukemia after retroviral infection” wrong here? High-risk HPV types such as 16 and 18 can cause which of the following?
back: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma follows infection with HTLV-1, a retrovirus that infects CD4 T cells.
extra: Confuses HPV with HTLV-1, an oncogenic retrovirus.

front: More than 90% of anogenital warts are caused by which low-risk HPV types?
back: HPV types 6 or 11
extra: CDC: more than 90% of cases of anogenital warts are caused by low-risk HPV types 6 or 11.

front: Why is “HPV types 1 or 2” wrong here? More than 90% of anogenital warts are caused by which low-risk HPV types?
back: HPV types 1 and 2 are cutaneous types that cause plantar and common warts on the hands and feet, not most anogenital warts.
extra: Confuses cutaneous wart types with anogenital wart types.

front: Why is “HPV types 16 or 18” wrong here? More than 90% of anogenital warts are caused by which low-risk HPV types?
back: HPV types 16 and 18 are high-risk oncogenic types linked to cervical and anogenital cancers rather than to most genital warts.
extra: Swaps the high-risk oncogenic types for the low-risk wart types.

front: Why is “HPV types 31 or 33” wrong here? More than 90% of anogenital warts are caused by which low-risk HPV types?
back: HPV types 31 and 33 are additional high-risk types associated with cervical precancer and cancer, not the typical genital wart.
extra: Assumes any common genital HPV genotype causes warts, ignoring risk class.

front:
A 34-year-old clinician recovers from influenza. Four winters later, immune testing shows poor recognition of a newly circulating strain. Surveillance indicates that the strain changed gradually across successive seasons rather than appearing as a wholly new subtype in one abrupt event.

Which of the following molecular findings most directly explains the reduced recognition of the newer strain?
back: Accumulation of point changes that alter surface antigens
extra: Antigenic drift is the accumulation of small viral-gene mutations that progressively change HA and NA.

front: Why is “Stable integration of viral RNA into the clinician’s genome” wrong here? A 34-year-old clinician recovers from influenza. Four winters later, immune testing shows poor recognition of a newly ci…

front: Why is “Spastic paralysis” wrong here? Paralytic poliomyelitis, which follows fewer than 1% of childhood poliovirus infections, produces which motor finding?

front: Why is “Cogwheel rigidity” wrong here? Paralytic poliomyelitis, which follows fewer than 1% of childhood poliovirus infections, produces which motor finding?

front: Why is “Intention tremor” wrong here? Paralytic poliomyelitis, which follows fewer than 1% of childhood poliovirus infections, produces which motor finding?

front: Why is “Blood transfusion and needle sharing” wrong here? Rotavirus spread is described as fecal-oral plus which other modes?

front: Why is “Sexual contact and vertical transmission” wrong here? Rotavirus spread is described as fecal-oral plus which other modes?

front: In the prevaccine era, rotavirus was described as the most common cause of which pediatric syndrome?

front: Why is “Acute bronchiolitis” wrong here? In the prevaccine era, rotavirus was described as the most common cause of which pediatric syndrome?

front: Why is “Hemolytic uremic syndrome” wrong here? In the prevaccine era, rotavirus was described as the most common cause of which pediatric syndrome?

extra: Links any severe pediatric diarrhea to HUS, which classically follows Shiga toxin-producing E. coli.

front: Why is “Aseptic meningitis” wrong here? In the prevaccine era, rotavirus was described as the most common cause of which pediatric syndrome?
back: Aseptic meningitis in children is most often caused by non-polio enteroviruses; rotavirus is an enteric diarrheal pathogen.
extra: Confuses rotavirus with the enteroviruses, which are acquired through the gut but cause aseptic meningitis.

front: The main objective of rubella vaccination programs is to prevent which outcome?

front: Why is “Rubella encephalitis in young children” wrong here? The main objective of rubella vaccination programs is to prevent which outcome?

front: Why is “Rubella arthritis in adult women” wrong here? The main objective of rubella vaccination programs is to prevent which outcome?

front: Why is “Rubella rash illness in schoolchildren” wrong here? The main objective of rubella vaccination programs is to prevent which outcome?

front: Congenital rubella syndrome includes deafness together with which other features?

front: Why is “Limb hypoplasia and cicatricial skin scars” wrong here? Congenital rubella syndrome includes deafness together with which other features?

front: Which named toxin causes the clinical manifestations of tetanus?
back: Tetanospasmin, a neurotoxin
extra: CDC states that tetanospasmin is a neurotoxin and is the cause of the clinical manifestations of tetanus.

front: Why is “Tetanolysin, a hemolysin” wrong here? Which named toxin causes the clinical manifestations of tetanus?
back: Tetanolysin is the second C. tetani exotoxin, a hemolysin of uncertain role; it does not produce the rigidity and spasms of tetanus.
extra: Picks the other C. tetani exotoxin, assuming both toxins drive the disease.

front: Why is “Botulinum toxin, a neurotoxin” wrong here? Which named toxin causes the clinical manifestations of tetanus?
back: Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, causing the flaccid paralysis of botulism rather than spasms.
extra: Confuses the two clostridial neurotoxins, which have opposite clinical effects.

front: Why is “Diphtheria toxin, an ADP-ribosylating exotoxin” wrong here? Which named toxin causes the clinical manifestations of tetanus?
back: Diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2 to halt protein synthesis, causing pseudomembrane and myocarditis, not tetanus.
extra: Groups tetanus with diphtheria because both are toxin-mediated diseases prevented by the same vaccines.

front:
A patient develops muscle stiffness that begins in the jaw and neck, then becomes generalized rigidity with convulsive spasms of skeletal muscles.

An exotoxin produced by which bacterium causes this disease?
back: Clostridium tetani
extra: CDC states tetanus is caused by an exotoxin of Clostridium tetani, with stiffness that begins in the jaw (lockjaw) and neck and then becomes generalized.

front: Why is “Corynebacterium diphtheriae” wrong here? A patient develops muscle stiffness that begins in the jaw and neck, then becomes generalized rigidity with convulsive s…
back: Corynebacterium diphtheriae exotoxin inhibits protein synthesis, causing pharyngeal pseudomembrane, myocarditis and neuropathy, not generalized rigidity.
extra: Groups the toxin-mediated diseases prevented by DTaP together and picks the wrong organism.

front: Why is “Clostridium botulinum” wrong here? A patient develops muscle stiffness that begins in the jaw and neck, then becomes generalized rigidity with convulsive s…
back: Clostridium botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release, producing descending flaccid paralysis, the opposite of rigidity and spasms.
extra: Confuses the two clostridial neurotoxin diseases; botulism is flaccid, tetanus is rigid.

front: Why is “Clostridium perfringens” wrong here? A patient develops muscle stiffness that begins in the jaw and neck, then becomes generalized rigidity with convulsive s…
back: Clostridium perfringens toxins cause gas gangrene and food poisoning; they do not produce lockjaw or generalized muscle spasms.
extra: Assumes any wound-associated Clostridium species can cause generalized rigidity.

front: Which of the following diagnoses is characterized by jaw and neck stiffness followed by rigidity and convulsive spasms of skeletal muscles?
back: Generalized tetanus
extra: The CDC passage characterizes tetanus by stiffness beginning in the jaw and neck, then becoming generalized with convulsive skeletal-muscle spasms.

front: Why is “Respiratory diphtheria” wrong here? Which of the following diagnoses is characterized by jaw and neck stiffness followed by rigidity and convulsive spasms o…
back: The jaw-first stiffness, generalized rigidity, and convulsive muscle spasms are the tetanus pattern described in the cited passage.
extra: Another toxin-mediated bacterial illness is selected without matching the cited neuromuscular pattern.

front: Why is “Paroxysmal pertussis” wrong here? Which of the following diagnoses is characterized by jaw and neck stiffness followed by rigidity and convulsive spasms o…
back: The cited passage identifies this progression of muscle stiffness and spasms as tetanus.
extra: A bacterial syndrome with episodic symptoms is chosen, but the source's defining rigidity pattern is missed.

front: Why is “Paralytic poliomyelitis” wrong here? Which of the following diagnoses is characterized by jaw and neck stiffness followed by rigidity and convulsive spasms o…
back: The source directly characterizes tetanus by lockjaw, neck stiffness, generalized rigidity, and convulsive skeletal-muscle spasms.
extra: A neurologic infectious diagnosis is selected without following the jaw-to-generalized-rigidity sequence.

front: A bacterial capsular polysaccharide undergoes covalent linkage in a conjugate vaccine. Which of the following immune changes is the main purpose of this linkage?
back: Conversion to a T-cell-dependent immune response
extra: The FDA passage states that covalent linkage makes an otherwise T-cell-independent polysaccharide antigen T-cell dependent, inducing long-term immunity.

front: Why is “Delivery of preformed pathogen-specific serum antibody” wrong here? A bacterial capsular polysaccharide undergoes covalent linkage in a conjugate vaccine. Which of the following immune cha…
back: Covalent linkage changes how the polysaccharide antigen elicits immunity; the cited mechanism is not delivery of preformed serum antibody.
extra: Confuses antigen conjugation with passive delivery of an already formed antibody.

front: Why is “Preservation of a T-cell-independent immune response” wrong here? A bacterial capsular polysaccharide undergoes covalent linkage in a conjugate vaccine. Which of the following immune cha…
back: The source describes the opposite change: covalent linkage converts the polysaccharide antigen from T-cell independent to T-cell dependent.
extra: Keeps the original response type instead of recognizing the conversion produced by conjugation.

front: Why is “Suppression of polysaccharide recognition by lymphocytes” wrong here? A bacterial capsular polysaccharide undergoes covalent linkage in a conjugate vaccine. Which of the following immune cha…
back: The FDA passage describes conversion to a durable T-cell-dependent response, not suppression of recognition of the polysaccharide antigen.
extra: Treats covalent linkage as a way to mask the antigen rather than change the immune response.

front: A vaccine contains an inactivated organism. Which of the following immune-response profiles is most characteristic of this vaccine class?
back: Mostly antibody production with little cellular immunity
extra: The cited passage describes the inactivated-vaccine response as mostly antibody production with little or no cellular immunity.

front: Why is “Sustained organism replication with persistent antigen production” wrong here? A vaccine contains an inactivated organism. Which of the following immune-response profiles is most characteristic of th…
back: An inactivated preparation does not match a profile based on sustained organism replication; its cited adaptive response is predominantly antibody production.
extra: Assigns a replicating-organism mechanism to a preparation defined here as inactivated.

front: Why is “Mostly cellular immunity with little antibody production” wrong here? A vaccine contains an inactivated organism. Which of the following immune-response profiles is most characteristic of th…
back: The CDC passage places antibody production, rather than cellular immunity, at the center of the inactivated-vaccine response.
extra: Reverses the relative humoral and cellular emphasis described for an inactivated vaccine.

front: Why is “Immediate protection from transferred donor antibodies” wrong here? A vaccine contains an inactivated organism. Which of the following immune-response profiles is most characteristic of th…
back: The passage describes the recipient producing a predominantly antibody response to inactivated antigen; it does not describe transferred donor antibody.
extra: Confuses an antigen-containing vaccine with direct transfer of an existing antibody pool.

front: A live attenuated vaccine is being engineered for safer use. Which of the following properties must the preparation retain in the vaccinated person to generate its intended immune response?
back: Replication within the recipient after administration
extra: The CDC passage states that a live attenuated vaccine must replicate in the vaccinated person to produce an immune response. That capacity therefore has to remain intact.

front: Why is “Polysaccharide signaling without T-cell participation” wrong here? A live attenuated vaccine is being engineered for safer use. Which of the following properties must the preparation reta…
back: The CDC passage grounds the response of this vaccine class in replication of the attenuated organism, not in an isolated polysaccharide signal.
extra: Imports a nonliving polysaccharide-response framework into a live attenuated vaccine question.

front: Why is “Transfer of preformed pathogen-specific antibody” wrong here? A live attenuated vaccine is being engineered for safer use. Which of the following properties must the preparation reta…
back: The cited requirement is replication of the attenuated organism in the recipient, not transfer of a ready-made antibody preparation.
extra: Confuses active vaccination with administration of an already formed immune product.

front: Why is “Placental transport of maternal antibody” wrong here? A live attenuated vaccine is being engineered for safer use. Which of the following properties must the preparation reta…
back: Placental transfer does not explain why the administered live attenuated preparation itself requires replication in the vaccinated person.
extra: Substitutes maternal antibody transfer for the mechanism of a vaccine given directly to the recipient.

front: Varicella-zoster virus entry is classically described via which portals?
back: Respiratory tract and conjunctiva
extra: CDC states VZV enters through the respiratory tract and conjunctiva, then replicates in the nasopharynx and regional lymph nodes before viremia.

front: Why is “Intestinal mucosa and Peyer patches” wrong here? Varicella-zoster virus entry is classically described via which portals?
back: Intestinal mucosa and Peyer patches are entry sites for enteric pathogens such as poliovirus and Salmonella Typhi, not varicella-zoster virus.
extra: Assumes VZV, like the enteroviruses, enters through the gut.

front: Why is “Urethral and cervical mucosa” wrong here? Varicella-zoster virus entry is classically described via which portals?
back: Urethral and cervical mucosa are portals for sexually transmitted pathogens such as HSV-2 and gonorrhea; VZV is not acquired this way.
extra: Confuses VZV with genital herpes simplex virus, a related herpesvirus acquired through sexual contact.

front: Why is “Bloodstream and injection sites” wrong here? Varicella-zoster virus entry is classically described via which portals?
back: Direct blood entry fits bloodborne viruses such as hepatitis B and HIV; VZV reaches the blood only after replicating at its mucosal entry sites.
extra: Mistakes the viremia of varicella for evidence that the virus enters directly through blood.

front: After primary varicella, latent VZV infection later results in which clinical syndrome?
back: Herpes zoster (shingles)
extra: CDC states that latent VZV infection results in herpes zoster (shingles); VZV is a DNA virus in the herpesvirus group.

front: Why is “Herpes labialis (cold sores)” wrong here? After primary varicella, latent VZV infection later results in which clinical syndrome?
back: Herpes labialis is reactivation of latent herpes simplex virus type 1 in the trigeminal ganglion, not varicella-zoster virus.
extra: Confuses latent VZV with latent HSV-1, since both herpesviruses persist in sensory ganglia.

front: Why is “Infectious mononucleosis” wrong here? After primary varicella, latent VZV infection later results in which clinical syndrome?
back: Infectious mononucleosis is typically a primary Epstein-Barr virus infection, not a reactivation of latent VZV.
extra: Assumes every herpesvirus syndrome, including Epstein-Barr virus mononucleosis, comes from VZV.

front: Why is “Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis” wrong here? After primary varicella, latent VZV infection later results in which clinical syndrome?
back: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is a late, fatal complication of persistent measles virus infection in the brain.
extra: Confuses the late sequel of measles with the late sequel of chickenpox.

front: What is the most common debilitating complication of shingles?
back: Postherpetic neuralgia
extra: CDC names postherpetic neuralgia, pain that persists where the rash was after the lesions resolve, as the most common and debilitating zoster complication.

front: Why is “Bacterial superinfection of skin lesions” wrong here? What is the most common debilitating complication of shingles?
back: Staphylococcal or streptococcal superinfection can complicate zoster lesions, but it is much less common than persistent pain.
extra: Assumes infection of the visible blisters, rather than nerve pain, is the main complication.

front: Why is “Ramsay Hunt syndrome” wrong here? What is the most common debilitating complication of shingles?
back: Ramsay Hunt syndrome is facial palsy with ear vesicles from geniculate ganglion reactivation; it is a recognized but uncommon zoster complication.
extra: Overweights a memorable eponymous syndrome over the common chronic pain complication.

front: Why is “VZV vasculopathy with stroke” wrong here? What is the most common debilitating complication of shingles?
back: VZV vasculopathy can cause stroke after zoster, especially ophthalmic zoster, but it is rare compared with postherpetic neuralgia.
extra: Overweights a rare but dramatic neurologic complication over the common one.

front: Shingles is caused by which viral process?
back: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus
extra: CDC states herpes zoster (shingles) is caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus that has stayed latent since the earlier infection.

front: Why is “Reactivation of herpes simplex virus” wrong here? Shingles is caused by which viral process?
back: Herpes simplex reactivation causes recurrent oral or genital herpes; it can mimic a dermatomal rash but is not shingles.
extra: Knows shingles is a herpesvirus reactivation but picks the wrong herpesvirus.

front: Why is “Primary infection with varicella-zoster virus” wrong here? Shingles is caused by which viral process?
back: Primary varicella-zoster infection causes chickenpox (varicella); shingles arises later, when the dormant virus reactivates.
extra: Confuses primary VZV infection (chickenpox) with its later reactivation (shingles).

front: Why is “Reactivation of Epstein-Barr virus” wrong here? Shingles is caused by which viral process?
back: Epstein-Barr virus causes infectious mononucleosis and is linked to several lymphomas; its reactivation does not cause shingles.
extra: Assumes any latent herpesvirus that reactivates can produce shingles.

front:
An unvaccinated 63-year-old man develops trismus and painful generalized muscle spasms several days after a contaminated puncture wound. Light touch triggers another sustained contraction.

Which of the following toxin effects most directly produces this motor pattern?
back: Reduced release of inhibitory neurotransmitters in motor pathways
extra: The toxin prevents inhibitory neural signals from being released normally. Removing this restraint permits excessive motor activity and stimulus-triggered spasms.

front: Why is “Increased release of inhibitory neurotransmitters in motor pathways” wrong here? An unvaccinated 63-year-old man develops trismus and painful generalized muscle spasms several days after a contaminated…
back: Increasing inhibition would suppress motor activity rather than produce the marked rigidity and spasms in this patient.
extra: Reverses the direction of the toxin's effect on inhibitory signaling.

front: Why is “Reduced acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction” wrong here? An unvaccinated 63-year-old man develops trismus and painful generalized muscle spasms several days after a contaminated…
back: Failure of acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction would impair contraction, which does not fit this patient's hyperactive motor state.
extra: Confuses tetanus with a disorder causing flaccid neuromuscular weakness.

front: Why is “Destruction of skeletal muscle contractile proteins” wrong here? An unvaccinated 63-year-old man develops trismus and painful generalized muscle spasms several days after a contaminated…
back: Direct loss of contractile proteins would cause weakness and muscle damage rather than disinhibited, stimulus-sensitive contraction.
extra: Attributes the syndrome to direct structural muscle injury.

front:
An unvaccinated 45-year-old farmer is brought to the emergency department with trismus, neck stiffness, and generalized painful spasms triggered by minor stimuli. He recalls a soil-contaminated puncture wound to his foot sustained while working in a barn ten days ago. Anaerobic conditions in the deep wound allowed Clostridium tetani spores to germinate and release tetanospasmin.

Which of the following synaptic effects of the toxin most directly produces the sustained muscle spasms?
back: Blockade of inhibitory neurotransmitter release onto motor neurons
extra: Tetanospasmin interferes with release of inhibitory neurotransmitters, blocking inhibitor impulses so motor neurons fire unchecked and skeletal muscles spasm.

front: Why is “Blockade of acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction” wrong here? An unvaccinated 45-year-old farmer is brought to the emergency department with trismus, neck stiffness, and generalized …
back: Botulinum toxin blocks ACh release and causes flaccid paralysis; tetanospasmin blocks inhibitory interneuron transmission, causing rigidity and spasms.
extra: Botulinum-like NMJ blockade is being confused with tetanus toxin action.

front: Why is “Irreversible activation of nicotinic receptors on skeletal muscle” wrong here? An unvaccinated 45-year-old farmer is brought to the emergency department with trismus, neck stiffness, and generalized …
back: Tetanospasmin acts inside inhibitory neurons to block transmitter release; it does not agonize muscle nicotinic receptors.
extra: A postsynaptic agonist effect is being invented for an intracellular toxin.

front: Why is “Destruction of dorsal-root sensory ganglia by spore germination” wrong here? An unvaccinated 45-year-old farmer is brought to the emergency department with trismus, neck stiffness, and generalized …
back: Spores germinate in the anaerobic wound; the clinical spasms come from tetanospasmin blocking inhibitory impulses to motor neurons.
extra: Sensory ganglion damage is being substituted for central disinhibition.

front:
A 52-year-old gardener sustains a deep puncture wound contaminated with soil. The narrow wound contains devitalized tissue and receives little blood flow.

Which of the following local features most strongly favors conversion of dormant tetanus spores into metabolically active bacteria?
back: Low oxygen tension within damaged tissue
extra: Poor perfusion and devitalized tissue create a low-oxygen niche. That anaerobic setting permits tetanus spores deposited in the wound to germinate.

front: Why is “High oxygen tension within intact tissue” wrong here? A 52-year-old gardener sustains a deep puncture wound contaminated with soil. The narrow wound contains devitalized tiss…
back: Well-oxygenated intact tissue does not provide the low-oxygen setting that favors tetanus spore germination.
extra: Assumes abundant oxygen promotes germination of an anaerobic organism.

front: Why is “Continuous ultraviolet exposure of the wound” wrong here? A 52-year-old gardener sustains a deep puncture wound contaminated with soil. The narrow wound contains devitalized tiss…
back: Ultraviolet exposure is not the local physiologic condition that permits spores in a deep wound to become active bacteria.
extra: Treats environmental light exposure as the key wound condition.

front: Why is “Rapid clearance of all devitalized tissue” wrong here? A 52-year-old gardener sustains a deep puncture wound contaminated with soil. The narrow wound contains devitalized tiss…
back: Clearing devitalized material improves the wound environment and would reduce, rather than promote, the conditions favorable to germination.
extra: Selects removal of the very tissue conditions that support bacterial growth.

front:
Developing skeletal tissue initially contains a hyaline cartilage model. Follow-up sections show removal of that template and deposition of bone in its place.

Which of the following interpretations best describes the process observed?
back: Endochondral ossification with replacement of a cartilage template
extra: Endochondral ossification replaces a pre-existing hyaline cartilage model with bone. Removal of the template followed by bone deposition is the defining sequence in this preparation.

front: Why is “Intramembranous ossification through a required cartilage template” wrong here? Developing skeletal tissue initially contains a hyaline cartilage model. Follow-up sections show removal of that templat…
back: Intramembranous ossification forms bone directly from mesenchymal tissue. A required hyaline cartilage template instead identifies the endochondral pathway described by these sequential observations.
extra: Assigns a required cartilage template to intramembranous ossification.

front: Why is “Endochondral ossification with direct conversion of cartilage matrix” wrong here? Developing skeletal tissue initially contains a hyaline cartilage model. Follow-up sections show removal of that templat…
back: The cartilage model provides a template that is removed and replaced by bone. It is not simply converted into bone matrix, as the separate removal and deposition observations demonstrate.
extra: Mistakes cartilage removal and replacement for direct matrix conversion.

front: Why is “Intramembranous ossification through osteoclast matrix deposition” wrong here? Developing skeletal tissue initially contains a hyaline cartilage model. Follow-up sections show removal of that templat…
back: Osteoclasts resorb bone rather than deposit its matrix. In addition, the observed cartilage template distinguishes this developmental process from direct intramembranous formation of bone.
extra: Assigns matrix deposition to osteoclasts and ignores the cartilage template.

front:
A volunteer changes from a short maximal effort to prolonged activity at a sustainable intensity. Oxygen delivery remains adequate during the prolonged phase.

Which of the following changes in the relative contribution of energy sources is most consistent with maintaining ATP supply?
back: Aerobic contribution rises while initial-store contribution falls
extra: Aerobic metabolism sustains ATP production when oxygen is available. Its relative contribution grows as the initial rapid energy stores cannot sustain the activity alone.

front: Why is “Creatine phosphate contribution rises while aerobic contribution falls” wrong here? A volunteer changes from a short maximal effort to prolonged activity at a sustainable intensity. Oxygen delivery remain…
back: Creatine phosphate supplies the early period of contraction. Its finite initial reserve cannot take over from aerobic regeneration during sustained activity.
extra: Assumes finite creatine phosphate reserves take over during sustained activity.

front: Why is “Anaerobic glycolysis contribution rises while aerobic contribution falls” wrong here? A volunteer changes from a short maximal effort to prolonged activity at a sustainable intensity. Oxygen delivery remain…
back: Brief intense activity can rely heavily on anaerobic production. Prolonged sustainable work with adequate oxygen instead favors a larger aerobic contribution.
extra: Extends a brief anaerobic energy pattern to prolonged oxygen-supported work.

front: Why is “Stored ATP contribution rises while metabolic regeneration falls” wrong here? A volunteer changes from a short maximal effort to prolonged activity at a sustainable intensity. Oxygen delivery remain…
back: Stored ATP requires replenishment during continuing contraction. Sustained activity cannot rely increasingly on the initial pool while regeneration declines.
extra: Treats stored ATP as a growing supply that needs progressively less replenishment.

front:
A cell is observed depositing collagen-rich bone matrix and contributing to mineral deposition. Later, it becomes surrounded by that matrix and occupies a mature position within bone.

Which of the following sequences of cell identities best explains these observations?
back: Osteoblast followed by osteocyte
extra: Osteoblasts produce bone matrix and contribute to mineral deposition. When an osteoblast becomes enclosed in that matrix, it becomes an osteocyte, matching the observed sequence.

front: Why is “Osteoclast followed by osteoblast” wrong here? A cell is observed depositing collagen-rich bone matrix and contributing to mineral deposition. Later, it becomes surrou…
back: Osteoclasts resorb bone rather than first depositing its collagen-rich matrix. The observed matrix-forming cell is an osteoblast, which becomes an osteocyte when enclosed by the matrix.
extra: Assigns initial matrix formation to bone-resorbing osteoclasts.

front: Why is “Osteocyte followed by osteoclast” wrong here? A cell is observed depositing collagen-rich bone matrix and contributing to mineral deposition. Later, it becomes surrou…
back: The cell begins with the matrix-forming role of an osteoblast. Its later enclosure corresponds to an osteocyte, not conversion into the bone-resorbing osteoclast lineage.
extra: Misidentifies both the matrix-forming cell and its later enclosed state.

front: Why is “Macrophage followed by osteocyte” wrong here? A cell is observed depositing collagen-rich bone matrix and contributing to mineral deposition. Later, it becomes surrou…
back: Macrophage-lineage cells give rise to osteoclasts involved in bone resorption. They do not explain the specified sequence of matrix deposition followed by enclosure as a mature bone cell.
extra: Assigns the osteoblast-to-osteocyte sequence to the macrophage lineage.

front:
Two muscle fiber populations are studied. Population X contracts slowly and relies heavily on aerobic ATP production. Population Y produces rapid, powerful contractions using substantial anaerobic glycolysis.

During a brief reduction in oxygen delivery, which of the following predictions best follows from their different energy pathways?
back: Y briefly maintains anaerobic ATP production but fatigues quickly
extra: Fast glycolytic fibers can obtain ATP through anaerobic glycolysis for brief activity. That route is compatible with low oxygen but with rapid fatigue.

front: Why is “Y loses anaerobic ATP production because it requires oxygen” wrong here? Two muscle fiber populations are studied. Population X contracts slowly and relies heavily on aerobic ATP production. Po…
back: Anaerobic glycolysis can produce ATP without oxygen. This option assigns the oxygen dependence of aerobic metabolism to the wrong pathway.
extra: Incorrectly makes anaerobic glycolysis dependent on oxygen.

front: Why is “X increases aerobic ATP production as oxygen delivery falls” wrong here? Two muscle fiber populations are studied. Population X contracts slowly and relies heavily on aerobic ATP production. Po…
back: Aerobic production uses oxygen. Reduced delivery does not directly increase the pathway on which the slow oxidative population relies.
extra: Assumes reduced oxygen directly increases oxygen-dependent ATP production.

front: Why is “X sustains aerobic ATP production independently of oxygen delivery” wrong here? Two muscle fiber populations are studied. Population X contracts slowly and relies heavily on aerobic ATP production. Po…
back: The oxidative pathway uses oxygen; its ATP production is not independent of oxygen availability. That distinguishes it from anaerobic glycolysis.
extra: Treats oxidative ATP production as independent of oxygen availability.

front:
In an isolated muscle preparation, myosin heads have hydrolyzed ATP but retain inorganic phosphate. An experimental reagent prevents phosphate release without preventing contact with actin.

Which of the following transitions in the cross-bridge cycle is most directly impaired?
back: Strengthening of actin attachment followed by the power stroke
extra: Phosphate release strengthens the actin–myosin attachment and precedes the power stroke. Preventing that release blocks this transition while allowing initial contact.

front: Why is “Hydrolysis of newly bound ATP into ADP and phosphate” wrong here? In an isolated muscle preparation, myosin heads have hydrolyzed ATP but retain inorganic phosphate. An experimental reag…
back: The stem establishes that ATP has already been hydrolyzed. The reagent blocks release of retained phosphate at a later step.
extra: Confuses completed ATP hydrolysis with subsequent phosphate release.

front: Why is “Binding of fresh ATP to a post-stroke myosin head” wrong here? In an isolated muscle preparation, myosin heads have hydrolyzed ATP but retain inorganic phosphate. An experimental reag…
back: The selective block concerns phosphate release before the force-generating stroke. It does not directly prevent the subsequent binding of another ATP molecule.
extra: Misplaces a pre-stroke phosphate block at later binding of fresh ATP.

front: Why is “Detachment of myosin from actin after fresh ATP binding” wrong here? In an isolated muscle preparation, myosin heads have hydrolyzed ATP but retain inorganic phosphate. An experimental reag…
back: Fresh ATP binding promotes detachment. That is a different step from phosphate release, which strengthens attachment and precedes the stroke.
extra: Confuses phosphate-dependent attachment strengthening with ATP-dependent detachment.

front:
A bone biopsy from a 45-year-old man shows cells trapped within small spaces in the calcified matrix, connected to one another by tiny channels.

These cells, the most common cell type in mature bone, are which of the following?
back: Osteocytes
extra: Osteocytes are the primary cells of mature bone and its most common type; each sits in a lacuna and exchanges nutrients and signals through long cytoplasmic processes in canaliculi.

front: Why is “Osteoblasts” wrong here? A bone biopsy from a 45-year-old man shows cells trapped within small spaces in the calcified matrix, connected to one a…
back: Osteoblasts synthesize and secrete collagen matrix and calcium salts at growing surfaces; once trapped in calcified matrix they CHANGE INTO osteocytes.
extra: The bone-forming cell is being cast as the trapped mature cell.

front: Why is “Osteogenic cells” wrong here? A bone biopsy from a 45-year-old man shows cells trapped within small spaces in the calcified matrix, connected to one a…
back: Osteogenic cells are undifferentiated, mitotically active precursors in the periosteum and endosteum that develop into osteoblasts; they are not embedded in lacunae.
extra: The stem-cell precursor is being cast as the mature matrix cell.

front: Why is “Osteoclasts” wrong here? A bone biopsy from a 45-year-old man shows cells trapped within small spaces in the calcified matrix, connected to one a…
back: Osteoclasts develop from monocytes and macrophages and resorb bone at its surfaces; they do not sit trapped within the matrix in lacunae.
extra: The resorbing cell is being cast as the matrix-embedded cell.

front:
A 68-year-old man has bone pain and an enlarging, deforming skull, and studies show markedly elevated osteoclast activity.

His weak, fracture-prone bones result from a remodeling imbalance in which his osteoclasts do which of the following?
back: Resorb more bone than the osteoblasts lay down
extra: This is Paget's disease: a remodeling disorder beginning with overactive osteoclasts, so more bone is resorbed than laid down; the compensating osteoblasts lay down weak, brittle bone prone to fracture.

front: Why is “Deposit excess collagen matrix on the periosteum” wrong here? A 68-year-old man has bone pain and an enlarging, deforming skull, and studies show markedly elevated osteoclast activit…
back: Osteoclasts resorb bone; deposition of collagen matrix is the work of osteoblasts at the periosteum and endosteum.
extra: A formative action is being assigned to osteoclasts.

front: Why is “Trap osteoblasts inside the calcified matrix” wrong here? A 68-year-old man has bone pain and an enlarging, deforming skull, and studies show markedly elevated osteoclast activit…
back: Osteoblasts trap THEMSELVES as the matrix they secrete calcifies, becoming osteocytes; osteoclasts play no part in that transition.
extra: The osteocyte transition is being attributed to osteoclasts.

front: Why is “Convert compact bone into hyaline cartilage” wrong here? A 68-year-old man has bone pain and an enlarging, deforming skull, and studies show markedly elevated osteoclast activit…
back: Osteoclasts break down bone matrix; they do not convert bone into any other tissue.
extra: Resorption is being cast as a tissue conversion.

front:
In an experiment, an isolated muscle fiber from a 26-year-old volunteer is exposed to a drug that prevents calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Stimulation now fails to produce contraction because calcium normally does which of the following?
back: Binds troponin so tropomyosin shifts off the actin sites
extra: Calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum activates the troponin-tropomyosin complex so that tropomyosin shifts away from actin's myosin-binding sites, allowing cross-bridges to form.

front: Why is “Binds actin so myosin heads detach from the filament” wrong here? In an experiment, an isolated muscle fiber from a 26-year-old volunteer is exposed to a drug that prevents calcium relea…
back: Detachment requires ATP binding to the myosin head; calcium's role is upstream, exposing the binding sites through troponin and tropomyosin.
extra: Calcium is being cast as the cross-bridge release factor.
