front: Why is “Opens sodium channels along the sarcolemma” wrong here? In an experiment, an isolated muscle fiber from a 26-year-old volunteer is exposed to a drug that prevents calcium relea…
back: Depolarization of the sarcolemma is driven by sodium entry after acetylcholine acts at the junction; calcium enters the sarcoplasm afterward, from the SR.
extra: The excitation step is being attributed to calcium.

front: Why is “Splits ATP to cock the myosin head” wrong here? In an experiment, an isolated muscle fiber from a 26-year-old volunteer is exposed to a drug that prevents calcium relea…
back: ATP is hydrolyzed by the myosin head's own intrinsic ATPase activity; calcium does not participate in the cocking step.
extra: The energy supply step is being attributed to calcium.

front: A 32-year-old woman fractures the shaft of her femur. The dense bone forming the walls of the shaft, which resists compressive forces, is organized into which of the following structural units?
back: Osteons with concentric lamellae
extra: Compact bone's microscopic structural unit is the osteon, or Haversian system: concentric rings of calcified matrix (lamellae) around a central canal; compact bone is dense and withstands compressive forces.

front: Why is “Trabeculae with open marrow spaces” wrong here? A 32-year-old woman fractures the shaft of her femur. The dense bone forming the walls of the shaft, which resists compr…
back: Spongy (cancellous) bone has open spaces and supports shifts in weight distribution; it fills the epiphyses, not the dense diaphyseal walls.
extra: The spongy architecture is being assigned to the dense shaft.

front: Why is “Osteoid seams of uncalcified matrix” wrong here? A 32-year-old woman fractures the shaft of her femur. The dense bone forming the walls of the shaft, which resists compr…
back: Osteoid is freshly secreted, not-yet-calcified matrix; it provides no compressive strength until mineralized.
extra: A formative precursor is being cast as the load-bearing structure.

front: Why is “Synchondroses of hyaline cartilage” wrong here? A 32-year-old woman fractures the shaft of her femur. The dense bone forming the walls of the shaft, which resists compr…
back: A synchondrosis joins bones with hyaline cartilage (e.g. the epiphyseal plate); it is a joint, not a structural unit of compact bone.
extra: A cartilaginous joint is being cast as a bone tissue.

front:
Several hours after death, a 55-year-old man's muscles become stiff and resist passive movement.

At the molecular level, this stiffness results from the absence of ATP preventing which of the following steps?
back: Detachment of myosin heads from the actin filaments
extra: A new molecule of ATP attaching to the myosin head causes the cross-bridge to detach; without ATP, actin and myosin remain locked together and the muscle stays rigid.

front:
Why is “Hydrolysis of ATP by the myosin head” wrong here? Several hours after death, a 55-year-old man's muscles become stiff and resist passive movement.

At the molecular level…
back: Hydrolysis returns the myosin head to its cocked, high-energy position; it requires ATP as substrate but is not the step whose loss locks the cross-bridge in place.
extra: The step that cocks the head is being cast as the step that releases it.

front:
Why is “Release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum” wrong here? Several hours after death, a 55-year-old man's muscles become stiff and resist passive movement.

At the molecular level…
back: Calcium release initiates contraction by exposing actin's binding sites; the rigidity after death comes from cross-bridges that cannot detach without ATP.
extra: The trigger for contraction is being cast as the cause of the persistent stiffness.

front:
Why is “Pivoting of the myosin head during the power stroke” wrong here? Several hours after death, a 55-year-old man's muscles become stiff and resist passive movement.

At the molecular level…
back: The power stroke is driven by phosphate release from the cocked head, pulling actin toward the M-line; it precedes and does not require the ATP binding that frees the cross-bridge.
extra: The force-generating step is being cast as the ATP-dependent release.

front:
A 24-year-old man receives a drug that prevents calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle. An action potential still propagates along the sarcolemma and T-tubules, but the fiber does not develop tension.

Which of the following steps fails as the direct consequence of blocked SR calcium release?
back: Exposure of myosin-binding sites on actin via troponin–tropomyosin shift
extra: SR calcium enters the sarcoplasm and activates the troponin–tropomyosin complex so tropomyosin shifts off myosin-binding sites on actin; without that Ca2+, cross-bridges cannot form and tension fails.

front: Why is “Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels at the motor end plate” wrong here? A 24-year-old man receives a drug that prevents calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle. An a…
back: The stem states the action potential still propagates; the block is downstream at SR calcium release needed to expose actin sites.
extra: The end-plate trigger is being blamed when the action potential already propagates.

front: Why is “Hydrolysis of ATP by the myosin head during the power stroke” wrong here? A 24-year-old man receives a drug that prevents calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle. An a…
back: Myosin ATPase acts after binding sites are exposed; the primary failure with blocked SR release is that tropomyosin never uncovers those sites.
extra: The ATPase step is being treated as the first failed event.

front: Why is “Shortening of the A band as thick filaments dissolve” wrong here? A 24-year-old man receives a drug that prevents calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle. An a…
back: The A band width stays constant during contraction; thick filaments do not dissolve, and the drug’s effect is upstream at Ca2+-dependent site exposure.
extra: A false description of sliding-filament geometry is being offered.

front: A 13-year-old boy grows 10 centimeters taller in one year. The lengthening of his femur during this period results mainly from cell division in which of the following zones?
back: The proliferative zone of the epiphyseal plate
extra: Longitudinal growth results from cellular division in the proliferative zone of the epiphyseal plate (plus maturation and hypertrophy of those cells); new bone is then added to the diaphysis.

front: Why is “The calcified matrix nearest the diaphysis” wrong here? A 13-year-old boy grows 10 centimeters taller in one year. The lengthening of his femur during this period results mainl…
back: In the zone of calcified matrix most chondrocytes are dead; capillaries and osteoblasts invade it to lay bone, but the divisions driving lengthening occur in the proliferative zone.
extra: The zone where cells have died is being cast as the growth engine.

front: Why is “The periosteal collar around the shaft” wrong here? A 13-year-old boy grows 10 centimeters taller in one year. The lengthening of his femur during this period results mainl…
back: The periosteum adds bone to the outer surface (appositional growth in diameter); length comes from the epiphyseal plate.
extra: A width-growth site is being cast as the length-growth site.

front: Why is “The articular cartilage at the joint surface” wrong here? A 13-year-old boy grows 10 centimeters taller in one year. The lengthening of his femur during this period results mainl…
back: Articular cartilage covers the bone ends to reduce friction; it does not contribute to longitudinal growth.
extra: A friction-reducing surface is being cast as a growth plate.

front: A 28-year-old mover picks up first a pencil and then a heavy box using the same arm muscles. The greater force needed for the box is generated mainly by which of the following?
back: Recruitment of larger, higher-threshold motor units
extra: Small, low-threshold motor units fire first; as more strength is needed, larger motor units with higher-threshold neurons are enlisted, and this recruitment makes the contraction progressively stronger.

front: Why is “Widening of the zone of filament overlap” wrong here? A 28-year-old mover picks up first a pencil and then a heavy box using the same arm muscles. The greater force needed fo…
back: Overlap affects the force each fiber can produce at a given length, but voluntary force grading in a working muscle comes from recruiting additional motor units.
extra: The length-tension relationship is being cast as the grading mechanism.

front: Why is “Shortening of every sarcomere by a greater distance” wrong here? A 28-year-old mover picks up first a pencil and then a heavy box using the same arm muscles. The greater force needed fo…
back: Each sarcomere shortens to an anatomical limit set by filament overlap; whole-muscle force is graded by how many motor units participate, not by extra sarcomere travel.
extra: A bigger per-sarcomere stroke is being cast as the grading mechanism.

front: Why is “Fusion of twitches into a continuous contraction” wrong here? A 28-year-old mover picks up first a pencil and then a heavy box using the same arm muscles. The greater force needed fo…
back: Tetanus (fused twitches) raises tension within an active unit, but picking up a heavier load engages MORE motor units through recruitment.
extra: Temporal summation is being cast as the main grading mechanism here.

front:
During the first few seconds of a 100-meter sprint at a collegiate track meet, a 19-year-old athlete's leg muscles demand ATP at their maximum rate.

Which of the following sources regenerates that ATP the fastest?
back: Creatine phosphate stores in the fibers
extra: Creatine phosphate provides about the first 15 seconds of ATP at the beginning of muscle contraction, before glycolysis and aerobic metabolism ramp up.

front: Why is “Anaerobic glycolysis of blood glucose” wrong here? During the first few seconds of a 100-meter sprint at a collegiate track meet, a 19-year-old athlete's leg muscles deman…
back: Muscles turn to glycolysis as creatine phosphate is depleted; glycolysis cannot generate ATP as quickly as the phosphagen system.
extra: The second-fastest source is being cast as the fastest.

front: Why is “Oxidation of circulating fatty acids” wrong here? During the first few seconds of a 100-meter sprint at a collegiate track meet, a 19-year-old athlete's leg muscles deman…
back: Fatty-acid oxidation feeds aerobic metabolism over longer efforts; it is far too slow for the opening seconds of a sprint.
extra: A slow sustained fuel is being cast as an immediate source.

front: Why is “Fermentation of muscle glycogen” wrong here? During the first few seconds of a 100-meter sprint at a collegiate track meet, a 19-year-old athlete's leg muscles deman…
back: Glycogen-derived glycolysis contributes after the phosphagen store is spent, not in the first seconds.
extra: A later anaerobic pathway is being cast as the immediate source.

front: A 24-year-old marathon runner has leg muscles dominated by fibers that resist fatigue over hours of continuous running. These fibers produce ATP mainly by which of the following?
back: Aerobic respiration in mitochondria
extra: Slow oxidative fibers contract relatively slowly and use aerobic respiration of oxygen and glucose to produce ATP, sustaining low-power contractions over long periods without fatiguing.

front: Why is “Anaerobic glycolysis in the cytosol” wrong here? A 24-year-old marathon runner has leg muscles dominated by fibers that resist fatigue over hours of continuous running. …
back: Fast glycolytic fibers rely on anaerobic glycolysis, which yields small amounts of ATP quickly but fatigues rapidly — the opposite of a marathoner's fibers.
extra: The fast glycolytic strategy is being assigned to endurance fibers.

front: Why is “Creatine phosphate transfer reactions” wrong here? A 24-year-old marathon runner has leg muscles dominated by fibers that resist fatigue over hours of continuous running. …
back: Creatine phosphate supplies roughly the first 15 seconds of contraction; it cannot sustain hours of endurance work.
extra: A seconds-long reserve is being cast as an hours-long supply.

front: Why is “Lactic acid fermentation alone” wrong here? A 24-year-old marathon runner has leg muscles dominated by fibers that resist fatigue over hours of continuous running. …
back: Lactic acid production marks anaerobic metabolism during strenuous effort; endurance fibers minimize it by using oxygen.
extra: A fatigue-promoting pathway is being assigned to fatigue-resistant fibers.

front:
A 20-year-old student examines a histology slide of a muscle that is striated, contracts without voluntary input, and has cells joined end-to-end by specialized junctions.

Which of the following muscle types is she viewing?
back: Cardiac muscle
extra: Cardiac muscle is striated, under involuntary control, and its cells are joined at intercalated discs containing gap junctions and desmosomes, contracting as one unit under pacemaker regulation.

front: Why is “Skeletal muscle” wrong here? A 20-year-old student examines a histology slide of a muscle that is striated, contracts without voluntary input, and ha…
back: Skeletal muscle is striated and multinucleated, but it requires signaling from the nervous system to trigger contraction (voluntary) and lacks intercalated discs.
extra: The other striated type is being chosen despite the involuntary control.

front: Why is “Smooth muscle” wrong here? A 20-year-old student examines a histology slide of a muscle that is striated, contracts without voluntary input, and ha…
back: Smooth muscle is involuntary but nonstriated and mononucleated; the striations on the slide exclude it.
extra: The involuntary visceral type is being chosen despite the striations.

front: Why is “Visceral muscle” wrong here? A 20-year-old student examines a histology slide of a muscle that is striated, contracts without voluntary input, and ha…
back: Visceral (single-unit) smooth muscle contracts as a unit through gap junctions, but it is nonstriated; the slide shows a striated tissue.
extra: A smooth-muscle subtype is being chosen despite the striations.

front:
A 34-year-old woman has double vision and fluctuating weakness that improves after she is given a drug that inhibits acetylcholinesterase.

At her neuromuscular junction, the chemical signal that acts directly on the muscle fiber is which of the following?
back: Acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors
extra: At the neuromuscular junction, the motor neuron's terminals release acetylcholine, which acts on the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor of the sarcolemma; acetylcholinesterase then eliminates it, so inhibiting that enzyme strengthens a weak signal.

front: Why is “Dopamine acting on D2 receptors” wrong here? A 34-year-old woman has double vision and fluctuating weakness that improves after she is given a drug that inhibits ace…
back: Dopamine acts in central pathways such as the basal nuclei; the neuromuscular junction uses acetylcholine.
extra: A basal-ganglia transmitter is being placed at the muscle junction.

front: Why is “Glutamate acting on NMDA receptors” wrong here? A 34-year-old woman has double vision and fluctuating weakness that improves after she is given a drug that inhibits ace…
back: Glutamate is excitatory within the central nervous system; skeletal muscle fibers are activated by acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors.
extra: The main central excitatory transmitter is being placed at the muscle junction.

front: Why is “GABA acting on ligand-gated chloride channels” wrong here? A 34-year-old woman has double vision and fluctuating weakness that improves after she is given a drug that inhibits ace…
back: GABA inhibits neurons in the brain and spinal cord; the junction on the muscle fiber is excitatory and cholinergic.
extra: An inhibitory central transmitter is being placed at the muscle junction.

front:
A 34-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of double vision and drooping eyelids that worsen after prolonged reading and improve after rest. Repetitive nerve stimulation shows a decremental response that partially corrects after edrophonium administration. Ice applied to a ptotic eyelid briefly lifts it.

Which of the following best describes the primary defect at her neuromuscular junction?
back: Autoimmune loss of functional nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the sarcolemma
extra: Myasthenia gravis autoantibodies reduce nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the muscle sarcolemma, so repeated stimulation depletes the safety margin; acetylcholinesterase inhibition temporarily restores transmission.

front: Why is “Irreversible blockade of presynaptic acetylcholine release by a bacterial toxin” wrong here? A 34-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of double vision and drooping eyelids that worsen after prolonged re…
back: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release, causing flaccid paralysis that does not improve with edrophonium or show fatigable ocular weakness.
extra: Botulinum flaccid paralysis is being confused with fatigable weakness.

front: Why is “Competitive antagonism of nicotinic receptors by a plant alkaloid” wrong here? A 34-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of double vision and drooping eyelids that worsen after prolonged re…
back: Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers competitively occupy nicotinic receptors but do not produce the autoimmune decremental response or edrophonium reversal pattern of myasthenia.
extra: Curare-like receptor blockade is being substituted for autoimmune receptor loss.

front: Why is “Deficiency of acetylcholinesterase causing receptor desensitization” wrong here? A 34-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of double vision and drooping eyelids that worsen after prolonged re…
back: Acetylcholinesterase eliminates acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction; myasthenia is postsynaptic receptor loss, and edrophonium works by inhibiting the esterase, not by replacing it.
extra: The enzyme that clears acetylcholine is being treated as deficient rather than inhibited therapeutically.

front:
At birth, a full-term newborn's skull bones remain incompletely ossified, allowing the head to deform during delivery.

These skull bones formed directly from mesenchymal sheets by which of the following processes?
back: Intramembranous ossification
extra: In intramembranous ossification, bone develops directly from sheets of mesenchymal connective tissue; the skull and clavicles form this way and are not fully ossified at birth, permitting deformation in the birth canal.

front:
Why is “Endochondral ossification” wrong here? At birth, a full-term newborn's skull bones remain incompletely ossified, allowing the head to deform during delivery.

…
back: Endochondral ossification replaces a hyaline cartilage model and produces long bones and the skull base; the flat skull bones form intramembranously.
extra: The cartilage-template pathway is being assigned to the skull vault.

front:
Why is “Calcification of a cartilage template” wrong here? At birth, a full-term newborn's skull bones remain incompletely ossified, allowing the head to deform during delivery.

…
back: Cartilage-template replacement defines endochondral ossification; the skull vault forms directly from mesenchymal membranes without a cartilage stage.
extra: The endochondral pathway is being described under another name.

front:
Why is “Appositional growth at the periosteum” wrong here? At birth, a full-term newborn's skull bones remain incompletely ossified, allowing the head to deform during delivery.

…
back: Appositional growth widens existing bone after it has formed; it is not the developmental pathway that first creates the skull bones.
extra: A growth-in-width process is being cast as initial bone formation.

front:
In a physiology laboratory, a 21-year-old student watches a stimulated skeletal muscle fiber contract under the microscope.

Which of the following describes the appearance of its sarcomeres during shortening?
back: The I band narrows while the A band stays constant
extra: When a sarcomere contracts, the Z lines move closer together and the I band becomes smaller, while the A band stays the same width because the thick filaments themselves do not change length.

front: Why is “Both bands narrow to half of their resting width” wrong here? In a physiology laboratory, a 21-year-old student watches a stimulated skeletal muscle fiber contract under the microsco…
back: The sliding filament model moves filaments past each other rather than shortening them; only the I band (and H zone) narrow, while the A band is unchanged.
extra: Shortening is being attributed to the filaments themselves.

front: Why is “The A band narrows while the I band stays constant” wrong here? In a physiology laboratory, a 21-year-old student watches a stimulated skeletal muscle fiber contract under the microsco…
back: The A band reflects the length of the myosin thick filaments, which does not change; it is the I band (thin filament only) that shrinks as the Z lines approach.
extra: The thick-filament band is being treated as the one that shortens.

front: Why is “The Z discs move farther apart as the filaments slide” wrong here? In a physiology laboratory, a 21-year-old student watches a stimulated skeletal muscle fiber contract under the microsco…
back: The Z lines move closer together during contraction, pulling the sarcomere's ends toward its center; moving apart would describe stretching.
extra: The direction of Z-disc movement is being reversed.

front:
During arthroscopy of a 27-year-old athlete's injured knee, the surgeon notes that the bone ends glide smoothly within a fluid-filled space.

Friction between these bone ends is normally minimized by which of the following?
back: Articular cartilage and the synovial fluid
extra: A thin layer of articular cartilage covers the articulating surfaces, and synovial fluid secreted by the synovial membrane lubricates the joint cavity, so the bone ends glide without grinding.

front: Why is “Intracapsular ligaments and the meniscus” wrong here? During arthroscopy of a 27-year-old athlete's injured knee, the surgeon notes that the bone ends glide smoothly within a…
back: Ligaments hold the bones together and resist abnormal motion, and a meniscus pads or smooths movement; neither coats the bone ends or lubricates the cavity.
extra: Stabilizing structures are being cast as the friction reducers.

front: Why is “The fibrous layer of the articular capsule” wrong here? During arthroscopy of a 27-year-old athlete's injured knee, the surgeon notes that the bone ends glide smoothly within a…
back: The fibrous capsule forms the walls of the joint cavity and provides strength; friction at the bone surfaces is handled by cartilage and synovial fluid.
extra: The joint's outer wall is being cast as the anti-friction element.

front: Why is “Bursae interposed between skin and bone” wrong here? During arthroscopy of a 27-year-old athlete's injured knee, the surgeon notes that the bone ends glide smoothly within a…
back: Bursae reduce friction OUTSIDE the joint (between skin, tendons, and bone); they do not lie between the articulating bone ends.
extra: Extra-articular cushions are being cast as intra-articular lubrication.

front: A 41-year-old man shakes his head side-to-side to signal 'no'. The movement occurring at the joint between his first and second cervical vertebrae is provided by which of the following joint types?
back: A pivot joint
extra: The atlantoaxial pivot joint (between C1 and C2) provides side-to-side rotation of the head around a single axis.

front: Why is “A hinge joint” wrong here? A 41-year-old man shakes his head side-to-side to signal 'no'. The movement occurring at the joint between his first and…
back: Hinge joints (knee, elbow, ankle) allow flexion and extension, not rotation; shaking the head 'no' is rotation at a pivot.
extra: A uniaxial flexion-extension joint is being assigned to head rotation.

front: Why is “A saddle joint” wrong here? A 41-year-old man shakes his head side-to-side to signal 'no'. The movement occurring at the joint between his first and…
back: Saddle joints (first carpometacarpal joint of the thumb) are biaxial, allowing flexion/extension and abduction/adduction with circumduction.
extra: A biaxial thumb joint is being assigned to the neck.

front: Why is “A ball-and-socket joint” wrong here? A 41-year-old man shakes his head side-to-side to signal 'no'. The movement occurring at the joint between his first and…
back: Ball-and-socket joints are found only at the shoulder and hip, where they permit multiaxial movement including rotation; the C1-C2 joint is a pivot.
extra: A multiaxial joint is being assigned to a uniaxial movement.

front:
In a muscle-physiology experiment, a 23-year-old student stimulates an isolated muscle at increasing frequencies until the relaxation phase between contractions disappears completely.

The resulting continuous maximal contraction is called which of the following?
back: Complete tetanus
extra: When stimulus frequency is so high that the relaxation phase disappears completely, contractions become continuous — complete tetanus — because sustained sarcoplasmic calcium lets nearly all sarcomeres keep cross-bridging.

front: Why is “Wave summation” wrong here? In a muscle-physiology experiment, a 23-year-old student stimulates an isolated muscle at increasing frequencies until t…
back: Wave summation is the adding together of successive stimuli to produce stronger contraction; when summation proceeds until relaxation vanishes, the result is complete tetanus.
extra: The additive process is being named where its endpoint belongs.

front: Why is “A single muscle twitch” wrong here? In a muscle-physiology experiment, a 23-year-old student stimulates an isolated muscle at increasing frequencies until t…
back: A twitch is the isolated contraction from a single action potential, with latent, contraction, and relaxation phases; repeated high-frequency stimulation fuses twitches into tetanus.
extra: The unit response is being applied to a fused train.

front: Why is “Incomplete tetanus” wrong here? In a muscle-physiology experiment, a 23-year-old student stimulates an isolated muscle at increasing frequencies until t…
back: Incomplete tetanus still shows quick cycles of contraction with short relaxation phases; here the relaxation phase has DISAPPEARED, defining complete tetanus.
extra: The partially fused state is being applied to a fully fused one.

front:
An action potential reaches a presynaptic terminal normally. A selective blocker prevents opening of the terminal's voltage-gated calcium channels.

Which of the following paired changes is most directly expected after stimulation?
back: Reduced terminal calcium entry with reduced transmitter exocytosis
extra: Presynaptic calcium entry triggers vesicle fusion. Preventing that entry reduces the calcium signal and therefore transmitter exocytosis despite arrival of the action potential.

front: Why is “Increased terminal calcium with increased transmitter exocytosis” wrong here? An action potential reaches a presynaptic terminal normally. A selective blocker prevents opening of the terminal's volt…
back: The blocked channels cannot generate the usual stimulation-induced calcium entry. Both proposed increases contradict the intervention.
extra: Reverses both consequences of blocking presynaptic calcium entry.

front: Why is “Preserved terminal calcium with increased transmitter exocytosis” wrong here? An action potential reaches a presynaptic terminal normally. A selective blocker prevents opening of the terminal's volt…
back: Preserved calcium entry is inconsistent with the selective channel block, and increased release lacks its normal calcium trigger.
extra: Preserves a blocked calcium signal while assuming increased transmitter release.

front: Why is “Increased terminal calcium with reduced transmitter exocytosis” wrong here? An action potential reaches a presynaptic terminal normally. A selective blocker prevents opening of the terminal's volt…
back: This pattern would require a downstream release defect with preserved or elevated calcium, rather than the channel-entry defect described.
extra: Substitutes a downstream release defect for the stated calcium-channel block.

front:
Tracer is applied to sensory fibers entering the right side of the spinal cord. Fibers in one pathway cross near entry, whereas those in another remain on the right until reaching the medulla.

Which of the following pairings correctly identifies the modalities conveyed by these pathways?
back: Spinal crossing: temperature; medullary crossing: proprioception
extra: Temperature fibers use the spinothalamic pathway and cross near spinal entry. Proprioceptive fibers ascend ipsilaterally in the dorsal column before crossing in the medulla, matching both observations.

front: Why is “Spinal crossing: proprioception; medullary crossing: pain” wrong here? Tracer is applied to sensory fibers entering the right side of the spinal cord. Fibers in one pathway cross near entry, …
back: Proprioceptive information follows the dorsal column pathway and crosses in the medulla. Pain information follows the spinothalamic pathway and crosses near spinal entry, reversing this proposed pairing.
extra: Reverses the medullary proprioception and spinal pain crossings.

front: Why is “Spinal crossing: pain; medullary crossing: temperature” wrong here? Tracer is applied to sensory fibers entering the right side of the spinal cord. Fibers in one pathway cross near entry, …
back: Pain information does cross near spinal entry, but temperature follows the same general spinothalamic crossing pattern. Temperature therefore does not distinguish the pathway that remains ipsilateral until the medulla.
extra: Incorrectly separates pain and temperature into different crossing patterns.

front: Why is “Spinal crossing: temperature; medullary crossing: pain” wrong here? Tracer is applied to sensory fibers entering the right side of the spinal cord. Fibers in one pathway cross near entry, …
back: Both pain and temperature use the spinothalamic crossing pattern described here. Pain therefore cannot identify the pathway remaining ipsilateral until the medulla.
extra: Assigns medullary crossing to pain despite its spinothalamic route.

front:
Three separate excitatory inputs reach a neuron simultaneously. Together they produce a larger depolarization than any one input alone. The investigator silences two inputs while preserving the timing and strength of the remaining input.

Which of the following changes best explains the smaller response?
back: Reduced spatial combination of signals from multiple input locations
extra: Silencing two locations removes their contributions to spatial summation. The surviving input can have unchanged strength while the total response falls.

front: Why is “Reduced temporal overlap of signals from the remaining input” wrong here? Three separate excitatory inputs reach a neuron simultaneously. Together they produce a larger depolarization than any o…
back: Timing at the remaining input is preserved. The manipulated feature is the number of active locations, not the spacing of repeated signals.
extra: Attributes fewer active locations to a timing change excluded by the experiment.

front: Why is “Increased temporal overlap of repeated signals at one input” wrong here? Three separate excitatory inputs reach a neuron simultaneously. Together they produce a larger depolarization than any o…
back: No increase in repeated signaling is described. Increased temporal overlap would tend to augment rather than explain the smaller combined response.
extra: Invents increased temporal overlap to explain a smaller total response.

front: Why is “Increased spatial combination of signals from newly recruited locations” wrong here? Three separate excitatory inputs reach a neuron simultaneously. Together they produce a larger depolarization than any o…
back: Inputs were silenced rather than newly recruited. The data support less spatial contribution, not more.
extra: Treats silenced input locations as newly recruited contributors.

front:
A presynaptic terminal has a normal action potential and a normal stimulation-induced calcium rise. Neurotransmitter-containing vesicles remain within the terminal, and little transmitter appears in the synaptic cleft.

Which of the following steps best localizes the defect?
back: Fusion of vesicle membranes with the presynaptic membrane
extra: Normal calcium with retained transmitter-containing vesicles and little cleft transmitter identifies failure of the fusion/exocytosis step.

front: Why is “Propagation of the action potential toward the axon terminal” wrong here? A presynaptic terminal has a normal action potential and a normal stimulation-induced calcium rise. Neurotransmitter-con…
back: The action potential is recorded at the terminal, so failure to arrive cannot explain vesicles being retained after a normal calcium signal.
extra: Attributes release failure to an action potential that demonstrably arrived.

front: Why is “Opening of calcium channels in the presynaptic terminal membrane” wrong here? A presynaptic terminal has a normal action potential and a normal stimulation-induced calcium rise. Neurotransmitter-con…
back: The stimulation-induced calcium rise is normal. A failure of the calcium-entry channels would not best match that preserved measurement.
extra: Places the defect at calcium-channel opening despite the normal calcium rise.

front: Why is “Entry of calcium through the stimulated terminal membrane” wrong here? A presynaptic terminal has a normal action potential and a normal stimulation-induced calcium rise. Neurotransmitter-con…
back: Calcium entry is upstream of fusion and its measured response is intact. The release failure occurs after that preserved event.
extra: Mistakes preserved calcium entry for the later failed release event.

front:
A small lesion interrupts the left dorsal column in the thoracic spinal cord. Ascending fibers above and below the lesion are otherwise intact.

Which of the following sensory findings below the lesion is most consistent with the crossing pattern of this pathway?
back: Reduced proprioception on the left side of the body
extra: Dorsal column fibers carry proprioceptive information and cross in the medulla. A left spinal cord lesion therefore interrupts information from the left side before the crossing.

front: Why is “Reduced proprioception on the right side of the body” wrong here? A small lesion interrupts the left dorsal column in the thoracic spinal cord. Ascending fibers above and below the lesio…
back: Right-sided proprioceptive information travels in the right dorsal column before crossing in the medulla. A lesion confined to the left thoracic dorsal column would spare those fibers.
extra: Assumes proprioceptive fibers have already crossed within the spinal cord.

front: Why is “Reduced pain sensation on the left side of the body” wrong here? A small lesion interrupts the left dorsal column in the thoracic spinal cord. Ascending fibers above and below the lesio…
back: Pain travels in the spinothalamic pathway, whose fibers cross near their spinal entry level. This lesion is restricted to a pathway carrying touch and proprioception.
extra: Assigns pain transmission to the lesioned dorsal-column pathway.

front: Why is “Reduced pain sensation on the right side of the body” wrong here? A small lesion interrupts the left dorsal column in the thoracic spinal cord. Ascending fibers above and below the lesio…
back: A left spinothalamic lesion can affect pain information from the opposite side after crossing. The specified lesion instead interrupts the dorsal column, which carries different sensory modalities.
extra: Applies contralateral spinothalamic pain loss to a dorsal-column lesion.

front:
A neuron receives input through one excitatory synapse. Widely spaced stimuli produce separate small depolarizations. When the same input fires more rapidly, successive depolarizations overlap and their combined effect becomes larger.

Which of the following mechanisms best explains this change?
back: Temporal summation from closely timed inputs at one location
extra: More frequent signals at one synapse allow graded depolarizations to overlap. Their timing, rather than recruitment of other sites, accounts for temporal summation.

front: Why is “Spatial summation as inputs combine at several different locations” wrong here? A neuron receives input through one excitatory synapse. Widely spaced stimuli produce separate small depolarizations. Wh…
back: The preparation stimulates one synapse. Spatial summation would combine input from different locations, which were not recruited here.
extra: Confuses repeated input at one site with input from several locations.

front: Why is “Temporal summation as repeated potentials become farther apart” wrong here? A neuron receives input through one excitatory synapse. Widely spaced stimuli produce separate small depolarizations. Wh…
back: The stimuli become closer together, not farther apart. Wider spacing would reduce overlap and does not explain the larger combined effect.
extra: Reverses the timing change that allows successive potentials to add.

front: Why is “Spatial summation as additional synaptic locations are recruited” wrong here? A neuron receives input through one excitatory synapse. Widely spaced stimuli produce separate small depolarizations. Wh…
back: No new synaptic location becomes active. The same site fires more rapidly, so an increase in spatial recruitment is not the observed change.
extra: Infers recruitment of new synapses when only firing frequency changes.

front: During the absolute refractory period, no new action potential can be initiated because which gate on voltage-gated sodium channels is closed?
back: The inactivation gate
extra: During the absolute refractory period the inactivation gate of voltage-gated Na+ channels is closed, so no stimulus can trigger another action potential until the channel resets below about −55 mV.

front: Why is “The activation gate” wrong here? During the absolute refractory period, no new action potential can be initiated because which gate on voltage-gated sodi…
back: The activation gate opens to start the action potential; absolute refractoriness reflects closure of the inactivation gate, which prevents reopening regardless of stimulus strength.
extra: The gate that opens during depolarization is being blamed for absolute refractoriness.

front: Why is “The voltage-gated potassium channel pore” wrong here? During the absolute refractory period, no new action potential can be initiated because which gate on voltage-gated sodi…
back: K+ channel opening contributes to repolarization and the relative refractory period; the absolute period reflects Na+ channel inactivation, not K+ pore closure.
extra: Potassium efflux is being assigned the primary block to Na+ reopening.

front: Why is “The ligand-gated sodium channel” wrong here? During the absolute refractory period, no new action potential can be initiated because which gate on voltage-gated sodi…
back: Action potential refractoriness is a property of voltage-gated Na+ channels on the axon, not ligand-gated channels at synapses.
extra: A synaptic channel type is being substituted for the voltage-gated channel gating the action potential.

front:
A 32-year-old man receives lidocaine infiltration before wound repair and loses sensation in the injected dermatome. Nerve conduction studies afterward show that rapidly firing axons are blocked preferentially.

Which of the following best explains why drugs that prolong the absolute refractory period prevent propagation of high-frequency impulses?
back: They hold voltage-gated sodium channels in the inactivated state between spikes
extra: Local anesthetics bind open and inactivated Na+ channels; high-frequency firing keeps channels in the inactivated state where drug affinity is highest, prolonging absolute refractoriness and blocking propagation.

front: Why is “They permanently depolarize the resting membrane potential up to firing threshold” wrong here? A 32-year-old man receives lidocaine infiltration before wound repair and loses sensation in the injected dermatome. Ner…
back: Local anesthetics block conduction by stabilizing inactivated Na+ channels, not by shifting resting potential to threshold.
extra: A tonic depolarization mechanism is being substituted for use-dependent channel block.

front: Why is “They open potassium channels and hyperpolarize the axon membrane beyond its resting potential” wrong here? A 32-year-old man receives lidocaine infiltration before wound repair and loses sensation in the injected dermatome. Ner…
back: Lidocaine acts primarily on voltage-gated Na+ channels; K+ hyperpolarization is not its principal local-anesthetic mechanism.
extra: A K+ channel opener mechanism is being attributed to lidocaine.

front: Why is “They strip myelin sheaths and convert saltatory conduction into continuous conduction” wrong here? A 32-year-old man receives lidocaine infiltration before wound repair and loses sensation in the injected dermatome. Ner…
back: Local anesthetics reversibly block Na+ channels in the membrane; they do not strip myelin like demyelinating disease.
extra: A demyelinating lesion is being confused with reversible pharmacologic block.

front:
While recording from an axon during a neurophysiology practical, a 26-year-old student delivers a second suprathreshold stimulus 1 millisecond after an action potential begins, yet no second action potential can be elicited no matter how strong the stimulus.

Which of the following best explains this absolute refractory period?
back: The inactivation gates of the voltage-gated sodium channels are closed
extra: Timed with the peak, the inactivation gate of each voltage-gated Na+ channel closes and cannot reopen until the membrane returns below about -55 mV, so no new action potential can start regardless of stimulus strength.

front: Why is “The axon hillock is busy integrating the first depolarizing signal” wrong here? While recording from an axon during a neurophysiology practical, a 26-year-old student delivers a second suprathreshold …
back: Integration determines whether threshold is reached; refractoriness persists even when a threshold-level stimulus is delivered directly, because inactivated Na+ channels cannot open.
extra: Summation at the initial segment is being confused with channel-level refractoriness.

front: Why is “The sodium-potassium pump has not yet restored the ionic gradients” wrong here? While recording from an axon during a neurophysiology practical, a 26-year-old student delivers a second suprathreshold …
back: A single action potential moves far too few ions to exhaust the gradients, and the pump works continuously; the block is the closed inactivation gate, not a lack of Na+ gradient.
extra: Gradient depletion is being blamed for a gating phenomenon.

front: Why is “Potassium efflux is opposing any further depolarization of the membrane” wrong here? While recording from an axon during a neurophysiology practical, a 26-year-old student delivers a second suprathreshold …
back: K+ leaving the cell explains the later relative refractory period, when a stronger-than-usual stimulus can fire the cell; during the absolute period no stimulus can work because the Na+ inactivation gates are shut.
extra: The mechanism of the relative refractory period is being applied to the absolute one.

front:
A 66-year-old man begins a medication that blocks beta-adrenergic receptors, slowing his heart rate.

Which of the following correctly characterizes the receptors bound by norepinephrine and epinephrine at sympathetic targets?
back: Alpha and beta classes, both of which are G protein-coupled receptors
extra: Norepinephrine and epinephrine share the alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors, and unlike the cholinergic nicotinic channel, every adrenergic receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor acting through second messengers.

front:
Why is “Alpha and beta classes, both of which are ligand-gated cation channels” wrong here? A 66-year-old man begins a medication that blocks beta-adrenergic receptors, slowing his heart rate.

Which of the follo…
back: Ligand-gated channels describe the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor; all alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors are G protein-coupled, hence slower second-messenger effects.
extra: The nicotinic receptor's structure is being attributed to adrenergic receptors.

front:
Why is “Nicotinic and muscarinic classes with no cross-reactivity between them” wrong here? A 66-year-old man begins a medication that blocks beta-adrenergic receptors, slowing his heart rate.

Which of the follo…
back: Nicotinic and muscarinic receptors bind acetylcholine; adrenergic targets express alpha and beta receptors, which are G protein-coupled.
extra: The cholinergic classification is being applied to catecholamines.

front:
Why is “Intracellular receptors that migrate to the nucleus when bound” wrong here? A 66-year-old man begins a medication that blocks beta-adrenergic receptors, slowing his heart rate.

Which of the follo…
back: Epinephrine and norepinephrine are ligands for surface G protein-coupled receptors and never enter the cell to bind nuclear receptors; that pattern fits lipophilic steroid hormones.
extra: Steroid-hormone signaling is being attributed to catecholamines.

front:
In a physiology laboratory, a 22-year-old student injects current into a neuron and depolarizes its membrane from -70 mV to -60 mV, but no action potential follows. A second, stronger injection depolarizes the membrane to -55 mV and a full action potential fires.

The critical difference at -55 mV is the opening of which of the following?
back: Voltage-gated sodium channels, initiating a full action potential
extra: At about -55 mV the activation gates of voltage-gated Na+ channels open, Na+ rushes in, and the action potential proceeds all-or-none to its peak near +30 mV; subthreshold depolarizations die out.

front: Why is “Leakage channels, initiating a steady sodium drift inward” wrong here? In a physiology laboratory, a 22-year-old student injects current into a neuron and depolarizes its membrane from -70 mV…
back: Leakage channels open and close at random to help set the resting potential; the regenerative upstroke begins only when voltage-gated Na+ channels open at threshold.
extra: Randomly gated background channels are being treated as a threshold device.

front: Why is “Voltage-gated calcium channels, initiating neurotransmitter release” wrong here? In a physiology laboratory, a 22-year-old student injects current into a neuron and depolarizes its membrane from -70 mV…
back: Ca2+ entry at the synaptic end bulb couples the arriving action potential to vesicle fusion; it does not set the axon's -55 mV firing threshold.
extra: The terminal's release machinery is being confused with the axon's firing trigger.

front: Why is “Voltage-gated potassium channels, initiating repolarization of the action potential” wrong here? In a physiology laboratory, a 22-year-old student injects current into a neuron and depolarizes its membrane from -70 mV…
back: Voltage-gated K+ channels open later, near the peak, to drive repolarization; threshold is defined by Na+ channel opening.
extra: The repolarizing channel is being cast as the trigger of the upstroke.

front:
A 35-year-old man suffers a right-sided spinal cord hemisection at T10. Below the lesion he loses fine touch and position sense on the right side but loses pain and temperature sensation on the left side.

Which of the following best explains this dissociated pattern?
back: Dorsal columns ascend uncrossed while spinothalamic fibers cross at entry
extra: Dorsal column fibers carrying touch and proprioception ascend ipsilaterally and cross only in the medulla, so a right hemisection removes right-sided fine touch; spinothalamic fibers for pain and temperature cross within the cord at the level they enter, so the right lesion removes left-sided pain and temperature below it.

front: Why is “Both ascending systems cross immediately upon entering the spinal cord” wrong here? A 35-year-old man suffers a right-sided spinal cord hemisection at T10. Below the lesion he loses fine touch and positio…
back: If both crossed at entry, a right hemisection would strip both modalities from the left side only; the preserved left-sided touch proves the dorsal columns ascend uncrossed until the medulla.
extra: A single crossing rule is being applied to both systems.

front: Why is “Both ascending systems cross together in the medulla” wrong here? A 35-year-old man suffers a right-sided spinal cord hemisection at T10. Below the lesion he loses fine touch and positio…
back: If both crossed in the medulla, the right lesion would remove both modalities on the right; the lost left-sided pain and temperature show that spinothalamic fibers already crossed in the cord.
extra: The spinothalamic crossing is being relocated upward.

front: Why is “Spinothalamic fibers ascend uncrossed while dorsal columns cross at entry” wrong here? A 35-year-old man suffers a right-sided spinal cord hemisection at T10. Below the lesion he loses fine touch and positio…
back: Swapping the rules would produce left-sided touch loss and right-sided pain loss — the mirror image of this patient's findings.
extra: The crossing rules of the two systems are being swapped.

front:
A pharmaceutical company finds that its new water-soluble antibiotic reaches high concentrations in most tissues but barely enters the cerebrospinal fluid of healthy 40-year-old volunteers.

Which of the following features of brain capillaries most accounts for this exclusion?
back: Tight junctions between endothelial cells, with few pores or transport vesicles
extra: Brain capillary endothelial cells are joined by tight junctions and have far fewer fenestra and pinocytotic vesicles than other capillaries, so water-soluble compounds cannot slip between or through the cells; the barrier preferentially blocks non-lipid-soluble drugs.

front: Why is “Astrocytes actively importing the drug before it can diffuse” wrong here? A pharmaceutical company finds that its new water-soluble antibiotic reaches high concentrations in most tissues but bar…
back: Astrocyte end feet help maintain the barrier but do not consume circulating drugs; exclusion is due to tight junctions and absent vesicular transport in the endothelium.
extra: Supporting glia are being cast as a sink that sequesters solutes.

front: Why is “Widely fenestrated endothelium that filters proteins into the tissue” wrong here? A pharmaceutical company finds that its new water-soluble antibiotic reaches high concentrations in most tissues but bar…
back: Fenestrations characterize permeable capillaries such as those of the kidney; cranial capillaries specifically lack them, which is the basis of the barrier.
extra: The leaky capillary design of other organs is being ascribed to the brain.

front: Why is “Ependymal cells filtering the blood into cerebrospinal fluid selectively” wrong here? A pharmaceutical company finds that its new water-soluble antibiotic reaches high concentrations in most tissues but bar…
back: Ependymal cells of the choroid plexus produce CSF, but the vascular barrier itself lies in the capillary endothelium's tight junctions; water-soluble drugs are blocked at the vessel wall.
extra: The CSF-producing epithelium is being treated as the vascular gatekeeper.

front:
A 34-year-old man receives a spinal anesthetic that blocks inhibitory interneurons synapsing on motor neurons. Recordings from an affected motor neuron now show repeated small graded potentials when several excitatory inputs fire together, and the cell reaches threshold more easily.

Each of these synaptic events is best classified as which of the following?
back: A depolarizing postsynaptic potential
extra: Excitatory postsynaptic potentials are depolarizing changes, usually from Na+ or Ca2+ entry, that bring the membrane closer to threshold; removing inhibition lets summated excitatory potentials trigger firing more readily.

front: Why is “An inhibitory postsynaptic potential” wrong here? A 34-year-old man receives a spinal anesthetic that blocks inhibitory interneurons synapsing on motor neurons. Recording…
back: Inhibitory postsynaptic potentials hyperpolarize the cell away from threshold, typically via Cl− influx or K+ efflux; the described depolarizations are excitatory.
extra: A hyperpolarizing event is being chosen for a depolarizing recording.

front: Why is “An action potential” wrong here? A 34-year-old man receives a spinal anesthetic that blocks inhibitory interneurons synapsing on motor neurons. Recording…
back: Action potentials are all-or-none overshoots; the small depolarizations described are subthreshold, graded EPSPs that can summate.
extra: A graded synaptic potential is being confused with the all-or-none spike.

front: Why is “A generator potential in a sensory dendrite” wrong here? A 34-year-old man receives a spinal anesthetic that blocks inhibitory interneurons synapsing on motor neurons. Recording…
back: Generator potentials occur in sensory receptors; motor neuron synaptic depolarizations are EPSPs.
extra: A sensory receptor event is being applied to a motor neuron synapse.

front:
A 41-year-old man with stiff-person syndrome has antibodies that reduce glycine release from spinal inhibitory interneurons. Intracellular recordings from an affected alpha motor neuron show that concurrent excitatory inputs now produce firing at lower stimulus intensity than in healthy controls, and postsynaptic hyperpolarization is absent.

Which of the following events is lost and best explains why excitatory input more readily reaches threshold?
back: Hyperpolarizing chloride-mediated signaling at the postsynaptic membrane
extra: Glycinergic inhibition hyperpolarizes motor neurons via Cl− entry; losing it removes opposition so excitatory depolarizations face less resistance and trigger action potentials at lower stimulus strength.

front: Why is “Loss of excitatory postsynaptic potentials at the neuromuscular junction” wrong here? A 41-year-old man with stiff-person syndrome has antibodies that reduce glycine release from spinal inhibitory interneur…
back: The neuromuscular junction is downstream of the motor neuron spike; the defect here is reduced central inhibition, not loss of EPSPs at the muscle endplate.
extra: The peripheral synapse is being blamed for a central integration defect.

front: Why is “Loss of saltatory conduction along the motor axon” wrong here? A 41-year-old man with stiff-person syndrome has antibodies that reduce glycine release from spinal inhibitory interneur…
back: Saltatory conduction affects spike propagation; the recording shows changed synaptic potentials at the soma before firing.
extra: Axonal propagation is being substituted for synaptic integration.

front: Why is “Loss of absolute refractory period in voltage-gated sodium channels” wrong here? A 41-year-old man with stiff-person syndrome has antibodies that reduce glycine release from spinal inhibitory interneur…
back: Refractory periods limit spike frequency after firing; the easier threshold crossing here reflects absent inhibitory IPSPs, not altered Na+ channel recovery.
extra: Channel refractoriness is being confused with synaptic inhibition.

front:
An interneuron releases glycine onto a motor neuron, and chloride flows into the postsynaptic cell, making its interior transiently more negative and an action potential less likely.

This recorded change is best classified as which of the following?
back: An inhibitory postsynaptic potential moving the cell away from threshold
extra: A hyperpolarizing graded potential at a synapse is an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) because it carries the membrane voltage farther from threshold; Cl- entry or K+ exit produces it.

front: Why is “A generator potential arising at the dendrites of a sensory neuron” wrong here? An interneuron releases glycine onto a motor neuron, and chloride flows into the postsynaptic cell, making its interior …
back: Generator potentials develop in the dendrites of unipolar sensory neurons to initiate afferent firing; the hyperpolarizing synaptic change in this motor neuron is an IPSP.
extra: A sensory-neuron depolarizing event is being applied to a synaptically inhibited motor cell.

front: Why is “An excitatory postsynaptic potential moving the cell toward threshold” wrong here? An interneuron releases glycine onto a motor neuron, and chloride flows into the postsynaptic cell, making its interior …
back: An EPSP depolarizes the cell toward threshold, typically via Na+ or Ca2+ entry; the chloride-driven hyperpolarization here is an IPSP.
extra: The excitatory category is being assigned to a hyperpolarizing event.

front: Why is “A receptor potential generated in a specialized sensory cell” wrong here? An interneuron releases glycine onto a motor neuron, and chloride flows into the postsynaptic cell, making its interior …
back: Receptor potentials occur in specialized receptor cells such as photoreceptors; a postsynaptic response to neurotransmitter from another neuron is a postsynaptic potential — inhibitory here.
extra: A sensory transduction event is being confused with synaptic input to a neuron.

front:
A 31-year-old researcher applies acetylcholine to an autonomic ganglion and records an immediate, rapid depolarization of the ganglionic neuron caused by cations flowing directly through the receptor protein itself.

The receptor mediating this fast response has which of the following structures?
back: A ligand-gated cation channel of the nicotinic type
extra: The nicotinic receptor is a ligand-gated cation channel: acetylcholine binding opens the pore and Na+ influx depolarizes the postsynaptic membrane within milliseconds, as at autonomic ganglia and the neuromuscular junction.

front: Why is “A G protein-coupled receptor of the muscarinic type” wrong here? A 31-year-old researcher applies acetylcholine to an autonomic ganglion and records an immediate, rapid depolarization o…
back: Muscarinic receptors act through G proteins and second messengers, producing slower, longer effects at postganglionic targets; a direct cation pore is the nicotinic channel.
extra: The slower metabotropic acetylcholine receptor is being matched to an immediate ion-flux recording.

front: Why is “An alpha-adrenergic receptor coupled to a G protein” wrong here? A 31-year-old researcher applies acetylcholine to an autonomic ganglion and records an immediate, rapid depolarization o…
back: Adrenergic receptors bind norepinephrine and epinephrine, not acetylcholine; the fast cholinergic ganglionic receptor is the nicotinic cation channel.
extra: A catecholamine receptor is being proposed for an acetylcholine response.

front: Why is “A beta-adrenergic receptor coupled to a G protein” wrong here? A 31-year-old researcher applies acetylcholine to an autonomic ganglion and records an immediate, rapid depolarization o…
back: Beta receptors respond to epinephrine and norepinephrine via G proteins; acetylcholine's direct channel action is mediated by the nicotinic receptor.
extra: A catecholamine receptor is being proposed for an acetylcholine response.

front:
A 55-year-old man has just finished a large meal, and vagal activity increases his gastric motility and secretion while slowing his heart.

Compared with the sympathetic wiring, the parasympathetic circuits mediating these effects are characterized by which of the following arrangements?
back: Long preganglionic fibers and short postganglionic fibers, with ganglia near or within the target
extra: Parasympathetic preganglionic neurons in brain stem nuclei or the sacral cord project long fibers to terminal ganglia near or within the target organ, so the postganglionic fibers are short — the mirror image of the sympathetic layout.

front: Why is “Short preganglionic fibers and long postganglionic fibers, with ganglia beside the spine” wrong here? A 55-year-old man has just finished a large meal, and vagal activity increases his gastric motility and secretion while …
back: Short myelinated preganglionics synapsing in paravertebral chain ganglia with long postganglionics describes the sympathetic system; parasympathetic ganglia sit near or inside the target.
extra: The sympathetic layout is being ascribed to the parasympathetic division.

front: Why is “Preganglionic neurons located in the thoracic and upper lumbar lateral horn” wrong here? A 55-year-old man has just finished a large meal, and vagal activity increases his gastric motility and secretion while …
back: The thoracolumbar lateral horn houses sympathetic preganglionics; parasympathetic preganglionic neurons occupy brain stem nuclei and the sacral lateral horn (craniosacral).
extra: The thoracolumbar origin of the opposing division is being claimed here.

front: Why is “Direct projection from the spinal cord to the adrenal medulla” wrong here? A 55-year-old man has just finished a large meal, and vagal activity increases his gastric motility and secretion while …
back: Only the sympathetic division has the preganglionic projection to the adrenal medulla, which releases catecholamines into blood; the parasympathetic division has no adrenal connection.
extra: A specialized sympathetic connection is being extended to the parasympathetic side.

front:
A 52-year-old woman with persistent vomiting presents with muscle weakness, and her serum potassium is low. The resting electrical state of her neurons depends on a predictable distribution of ions across the cell membrane.

Which of the following distributions most directly establishes the negative resting membrane potential of a neuron?
back: Potassium concentrated inside the cell, with large anions trapped in the cytosol
extra: K+ is more concentrated inside the cell, Na+ outside, and the cytosol holds negatively charged proteins and phosphates that cannot leave, so the interior measures about -70 mV relative to the outside.

front: Why is “Equal ion concentrations on both sides, with the membrane selecting charge” wrong here? A 52-year-old woman with persistent vomiting presents with muscle weakness, and her serum potassium is low. The resting …
back: Bulk fluids are nearly neutral, but unequal Na+ and K+ gradients plus trapped intracellular anions produce the charge difference at the membrane surface.
extra: The resting voltage arises from gradients, not from uniform concentrations.

front: Why is “Sodium concentrated inside the cell, with chloride balancing the charge” wrong here? A 52-year-old woman with persistent vomiting presents with muscle weakness, and her serum potassium is low. The resting …
back: Na+ is about ten times more concentrated outside the cell than inside; reversing this gradient would depolarize, not establish, the resting state.
extra: The dominant extracellular cation is being placed on the wrong side of the membrane.

front: Why is “Calcium pumped into the cytosol until the interior turns negative” wrong here? A 52-year-old woman with persistent vomiting presents with muscle weakness, and her serum potassium is low. The resting …
back: Cytosolic Ca2+ is kept extremely low by extrusion; the resting potential reflects K+ and Na+ gradients with fixed intracellular anions, not calcium accumulation.
extra: A signaling cation kept very low in the cytosol is being given a voltage-setting role.

front: Which of the following best describes the typical resting membrane potential of a neuron relative to the extracellular fluid?
back: About −70 mV, with the interior more negative
extra: K+ is concentrated inside, Na+ outside, and trapped intracellular anions leave the cytosol negative — typically about −70 mV at rest.

front: Why is “About +30 mV, with the interior more positive” wrong here? Which of the following best describes the typical resting membrane potential of a neuron relative to the extracellular f…
back: +30 mV is near the peak of an action potential; at rest the interior is negative, about −70 mV.
extra: The action-potential peak is being reported as the resting value.

front: Why is “About 0 mV, with no charge separation” wrong here? Which of the following best describes the typical resting membrane potential of a neuron relative to the extracellular f…
back: Fluids are macroscopically neutral, but unequal ion distributions create a voltage across the membrane near −70 mV at rest.
extra: Bulk electroneutrality is being confused with the membrane potential.

front: Why is “About −110 mV, matching the potassium equilibrium potential exactly” wrong here? Which of the following best describes the typical resting membrane potential of a neuron relative to the extracellular f…
back: Resting potential is near but not exactly at E_K because some Na+ leak and other ions contribute; −70 mV is the usual resting value cited.
extra: The pure K+ equilibrium potential is being reported as the observed resting value.

front:
A 61-year-old researcher records a stable −70 mV resting potential from a neuron. Chemical analysis shows abundant phosphate ions and negatively charged proteins in the cytosol, but the labels identifying sodium and potassium samples from each side of the membrane are lost. The investigator must reconstruct the ion map associated with this voltage.

Which of the following distributions is most consistent with the recorded resting state?
back: Extracellular Na+ tenfold higher; intracellular K+ higher
extra: At the resting potential, extracellular sodium is about tenfold higher than intracellular sodium, while potassium is more concentrated inside.

front: Why is “Intracellular Na+ tenfold higher; intracellular K+ higher” wrong here? A 61-year-old researcher records a stable −70 mV resting potential from a neuron. Chemical analysis shows abundant phosp…
back: The source places sodium at a tenfold higher concentration outside, not inside, the cell.
extra: Places sodium on the wrong side while preserving the potassium distribution.

front: Why is “Extracellular Na+ tenfold higher; extracellular K+ higher” wrong here? A 61-year-old researcher records a stable −70 mV resting potential from a neuron. Chemical analysis shows abundant phosp…
back: The source places potassium at a higher concentration inside, not outside, the cell.
extra: Places potassium on the wrong side while preserving the sodium distribution.

front: Why is “Equal Na+ across the membrane; intracellular K+ higher” wrong here? A 61-year-old researcher records a stable −70 mV resting potential from a neuron. Chemical analysis shows abundant phosp…
back: The source describes sodium outside the cell as ten times more concentrated than sodium inside, not equal across the membrane.
extra: Removes the sodium asymmetry while preserving the potassium distribution.

front:
A 29-year-old woman develops demyelination of central axons, and her nerve conduction studies show slowed signal propagation.

In a healthy myelinated axon, propagation is fast because the action potential travels by which of the following mechanisms?
back: Regenerating only at the nodes of Ranvier, leaping from node to node
extra: Voltage-gated Na+ channels cluster at the nodes of Ranvier; the depolarization spreads passively under the myelin and is renewed at each node, so the signal effectively jumps node to node and is much faster than continuous conduction.

front: Why is “Glial cells actively propelling the depolarization down the fiber” wrong here? A 29-year-old woman develops demyelination of central axons, and her nerve conduction studies show slowed signal propaga…
back: Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes only wrap and insulate the axon; the signal still propagates by voltage-gated Na+ channel opening, concentrated at the nodes.
extra: A passive insulating sheath is being given an active transport role.

front: Why is “Opening voltage-gated channels continuously along the entire membrane” wrong here? A 29-year-old woman develops demyelination of central axons, and her nerve conduction studies show slowed signal propaga…
back: Continuous conduction, with channels opening along the whole membrane, characterizes unmyelinated axons and is slower; myelinated segments regenerate the signal only at nodes.
extra: The slower unmyelinated strategy is being ascribed to myelinated fibers.

front: Why is “Widening the axon so that internal resistance to ion flow falls” wrong here? A 29-year-old woman develops demyelination of central axons, and her nerve conduction studies show slowed signal propaga…
back: Larger diameter does speed conduction by lowering resistance, but that applies to any axon; the specific advantage of myelination is saltatory, node-to-node propagation.
extra: A separate, size-based determinant of speed is being substituted for the myelin mechanism.

front:
A 28-year-old woman has had two episodes of monocular vision loss that resolved over weeks, and MRI now shows multifocal white-matter lesions. Nerve conduction studies of affected central pathways show slowed propagation.

Loss of which of the following properties of myelinated axons most directly accounts for the slowed conduction?
back: Saltatory regeneration of the action potential at nodes of Ranvier
extra: In myelinated axons the action potential regenerates only at nodes of Ranvier and jumps between them; demyelination disrupts that saltatory pattern and slows conduction.

front: Why is “Continuous opening of channels along the entire axonal membrane” wrong here? A 28-year-old woman has had two episodes of monocular vision loss that resolved over weeks, and MRI now shows multifocal…
back: Continuous conduction is the slower unmyelinated strategy; demyelination removes the insulation that enables saltatory, node-to-node renewal.
extra: The unmyelinated pattern is being treated as what demyelination removes.

front: Why is “Active glial pumping of depolarization down the fiber” wrong here? A 28-year-old woman has had two episodes of monocular vision loss that resolved over weeks, and MRI now shows multifocal…
back: Oligodendrocytes insulate; they do not pump the signal. Slowing after demyelination reflects loss of saltatory node-to-node renewal.
extra: Glia are being given an active propulsive role they do not have.

front: Why is “Amplification of action-potential peak voltage at each segment” wrong here? A 28-year-old woman has had two episodes of monocular vision loss that resolved over weeks, and MRI now shows multifocal…
back: Action potentials are all-or-none at a fixed peak; nodes renew the same amplitude rather than amplifying it, and demyelination slows by breaking saltatory jump.
extra: All-or-none spikes are being treated as size-adjustable amplifiers.

front:
A 23-year-old graduate student records from a postsynaptic cell contacted by three presynaptic neurons, each synapsing at a different site and each alone producing a depolarization too small to reach threshold.

When all three fire simultaneously, their combined input brings the axon hillock to threshold and an action potential fires. This integration is best described as which of the following?
back: Spatial summation of graded potentials arriving from separate locations
extra: Spatial summation combines graded potentials generated at different locations on the neuron at the same time; their voltages add at the axon hillock and can reach threshold.

front: Why is “Temporal summation of graded potentials from one repeated input” wrong here? A 23-year-old graduate student records from a postsynaptic cell contacted by three presynaptic neurons, each synapsing a…
back: Temporal summation is the adding of successive signals from the same input separated in time; three different presynaptic cells firing at three sites is spatial summation.
extra: The single-site, time-separated pattern is being applied to a multi-site event.

front: Why is “Frequency coding of signal intensity by the presynaptic cells” wrong here? A 23-year-old graduate student records from a postsynaptic cell contacted by three presynaptic neurons, each synapsing a…
back: Frequency coding describes how a stronger stimulus raises firing rate in one neuron; threshold here was reached because several simultaneous, spatially separated inputs summed.
extra: The rate code for stimulus strength is being confused with input integration.

front: Why is “Saltatory propagation of the graded potentials between the sites” wrong here? A 23-year-old graduate student records from a postsynaptic cell contacted by three presynaptic neurons, each synapsing a…
back: Saltatory conduction describes action potentials jumping between nodes of Ranvier; graded potentials simply spread and add, and their combination across sites is spatial summation.
extra: A conduction mode of myelinated axons is being invoked at the dendrites.

front:
During a physical examination of a 40-year-old woman, a tap on the patellar ligament produces an immediate kick of the lower leg.

Within this reflex, the afferent signal from the muscle spindle reaches the spinal cord and then does which of the following?
back: Synapses directly on the ventral horn motor neuron supplying the same muscle
extra: The muscle-spindle afferent enters through the dorsal root and synapses directly on the ventral horn motor neuron that activates the stretched muscle, causing contraction; a collateral branch also inhibits the antagonist's motor neuron via an interneuron.

front: Why is “Ascends to the motor cortex, which then commands the muscle to extend the leg” wrong here? During a physical examination of a 40-year-old woman, a tap on the patellar ligament produces an immediate kick of the l…
back: The knee-jerk is a spinal reflex that does not require the brain; the afferent synapses on the motor neuron in the ventral horn, which is why the response is immediate.
extra: A spinal reflex is being routed through the cerebrum.

front: Why is “Relays through a chain of dorsal horn interneurons before reaching any motor neuron” wrong here? During a physical examination of a 40-year-old woman, a tap on the patellar ligament produces an immediate kick of the l…
back: Multi-interneuron arcs describe withdrawal reflexes; the stretch reflex's defining feature is the single synapse from spindle afferent to ventral horn motor neuron.
extra: A polysynaptic withdrawal pattern is being substituted for the monosynaptic stretch reflex.

front: Why is “Activates Golgi tendon organs, which drive the contraction instead” wrong here? During a physical examination of a 40-year-old woman, a tap on the patellar ligament produces an immediate kick of the l…
back: Golgi tendon organs sense tension and inhibit the homonymous muscle (the inverse stretch reflex); the tapped patellar ligament stretches the quadriceps spindle, which excites its own motor neuron.
extra: A different receptor with the opposite protective action is being invoked.

front: Which of the following sudden symptom pairs should make a bystander suspect a stroke?
back: Trouble walking with loss of balance
extra: The CDC lists sudden trouble walking and sudden loss of balance or coordination among the warning signs of stroke.

front: Why is “Sneezing with itchy eyes” wrong here? Which of the following sudden symptom pairs should make a bystander suspect a stroke?
back: Sneezing and itchy eyes do not match the CDC warning signs of sudden trouble walking, balance loss, or trouble seeing.
extra: An allergic symptom pair is being mistaken for an abrupt neurologic deficit.

front: Why is “Heartburn with belching” wrong here? Which of the following sudden symptom pairs should make a bystander suspect a stroke?
back: The cited stroke warning signs concern sudden walking, balance, coordination, or vision problems rather than heartburn and belching.
extra: A gastrointestinal symptom pair is being substituted for a neurologic warning pattern.

front: Why is “Knee soreness with stair climbing” wrong here? Which of the following sudden symptom pairs should make a bystander suspect a stroke?
back: The CDC describes sudden trouble walking and balance loss, not predictable knee soreness during stair climbing.
extra: Activity-related joint discomfort is being confused with sudden neurologic dysfunction.

front: During a B.E. F.A.S.T. check, both arms are raised and one arm drifts downward. Which of the following interpretations is most appropriate?
back: This is a stroke warning sign; call 9-1-1
extra: One arm drifting downward is the arm finding in the CDC B.E. F.A.S.T. check. Seeing this sign should prompt an immediate emergency call.

front: Why is “This excludes stroke because both arms moved” wrong here? During a B.E. F.A.S.T. check, both arms are raised and one arm drifts downward. Which of the following interpretations i…
back: The CDC specifically identifies one arm drifting downward during the arm test as a stroke warning sign.
extra: Any movement is being treated as reassurance despite asymmetric arm drift.

front: Why is “This matters only when both arms drift” wrong here? During a B.E. F.A.S.T. check, both arms are raised and one arm drifts downward. Which of the following interpretations i…
back: The cited B.E. F.A.S.T. test asks whether one arm drifts downward; bilateral drift is not required.
extra: The one-sided nature of the warning sign is being reversed.

front: Why is “This is reassuring if speech remains clear” wrong here? During a B.E. F.A.S.T. check, both arms are raised and one arm drifts downward. Which of the following interpretations i…
back: The CDC directs action when any of the listed face, arm, or speech signs is present, not only when all appear together.
extra: One normal component is being used to dismiss a different positive stroke sign.

front: A person suddenly develops one-sided facial weakness and trouble speaking. Which of the following actions should a nearby person take?
back: Call emergency services right away
extra: Sudden unilateral facial weakness and trouble speaking are stroke warning signs. The CDC directs bystanders to call emergency services right away.

front: Why is “Offer water and watch for improvement” wrong here? A person suddenly develops one-sided facial weakness and trouble speaking. Which of the following actions should a nearb…
back: The CDC advises calling emergency services right away rather than waiting to see whether sudden stroke symptoms improve.
extra: Observation is being chosen despite a time-sensitive stroke warning pattern.

front: Why is “Ask the person to sleep briefly” wrong here? A person suddenly develops one-sided facial weakness and trouble speaking. Which of the following actions should a nearb…
back: Sleep delays emergency evaluation; the cited action for sudden one-sided weakness or speech trouble is an immediate emergency call.
extra: Rest is being substituted for urgent assessment of sudden focal neurologic symptoms.

front: Why is “Arrange a routine clinic visit later” wrong here? A person suddenly develops one-sided facial weakness and trouble speaking. Which of the following actions should a nearb…
back: A later appointment is inappropriate for this sudden pattern; the cited response is to call emergency services immediately.
extra: A routine timeline is being applied to an acute neurologic emergency.
