front: Why is “Respiratory acidosis following carbon dioxide retention” wrong here? A 33-year-old patient has repeated vomiting. Testing shows a blood pH of 7.51 and an elevated bicarbonate concentration.…
back: Carbon dioxide retention shifts the blood toward acidosis. It cannot explain the primary high-pH, high-bicarbonate disturbance following loss of gastric hydrochloric acid.
extra: Uses carbon dioxide retention and respiratory acidosis to explain a primary high-pH disturbance.

front: An adult has generalized edema, marked proteinuria, and hypoalbuminemia due to glomerular disease. Which of the following additional laboratory findings is characteristic of nephrotic syndrome?
back: Elevated serum cholesterol
extra: Nephrotic syndrome commonly includes elevated cholesterol and other circulating lipids.

front: Why is “Reduced serum complement C3” wrong here? An adult has generalized edema, marked proteinuria, and hypoalbuminemia due to glomerular disease. Which of the followin…
back: Low complement can support selected immune-complex glomerulonephritides but is not a characteristic component of nephrotic syndrome.
extra: A complement-consuming nephritic process is being confused with the defining nephrotic laboratory pattern.

front: Why is “Urinary red blood cell casts” wrong here? An adult has generalized edema, marked proteinuria, and hypoalbuminemia due to glomerular disease. Which of the followin…
back: Red blood cell casts indicate glomerular inflammation and a nephritic sediment rather than the characteristic nephrotic laboratory constellation.
extra: A nephritic urine-sediment finding is being substituted for the nephrotic lipid abnormality.

front: Why is “Circulating anti-GBM antibodies” wrong here? An adult has generalized edema, marked proteinuria, and hypoalbuminemia due to glomerular disease. Which of the followin…
back: Anti-GBM antibodies support anti-glomerular-basement-membrane disease, not the characteristic nephrotic lipid pattern.
extra: A disease-specific marker of rapidly progressive nephritis is being mistaken for a general nephrotic finding.

front: A 7-year-old child has periorbital edema, 4+ protein on urine dipstick, and a serum albumin concentration of 2.0 g/dL. Which of the following mechanisms most directly accounts for the hypoalbuminemia?
back: Urinary albumin loss through a damaged glomerular filtration barrier
extra: Damage to the glomerular filtration barrier permits albumin and other plasma proteins to pass from blood into urine, producing heavy proteinuria and lowering the serum albumin concentration.

front: Why is “Reduced albumin synthesis by hepatocytes without urinary protein loss” wrong here? A 7-year-old child has periorbital edema, 4+ protein on urine dipstick, and a serum albumin concentration of 2.0 g/dL. W…
back: Severe liver dysfunction can reduce albumin synthesis, but the marked proteinuria here identifies urinary protein loss.
extra: A hepatic cause of hypoalbuminemia is being selected despite direct evidence of renal protein loss.

front: Why is “Accelerated systemic albumin catabolism without urinary protein loss” wrong here? A 7-year-old child has periorbital edema, 4+ protein on urine dipstick, and a serum albumin concentration of 2.0 g/dL. W…
back: The renal findings directly support urinary protein loss rather than accelerated albumin breakdown elsewhere in the body.
extra: General protein catabolism is being substituted for the glomerular leak demonstrated by the urinalysis.

front: Why is “Gastrointestinal albumin loss from protein-losing enteropathy” wrong here? A 7-year-old child has periorbital edema, 4+ protein on urine dipstick, and a serum albumin concentration of 2.0 g/dL. W…
back: Intestinal protein loss can lower albumin, but it does not explain this child's marked urinary protein finding.
extra: Protein-losing enteropathy is being selected even though the vignette localizes protein loss to the kidney.

front:
A 64-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has chronic CO2 retention. Arterial blood shows pH 7.34, elevated pCO2, and a bicarbonate concentration above the normal range.

His elevated bicarbonate most directly reflects which of the following?
back: Renal compensation raising bicarbonate to offset carbonic acid
extra: In respiratory acidosis, excess CO2 is present; bicarbonate is normal at first, but with renal compensation it increases to reestablish the proper bicarbonate-to-carbonic-acid ratio — a large-capacity response that takes minutes to hours.

front: Why is “Hyperventilation that converts carbonic acid into bicarbonate” wrong here? A 64-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has chronic CO2 retention. Arterial blood shows pH 7…
back: His lungs cannot blow off the CO2 load — that is the primary problem; the compensation comes from the kidneys raising bicarbonate, not from breathing.
extra: A ventilatory fix is being proposed for a patient whose defect is ventilatory.

front: Why is “Bone buffering that releases bicarbonate within seconds” wrong here? A 64-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has chronic CO2 retention. Arterial blood shows pH 7…
back: Chemical buffers act within fractions of a second but with limited capacity; the sustained rise in bicarbonate with chronic CO2 retention is renal compensation.
extra: A rapid buffer is being credited with a sustained compensatory change.

front: Why is “Increased aldosterone causing bicarbonate loss in the urine” wrong here? A 64-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has chronic CO2 retention. Arterial blood shows pH 7…
back: Compensation requires gaining, not losing, bicarbonate; the kidneys increase bicarbonate generation and hydrogen-ion secretion during respiratory acidosis.
extra: Bicarbonate loss could not explain an elevated blood level, and aldosterone is not the compensatory driver.

front:
A 22-year-old woman with central diabetes insipidus produces large volumes of dilute urine because her posterior pituitary fails to release antidiuretic hormone (ADH).

At the cellular level, her collecting duct principal cells fail to perform which of the following actions?
back: Insert aquaporin water channels into their apical membranes
extra: Stimulated by ADH, aquaporin channels are inserted into the apical membrane of principal cells lining the collecting ducts; with less ADH, fewer channels are inserted and less water is recovered, producing dilute urine.

front: Why is “Synthesize Na+/K+ ATPase pumps for their basal membranes” wrong here? A 22-year-old woman with central diabetes insipidus produces large volumes of dilute urine because her posterior pituita…
back: Aldosterone drives principal cells to manufacture sodium channels, potassium channels, and Na+/K+ ATPase pumps; ADH controls aquaporin insertion instead.
extra: Aldosterone's action is being attributed to ADH.

front: Why is “Secrete hydrogen ions through apical proton pumps” wrong here? A 22-year-old woman with central diabetes insipidus produces large volumes of dilute urine because her posterior pituita…
back: Proton secretion is the work of intercalated cells regulating blood pH; principal cells respond to ADH by inserting aquaporin channels for water recovery.
extra: Intercalated-cell acid handling is being attributed to principal cells.

front: Why is “Actively pump sodium from the tubular fluid into the medullary interstitium” wrong here? A 22-year-old woman with central diabetes insipidus produces large volumes of dilute urine because her posterior pituita…
back: Collecting duct water recovery is osmotic and passive through aquaporins; ADH does not switch on salt pumps — it inserts water channels.
extra: The ascending limb's salt extrusion is being assigned to the collecting duct.

front: Which of the following hormones is released from the posterior pituitary when plasma osmolality rises?
back: Vasopressin from the posterior pituitary
extra: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect rising plasma osmolality and signal release of vasopressin (ADH) from the posterior pituitary to conserve water.

front: Why is “Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex” wrong here? Which of the following hormones is released from the posterior pituitary when plasma osmolality rises?
back: Aldosterone acts on principal cells for sodium retention; the osmolality-triggered posterior-pituitary release is ADH.
extra: A sodium-retaining cortical steroid is being substituted for the water-retaining peptide.

front: Why is “Atrial natriuretic peptide from the atria” wrong here? Which of the following hormones is released from the posterior pituitary when plasma osmolality rises?
back: ANP responds to atrial stretch; rising osmolality triggers hypothalamic osmoreceptors to release ADH from the posterior pituitary.
extra: A volume-overload natriuretic peptide is being treated as the high-osmolality response.

front: Why is “Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary” wrong here? Which of the following hormones is released from the posterior pituitary when plasma osmolality rises?
back: Oxytocin drives uterine contraction and milk ejection; the osmolality-response peptide is ADH.
extra: The neighboring posterior-pituitary peptide is being confused with ADH.

front:
A 45-year-old man with primary hyperaldosteronism has hypertension and a low serum potassium concentration.

His elevated aldosterone acts on principal cells of the collecting duct to produce which of the following changes?
back: More sodium and potassium channels plus more Na+/K+ ATPase pumps
extra: Aldosterone stimulates principal cells to manufacture luminal Na+ and K+ channels and basal Na+/K+ ATPase pumps; more Na+ is recovered (with water following) while more K+ is pumped into the forming urine, explaining his hypertension and hypokalemia.

front:
Why is “Fewer sodium channels, so less sodium and water are recovered” wrong here? A 45-year-old man with primary hyperaldosteronism has hypertension and a low serum potassium concentration.

His elevate…
back: Aldosterone increases, not decreases, sodium-channel production; excess aldosterone therefore expands volume (hypertension) rather than shrinking it.
extra: The hormone's effect on sodium handling is being stated backward.

front:
Why is “Insertion of aquaporin water channels into the apical membrane” wrong here? A 45-year-old man with primary hyperaldosteronism has hypertension and a low serum potassium concentration.

His elevate…
back: Aquaporin insertion is controlled by ADH; aldosterone builds sodium/potassium channels and pumps, and water then follows the recovered sodium passively.
extra: ADH's signature action is being attributed to aldosterone.

front:
Why is “Suppression of potassium secretion, conserving serum potassium” wrong here? A 45-year-old man with primary hyperaldosteronism has hypertension and a low serum potassium concentration.

His elevate…
back: Aldosterone promotes potassium loss: as the Na+/K+ pump recovers Na+, K+ moves the opposite way into the forming urine, which is why hyperaldosteronism causes hypokalemia.
extra: The direction of potassium handling is being reversed.

front: Because renal tubule cells are impermeable to bicarbonate, filtered bicarbonate is recovered primarily by converting it to which molecule that can enter the cell?
back: Carbon dioxide
extra: Filtered bicarbonate reacts to form carbonic acid, which yields CO2 that enters the cell; intracellular carbonic anhydrase regenerates bicarbonate for return to blood while H+ is secreted.

front: Why is “Ammonia” wrong here? Because renal tubule cells are impermeable to bicarbonate, filtered bicarbonate is recovered primarily by converting it …
back: Ammonia buffers secreted H+ in the collecting duct during chronic acidosis; proximal bicarbonate conservation uses the CO2/carbonic anhydrase pathway.
extra: A buffer used in chronic acid excretion is being confused with proximal bicarbonate recovery.

front: Why is “Phosphate” wrong here? Because renal tubule cells are impermeable to bicarbonate, filtered bicarbonate is recovered primarily by converting it …
back: Phosphate buffers filtered H+ in the urine; bicarbonate reabsorption depends on CO2 entry and intracellular regeneration.
extra: A titratable acid buffer is being substituted for the primary bicarbonate recovery intermediate.

front: Why is “Urea” wrong here? Because renal tubule cells are impermeable to bicarbonate, filtered bicarbonate is recovered primarily by converting it …
back: Urea contributes to medullary tonicity but plays no role in proximal bicarbonate reabsorption via carbonic anhydrase.
extra: A medullary osmole is being confused with an acid-base intermediate.

front:
In the proximal tubule, filtered bicarbonate cannot cross the apical membrane directly.

After carbon dioxide enters the cell, carbonic anhydrase catalyzes which of the following paired ion movements that together return bicarbonate to the blood?
back: Luminal hydrogen ion secretion with basolateral bicarbonate exit to blood
extra: After CO2 enters the cell, carbonic anhydrase forms carbonic acid, which dissociates; bicarbonate exits basolaterally to the blood and hydrogen ions are secreted apically, conserving filtered bicarbonate indirectly.

front:
Why is “Direct bicarbonate channel reabsorption without any hydrogen ion secretion” wrong here? In the proximal tubule, filtered bicarbonate cannot cross the apical membrane directly.

After carbon dioxide enters the…
back: Tubule cells are not permeable to bicarbonate; recovery requires the carbonic anhydrase-coupled H+ secretion pathway.
extra: A direct channel is being proposed despite tubule impermeability to bicarbonate.

front:
Why is “Luminal bicarbonate secretion with hydrogen ion absorption from filtrate” wrong here? In the proximal tubule, filtered bicarbonate cannot cross the apical membrane directly.

After carbon dioxide enters the…
back: Bicarbonate is returned to the blood, not secreted; H+ moves into the lumen to titrate filtered bicarbonate.
extra: The direction of ion movement is reversed.

front:
Why is “Luminal bicarbonate-for-chloride exchange without carbonic anhydrase activity” wrong here? In the proximal tubule, filtered bicarbonate cannot cross the apical membrane directly.

After carbon dioxide enters the…
back: The canonical proximal mechanism uses carbonic anhydrase to convert CO2 to bicarbonate inside the cell; direct bicarbonate exchange is not the primary route.
extra: A chloride-bicarbonate exchanger is being proposed without the required enzymatic step.

front:
A 58-year-old man is treated with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and develops a mild metabolic acidosis with an alkaline urine. In the untreated kidney, filtered bicarbonate is recovered even though tubule cells are impermeable to it.

Which of the following sequences most directly describes this recovery?
back: Filtered bicarbonate becomes luminal CO2, which cells convert back to bicarbonate for the blood
extra: Tubule cells are not permeable to bicarbonate, so it is conserved indirectly: when CO2 is available, carbonic acid forms and dissociates; the bicarbonate ion passes into the peritubular capillaries while the hydrogen ion is secreted into the filtrate — the reaction the inhibitor blocks.

front: Why is “Bicarbonate crosses the apical membrane directly through a dedicated channel” wrong here? A 58-year-old man is treated with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and develops a mild metabolic acidosis with an alkaline…
back: The tubule cells are not permeable to bicarbonate; it is conserved by intracellular regeneration via carbonic acid chemistry, not by direct channel-mediated uptake.
extra: A direct channel is being proposed for an ion the membrane cannot pass.

front: Why is “The ascending limb uses carbonic anhydrase to pump bicarbonate into the interstitium” wrong here? A 58-year-old man is treated with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and develops a mild metabolic acidosis with an alkaline…
back: The ascending limb extrudes Na+ to build the medullary gradient; bicarbonate conservation occurs through the proximal tubule's carbonic anhydrase-coupled mechanism.
extra: The loop's salt extrusion is being extended to an acid-base solute.

front: Why is “Aldosterone stimulates principal cells to absorb bicarbonate with potassium” wrong here? A 58-year-old man is treated with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and develops a mild metabolic acidosis with an alkaline…
back: Aldosterone regulates sodium recovery and potassium secretion; bicarbonate is conserved by the carbonic anhydrase mechanism that trades secreted H+ for regenerated bicarbonate.
extra: The mineralocorticoid's Na+/K+ program is being applied to acid handling.

front: Which of the following best describes symptoms during the early stages of chronic kidney disease (CKD)?
back: Symptoms can remain absent until the condition is advanced
extra: Many people have no symptoms during early CKD and may remain unaware of symptoms until the disease is advanced.

front: Why is “Symptoms begin with severe pain over both kidneys” wrong here? Which of the following best describes symptoms during the early stages of chronic kidney disease (CKD)?
back: The cited NIDDK passage emphasizes that early CKD can be clinically quiet rather than beginning with severe kidney pain.
extra: Kidney disease is being treated as a condition that must announce itself with pain.

front: Why is “Symptoms first appear as sudden loss of vision” wrong here? Which of the following best describes symptoms during the early stages of chronic kidney disease (CKD)?
back: Sudden visual loss is not the early pattern described in the cited CKD passage; many people have no early symptoms.
extra: An unrelated acute symptom is being substituted for the often-silent early course of CKD.

front: Why is “Symptoms reliably identify disease before filtration changes” wrong here? Which of the following best describes symptoms during the early stages of chronic kidney disease (CKD)?
back: Early CKD may produce no symptoms, so symptoms do not reliably announce the disease before it becomes advanced.
extra: Symptoms are being assumed to provide an early warning before kidney dysfunction develops.

front: Which of the following retained pairs most directly contributes to edema in chronic kidney disease?
back: Extra fluid and salt
extra: When damaged kidneys cannot remove extra fluid and salt, those retained substances contribute directly to edema.

front: Why is “Glucose and insulin” wrong here? Which of the following retained pairs most directly contributes to edema in chronic kidney disease?
back: The cited CKD passage links edema to impaired removal of fluid and salt, not retention of glucose and insulin.
extra: Glucose regulation is being substituted for the kidney's role in volume and salt balance.

front: Why is “Calcium and vitamin D” wrong here? Which of the following retained pairs most directly contributes to edema in chronic kidney disease?
back: This pair does not match the passage's direct explanation for CKD-related edema: failure to remove extra fluid and salt.
extra: Mineral metabolism is being confused with the retained substances that directly expand body fluid.

front: Why is “Oxygen and carbon dioxide” wrong here? Which of the following retained pairs most directly contributes to edema in chronic kidney disease?
back: Oxygen and carbon dioxide are respiratory gases; the cited renal explanation is retention of extra fluid and salt.
extra: Respiratory gas exchange is being substituted for renal fluid handling.

front:
A 70-year-old woman with advanced chronic kidney disease develops a normocytic anemia that improves with injections of recombinant erythropoietin.

Her native deficiency arose because the failing kidneys are normally responsible for which of the following?
back: Producing the majority of the body's erythropoietin
extra: Eighty-five percent of the erythropoietin produced to stimulate red blood cell production is made in the kidneys; failing kidneys therefore cause an anemia that exogenous erythropoietin can replace.

front: Why is “Synthesizing the heme moiety incorporated into hemoglobin” wrong here? A 70-year-old woman with advanced chronic kidney disease develops a normocytic anemia that improves with injections of r…
back: Heme synthesis occurs in developing erythroid cells and the liver; the kidney's contribution to red-cell production is the hormone erythropoietin.
extra: A bone-marrow/liver biosynthetic pathway is being assigned to the kidney.

front: Why is “Secreting thrombopoietin, the marrow hormone parallel to erythropoietin” wrong here? A 70-year-old woman with advanced chronic kidney disease develops a normocytic anemia that improves with injections of r…
back: Thrombopoietin comes mainly from the liver and acts on platelets; the kidney supplies erythropoietin for the erythroid line.
extra: The platelet lineage hormone, made by the liver, is being confused with the red-cell hormone.

front: Why is “Storing iron as ferritin for later release to the marrow” wrong here? A 70-year-old woman with advanced chronic kidney disease develops a normocytic anemia that improves with injections of r…
back: Iron stores reside mainly in the liver and macrophages; renal anemia of chronic kidney disease reflects lost erythropoietin production, not iron storage.
extra: The liver's iron-storage role is being moved to the kidney.

front: A 70-kg healthy 25-year-old man has about 42 liters of total body water. Which of the following best estimates the distribution of this water between his intracellular fluid and his plasma?
back: About 25 liters intracellular and about 3 liters as plasma
extra: The ICF holds about 60 percent of total body water (~25 L here). The ECF holds the remaining third (~17 L), and only about 20 percent of the ECF is plasma (~3 L), the rest being interstitial fluid.

front: Why is “About 17 liters intracellular and about 8 liters as plasma” wrong here? A 70-kg healthy 25-year-old man has about 42 liters of total body water. Which of the following best estimates the distr…
back: The larger share is intracellular (about 60 percent), and plasma is only a fifth of the extracellular third — far less than 8 liters.
extra: The two compartments' shares are being swapped and plasma overestimated.

front: Why is “About 25 liters intracellular and about 17 liters as plasma” wrong here? A 70-kg healthy 25-year-old man has about 42 liters of total body water. Which of the following best estimates the distr…
back: The 17-liter extracellular volume is mostly interstitial fluid; plasma is only about 20 percent of the ECF, roughly 3 liters.
extra: The whole extracellular compartment is being counted as plasma.

front: Why is “About 10 liters intracellular and about 10 liters as plasma” wrong here? A 70-kg healthy 25-year-old man has about 42 liters of total body water. Which of the following best estimates the distr…
back: Body water is not evenly divided: the ICF predominates at about 60 percent, while plasma is a small fraction (about 20 percent) of the extracellular third.
extra: The compartments are being split evenly, contrary to their measured proportions.

front: Which of the following properties of the glomerular capillary wall most selectively restricts negatively charged plasma proteins?
back: Fixed negative charges on the capillary wall
extra: The glomerular barrier carries fixed negative charges that electrostatically restrict passage of negatively charged plasma proteins while permitting water and small solutes.

front: Why is “Fenestrations in the capillary endothelium that admit only cells, not fluid” wrong here? Which of the following properties of the glomerular capillary wall most selectively restricts negatively charged plasma …
back: Fenestrae allow plasma fluid and small solutes; charge selectivity against proteins comes mainly from negatively charged barrier elements.
extra: Endothelial fenestrae are being described as cell-only pores.

front: Why is “Positive charges that attract albumin into the filtrate” wrong here? Which of the following properties of the glomerular capillary wall most selectively restricts negatively charged plasma …
back: A positively charged barrier would favor albumin filtration; the real barrier is anionic and restricts albumin.
extra: The barrier polarity is being reversed.

front: Why is “Active tubular secretion of albumin in the PCT” wrong here? Which of the following properties of the glomerular capillary wall most selectively restricts negatively charged plasma …
back: Albumin is normally kept out of the filtrate by the glomerular barrier; PCT handling is not the primary charge-selective gate.
extra: A tubular process is being substituted for glomerular restriction.

front:
A 34-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome loses large amounts of albumin in his urine. In a healthy kidney, albumin is nearly excluded from the filtrate even though its molecular size is close to the filtration limit.

Which of the following properties of the filtration membrane most contributes to this selective exclusion of albumin?
back: Pore-associated proteins carry a negative charge that repels anionic molecules
extra: The proteins associated with the filtration pores are negatively charged, so they tend to repel negatively charged substances and allow positively charged substances to pass more readily; albumin carries a negative charge and is repelled.

front: Why is “Mesangial cells actively phagocytose albumin from the passing filtrate” wrong here? A 34-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome loses large amounts of albumin in his urine. In a healthy kidney, albumin is n…
back: Mesangial cells contract to regulate the rate of filtration; the charge-based repulsion of anionic proteins is what excludes albumin.
extra: A contractile regulatory cell is being assigned a scavenging role.

front: Why is “Fenestrations bind albumin with high-affinity transmembrane receptors” wrong here? A 34-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome loses large amounts of albumin in his urine. In a healthy kidney, albumin is n…
back: Fenestrations filter primarily by size and do not bind specific solutes; albumin exclusion additionally depends on electrostatic repulsion by negatively charged pore proteins.
extra: Passive pores are being given a receptor-mediated uptake function.

front: Why is “Podocyte foot processes fuse into an impermeable lipid sheet over each capillary” wrong here? A 34-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome loses large amounts of albumin in his urine. In a healthy kidney, albumin is n…
back: Podocyte pedicels interdigitate to form filtration slits, not a sealed sheet; molecules cross by size and charge, with charge repelling anions such as albumin.
extra: The slit architecture is being described as sealed.

front:
A researcher measures glomerular filtration rate in a healthy 27-year-old volunteer by infusing inulin and tracking its urinary appearance.

Inulin is the reference marker for this measurement because it has which of the following properties?
back: It is filtered freely but neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the nephron
extra: Inulin is a plant polysaccharide that is neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the kidney, so its appearance in the urine is directly proportional to the rate at which it is filtered by the renal corpuscle.

front: Why is “It binds plasma proteins, restricting it to the vascular compartment” wrong here? A researcher measures glomerular filtration rate in a healthy 27-year-old volunteer by infusing inulin and tracking its …
back: A GFR marker must be freely filtered, so it cannot be protein-bound; inulin filters freely and then undergoes no tubular handling.
extra: Protein binding would prevent filtration entirely, the opposite of the required behavior.

front: Why is “It is filtered and then fully reabsorbed in the proximal tubule” wrong here? A researcher measures glomerular filtration rate in a healthy 27-year-old volunteer by infusing inulin and tracking its …
back: Full reabsorption (as with glucose) removes the marker from the urine; inulin works precisely because none of its filtered load is recovered or added to.
extra: A substance returned to the blood cannot report filtration in the urine.

front: Why is “It is secreted by the tubules in proportion to renal blood flow” wrong here? A researcher measures glomerular filtration rate in a healthy 27-year-old volunteer by infusing inulin and tracking its …
back: Tubular secretion would add marker beyond the filtered amount, breaking the proportionality with GFR; inulin is not secreted.
extra: A secretion-based flow marker is being confused with a filtration marker.

front: Which of the following nephron segments is impermeable to water while actively extruding sodium into the medullary interstitium?
back: Ascending limb of the loop of Henle in the medulla
extra: The ascending limb is impermeable to water yet actively pumps Na+ into the interstitium, creating the hyperosmotic medulla of the countercurrent multiplier.

front: Why is “Proximal convoluted tubule in the renal cortex” wrong here? Which of the following nephron segments is impermeable to water while actively extruding sodium into the medullary inter…
back: The proximal tubule reabsorbs most filtered solute and water isosmotically; the medullary gradient is built in the loop of Henle.
extra: The bulk reabsorption site is being assigned the countercurrent multiplier role.

front: Why is “Descending limb of the loop of Henle in the medulla” wrong here? Which of the following nephron segments is impermeable to water while actively extruding sodium into the medullary inter…
back: The descending limb is freely water-permeable via aquaporins and loses water to the interstitium; it does not actively extrude sodium.
extra: The water-permeable limb is being confused with the salt-pumping limb.

front: Why is “Distal convoluted tubule in the renal cortex” wrong here? Which of the following nephron segments is impermeable to water while actively extruding sodium into the medullary inter…
back: The distal tubule adjusts sodium under aldosterone control but does not generate the medullary osmolar gradient.
extra: A downstream fine-tuning segment is being assigned the gradient-building role.

front:
A 55-year-old man with heart failure is started on furosemide and later reports polyuria with urine that remains dilute despite dehydration. Laboratory studies show hyponatremia and hypokalemia.

Blockade of which of the following transport processes most directly explains his inability to generate a concentrated medullary gradient?
back: Na+/K+/2Cl− cotransport in the thick ascending limb
extra: Furosemide blocks the Na+/K+/2Cl− cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, preventing Na+ extrusion into the interstitium and dissipating the hyperosmotic medulla needed for water reabsorption under ADH.

front: Why is “Aquaporin-2 insertion in the collecting duct” wrong here? A 55-year-old man with heart failure is started on furosemide and later reports polyuria with urine that remains dilute …
back: ADH regulates collecting-duct aquaporins, but without a medullary gradient even open channels cannot reclaim much water; loop diuretics act upstream on salt pumping.
extra: The downstream water channel is being blamed instead of the gradient generator.

front: Why is “Na+/H+ exchange in the proximal tubule” wrong here? A 55-year-old man with heart failure is started on furosemide and later reports polyuria with urine that remains dilute …
back: Proximal Na+/H+ exchange reclaims filtered bicarbonate; it does not generate the medullary osmolar gradient blocked by loop diuretics.
extra: Proximal acid-base transport is being substituted for the countercurrent multiplier.

front: Why is “Epithelial sodium channels in principal cells” wrong here? A 55-year-old man with heart failure is started on furosemide and later reports polyuria with urine that remains dilute …
back: Principal-cell ENaC reabsorbs sodium distally; loop diuretics act on the thick ascending limb, not the collecting duct.
extra: Aldosterone-regulated distal reabsorption is being confused with the loop mechanism.

front:
A 30-year-old man becomes dehydrated during a desert trek, and his kidneys produce a small volume of highly concentrated urine. The ability to concentrate urine depends on a hyperosmolar renal medulla.

Which of the following properties of the loop of Henle most directly builds this medullary gradient?
back: The ascending limb extrudes sodium while remaining impermeable to water
extra: The ascending limb is completely impermeable to water (no aquaporins) yet actively pumps Na+ into the interstitium; the movement of Na+ and urea into the interstitial spaces creates the hyperosmotic environment of the medulla.

front: Why is “The vasa recta rapidly wash solutes out of the medullary interstitium” wrong here? A 30-year-old man becomes dehydrated during a desert trek, and his kidneys produce a small volume of highly concentrated…
back: Slow flow in the vasa recta preserves the osmolar gradient while recovering solutes and water; rapid washout would dissipate the medullary hyperosmolarity.
extra: The gradient-preserving vessel is being described as gradient-destroying.

front: Why is “The collecting duct pumps sodium against its gradient under ADH control” wrong here? A 30-year-old man becomes dehydrated during a desert trek, and his kidneys produce a small volume of highly concentrated…
back: ADH regulates water channels, not the salt pumping that builds the gradient; the multiplier is generated by the ascending limb (with urea from the collecting duct).
extra: The site of medullary solute deposition is being misassigned.

front: Why is “The descending limb is impermeable to water, trapping solute in the lumen” wrong here? A 30-year-old man becomes dehydrated during a desert trek, and his kidneys produce a small volume of highly concentrated…
back: The descending limb is freely water-permeable via permanent aquaporins; it is the ascending limb that is impermeable to water while extruding Na+.
extra: The water permeabilities of the two limbs are being reversed.

front:
A 4-year-old boy is being toilet trained.

His micturition reflex, triggered when bladder stretch receptors signal the sacral spinal cord, produces voiding through which of the following effector responses?
back: Parasympathetic outflow contracts the detrusor, relaxing the internal sphincter
extra: Bladder stretch receptors trigger a sacral spinal reflex whose parasympathetic outflow contracts the detrusor muscle and relaxes the involuntary internal urethral sphincter, while somatic motor neurons to the external sphincter are inhibited.

front:
Why is “Sympathetic outflow contracts the detrusor and closes the external sphincter” wrong here? A 4-year-old boy is being toilet trained.

His micturition reflex, triggered when bladder stretch receptors signal the s…
back: Sympathetic activity via the hypogastric nerves suppresses detrusor contraction during filling; voiding is a parasympathetic event with sphincter relaxation.
extra: The filling-phase autonomic pattern is being applied to voiding.

front:
Why is “Cortical inhibition of the sacral micturition center” wrong here? A 4-year-old boy is being toilet trained.

His micturition reflex, triggered when bladder stretch receptors signal the s…
back: Higher centers delay voiding by holding the external sphincter; the reflex being trained away is the parasympathetic detrusor contraction with sphincter relaxation.
extra: The learned override is being confused with the reflex itself.

front:
Why is “Stretch-activated contraction of the abdominal wall muscles” wrong here? A 4-year-old boy is being toilet trained.

His micturition reflex, triggered when bladder stretch receptors signal the s…
back: Abdominal contraction can raise intra-abdominal pressure to aid emptying, but the reflex arc itself runs through sacral parasympathetic outflow to the detrusor and internal sphincter.
extra: A voluntary assist maneuver is being named as the reflex mechanism.

front:
A physiologist measures pressures across the glomerular capillaries of a healthy 28-year-old woman: glomerular blood hydrostatic pressure 55 mm Hg, capsular hydrostatic pressure 15 mm Hg, and blood colloid osmotic pressure 30 mm Hg.

Which of the following is her net filtration pressure?
back: 10 mm Hg favoring filtration
extra: Net filtration pressure equals glomerular blood hydrostatic pressure minus the sum of capsular hydrostatic pressure and blood colloid osmotic pressure: 55 − (15 + 30) = 10 mm Hg, driving fluid into Bowman's space.

front: Why is “40 mm Hg favoring filtration” wrong here? A physiologist measures pressures across the glomerular capillaries of a healthy 28-year-old woman: glomerular blood hyd…
back: Subtracting only the capsular hydrostatic pressure gives 40 mm Hg, but the blood colloid osmotic pressure also opposes filtration and must be subtracted as well.
extra: Only the capsular pressure was subtracted; the osmotic force was ignored.

front: Why is “25 mm Hg favoring filtration” wrong here? A physiologist measures pressures across the glomerular capillaries of a healthy 28-year-old woman: glomerular blood hyd…
back: Subtracting only the osmotic pressure gives 25 mm Hg; both the capsular hydrostatic and the colloid osmotic pressures oppose filtration and must both be subtracted.
extra: Only the colloid osmotic pressure was subtracted; the capsular pressure was ignored.

front: Why is “100 mm Hg favoring filtration” wrong here? A physiologist measures pressures across the glomerular capillaries of a healthy 28-year-old woman: glomerular blood hyd…
back: Adding all three pressures gives 100 mm Hg, but capsular hydrostatic and colloid osmotic pressures oppose the glomerular hydrostatic pressure and are subtracted.
extra: The opposing pressures were added to, rather than subtracted from, the hydrostatic pressure.

front: A 75-year-old woman with gastroenteritis becomes volume-depleted, and her plasma osmolality rises above its ideal value. Which of the following hypothalamic responses most directly follows this rise?
back: Osmoreceptors trigger thirst and ADH release from the posterior pituitary
extra: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamic thirst center monitor blood osmolality; when it rises, the hypothalamus generates conscious thirst and signals the release of ADH from the posterior pituitary to recover water in the collecting ducts.

front: Why is “Paraventricular neurons release oxytocin to constrict renal arterioles” wrong here? A 75-year-old woman with gastroenteritis becomes volume-depleted, and her plasma osmolality rises above its ideal value.…
back: Oxytocin drives uterine contraction and milk ejection; the osmolality-response peptide released from the posterior pituitary is ADH, triggered by hypothalamic osmoreceptors.
extra: The neighboring posterior-pituitary peptide is being substituted for ADH.

front: Why is “The anterior pituitary secretes ACTH, stimulating aldosterone release” wrong here? A 75-year-old woman with gastroenteritis becomes volume-depleted, and her plasma osmolality rises above its ideal value.…
back: The immediate hypothalamic response to rising osmolality is osmoreceptor-driven thirst and ADH release; aldosterone responds to angiotensin II and plasma potassium, not directly to osmolality.
extra: A cortisol axis is being recruited as the direct osmolality sensor.

front: Why is “Juxtaglomerular cells release renin in direct response to osmolality” wrong here? A 75-year-old woman with gastroenteritis becomes volume-depleted, and her plasma osmolality rises above its ideal value.…
back: Renin release responds to decreased blood flow and pressure, and it is renal, not hypothalamic; osmolality is sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors that drive thirst and ADH.
extra: A renal pressure/flow sensor is being recast as the hypothalamic osmolality response.

front: Approximately what fraction of filtered water, sodium, and potassium is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule under normal conditions?
back: About 67 percent
extra: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs about 67 percent of filtered water, sodium, and potassium, making it the dominant reclamation site.

front: Why is “About 10 percent” wrong here? Approximately what fraction of filtered water, sodium, and potassium is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule und…
back: The proximal tubule reclaims the majority of filtered solutes and water; about two-thirds, not one-tenth, is reabsorbed here.
extra: The PCT share is being grossly underestimated.

front: Why is “About 25 percent” wrong here? Approximately what fraction of filtered water, sodium, and potassium is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule und…
back: Only about one-quarter would leave most filtrate downstream; the PCT handles roughly 67 percent of filtered Na+, K+, and water.
extra: A minority fraction is being assigned to the major reabsorptive segment.

front: Why is “About 90 percent” wrong here? Approximately what fraction of filtered water, sodium, and potassium is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule und…
back: Fine-tuning continues in the loop, distal tubule, and collecting duct; the PCT handles about two-thirds, not almost all, of filtration.
extra: Nearly complete reabsorption is being assigned to the PCT alone.

front:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus starts canagliflozin and develops glucosuria despite adequate insulin therapy. Before treatment, his proximal tubule cells recovered essentially all filtered glucose at normal plasma concentrations.

Inhibition of which of the following proximal-tubule transport steps most directly explains the new glucosuria?
back: Apical sodium-linked glucose uptake at the brush border
extra: Filtered glucose is normally reclaimed by apical symporters powered by the sodium gradient; inhibitors of these transporters leave glucose in the filtrate even when insulin is present.

front: Why is “Basolateral facilitative glucose export into peritubular blood” wrong here? A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus starts canagliflozin and develops glucosuria despite adequate insulin th…
back: GLUT transporters move glucose out of the cell after apical uptake; the drug acts on apical SGLT symporters, not basolateral export alone.
extra: The exit step is being blocked instead of the apical entry step targeted by the drug class.

front: Why is “Thick ascending limb sodium-potassium-chloride cotransport in the loop” wrong here? A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus starts canagliflozin and develops glucosuria despite adequate insulin th…
back: NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb handles salt, not glucose; glucosuria reflects proximal Na+/glucose symport blockade.
extra: A loop diuretic target is being substituted for a proximal glucose transporter.

front: Why is “ADH-regulated aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting-duct principal cells” wrong here? A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus starts canagliflozin and develops glucosuria despite adequate insulin th…
back: Aquaporin-2 governs water reabsorption downstream; glucose handling fails at the proximal Na+/glucose symporter.
extra: ADH-regulated water channels are being blamed for glucose loss.

front:
A 52-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus has glucose in her urine despite a normal filtration rate. In her proximal convoluted tubule cells, the transporters that normally recover filtered glucose have reached their maximum capacity.

Glucose uptake at the apical membrane of these cells is powered directly by which of the following?
back: The sodium electrochemical gradient via a shared symport protein
extra: Glucose and Na+ bind simultaneously to the same apical symport proteins; sodium moves down its electrochemical gradient into the cell and carries glucose with it, a secondary active transport driven ultimately by the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase.

front: Why is “Hydrolysis of ATP by the apical glucose carrier itself” wrong here? A 52-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus has glucose in her urine despite a normal filtration rate. …
back: The apical symporter does not hydrolyze ATP; it harvests the sodium gradient that the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase maintains.
extra: A secondary active transporter is being described as a primary ATP-driven pump.

front: Why is “Facilitated diffusion of glucose down its own concentration gradient” wrong here? A 52-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus has glucose in her urine despite a normal filtration rate. …
back: Facilitated diffusion moves glucose out of the cell at the basal surface; apical entry against the glucose gradient requires cotransport with sodium.
extra: The basolateral exit mechanism is being confused with the apical entry step.

front: Why is “Pinocytosis of glucose-containing tubular fluid at the brush border” wrong here? A 52-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus has glucose in her urine despite a normal filtration rate. …
back: Glucose is recovered by the Na+/glucose symport across the apical membrane, not by vesicular uptake; saturation of that carrier is what produces glycosuria.
extra: A bulk-uptake route is being proposed for a carrier-mediated solute.

front:
A 62-year-old man with chronic heart failure and an ejection fraction of 30% is started on lisinopril. At a follow-up visit two weeks later he reports mild fatigue but no angioedema. Repeat electrolytes show a serum concentration of 5.6 mEq/L, up from 4.1 mEq/L at baseline.

Reduced activity of which of the following collecting-duct processes most directly explains the new hyperkalemia?
back: Aldosterone-driven principal-cell sodium recovery and potassium secretion
extra: ACE blockade reduces angiotensin II formation and thereby aldosterone; aldosterone normally stimulates principal cells to recover Na+ and secrete K+, so its fall raises serum potassium.

front: Why is “ADH-dependent insertion of apical aquaporin channels” wrong here? A 62-year-old man with chronic heart failure and an ejection fraction of 30% is started on lisinopril. At a follow-up vi…
back: Aquaporin insertion controls water recovery, not potassium secretion; ACE inhibition lowers angiotensin II and aldosterone, which reduces principal-cell Na+/K+ exchange.
extra: A water-permeability step is being blamed for a potassium change.

front: Why is “Intercalated-cell apical proton secretion into the tubular lumen” wrong here? A 62-year-old man with chronic heart failure and an ejection fraction of 30% is started on lisinopril. At a follow-up vi…
back: Intercalated cells secrete H+; the ACE-inhibitor hyperkalemia reflects reduced aldosterone-driven K+ secretion by principal cells.
extra: Acid handling is being substituted for potassium handling.

front: Why is “Macula densa sensing of tubular sodium chloride delivery” wrong here? A 62-year-old man with chronic heart failure and an ejection fraction of 30% is started on lisinopril. At a follow-up vi…
back: Macula densa signaling modulates renin release; the proximate cause of the potassium rise is reduced aldosterone action on principal cells.
extra: The afferent sensing step is being treated as the effector that moves potassium.

front: Angiotensin I becomes biologically active after cleavage by which enzyme?
back: Pulmonary ACE turning angiotensin I into form II
extra: Angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II by ACE from the lungs.

front: Why is “Renin enzyme acting on circulating angiotensinogen” wrong here? Angiotensin I becomes biologically active after cleavage by which enzyme?
back: Renin produces angiotensin I from angiotensinogen; ACE converts angiotensin I to II.
extra: The angiotensinogen-cleaving enzyme is being confused with ACE.

front: Why is “Adrenal enzyme synthesizing aldosterone steroid hormone” wrong here? Angiotensin I becomes biologically active after cleavage by which enzyme?
back: Aldosterone synthase makes aldosterone; ACE performs the I→II conversion.
extra: A downstream steroid enzyme is being credited with I→II conversion.

front: Why is “Kallikrein enzyme generating angiotensin-like kinins” wrong here? Angiotensin I becomes biologically active after cleavage by which enzyme?
back: Kallikrein is not the enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.
extra: The kinin system is being confused with ACE conversion.

front: Renin cleaves several amino acids from which circulating precursor to produce angiotensin I?
back: Angiotensinogen in the plasma
extra: Renin cleaves amino acids from angiotensinogen to produce angiotensin I.

front: Why is “Angiotensin II already formed” wrong here? Renin cleaves several amino acids from which circulating precursor to produce angiotensin I?
back: Angiotensin II is produced from angiotensin I by ACE, not by renin from II.
extra: The active product is being treated as the renin substrate.

front: Why is “Bradykinin from kininogen” wrong here? Renin cleaves several amino acids from which circulating precursor to produce angiotensin I?
back: Bradykinin is not the precursor cleaved by renin to make angiotensin I.
extra: A kinin peptide is being confused with angiotensinogen.

front: Why is “Aldosterone from the cortex” wrong here? Renin cleaves several amino acids from which circulating precursor to produce angiotensin I?
back: Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid product, not the renin substrate.
extra: A steroid hormone is being treated as a peptide precursor.

front:
A 58-year-old man with longstanding hypertension starts a new oral drug that inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme. Two weeks later, laboratory studies show a rise in plasma angiotensin I with a concurrent fall in angiotensin II, and his blood pressure improves.

Which step did the drug most directly interrupt?
back: Pulmonary ACE changing angiotensin I into II
extra: ACE from the lungs converts angiotensin I to biologically active angiotensin II; blocking ACE stops that step.

front: Why is “Renin making angiotensin I from angiotensinogen” wrong here? A 58-year-old man with longstanding hypertension starts a new oral drug that inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme. Two…
back: Renin still forms angiotensin I; ACE inhibition blocks the subsequent I→II conversion.
extra: The upstream renin step is being confused with ACE blockade.

front: Why is “Adrenal making aldosterone after angiotensin II” wrong here? A 58-year-old man with longstanding hypertension starts a new oral drug that inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme. Two…
back: Aldosterone synthesis is downstream of angiotensin II, not the ACE cleavage itself.
extra: A downstream steroid step is being treated as the ACE target.

front: Why is “Liver secreting more angiotensinogen into plasma” wrong here? A 58-year-old man with longstanding hypertension starts a new oral drug that inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme. Two…
back: Angiotensinogen supply is not the ACE-catalyzed I→II conversion interrupted here.
extra: Precursor production is being confused with ACE activity.

front:
A 60-year-old man with hypertension is prescribed an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor.

The blocked enzyme normally catalyzes which of the following conversions, and in which organ is it chiefly produced?
back: Angiotensin I to angiotensin II, produced in the lungs
extra: Angiotensin I is not biologically active until converted to angiotensin II by angiotensin-converting enzyme from the lungs; inhibiting ACE reduces the vasoconstrictor and aldosterone drive.

front:
Why is “Angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, produced in the kidneys” wrong here? A 60-year-old man with hypertension is prescribed an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor.

The blocked enzyme …
back: Renin, secreted by juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole, cleaves angiotensinogen into angiotensin I; ACE performs the next step and comes from the lungs.
extra: Renin's reaction and source are being attributed to ACE.

front:
Why is “Angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, produced in the liver” wrong here? A 60-year-old man with hypertension is prescribed an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor.

The blocked enzyme …
back: The liver makes angiotensinogen, the circulating substrate; converting it to angiotensin I is renin's job, and ACE converts angiotensin I to II in the lungs.
extra: The substrate's origin is being confused with the enzyme that converts it.

front:
Why is “Angiotensin II to angiotensin III, produced in the adrenal cortex” wrong here? A 60-year-old man with hypertension is prescribed an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor.

The blocked enzyme …
back: ACE activates rather than degrades: it converts inactive angiotensin I into the potent vasoconstrictor angiotensin II, and it is produced in the lungs.
extra: A downstream degradation step is being offered as the blocked reaction.

front:
In an experiment on a healthy 26-year-old volunteer, a sustained rise in glomerular filtration rate increases the flow of tubular fluid past the macula densa.

Which of the following sequences most directly restores the filtration rate toward baseline?
back: Macula densa cells release ATP and adenosine, constricting the afferent arteriole
extra: When filtration rises, more NaCl reaches the macula densa; the activated cells release ATP and adenosine, which act as paracrine factors that constrict the afferent arteriole, slowing blood flow and reducing GFR.

front: Why is “Juxtaglomerular cells increase renin secretion, raising systemic angiotensin II” wrong here? In an experiment on a healthy 26-year-old volunteer, a sustained rise in glomerular filtration rate increases the flow o…
back: Tubuloglomerular feedback acts locally through ATP and adenosine on the afferent arteriole; renin release responds to decreased perfusion, not to an acute rise in filtration.
extra: A slower endocrine pressor pathway is being substituted for the local feedback loop.

front: Why is “Macula densa cells release nitric oxide, dilating the efferent arteriole” wrong here? In an experiment on a healthy 26-year-old volunteer, a sustained rise in glomerular filtration rate increases the flow o…
back: Nitric oxide relaxes the afferent arteriole and opposes the ATP/adenosine signal; the feedback that lowers an elevated GFR is adenosine-mediated constriction of the afferent vessel.
extra: The fine-tuning vasodilator is being cast as the primary negative-feedback signal, and at the wrong arteriole.

front: Why is “Principal cells insert aquaporin channels, diverting water from the tubule” wrong here? In an experiment on a healthy 26-year-old volunteer, a sustained rise in glomerular filtration rate increases the flow o…
back: Aquaporin insertion alters water recovery downstream of the glomerulus; it does not feed back on the filtration rate, which is controlled at the afferent arteriole.
extra: A collecting-duct water mechanism is being credited with changing glomerular filtration.

front:
A 26-year-old patient is studied during the preovulatory portion of a menstrual cycle. Follicular estrogen production is lower than in the comparison cycle.

Which of the following endometrial changes would most directly reflect loss of this hormonal stimulus?
back: Reduced proliferative growth before the postovulatory secretory phase
extra: Follicular estrogen stimulates endometrial rebuilding. Reducing that stimulus most directly reduces preovulatory proliferation rather than advancing the postovulatory secretory phase.

front: Why is “Increased proliferative growth with unchanged postovulatory gland secretion” wrong here? A 26-year-old patient is studied during the preovulatory portion of a menstrual cycle. Follicular estrogen production is…
back: Estrogen supports proliferative rebuilding. Less follicular estrogen does not directly predict greater rebuilding; the later secretory state is a separate phase.
extra: Reverses the proliferative effect of reducing follicular estrogen.

front: Why is “Preserved proliferative growth with reduced postovulatory gland secretion” wrong here? A 26-year-old patient is studied during the preovulatory portion of a menstrual cycle. Follicular estrogen production is…
back: This assigns the change to a later secretory state while leaving the directly estrogen-dependent proliferative response unchanged.
extra: Moves the effect to a later secretory phase while preserving estrogen-driven growth.

front: Why is “Preserved proliferative growth with increased preovulatory gland secretion” wrong here? A 26-year-old patient is studied during the preovulatory portion of a menstrual cycle. Follicular estrogen production is…
back: The measured reduction is in a stimulus for preovulatory rebuilding. Neither preserved growth nor increased glandular secretion follows directly from that loss.
extra: Preserves estrogen-dependent growth and assumes unsupported increased secretion.

front:
A postpartum patient has milk within the mammary alveoli. Suckling produces an appropriate rise in circulating oxytocin, but the surrounding myoepithelial cells fail to contract.

Which of the following steps is most directly impaired?
back: Expulsion of milk from glandular storage spaces
extra: Oxytocin normally drives myoepithelial contraction, which ejects milk from alveoli. The reported lack of contraction localizes the failure to that response.

front: Why is “Production of oxytocin within hypothalamic neurons” wrong here? A postpartum patient has milk within the mammary alveoli. Suckling produces an appropriate rise in circulating oxytocin,…
back: The observed oxytocin rise argues against deficient hormone production as the most direct explanation.
extra: Attributes a target-cell defect to synthesis despite the measured oxytocin rise.

front: Why is “Storage of oxytocin within posterior-pituitary terminals” wrong here? A postpartum patient has milk within the mammary alveoli. Suckling produces an appropriate rise in circulating oxytocin,…
back: An appropriate stimulated circulating response makes terminal storage failure a less direct explanation than the observed target-cell defect.
extra: Places the failure in terminal storage despite an appropriate circulating response.

front: Why is “Release of oxytocin after the suckling stimulus” wrong here? A postpartum patient has milk within the mammary alveoli. Suckling produces an appropriate rise in circulating oxytocin,…
back: The hormone concentration rises after suckling, so the release step occurred. The abnormal observation follows it.
extra: Attributes the defect to release even though stimulated oxytocin rises.

front:
An endometrial sample from a 29-year-old patient shows glands releasing nutrient-rich fluid that prepares the tissue for implantation.

Which of the following ovarian and endometrial states best fits this finding?
back: Ovarian luteal phase with a secretory endometrium
extra: The secretory endometrium prepares for implantation and corresponds to the postovulatory luteal phase with progesterone secretion.

front: Why is “Ovarian follicular phase with a secretory endometrium” wrong here? An endometrial sample from a 29-year-old patient shows glands releasing nutrient-rich fluid that prepares the tissue for…
back: This pairs the postovulatory secretory finding with the wrong ovarian phase. Follicular estrogen primarily supports proliferative rebuilding.
extra: Pairs a postovulatory endometrial finding with the follicular ovarian phase.

front: Why is “Ovarian luteal phase with a proliferative endometrium” wrong here? An endometrial sample from a 29-year-old patient shows glands releasing nutrient-rich fluid that prepares the tissue for…
back: The ovarian timing fits, but the endometrial label does not: nutrient-rich glandular secretion identifies a secretory state.
extra: Identifies ovarian timing correctly but mislabels glandular secretion as proliferation.

front: Why is “Preovulatory follicular phase with endometrial shedding” wrong here? An endometrial sample from a 29-year-old patient shows glands releasing nutrient-rich fluid that prepares the tissue for…
back: The observed glandular preparation for implantation is not endometrial shedding during a preovulatory state.
extra: Confuses implantation preparation with endometrial shedding.

front:
An experimental lesion interrupts axons reaching the posterior pituitary while sparing the hypothalamic neurons that produce oxytocin.

After hormone already stored in the disconnected terminals has been depleted, which of the following patterns best distinguishes the roles of these two structures?
back: Oxytocin synthesis can persist, while terminal storage and release are impaired
extra: The hypothalamus synthesizes oxytocin, while posterior-pituitary axon terminals provide storage and release. Disrupting terminals can therefore separate synthesis from secretion.

front: Why is “Oxytocin synthesis stops, but release from damaged terminals increases” wrong here? An experimental lesion interrupts axons reaching the posterior pituitary while sparing the hypothalamic neurons that pro…
back: The hormone-producing hypothalamic neurons are spared. Damaging their axonal output does not imply increased terminal release.
extra: Confuses terminal injury with loss of spared hypothalamic synthesis.

front: Why is “Both oxytocin synthesis and release shift into the anterior pituitary” wrong here? An experimental lesion interrupts axons reaching the posterior pituitary while sparing the hypothalamic neurons that pro…
back: The intervention does not create a new synthesis or release pathway in the anterior pituitary.
extra: Assumes injury transfers oxytocin production and release to the anterior pituitary.

front: Why is “Oxytocin synthesis begins in the posterior pituitary after axonal injury” wrong here? An experimental lesion interrupts axons reaching the posterior pituitary while sparing the hypothalamic neurons that pro…
back: The posterior pituitary is a storage-and-release site; it does not replace the hypothalamus as the synthesis site after injury.
extra: Treats the posterior storage-and-release site as a replacement synthesis site.

front:
A 28-year-old woman conceives, and one week after fertilization her conceptus adheres to the uterine wall and embeds into the endometrial lining.

Which of the following developmental stages has her conceptus reached at the time of this implantation?
back: The blastocyst stage of development
extra: At the end of the first week, the blastocyst comes in contact with the uterine wall and adheres to it, embedding itself in the uterine lining via the trophoblast cells.

front: Why is “The zygote stage of development” wrong here? A 28-year-old woman conceives, and one week after fertilization her conceptus adheres to the uterine wall and embeds int…
back: The zygote is the single diploid cell formed at fertilization; a week of cleavage produces the blastocyst before implantation can occur.
extra: The fertilized single cell is being placed at implantation.

front: Why is “The morula stage of development” wrong here? A 28-year-old woman conceives, and one week after fertilization her conceptus adheres to the uterine wall and embeds int…
back: The morula is the tightly packed sphere present on reaching the uterus; it then forms the blastocyst, and it is the blastocyst that implants.
extra: An earlier solid-ball stage is being sequenced at implantation.

front: Why is “The gastrula stage of development” wrong here? A 28-year-old woman conceives, and one week after fertilization her conceptus adheres to the uterine wall and embeds int…
back: Gastrulation establishes the three germ layers after implantation; the structure that embeds in the endometrium is the blastocyst.
extra: A post-implantation stage is being placed before it.

front: A 33-year-old woman is 8 weeks pregnant by her last menstrual period. At this stage, her pregnancy is being sustained primarily by progesterone from which of the following structures?
back: The corpus luteum of the ovary
extra: During weeks 7–12 from the last menstrual period, the pregnancy hormones are primarily generated by the corpus luteum, whose progesterone stimulates decidual cells that nourish the conceptus before placentation.

front: Why is “The fully developed placenta” wrong here? A 33-year-old woman is 8 weeks pregnant by her last menstrual period. At this stage, her pregnancy is being sustained pr…
back: The placenta gradually takes over as the endocrine organ of pregnancy during weeks 12–17 as the corpus luteum degenerates; at 8 weeks the corpus luteum predominates.
extra: The later endocrine organ is being credited too early.

front: Why is “The dominant follicle of the ovary” wrong here? A 33-year-old woman is 8 weeks pregnant by her last menstrual period. At this stage, her pregnancy is being sustained pr…
back: Ovulation transforms the follicle into the corpus luteum; it is this luteinized structure, not a persisting follicle, that secretes early-pregnancy progesterone.
extra: A pre-ovulatory estrogen source is being assigned a gestational role.

front: Why is “The maternal adrenal cortex” wrong here? A 33-year-old woman is 8 weeks pregnant by her last menstrual period. At this stage, her pregnancy is being sustained pr…
back: Adrenal androgens serve later as substrates for placental estrogen synthesis; the progesterone sustaining weeks 7–12 comes from the corpus luteum.
extra: An auxiliary androgen source is being cast as the progesterone source.

front:
During in vitro fertilization of a 34-year-old woman's oocyte, a single sperm fuses with the oocyte membrane. Within minutes, cortical granules beneath the oocyte membrane fuse with it and release their contents.

Which of the following is the direct purpose of this cortical reaction?
back: Blocking entry of any additional sperm cells
extra: In the cortical reaction, cortical granules sitting immediately below the oocyte plasma membrane fuse with it and release zonal inhibiting proteins, hardening the zona pellucida to prevent polyspermy — which would produce a nonviable triploid zygote.

front: Why is “Digesting the oocyte's surrounding corona radiata” wrong here? During in vitro fertilization of a 34-year-old woman's oocyte, a single sperm fuses with the oocyte membrane. Within min…
back: Acrosomal enzymes from sperm digest the corona radiata and zona path; the oocyte's cortical granules modify the zona to exclude further sperm.
extra: Sperm-side enzymes are being attributed to the oocyte.

front: Why is “Triggering the first cleavage division of the zygote” wrong here? During in vitro fertilization of a 34-year-old woman's oocyte, a single sperm fuses with the oocyte membrane. Within min…
back: Cleavage begins later as the conceptus travels toward the uterus; the cortical reaction's immediate role is the slow block to polyspermy.
extra: A fertilization defense is being mistaken for a cell-cycle trigger.

front: Why is “Signaling the corpus luteum to secrete progesterone” wrong here? During in vitro fertilization of a 34-year-old woman's oocyte, a single sperm fuses with the oocyte membrane. Within min…
back: The corpus luteum is maintained by hCG from the implanting trophoblast days later; cortical granule release acts locally on the zona pellucida within minutes.
extra: An endocrine rescue is being assigned to a membrane event.

front:
A 35-year-old man undergoes vasectomy, during which the ductus deferens is transected.

Sperm leaving the seminiferous tubules are still immotile and immature; They complete their maturation before entering the ductus deferens in which of the following structures?
back: The epididymis on the posterior testis
extra: Upon release from the seminiferous tubules, sperm are moved to the epididymis where they continue to mature; during ejaculation they exit the epididymis through the ductus deferens.

front:
Why is “The seminiferous tubules themselves” wrong here? A 35-year-old man undergoes vasectomy, during which the ductus deferens is transected.

Sperm leaving the seminiferous t…
back: Sperm leaving the seminiferous tubules are still immotile; functional maturation occurs downstream in the epididymis during transit.
extra: The production site is being credited with final maturation.

front:
Why is “The rete testis within the mediastinum” wrong here? A 35-year-old man undergoes vasectomy, during which the ductus deferens is transected.

Sperm leaving the seminiferous t…
back: The rete testis merely channels sperm from the tubules toward the efferent ductules; maturation takes place in the epididymis.
extra: A transit meshwork is being elevated to a maturation organ.

front:
Why is “The seminal vesicles beside the bladder” wrong here? A 35-year-old man undergoes vasectomy, during which the ductus deferens is transected.

Sperm leaving the seminiferous t…
back: Seminal vesicles contribute fructose-rich fluid at ejaculation; sperm have already matured in the epididymis before reaching them.
extra: A secretory gland is being confused with a maturation duct.

front:
A 27-year-old woman with a history of chlamydial pelvic inflammatory disease has tubal scarring and is now being evaluated for infertility.

In an unscarred reproductive tract, fertilization of an ovulated oocyte usually occurs in which of the following locations?
back: The distal portion of the uterine tube
extra: Sperm enter through the vagina, and fertilization of an ovulated oocyte usually occurs in the distal uterine tube — the reason tubal scarring from pelvic inflammatory disease causes infertility.

front: Why is “The fundus of the uterine body” wrong here? A 27-year-old woman with a history of chlamydial pelvic inflammatory disease has tubal scarring and is now being evaluat…
back: The blastocyst typically implants in the fundus, but fertilization happened days earlier in the distal uterine tube.
extra: The implantation region is being confused with the fertilization site.

front: Why is “The cervix at the uterine outlet” wrong here? A 27-year-old woman with a history of chlamydial pelvic inflammatory disease has tubal scarring and is now being evaluat…
back: Cervical mucus filters and blocks many sperm; the surviving sperm meet the oocyte far upstream in the distal uterine tube.
extra: A sperm barrier is being cast as the fertilization site.

front: Why is “The vaginal fornix around the cervix” wrong here? A 27-year-old woman with a history of chlamydial pelvic inflammatory disease has tubal scarring and is now being evaluat…
back: Semen is deposited in the vagina, but the oocyte never descends there; sperm must ascend to the distal uterine tube to fertilize it.
extra: The deposition site is being confused with the fertilization site.

front: A 19-year-old man is being evaluated for delayed puberty, and laboratory studies show a low serum testosterone. Within the testis, testosterone is produced by which of the following cell types?
back: Leydig cells between the seminiferous tubules
extra: Leydig cells are the cells between the seminiferous tubules of the testes that produce testosterone; this steroid drives the male reproductive system's development, sperm maturation, and secondary sex characteristics.

front: Why is “Sertoli cells lining the tubular walls” wrong here? A 19-year-old man is being evaluated for delayed puberty, and laboratory studies show a low serum testosterone. Within t…
back: Sertoli (sustentacular) cells support and nourish developing sperm and respond to FSH; androgen synthesis belongs to the interstitial Leydig cells.
extra: The nurse cells are being assigned the steroid role.

front: Why is “Spermatogonia at the basement membrane” wrong here? A 19-year-old man is being evaluated for delayed puberty, and laboratory studies show a low serum testosterone. Within t…
back: Spermatogonia are the diploid stem cells that enter spermatogenesis; they do not secrete testosterone, which comes from Leydig cells.
extra: The germ stem cells are being cast as hormone producers.

front: Why is “Epididymal epithelial cells of the duct” wrong here? A 19-year-old man is being evaluated for delayed puberty, and laboratory studies show a low serum testosterone. Within t…
back: The epididymis matures and stores sperm; testicular testosterone is synthesized by Leydig cells lying between the seminiferous tubules.
extra: A storage-site lining is being treated as an endocrine source.

front: Which hormone signal triggers the anterior-pituitary switch that produces the preovulatory LH surge?
back: Extremely high systemic estrogen
extra: Extremely high plasma estrogen switches anterior-pituitary regulation to positive feedback, producing the LH surge.

front: Why is “Very low systemic estrogen” wrong here? Which hormone signal triggers the anterior-pituitary switch that produces the preovulatory LH surge?
back: The checked passage identifies extremely high, not very low, systemic estrogen as the surge trigger.
extra: Reverses the direction of the estrogen signal required for the switch.

front: Why is “Sustained high systemic progesterone” wrong here? Which hormone signal triggers the anterior-pituitary switch that produces the preovulatory LH surge?
back: The regulatory switch described in the passage is triggered by extremely high estrogen.
extra: Substitutes progesterone for the estrogen signal named by the source.

front: Why is “Sudden low systemic progesterone” wrong here? Which hormone signal triggers the anterior-pituitary switch that produces the preovulatory LH surge?
back: The source links the LH surge to extremely high systemic estrogen rather than low progesterone.
extra: Substitutes progesterone withdrawal for the preovulatory estrogen signal.

front:
A 29-year-old woman undergoing evaluation of ovulatory timing has serial plasma hormone measurements. Estrogen rises gradually, then reaches an extremely high sustained concentration. An experimental antagonist now prevents the anterior pituitary from switching its response to that estrogen signal. No large burst of luteinizing hormone or follicle-stimulating hormone occurs.

Which of the following reproductive events is most directly prevented by this intervention?
back: Release of the dominant follicle at ovulation
extra: The source states that extremely high estrogen triggers a pituitary switch and large LH burst, and that this LH surge leads to ovulation of the dominant follicle.

front: Why is “Growth of the dominant follicle before the estrogen peak” wrong here? A 29-year-old woman undergoing evaluation of ovulatory timing has serial plasma hormone measurements. Estrogen rises gra…
back: A dominant follicle and its extremely high estrogen signal already exist before the intervention; the blocked LH surge normally acts afterward to produce ovulation.
extra: Places an upstream follicular event downstream of the blocked pituitary switch.

front: Why is “Production of estrogen by the dominant follicle” wrong here? A 29-year-old woman undergoing evaluation of ovulatory timing has serial plasma hormone measurements. Estrogen rises gra…
back: The extremely high estrogen concentration already exists before the pituitary switch is blocked; the source places ovulation after the LH surge.
extra: Places an upstream estrogen signal downstream of the blocked pituitary response.

front: Why is “Entry of estrogen into the systemic circulation” wrong here? A 29-year-old woman undergoing evaluation of ovulatory timing has serial plasma hormone measurements. Estrogen rises gra…
back: Systemic estrogen is already extremely high in the stem; the blocked sequence is the pituitary burst followed by ovulation.
extra: Places the already measured upstream signal after the pituitary blockade.

front: A 31-year-old woman has an abrupt pituitary burst of LH and FSH followed by ovulation. Which circulating signal most directly triggered the pituitary regulatory switch?
back: Extremely high systemic estrogen
extra: Extremely high systemic estrogen triggers the anterior-pituitary switch, producing the LH and FSH burst that precedes ovulation.

front: Why is “Extremely high systemic progesterone” wrong here? A 31-year-old woman has an abrupt pituitary burst of LH and FSH followed by ovulation. Which circulating signal most dir…
back: The checked passage identifies extremely high systemic estrogen, not progesterone, as the signal that triggers the pituitary switch.
extra: Substitutes progesterone for the source-defined estrogen signal.

front: Why is “Very low systemic estrogen” wrong here? A 31-year-old woman has an abrupt pituitary burst of LH and FSH followed by ovulation. Which circulating signal most dir…
back: The cited regulatory switch occurs at extremely high rather than very low systemic estrogen concentrations.
extra: Reverses the direction of the source-defined estrogen signal.

front: Why is “Extremely high systemic inhibin” wrong here? A 31-year-old woman has an abrupt pituitary burst of LH and FSH followed by ovulation. Which circulating signal most dir…
back: The checked passage identifies extremely high systemic estrogen, not inhibin, as the trigger.
extra: Substitutes another circulating signal for the estrogen named by the source.

front: A 51-year-old woman has not had a menstrual period for 12 months and is experiencing hot flashes. Her transition to menopause is best explained by which of the following changes in her ovaries?
back: Exhaustion of her remaining pool of primary oocytes
extra: The number of primary oocytes in the ovaries declines from one to two million in an infant, to approximately 400,000 at puberty, to zero by the end of menopause; with no follicles left, cycles cease.

front: Why is “Failure of the pituitary to secrete FSH and LH” wrong here? A 51-year-old woman has not had a menstrual period for 12 months and is experiencing hot flashes. Her transition to meno…
back: In menopause the depleted ovary stops responding, and FSH and LH actually rise from lost negative feedback; the initiating event is oocyte-pool exhaustion.
extra: The axis is being inverted — the ovary fails, not the pituitary.

front: Why is “Atresia of the uterine endometrial lining” wrong here? A 51-year-old woman has not had a menstrual period for 12 months and is experiencing hot flashes. Her transition to meno…
back: Endometrial thinning follows the loss of ovarian estrogen; the primary change is depletion of the ovarian follicle pool.
extra: A downstream target is being mistaken for the cause.

front: Why is “Autoimmune destruction of ovarian theca cells” wrong here? A 51-year-old woman has not had a menstrual period for 12 months and is experiencing hot flashes. Her transition to meno…
back: Ordinary menopause is the programmed exhaustion of the finite oocyte pool formed in fetal life, not an immune attack on the ovary.
extra: A rare pathological cause is being substituted for the physiological one.

front:
A 24-year-old woman ovulates, releasing an oocyte that completes its first meiotic division.

The arrested meiotic process that resumes at this ovulation actually began in her ovaries during which of the following periods?
back: During her fetal development, before birth
extra: Oogonia form primary oocytes in the fetal ovary prior to birth; these primary oocytes are then arrested in meiosis I, resuming only years later at each ovulation from puberty onward.

front:
Why is “At the onset of puberty, with menarche” wrong here? A 24-year-old woman ovulates, releasing an oocyte that completes its first meiotic division.

The arrested meiotic proce…
back: Puberty marks when arrested oocytes resume meiosis at each cycle, not when they first entered meiosis; entry into meiosis I occurred during fetal life.
