extra: The resumption of meiosis is being confused with its initiation.

front:
Why is “At the moment of the LH surge” wrong here? A 24-year-old woman ovulates, releasing an oocyte that completes its first meiotic division.

The arrested meiotic proce…
back: The LH surge triggers resumption of a meiotic process that was initiated and arrested in the fetal ovary decades earlier.
extra: The trigger for resumption is being mistaken for the start.

front:
Why is “During the follicular phase of that cycle” wrong here? A 24-year-old woman ovulates, releasing an oocyte that completes its first meiotic division.

The arrested meiotic proce…
back: Follicular growth in a given cycle recruits an oocyte whose meiotic arrest began in fetal life; meiosis does not start anew each month.
extra: Meiosis is being treated as a per-cycle event.

front:
A 29-year-old woman is breastfeeding her 2-month-old infant. When the infant suckles, milk is ejected from the alveoli into the ducts toward the nipple.

Which of the following hormones, released in response to suckling, produces this milk ejection?
back: Oxytocin acting on myoepithelial cells
extra: Following childbirth, suckling triggers oxytocin release, which stimulates myoepithelial cells to squeeze milk from alveoli — the let-down reflex that drains milk toward the nipple.

front: Why is “Prolactin acting on the lactocytes” wrong here? A 29-year-old woman is breastfeeding her 2-month-old infant. When the infant suckles, milk is ejected from the alveoli i…
back: Prolactin drives milk synthesis by the alveolar lactocytes; the mechanical ejection of stored milk is triggered by oxytocin contracting myoepithelial cells.
extra: The synthesis hormone is being assigned the ejection role.

front: Why is “Estrogen acting on the duct epithelium” wrong here? A 29-year-old woman is breastfeeding her 2-month-old infant. When the infant suckles, milk is ejected from the alveoli i…
back: Estrogen promotes ductal growth during pregnancy but falls after childbirth; suckling-induced milk ejection is mediated by oxytocin.
extra: A pregnancy growth signal is being cast as the let-down trigger.

front: Why is “Progesterone acting on the alveoli” wrong here? A 29-year-old woman is breastfeeding her 2-month-old infant. When the infant suckles, milk is ejected from the alveoli i…
back: Progesterone supports alveolar development in pregnancy and its withdrawal permits lactation; the ejection reflex itself runs on oxytocin.
extra: A gestational hormone is being linked to postpartum ejection.

front:
A 29-year-old woman is on day 9 of a regular 28-day menstrual cycle, several days after her menstrual flow ceased. Her endometrium is actively rebuilding and thickening.

Which of the following hormones, secreted by the developing ovarian follicles, is driving this endometrial proliferation?
back: Estrogen from granulosa and theca cells
extra: During the proliferative phase, granulosa and theca cells of the tertiary follicles produce increased amounts of estrogen, and these rising estrogen concentrations stimulate the endometrial lining to rebuild.

front: Why is “Follicle-stimulating hormone from the pituitary” wrong here? A 29-year-old woman is on day 9 of a regular 28-day menstrual cycle, several days after her menstrual flow ceased. Her e…
back: FSH stimulates follicular growth and thereby raises estrogen, but the endometrium responds to the estrogen itself, not to FSH.
extra: The follicle recruiter is being confused with the endometrial effector.

front: Why is “Progesterone from the corpus luteum” wrong here? A 29-year-old woman is on day 9 of a regular 28-day menstrual cycle, several days after her menstrual flow ceased. Her e…
back: Progesterone dominates after ovulation and drives the secretory phase; on day 9 the follicles' estrogen, not luteal progesterone, is rebuilding the lining.
extra: The luteal-phase hormone is being applied to the pre-ovulatory phase.

front: Why is “Luteinizing hormone from the pituitary” wrong here? A 29-year-old woman is on day 9 of a regular 28-day menstrual cycle, several days after her menstrual flow ceased. Her e…
back: LH acts on the ovary to promote steroidogenesis and trigger ovulation; the hormone acting directly on the endometrium during proliferation is estrogen.
extra: A gonadotropin is being credited with direct endometrial action.

front: Which menstrual-cycle phase features endometrial secretion of nutrient-rich fluid in preparation for implantation?
back: The secretory phase of the cycle
extra: The secretory phase features endometrial secretion of nutrient-rich fluid in preparation for embryo implantation.

front: Why is “The proliferative phase of the cycle” wrong here? Which menstrual-cycle phase features endometrial secretion of nutrient-rich fluid in preparation for implantation?
back: The checked passage names the nutrient-secreting endometrial stage the secretory phase, not the proliferative phase.
extra: Substitutes a different cycle label for the source-defined secretory phase.

front: Why is “The menses phase of the cycle” wrong here? Which menstrual-cycle phase features endometrial secretion of nutrient-rich fluid in preparation for implantation?
back: The checked passage names the nutrient-secreting endometrial stage the secretory phase, not the menses phase.
extra: Substitutes a different cycle label for the source-defined secretory phase.

front: Why is “The ischemic phase of the cycle” wrong here? Which menstrual-cycle phase features endometrial secretion of nutrient-rich fluid in preparation for implantation?
back: The checked passage names the nutrient-secreting endometrial stage the secretory phase, not the ischemic phase.
extra: Substitutes a different cycle label for the source-defined secretory phase.

front:
A 32-year-old man has a semen analysis showing an abnormally low ejaculate volume with poorly motile sperm.

The fructose that sperm mitochondria use to generate ATP for movement is contributed primarily by which of the following accessory glands?
back: The paired seminal vesicles
extra: The paired seminal vesicles contribute approximately 60 percent of semen volume, and their fluid contains large amounts of fructose, which sperm mitochondria use to generate ATP for movement through the female reproductive tract.

front:
Why is “The bulbourethral glands of the perineum” wrong here? A 32-year-old man has a semen analysis showing an abnormally low ejaculate volume with poorly motile sperm.

The fructos…
back: Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands secrete lubricating mucus before ejaculation; fructose for sperm ATP comes from the seminal vesicles.
extra: Lubricating glands are being cast as the energy supplier.

front:
Why is “The epididymal duct lining” wrong here? A 32-year-old man has a semen analysis showing an abnormally low ejaculate volume with poorly motile sperm.

The fructos…
back: The epididymis matures sperm but does not supply the ejaculate's fructose; that sugar arrives with seminal vesicle fluid at emission.
extra: The maturation duct is being credited with seminal fuel.

front:
Why is “The testicular interstitial cells” wrong here? A 32-year-old man has a semen analysis showing an abnormally low ejaculate volume with poorly motile sperm.

The fructos…
back: Leydig cells secrete testosterone, not seminal fluid; fructose-rich fluid contributing most of semen volume comes from the seminal vesicles.
extra: Steroid-producing cells are being assigned a secretory-fluid role.

front:
A 30-year-old man has a semen analysis showing sperm with markedly reduced motility. Electron microscopy reveals defective mitochondria.

The mitochondria that power its movement are housed in which of the following regions of the sperm cell?
back: The mid-piece of the sperm
extra: Sperm cells are divided into a head containing DNA, a mid-piece containing mitochondria, and a tail providing motility; ATP produced by these mitochondria powers the flagellum.

front: Why is “The acrosome at the sperm head tip” wrong here? A 30-year-old man has a semen analysis showing sperm with markedly reduced motility. Electron microscopy reveals defecti…
back: The acrosome holds digestive enzymes for penetrating the oocyte's coverings; locomotive ATP comes from mid-piece mitochondria.
extra: The enzyme cap is being cast as the energy source.

front: Why is “The nucleus within the sperm head” wrong here? A 30-year-old man has a semen analysis showing sperm with markedly reduced motility. Electron microscopy reveals defecti…
back: The head carries the haploid DNA; it contains no mitochondria, which are packed into the mid-piece behind it.
extra: The genetic compartment is being assigned a bioenergetic role.

front: Why is “The axial filament of the tail” wrong here? A 30-year-old man has a semen analysis showing sperm with markedly reduced motility. Electron microscopy reveals defecti…
back: The axial filament is the flagellar core that moves the cell; it consumes ATP generated by the mid-piece mitochondria rather than producing it.
extra: The motility apparatus is being confused with the ATP supply.

front:
A 27-year-old man undergoes fertility testing, and a testicular biopsy shows active spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules.

Starting from one primary spermatocyte, which of the following is the number of haploid spermatids that will ultimately be produced?
back: Four haploid spermatids
extra: Meiosis has two rounds of cell division — primary spermatocyte to secondary spermatocyte, then secondary spermatocyte to spermatid — producing four haploid daughter cells from each primary spermatocyte.

front: Why is “Two haploid spermatids” wrong here? A 27-year-old man undergoes fertility testing, and a testicular biopsy shows active spermatogenesis in the seminiferous …
back: Meiosis I alone yields two secondary spermatocytes, but each then completes meiosis II, doubling the final yield to four haploid spermatids.
extra: Only the first meiotic division is being counted.

front: Why is “One haploid spermatid” wrong here? A 27-year-old man undergoes fertility testing, and a testicular biopsy shows active spermatogenesis in the seminiferous …
back: Female meiosis yields one ovum plus polar bodies; male meiosis conserves all four products as functional spermatids.
extra: The oogenesis pattern of one ovum is being applied to sperm.

front: Why is “Eight haploid spermatids” wrong here? A 27-year-old man undergoes fertility testing, and a testicular biopsy shows active spermatogenesis in the seminiferous …
back: Meiosis comprises exactly two divisions after the single mitotic amplification; 2 × 2 gives four, not eight, spermatids per primary spermatocyte.
extra: An extra division round is being inserted into meiosis.

front:
A 25-year-old woman at 20 weeks of gestation undergoes ultrasound examination of the umbilical cord, which shows two arteries and one vein.

Which of the following correctly describes the direction of oxygenated blood flow in these vessels?
back: The single umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood toward the fetus
extra: The umbilical cord carries deoxygenated blood and wastes from the fetus through two umbilical arteries, while nutrients and oxygen are carried from the mother to the fetus through the single umbilical vein.

front: Why is “The two umbilical arteries carry oxygenated blood toward the fetus” wrong here? A 25-year-old woman at 20 weeks of gestation undergoes ultrasound examination of the umbilical cord, which shows two art…
back: The umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the fetus to the placenta — the reverse of the postnatal pattern; oxygenated blood arrives via the vein.
extra: The fetal arteries are being assigned the vein's cargo.

front: Why is “All three vessels carry oxygenated blood toward the fetus” wrong here? A 25-year-old woman at 20 weeks of gestation undergoes ultrasound examination of the umbilical cord, which shows two art…
back: Only the vein delivers oxygenated blood; the two arteries remove deoxygenated blood and metabolic wastes from the fetus to the placenta.
extra: The fetal waste-removal limb is being overlooked.

front: Why is “The single umbilical vein carries deoxygenated blood to the placenta” wrong here? A 25-year-old woman at 20 weeks of gestation undergoes ultrasound examination of the umbilical cord, which shows two art…
back: The umbilical vein flows toward the fetus carrying oxygen and nutrients; deoxygenated blood leaves the fetus through the two arteries.
extra: The vein's contents and direction are both being reversed.

front:
During vigorous exercise, a 25-year-old man's active skeletal muscle produces increased amounts of carbon dioxide and lactic acid. Compared with resting muscle, oxygen release from hemoglobin within the exercising muscle's capillaries is enhanced.

Which of the following mechanisms most directly accounts for this enhanced release?
back: Local tissue acidosis reduces the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen
extra: Carbon dioxide conversion and lactic acid lower local pH; a lower, more acidic pH promotes oxygen dissociation from hemoglobin, delivering more oxygen to the active tissue.

front: Why is “Increased tissue temperature raises hemoglobin's oxygen saturation” wrong here? During vigorous exercise, a 25-year-old man's active skeletal muscle produces increased amounts of carbon dioxide and la…
back: Rising temperature shifts the dissociation curve to lower saturation at a given partial pressure; it does not raise saturation.
extra: Temperature's effect on saturation is being stated backward.

front: Why is “Carbon monoxide produced by metabolism displaces oxygen from hemoglobin” wrong here? During vigorous exercise, a 25-year-old man's active skeletal muscle produces increased amounts of carbon dioxide and la…
back: Exercising muscle does not produce carbon monoxide; the physiologic driver of release is the fall in local pH from carbon dioxide and lactic acid.
extra: A pathologic competitor is being invoked for a physiologic response.

front: Why is “An increased partial pressure of oxygen in the tissue drives unloading” wrong here? During vigorous exercise, a 25-year-old man's active skeletal muscle produces increased amounts of carbon dioxide and la…
back: Active muscle consumes oxygen, so tissue partial pressure falls; release is enhanced by acidity, not by a rise in tissue oxygen tension.
extra: Tissue oxygen tension is being described in the wrong direction.

front:
In a physiology laboratory, a 21-year-old student compresses a gas-filled syringe to one-half of its original volume while temperature is held constant and no gas escapes.

According to Boyle's law, which of the following best describes the resulting change in the pressure of the trapped gas?
back: It doubles
extra: Boyle's law states that the pressure of a gas is inversely proportional to its volume at constant temperature: if volume decreases to one-half, pressure increases twofold.

front: Why is “It remains unchanged” wrong here? In a physiology laboratory, a 21-year-old student compresses a gas-filled syringe to one-half of its original volume whi…
back: At constant temperature, changing the volume occupied by a gas changes its pressure; the two cannot remain independent.
extra: Pressure is being treated as independent of volume.

front: Why is “It increases by half” wrong here? In a physiology laboratory, a 21-year-old student compresses a gas-filled syringe to one-half of its original volume whi…
back: The relationship is inverse and proportional: halving the volume doubles the pressure, not a one-half increase.
extra: A linear rather than inverse proportional relationship is being applied.

front: Why is “It is halved” wrong here? In a physiology laboratory, a 21-year-old student compresses a gas-filled syringe to one-half of its original volume whi…
back: Pressure and volume are inversely related; reducing volume raises rather than lowers pressure.
extra: Pressure is being treated as proportional to volume.

front:
A 59-year-old man with a brainstem stroke loses his normal automatic breathing rhythm and must consciously initiate each breath.

A lesion in which of the following structures most directly explains the loss of his involuntary breathing rhythm?
back: Dorsal respiratory group in the medulla oblongata
extra: The dorsal respiratory group is involved in maintaining a constant breathing rhythm by stimulating the diaphragm and intercostal muscles to contract; destroying it abolishes automatic inspiration.

front: Why is “Primary motor cortex projections to the diaphragm” wrong here? A 59-year-old man with a brainstem stroke loses his normal automatic breathing rhythm and must consciously initiate each…
back: He can still breathe consciously, so voluntary cortical control is intact; the lost function is the medullary rhythm generator.
extra: The voluntary pathway is being blamed for loss of the automatic one.

front: Why is “Ventral respiratory group in the medulla oblongata” wrong here? A 59-year-old man with a brainstem stroke loses his normal automatic breathing rhythm and must consciously initiate each…
back: The ventral respiratory group is involved in forced breathing, stimulating accessory muscles; baseline quiet rhythm depends on the dorsal group.
extra: The forced-breathing group is being confused with the quiet-rhythm group.

front: Why is “Apneustic center in the pons” wrong here? A 59-year-old man with a brainstem stroke loses his normal automatic breathing rhythm and must consciously initiate each…
back: Pontine centers influence and modify the medullary pattern; the constant rhythm itself is generated by the medullary dorsal respiratory group.
extra: A pontine modulatory center is being assigned the rhythm-generating role.

front:
A 60-year-old man with severe hypoventilation has a steadily rising arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide, and his ventilatory drive increases in response.

Which of the following sequences most directly links his hypercapnia to the increased drive?
back: Carbon dioxide diffuses into the brain's extracellular fluid, generating hydrogen ions that stimulate central chemoreceptors
extra: As blood CO2 rises, it readily diffuses across the blood-brain barrier into the extracellular fluid; increased carbon dioxide generates hydrogen ions, and the increase in hydrogen ions in the brain triggers the central chemoreceptors.

front: Why is “Hydrogen ions from the blood cross the blood-brain barrier and directly stimulate the central chemoreceptors” wrong here? A 60-year-old man with severe hypoventilation has a steadily rising arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide, and his…
back: It is carbon dioxide that readily diffuses across the blood-brain barrier; the hydrogen ions that trigger the chemoreceptors are generated within the brain's extracellular fluid.
extra: The crossing species is being misidentified.

front: Why is “Oxygen sensors in the carotid bodies activate the phrenic nerve directly” wrong here? A 60-year-old man with severe hypoventilation has a steadily rising arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide, and his…
back: Peripheral chemoreceptors signal the respiratory centers rather than the phrenic nerve directly, and the stimulus here is carbon dioxide, not oxygen.
extra: A peripheral reflex arc is being substituted for the central CO2 pathway, and the wiring is wrong.

front: Why is “Lung stretch receptors signal the pons to accelerate the inspiratory rate” wrong here? A 60-year-old man with severe hypoventilation has a steadily rising arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide, and his…
back: The inflation reflex protects the lungs from over-inflating by limiting inspiration; it does not accelerate ventilation in response to carbon dioxide.
extra: The inflation reflex is being described with the opposite effect.

front:
In the venous blood of a 33-year-old woman, carbon dioxide enters erythrocytes and is converted to bicarbonate, which then moves out of the cells into the plasma.

Which of the following ion movements accompanies this efflux of bicarbonate from the erythrocytes?
back: Movement of chloride ions into the erythrocytes
extra: Bicarbonate is moved across the membrane into the plasma in exchange for chloride ions, a mechanism called the chloride shift; in the pulmonary capillaries the exchange reverses.

front: Why is “Movement of chloride ions out of the erythrocytes” wrong here? In the venous blood of a 33-year-old woman, carbon dioxide enters erythrocytes and is converted to bicarbonate, which th…
back: In systemic capillaries, where bicarbonate is generated and exported, chloride enters the cell; chloride exits only in the pulmonary capillaries, where the cycle reverses.
extra: The direction of the exchange is being reversed.

front: Why is “Movement of sodium ions into the erythrocytes” wrong here? In the venous blood of a 33-year-old woman, carbon dioxide enters erythrocytes and is converted to bicarbonate, which th…
back: The bicarbonate exchange partner across the erythrocyte membrane is chloride, not sodium.
extra: The wrong counter-ion is being paired with bicarbonate efflux.

front: Why is “Movement of potassium ions out of the erythrocytes” wrong here? In the venous blood of a 33-year-old woman, carbon dioxide enters erythrocytes and is converted to bicarbonate, which th…
back: Potassium is not the ion exchanged for bicarbonate in the chloride shift; the exchange is bicarbonate for chloride.
extra: An unrelated cation movement is being proposed.

front:
A researcher measures the forms in which carbon dioxide is carried in the venous blood of a healthy 30-year-old man.

Which of the following forms accounts for the largest fraction of the carbon dioxide transported to the lungs?
back: Bicarbonate ions produced within erythrocytes
extra: A large fraction — about 70 percent — of the carbon dioxide molecules that diffuse into the blood is transported to the lungs as bicarbonate, produced in erythrocytes by carbonic anhydrase.

front:
Why is “Carboxyhemoglobin formed at the heme iron” wrong here? A researcher measures the forms in which carbon dioxide is carried in the venous blood of a healthy 30-year-old man.

Wh…
back: Carboxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide, a different molecule; carbon dioxide is carried mainly as bicarbonate.
extra: Carbon monoxide binding is being confused with carbon dioxide carriage.

front:
Why is “Carbon dioxide gas dissolved directly in the plasma” wrong here? A researcher measures the forms in which carbon dioxide is carried in the venous blood of a healthy 30-year-old man.

Wh…
back: Only a small fraction of carbon dioxide travels dissolved; the great majority is converted to bicarbonate.
extra: The physically dissolved fraction is being overestimated.

front:
Why is “Carbaminohemoglobin within the erythrocytes” wrong here? A researcher measures the forms in which carbon dioxide is carried in the venous blood of a healthy 30-year-old man.

Wh…
back: An intermediate amount of carbon dioxide binds hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin; bicarbonate remains the largest fraction.
extra: The hemoglobin-bound fraction is being confused with the dominant form.

front:
A 26-year-old mountaineer breathes ambient air at an altitude where the barometric pressure is 380 mm Hg. The composition of the air is unchanged from sea level, with oxygen making up about 21 percent of the gas mixture.

According to Dalton's law, which of the following is the partial pressure of oxygen in the inspired air?
back: 80 mm Hg
extra: Dalton's law states that each gas in a mixture exerts its own pressure, and the total is the sum of the partial pressures; oxygen's share is 0.21 × 380 ≈ 80 mm Hg.

front: Why is “40 mm Hg” wrong here? A 26-year-old mountaineer breathes ambient air at an altitude where the barometric pressure is 380 mm Hg. The compositio…
back: The partial pressure of a gas in a mixture equals its fractional concentration times the total pressure: 0.21 × 380 mm Hg ≈ 80 mm Hg.
extra: The oxygen fraction is being applied twice, or to half the barometric pressure.

front: Why is “160 mm Hg” wrong here? A 26-year-old mountaineer breathes ambient air at an altitude where the barometric pressure is 380 mm Hg. The compositio…
back: About 160 mm Hg is oxygen's partial pressure at sea level (0.21 × 760); at 380 mm Hg barometric pressure the value halves to about 80 mm Hg.
extra: Sea-level oxygen partial pressure is being recalled instead of computed.

front: Why is “190 mm Hg” wrong here? A 26-year-old mountaineer breathes ambient air at an altitude where the barometric pressure is 380 mm Hg. The compositio…
back: Dividing 380 by two ignores the oxygen fraction; only 21 percent of the mixture is oxygen.
extra: Half the barometric pressure is being reported as the oxygen partial pressure.

front:
A 45-year-old man develops shortness of breath after neck surgery during which the phrenic nerve was injured. Examination shows paradoxical upward movement of the affected hemidiaphragm during inspiration, and air entry into the ipsilateral lung is markedly reduced.

Loss of which of the following events most directly accounts for this reduction in ventilation?
back: Expansion of the pleural cavities with a fall in their internal pressure
extra: When the diaphragm contracts and flattens, the volume inside the pleural cavities increases, which decreases the pressure within them; as a result, air flows into the lungs.

front: Why is “Contraction of the abdominal wall muscles forcing the diaphragm upward” wrong here? A 45-year-old man develops shortness of breath after neck surgery during which the phrenic nerve was injured. Examinatio…
back: Abdominal muscle contraction pushes the diaphragm upward and drives air out during forced expiration; it opposes rather than supports inspiration.
extra: A forced-expiration mechanism is being credited with moving air inward.

front: Why is “Relaxation of the external intercostal muscles narrowing the rib cage” wrong here? A 45-year-old man develops shortness of breath after neck surgery during which the phrenic nerve was injured. Examinatio…
back: Relaxation of the inspiratory muscles allows recoil during expiration; reduced air entry reflects loss of active expansion, not of a relaxation step.
extra: A passive-expiration event is being assigned to the inspiratory phase.

front: Why is “An increase in intra-alveolar pressure above atmospheric pressure” wrong here? A 45-year-old man develops shortness of breath after neck surgery during which the phrenic nerve was injured. Examinatio…
back: Air flows from higher to lower pressure; inspiration requires intra-alveolar pressure to fall below atmospheric pressure, not rise above it.
extra: The pressure gradient is being described in the expiratory direction.

front:
A sleep study shows intermittent pauses in breathing while the upper airway remains patent. During an episode, rising blood carbon dioxide produces little increase in inspiratory stimulation.

Which of the following failures most directly accounts for this pattern?
back: Reduced respiratory-center response to carbon dioxide
extra: The airway remains open, so a mechanical obstruction does not explain the pauses. An inadequate respiratory-center response to carbon dioxide accounts for absent inspiratory stimulation.

front: Why is “Excessive inspiratory stimulation despite a patent airway” wrong here? A sleep study shows intermittent pauses in breathing while the upper airway remains patent. During an episode, rising bl…
back: The airway condition matches the study, but the stimulation direction is reversed. The observed episodes occur with inadequate inspiratory activation rather than excessive drive.
extra: Reverses the measured drive abnormality by calling inadequate inspiratory stimulation excessive.

front: Why is “Excessive pharyngeal relaxation closing the upper airway” wrong here? A sleep study shows intermittent pauses in breathing while the upper airway remains patent. During an episode, rising bl…
back: This would produce an obstructive mechanism, but the study confirms a patent airway during the event. The measured defect instead concerns the response driving inspiration.
extra: Assumes pharyngeal obstruction despite documented airway patency during the pause.

front: Why is “Increased respiratory-center response to carbon dioxide” wrong here? A sleep study shows intermittent pauses in breathing while the upper airway remains patent. During an episode, rising bl…
back: An increased response would strengthen the drive to breathe as carbon dioxide rises. It conflicts with the recorded failure to increase inspiratory stimulation.
extra: Predicts an increased carbon dioxide response despite the recorded failure to increase inspiratory drive.

front:
A lung model contains 140 mL in conducting airways and 60 mL in ventilated alveoli that receive no effective blood flow. Investigators classify the inspired volume that does not participate in gas exchange.

Which of the following correctly reports the anatomical, alveolar, and total dead spaces?
back: 140 mL anatomical; 60 mL alveolar; 200 mL total
extra: Conducting-airway volume is anatomical dead space. The ventilated but ineffective alveolar compartment contributes additional dead space, and adding the two compartments gives 200 mL.

front: Why is “60 mL anatomical; 140 mL alveolar; 200 mL total” wrong here? A lung model contains 140 mL in conducting airways and 60 mL in ventilated alveoli that receive no effective blood flow.…
back: The combined volume is correct, but the compartments are reversed. Conducting airways supply anatomical dead space; the ineffective alveoli supply the alveolar component.
extra: Reverses the conducting-airway and ineffective-alveolar compartment labels while preserving their sum.

front: Why is “140 mL anatomical; 60 mL alveolar; 140 mL total” wrong here? A lung model contains 140 mL in conducting airways and 60 mL in ventilated alveoli that receive no effective blood flow.…
back: Both compartments are classified correctly, but the total omits the alveolar contribution. Total dead space includes the conducting-airway and ineffective alveolar volumes together.
extra: Omits the ineffective alveolar compartment when adding total dead space.

front: Why is “140 mL anatomical; 60 mL alveolar; 60 mL total” wrong here? A lung model contains 140 mL in conducting airways and 60 mL in ventilated alveoli that receive no effective blood flow.…
back: The individual labels are correct, but the total excludes conducting-airway volume. Gas fails to exchange in both specified compartments, so both contribute to the total.
extra: Omits conducting-airway volume when adding total dead space.

front:
A ventilation model compares two breathing patterns at the same total inspired volume per minute. Pattern X uses 12 breaths/min of 500 mL each; pattern Y uses 20 breaths/min of 300 mL each. Dead space is 150 mL per breath in both.

Which of the following correctly compares gas-exchanging inspired volume per minute?
back: 4.2 L/min for X; 3.0 L/min for Y
extra: Subtract dead space before multiplying by rate. Pattern X supplies 12 times 350 mL, while pattern Y supplies 20 times 150 mL, yielding different effective volumes.

front: Why is “3.0 L/min for X; 4.2 L/min for Y” wrong here? A ventilation model compares two breathing patterns at the same total inspired volume per minute. Pattern X uses 12 brea…
back: This reverses the calculated effective volumes. Larger individual breaths devote a smaller fraction to the same dead-space volume, favoring pattern X in this comparison.
extra: Reverses the two effective minute volumes despite the larger breaths losing a smaller fraction to dead space.

front: Why is “5.8 L/min for X; 5.8 L/min for Y” wrong here? A ventilation model compares two breathing patterns at the same total inspired volume per minute. Pattern X uses 12 brea…
back: This approximates subtracting dead space just once from the minute total. Dead space must instead be subtracted from every breath before multiplying by breathing rate.
extra: Subtracts dead space only once per minute instead of subtracting it from every breath.

front: Why is “1.8 L/min for X; 3.0 L/min for Y” wrong here? A ventilation model compares two breathing patterns at the same total inspired volume per minute. Pattern X uses 12 brea…
back: The first value is the nonexchanging minute volume for pattern X, while the second is the exchanging volume for Y. The comparison must use the same quantity.
extra: Compares nonexchanging volume for one pattern with gas-exchanging volume for the other.

front:
During lung-volume testing, a 29-year-old patient exhales normally and then forcefully expels another 1.2 L. A separate measurement shows that 1.4 L remains after maximal expiration.

Which of the following was the lung volume immediately after the normal exhalation?
extra: At the end of normal expiration, the lungs contain the additional expiratory reserve plus the residual. Adding 1.2 L and 1.4 L gives 2.6 L.

front: Why is “1.2 L” wrong here? During lung-volume testing, a 29-year-old patient exhales normally and then forcefully expels another 1.2 L. A separate …
back: This is the extra volume expelled after normal expiration. It excludes the 1.4 L that remains even after the patient completes maximal expiration.
extra: Counts the extra expiratory reserve but omits the volume remaining after maximal expiration.

front: Why is “1.4 L” wrong here? During lung-volume testing, a 29-year-old patient exhales normally and then forcefully expels another 1.2 L. A separate …
back: This measures the volume remaining after maximal expiration. At the earlier end of normal expiration, the additional expiratory reserve was still present in the lungs.
extra: Uses the volume after maximal expiration for the earlier volume after normal expiration.

front: Why is “0.2 L” wrong here? During lung-volume testing, a 29-year-old patient exhales normally and then forcefully expels another 1.2 L. A separate …
back: Subtracting the reserve from the residual does not produce functional residual capacity. The two volumes occupy complementary portions of the lung volume after normal expiration.
extra: Subtracts complementary reserve and residual compartments instead of adding them.

front:
Two identical fluid samples are equilibrated separately with oxygen and carbon dioxide. The oxygen partial pressure is 100 units and the carbon dioxide partial pressure is 10 units. Assume the carbon dioxide solubility coefficient is 20 times the oxygen coefficient in this model.

Which of the following is the dissolved carbon dioxide-to-oxygen concentration ratio?
extra: Dissolved concentration equals solubility times partial pressure. The ratio is therefore 20 times 10 divided by 100, so dissolved carbon dioxide is twice dissolved oxygen.

front: Why is “0.1 to 1” wrong here? Two identical fluid samples are equilibrated separately with oxygen and carbon dioxide. The oxygen partial pressure is 1…
back: This uses the partial-pressure ratio without accounting for different solubilities. The twentyfold solubility advantage more than offsets the tenfold lower carbon dioxide pressure.
extra: Uses the partial-pressure ratio alone and ignores the gases' different solubility coefficients.

front: Why is “0.5 to 1” wrong here? Two identical fluid samples are equilibrated separately with oxygen and carbon dioxide. The oxygen partial pressure is 1…
back: This is the reciprocal of the requested concentration ratio. The question asks for carbon dioxide relative to oxygen, so the product comparison gives two rather than one-half.
extra: Inverts the requested carbon dioxide-to-oxygen dissolved-concentration ratio.

front: Why is “20.0 to 1” wrong here? Two identical fluid samples are equilibrated separately with oxygen and carbon dioxide. The oxygen partial pressure is 1…
back: This treats the gases as if their partial pressures were equal. The solubility advantage must be multiplied by the stated pressure ratio of one-tenth.
extra: Uses the solubility ratio alone as though the two gas partial pressures were equal.

front:
A respiratory-membrane model is tested under the same gas gradients before and after a change in geometry. The altered membrane has a smaller exchange surface and a longer diffusion path. Cellular ATP availability is maintained.

Which of the following best predicts the effect on gas transfer?
back: Reduced transfer from less favorable passive diffusion
extra: A large surface area and thin membrane favor gas exchange. Reducing area and increasing path length make diffusion less efficient even when cellular ATP availability is unchanged.

front: Why is “Unchanged transfer because cellular ATP remains available” wrong here? A respiratory-membrane model is tested under the same gas gradients before and after a change in geometry. The altered m…
back: Gas exchange occurs by passive diffusion rather than direct ATP consumption. Preserving ATP therefore does not cancel the effects of an unfavorable change in membrane geometry.
extra: Assumes that preserved cellular ATP cancels unfavorable changes in a passive diffusion pathway.

front: Why is “Reduced transfer from greater direct ATP consumption” wrong here? A respiratory-membrane model is tested under the same gas gradients before and after a change in geometry. The altered m…
back: Reduced transfer is expected, but the proposed energy explanation is incorrect. The specified exchange process is passive, and the intervention changes geometry rather than ATP-dependent transport.
extra: Attributes reduced gas transfer to direct ATP consumption instead of the altered diffusion geometry.

front: Why is “Increased transfer from reduced direct ATP consumption” wrong here? A respiratory-membrane model is tested under the same gas gradients before and after a change in geometry. The altered m…
back: Gas diffusion does not become more efficient by consuming less ATP because it does not directly require ATP. The geometric changes instead hinder the passive process.
extra: Treats reduced ATP consumption as a way to improve a process that does not directly consume ATP.

front:
A 52-year-old patient has recurrent pauses in airflow during sleep. A monitored episode shows marked loss of muscle tone around the pharynx and closure of the upper airway, while the study separately confirms continuing signals to the inspiratory apparatus.

Which of the following best identifies the defect responsible for these episodes?
back: Obstructive apnea from excessive pharyngeal relaxation
extra: The study documents closure of the upper airway despite continuing inspiratory stimulation. Excessive pharyngeal relaxation therefore explains interruption of airflow through an obstructive mechanism.

front: Why is “Obstructive apnea from sustained pharyngeal contraction” wrong here? A 52-year-old patient has recurrent pauses in airflow during sleep. A monitored episode shows marked loss of muscle tone…
back: The study identifies excessive relaxation, not sustained contraction. Reversing the observed muscle behavior fails to explain the specific airway obstruction demonstrated during sleep.
extra: Attributes the airway closure to sustained contraction despite the observed loss of pharyngeal tone.

front: Why is “Central apnea from heightened chemoreceptor activation” wrong here? A 52-year-old patient has recurrent pauses in airflow during sleep. A monitored episode shows marked loss of muscle tone…
back: Heightened activation would not explain preserved inspiratory signaling interrupted by a closed airway. The discriminating observation is mechanical closure at the pharyngeal level.
extra: Treats heightened central activation as the defect despite continuing drive and directly observed airway closure.

front: Why is “Central apnea from absent inspiratory stimulation” wrong here? A 52-year-old patient has recurrent pauses in airflow during sleep. A monitored episode shows marked loss of muscle tone…
back: This mechanism requires impaired stimulation of inspiration, whereas the study confirms continuing signals during the event. The directly observed airway closure better explains the pause.
extra: Assumes absent inspiratory stimulation even though the study directly confirms continuing signals.

front:
A 40-year-old patient receives morphine and develops a lower respiratory rate. The airway remains open. The team considers why increasing carbon dioxide has not restored the prior breathing rate.

Which of the following drug effects best explains the observation?
back: Depression of respiratory-center activity controlling rate
extra: Morphine can decrease respiratory rate through its effect on respiratory centers. This explains reduced breathing despite a patent airway and an accumulating stimulus for ventilation.

front: Why is “Enhancement of respiratory-center activity controlling rate” wrong here? A 40-year-old patient receives morphine and develops a lower respiratory rate. The airway remains open. The team conside…
back: Enhanced respiratory-center activity would oppose the observed slowing. Morphine’s relevant action in this mechanism is a reduction in respiratory rate through these centers.
extra: Explains a lower rate through enhanced rather than depressed respiratory-center activity.

front: Why is “Obstruction of the pharynx despite maintained airway patency” wrong here? A 40-year-old patient receives morphine and develops a lower respiratory rate. The airway remains open. The team conside…
back: The proposed mechanism conflicts with the directly observed patent airway. A central rate effect explains the respiratory change without requiring an unobserved mechanical obstruction.
extra: Assumes pharyngeal obstruction despite the directly observed patent airway.

front: Why is “Enhanced carbon dioxide conversion into central hydrogen ions” wrong here? A 40-year-old patient receives morphine and develops a lower respiratory rate. The airway remains open. The team conside…
back: Increasing the hydrogen-ion stimulus would ordinarily activate central chemoreceptors. That direction does not explain why morphine exposure is followed by a lower breathing rate.
extra: Explains reduced breathing through an increased hydrogen-ion stimulus that would activate central chemoreceptors.

front:
A 45-year-old patient completes lung-volume testing. The volume present after maximal inspiration is 6.0 L. The patient can then expel 4.5 L during a maximal expiration.

Which of the following volumes remains in the lungs at the end of that effort?
extra: The difference between total lung capacity and vital capacity is residual volume. Subtracting the maximally expelled 4.5 L from the initial 6.0 L leaves 1.5 L.

front: Why is “0.5 L” wrong here? A 45-year-old patient completes lung-volume testing. The volume present after maximal inspiration is 6.0 L. The patient …
back: This would require an expelled volume of 5.5 L from the stated starting volume. The measured maximal expiration removes 4.5 L, leaving a larger residual.
extra: Assumes a larger maximally expelled volume than the lung-volume test actually measured.

front: Why is “4.5 L” wrong here? A 45-year-old patient completes lung-volume testing. The volume present after maximal inspiration is 6.0 L. The patient …
back: This is the volume expelled between maximal inspiration and maximal expiration. The question asks for the volume that remains after that maximal expiratory effort.
extra: Confuses the volume expelled during maximal expiration with the volume left in the lungs.

front: Why is “6.0 L” wrong here? A 45-year-old patient completes lung-volume testing. The volume present after maximal inspiration is 6.0 L. The patient …
back: This is the total volume present at maximal inspiration. Using it as the residual ignores the 4.5 L removed during the subsequent maximal expiration.
extra: Uses the maximal inspiratory volume as the residual and ignores the subsequent measured expiration.

front:
At the placenta of a healthy 24-year-old woman at 36 weeks of gestation, the partial pressure of oxygen in the fetal blood is only about 20 mm Hg, far below the maternal arterial partial pressure. Despite this shallow gradient, the fetus loads adequate oxygen.

Which of the following properties most directly enables this uptake?
back: Fetal hemoglobin has a greater affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin
extra: Two of the subunits of fetal hemoglobin have a different structure that causes fetal hemoglobin to have a greater affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin, overcoming the shallow placental gradient.

front: Why is “Fetal blood has a lower hemoglobin concentration than maternal blood” wrong here? At the placenta of a healthy 24-year-old woman at 36 weeks of gestation, the partial pressure of oxygen in the fetal blo…
back: A lower concentration would reduce oxygen carriage; the fetus compensates for the gradient through higher hemoglobin affinity, not lower content.
extra: A reduced carrying capacity is being offered as an uptake advantage.

front: Why is “Fetal hemoglobin releases oxygen more readily at low pH” wrong here? At the placenta of a healthy 24-year-old woman at 36 weeks of gestation, the partial pressure of oxygen in the fetal blo…
back: Enhanced release would impair uptake at the placenta; the fetus loads oxygen because its hemoglobin binds oxygen more avidly.
extra: A tissue-unloading property is being applied to placental loading.

front: Why is “The placenta actively transports oxygen using ATP” wrong here? At the placenta of a healthy 24-year-old woman at 36 weeks of gestation, the partial pressure of oxygen in the fetal blo…
back: Oxygen crosses the placental barrier by diffusion down its partial-pressure gradient; fetal hemoglobin's affinity captures it.
extra: An energy-requiring pump is being proposed for a diffusive process.

front:
A 29-year-old scuba diver ascends rapidly from a deep dive and develops joint pain and shortness of breath. During the dive, the elevated ambient pressure increased the amount of nitrogen dissolved in his blood and tissues; during the rapid ascent, that nitrogen came out of solution as bubbles.

Which of the following principles most directly explains why more nitrogen dissolved in his tissues at depth?
back: The quantity of gas that dissolves in a liquid rises with the partial pressure of that gas
extra: Henry's law states that the amount of a specific gas that dissolves in a liquid is a function of its partial pressure; the greater the partial pressure, the more gas dissolves, as at depth.

front: Why is “The total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures of its components” wrong here? A 29-year-old scuba diver ascends rapidly from a deep dive and develops joint pain and shortness of breath. During the d…
back: Dalton's law relates component pressures to total pressure in a gas mixture; it does not describe how much gas enters solution in a liquid.
extra: Dalton's law, which describes mixtures, is being used to explain dissolution.

front: Why is “Gas pressure varies inversely with the volume of its container at constant temperature” wrong here? A 29-year-old scuba diver ascends rapidly from a deep dive and develops joint pain and shortness of breath. During the d…
back: Boyle's law describes the pressure-volume behavior of a trapped gas; the question concerns gas dissolving into blood and tissue, which is Henry's law.
extra: Boyle's law, which links gas pressure and volume, is being applied to solubility.

front: Why is “Once one oxygen molecule binds hemoglobin, additional molecules bind more readily” wrong here? A 29-year-old scuba diver ascends rapidly from a deep dive and develops joint pain and shortness of breath. During the d…
back: Hemoglobin cooperativity concerns oxygen carriage by erythrocytes, not the physical dissolution of nitrogen gas in body fluids.
extra: Cooperative oxygen binding is being invoked for dissolved nitrogen.

front:
A 68-year-old man with pulmonary fibrosis has lungs that resist expansion, and his work of breathing is increased.

Compared with a healthy lung, which of the following best describes the effect of his reduced lung compliance on pulmonary ventilation?
back: A smaller potential lung volume for any given distending force
extra: Lung compliance is the ability of the lungs to stretch; the more the lungs can stretch, the greater the potential volume, so a stiff, low-compliance lung achieves a smaller volume.

front:
Why is “A larger potential lung volume for any given distending force” wrong here? A 68-year-old man with pulmonary fibrosis has lungs that resist expansion, and his work of breathing is increased.

Comp…
back: Greater compliance permits greater stretch and volume; reduced compliance, as in fibrosis, limits both.
extra: The direction of the compliance-volume relationship is being reversed.

front:
Why is “An increase in the resting pressure gradient driving airflow” wrong here? A 68-year-old man with pulmonary fibrosis has lungs that resist expansion, and his work of breathing is increased.

Comp…
back: A low-compliance lung requires more effort to generate the same volume change; the resting gradient is not increased as a compensatory feature.
extra: A stiffer lung is being assigned a larger driving gradient.

front:
Why is “An increase in alveolar surface tension from excess surfactant” wrong here? A 68-year-old man with pulmonary fibrosis has lungs that resist expansion, and his work of breathing is increased.

Comp…
back: Surfactant reduces surface tension; fibrosis stiffens the lung through tissue change, not through surfactant excess.
extra: Surfactant's effect on surface tension is being inverted.

front:
A 55-year-old woman with severe iron-deficiency anemia has a hemoglobin concentration half of normal, yet her measured arterial oxygen partial pressure is normal.

Which of the following best explains why oxygen delivery to her tissues is nevertheless substantially reduced?
back: Most oxygen is carried bound to hemoglobin rather than dissolved in plasma
extra: Only about 1.5% of oxygen is transported dissolved in the blood; the majority is bound to hemoglobin, so halving hemoglobin nearly halves oxygen content even though the partial pressure is unchanged.

front: Why is “Anemia increases the partial-pressure gradient across the respiratory membrane” wrong here? A 55-year-old woman with severe iron-deficiency anemia has a hemoglobin concentration half of normal, yet her measured a…
back: The gradient governs how fast oxygen loads; with normal arterial partial pressure, loading is intact and the limiting step is the reduced hemoglobin reservoir.
extra: The alveolar-to-blood gradient is being invoked where carriage is limiting.

front: Why is “Low hemoglobin prevents oxygen from diffusing into the blood” wrong here? A 55-year-old woman with severe iron-deficiency anemia has a hemoglobin concentration half of normal, yet her measured a…
back: Her arterial partial pressure is normal, proving oxygen enters the blood normally; the defect is in carriage capacity, not diffusion.
extra: Uptake across the respiratory membrane is being blamed for a carriage problem.

front: Why is “Dissolved oxygen cannot leave the bloodstream without hemoglobin” wrong here? A 55-year-old woman with severe iron-deficiency anemia has a hemoglobin concentration half of normal, yet her measured a…
back: Dissolved oxygen diffuses freely into tissues; the problem is that the dissolved pool is only about 1.5% of total oxygen content.
extra: Dissolved oxygen is being described as trapped in the vasculature.

front:
Blood entering a pulmonary capillary of a healthy 40-year-old man has a partial pressure of oxygen of 40 mm Hg, while the adjacent alveolar air has a partial pressure of oxygen of 104 mm Hg.

Which of the following best describes the resulting movement of oxygen across the respiratory membrane in this region?
back: Rapid diffusion from the alveolus into the capillary blood
extra: The roughly 64 mm Hg difference creates a very strong pressure gradient that causes oxygen to rapidly cross the respiratory membrane from the alveoli into the blood.

front: Why is “Diffusion from the capillary blood into the alveolus” wrong here? Blood entering a pulmonary capillary of a healthy 40-year-old man has a partial pressure of oxygen of 40 mm Hg, while th…
back: Gases move from higher to lower partial pressure; alveolar pressure (104) exceeds blood pressure (40), so oxygen moves into the blood, not out of it.
extra: The direction of the partial-pressure gradient is being reversed.

front: Why is “Active transport of oxygen into the capillary blood” wrong here? Blood entering a pulmonary capillary of a healthy 40-year-old man has a partial pressure of oxygen of 40 mm Hg, while th…
back: Oxygen crosses the respiratory membrane by simple diffusion down its partial-pressure gradient; no active transport is involved.
extra: An energy-requiring carrier process is being proposed for oxygen uptake.

front: Why is “Facilitated diffusion of oxygen through membrane carrier proteins” wrong here? Blood entering a pulmonary capillary of a healthy 40-year-old man has a partial pressure of oxygen of 40 mm Hg, while th…
back: Oxygen diffuses directly through the membrane lipids without carriers; the rate is set by the partial-pressure gradient.
extra: A carrier-mediated mechanism is being assigned to a directly permeable gas.

front: Which of the following diagnoses is defined by airways that become inflamed and narrowed at times, making exhalation harder?
back: Bronchial asthma
extra: NHLBI describes asthma as airways becoming inflamed and narrowed at times, which makes it harder for air to flow out during exhalation.

front: Why is “Bronchiectasis” wrong here? Which of the following diagnoses is defined by airways that become inflamed and narrowed at times, making exhalation har…
back: The cited passage assigns the combination of intermittent airway inflammation, narrowing, and harder expiratory airflow to asthma, not bronchiectasis.
extra: An airway diagnosis is selected without matching the complete source-defined pattern.

front: Why is “Chronic bronchitis” wrong here? Which of the following diagnoses is defined by airways that become inflamed and narrowed at times, making exhalation har…
back: The evidence directly identifies asthma when episodic airway inflammation and narrowing make exhalation harder; it does not identify chronic bronchitis.
extra: The general airway wording is noticed, but the passage's named diagnosis is missed.

front: Why is “Pulmonary emphysema” wrong here? Which of the following diagnoses is defined by airways that become inflamed and narrowed at times, making exhalation har…
back: The passage links harder outward airflow specifically to airways that become inflamed and narrowed at times, and names that condition asthma.
extra: Expiratory difficulty is isolated from the paired inflammation and narrowing cues.

front: Which change promotes oxygen dissociation from hemoglobin?
back: A more acidic blood pH
extra: A lower, more acidic pH promotes oxygen dissociation from hemoglobin.

front: Why is “A more basic blood pH” wrong here? Which change promotes oxygen dissociation from hemoglobin?
back: A higher, more basic pH inhibits oxygen dissociation from hemoglobin.
extra: Alkalosis is being treated as the unloading signal.

front: Why is “A fall in tissue temperature” wrong here? Which change promotes oxygen dissociation from hemoglobin?
back: The grounded unloading cue here is acidic pH, not a temperature decrease.
extra: Cooling is being confused with the acid-driven Bohr effect.

front: Why is “A rise in inspired oxygen only” wrong here? Which change promotes oxygen dissociation from hemoglobin?
back: Higher inspired oxygen raises loading pressure; acidic pH promotes dissociation.
extra: Raised alveolar PO2 is being confused with hemoglobin unloading.

front: Working skeletal muscle generates lactic acid. How does the local pH change affect hemoglobin?
back: It promotes oxygen dissociation from hemoglobin
extra: A lower, more acidic pH promotes oxygen dissociation, matching local metabolic acid production.

front: Why is “It inhibits oxygen release to myocytes” wrong here? Working skeletal muscle generates lactic acid. How does the local pH change affect hemoglobin?
back: Acidic pH promotes dissociation; it does not inhibit unloading to tissues.
extra: Acid is being treated as a loading signal.

front: Why is “It raises hemoglobin's oxygen affinity” wrong here? Working skeletal muscle generates lactic acid. How does the local pH change affect hemoglobin?
back: Acidosis lowers affinity and promotes dissociation rather than raising affinity.
extra: A left shift is being inferred from acidosis.

front: Why is “It blocks carbon dioxide binding to globin” wrong here? Working skeletal muscle generates lactic acid. How does the local pH change affect hemoglobin?
back: The described effect is acid-driven oxygen dissociation, not blocked CO2 binding.
extra: CO2 carriage is being confused with the Bohr unloading effect.

front:
A 24-year-old recreational runner finishes a 400-meter sprint and reports burning pain in both thighs with heavy breathing. Capillary blood sampled from the working muscle is more acidic than an arterial sample drawn at rest a few minutes earlier.

Which mechanism most directly improves oxygen delivery in this setting?
back: Acidic pH promotes oxygen dissociation from hemoglobin
extra: A lower, more acidic pH promotes oxygen dissociation from hemoglobin, aiding delivery to active muscle.

front: Why is “Basic pH inhibits oxygen dissociation from hemoglobin” wrong here? A 24-year-old recreational runner finishes a 400-meter sprint and reports burning pain in both thighs with heavy breathi…
back: A higher, more basic pH inhibits dissociation; working muscle is acidic, not basic.
extra: The alkalotic Bohr limb is being applied to acidifying muscle.

front: Why is “Acidic pH permanently denatures hemoglobin tetramers” wrong here? A 24-year-old recreational runner finishes a 400-meter sprint and reports burning pain in both thighs with heavy breathi…
back: The Bohr effect is a reversible affinity change, not permanent denaturation.
extra: Irreversible protein damage is being inferred from physiologic acidosis.

front: Why is “Acidic pH stops erythrocyte glycolysis entirely” wrong here? A 24-year-old recreational runner finishes a 400-meter sprint and reports burning pain in both thighs with heavy breathi…
back: Oxygen unloading via lower pH does not require stopping red-cell glycolysis.
extra: Metabolic shutdown is being confused with unloading.

front: Which of the following forms accounts for most carbon dioxide transport in human blood?
back: Bicarbonate ion in plasma
extra: Most carbon dioxide is converted in red cells to bicarbonate, which then travels in plasma as the main transport form.

front: Why is “Dissolved CO2 gas in plasma alone” wrong here? Which of the following forms accounts for most carbon dioxide transport in human blood?
back: Only a small fraction of CO2 travels as dissolved gas; about 70% is carried as bicarbonate.
extra: The small dissolved fraction is being treated as the majority.

front: Why is “Carbamino compounds on plasma albumin only” wrong here? Which of the following forms accounts for most carbon dioxide transport in human blood?
back: Some CO2 binds proteins as carbamino compounds, but bicarbonate is the predominant transport form.
extra: A minority carbamino route is being overstated.

front: Why is “Bound CO2 inside platelets” wrong here? Which of the following forms accounts for most carbon dioxide transport in human blood?
back: CO2 transport is a red-cell/plasma process (dissolved, carbamino, bicarbonate), not a platelet function.
extra: Platelets are being invented as a CO2 carrier.

front: Which of the following cell types secretes pulmonary surfactant that reduces alveolar surface tension?
back: Type II alveolar epithelial cells
extra: Type II alveolar cells secrete pulmonary surfactant, which reduces the surface tension of the alveoli and stabilizes them against collapse.

front: Why is “Type I alveolar epithelial cells” wrong here? Which of the following cell types secretes pulmonary surfactant that reduces alveolar surface tension?
back: Type I cells form the thin gas-exchange surface; surfactant comes from type II alveolar cells.
extra: The gas-exchange epithelium is being confused with the secretory cell.

front: Why is “Alveolar macrophages” wrong here? Which of the following cell types secretes pulmonary surfactant that reduces alveolar surface tension?
back: Alveolar macrophages clear debris; they do not secrete the surfactant that reduces surface tension.
extra: A phagocyte is being treated as the surfactant source.

front: Why is “Bronchial smooth-muscle cells” wrong here? Which of the following cell types secretes pulmonary surfactant that reduces alveolar surface tension?
back: Smooth muscle regulates airway caliber; surfactant is an alveolar type II epithelial secretion.
extra: Airway muscle is being confused with alveolar secretory epithelium.

front:
A 19-year-old man who is 193 cm tall presents to the emergency department with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath after bench-pressing. Vital signs are stable. Examination shows diminished breath sounds, hyperresonance, and reduced chest expansion on the right. Chest radiography shows complete collapse of the right lung with a visible pleural line and no mediastinal shift.

Which of the following best explains why voluntary inspiration fails to reinflate the affected lung?
back: Loss of the subatmospheric pressure gradient required for lung inflation
extra: Normally diaphragm contraction enlarges the pleural cavities and lowers their pressure, drawing air in; when air enters the pleural space the lung collapses and that subatmospheric gradient vanishes, so increasing thoracic volume no longer creates the pressure fall needed for inspiration.

front: Why is “Paralysis of the diaphragm prevents any change in thoracic volume” wrong here? A 19-year-old man who is 193 cm tall presents to the emergency department with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain a…
back: Diaphragmatic paralysis reduces ventilation by preventing thoracic expansion; this patient can inspire, but air cannot enter the collapsed lung because the pleural pressure gradient is lost.
extra: Phrenic nerve injury is being invoked despite an intact inspiratory pump.

front: Why is “Surfactant deficiency raises alveolar surface tension and prevents expansion” wrong here? A 19-year-old man who is 193 cm tall presents to the emergency department with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain a…
back: Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension in immature lungs; pneumothorax fails because pleural air eliminates the negative intrapleural pressure that drives inflation, not because of surfactant loss.
extra: Neonatal respiratory distress mechanism is being applied to traumatic pneumothorax.

front: Why is “Bronchospasm raises airway resistance above the driving pressure gradient” wrong here? A 19-year-old man who is 193 cm tall presents to the emergency department with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain a…
back: Bronchospasm impedes airflow through patent airways; complete lung collapse from pneumothorax reflects loss of the pleural pressure gradient, not increased airway resistance alone.
extra: Obstructive airflow limitation is being substituted for a pleural-space defect.

front: For alveolar gas exchange to be efficient, ventilation and perfusion in a given lung region must be which of the following?
back: Matched in compatible volumes
extra: For gas exchange to be efficient, the volumes involved in ventilation and perfusion should be compatible in each region.

front: Why is “Maximized independently regardless of the other variable” wrong here? For alveolar gas exchange to be efficient, ventilation and perfusion in a given lung region must be which of the followi…
back: High ventilation with no perfusion, or high perfusion with no ventilation, wastes one component; compatibility is required.
extra: Each process is being optimized in isolation.

front: Why is “Equal to dead-space ventilation only” wrong here? For alveolar gas exchange to be efficient, ventilation and perfusion in a given lung region must be which of the followi…
back: Dead-space ventilation does not participate in gas exchange; efficient regions require both ventilation and perfusion.
extra: Dead space is being treated as the target for all regions.

front: Why is “Absent in the upper lobes at rest” wrong here? For alveolar gas exchange to be efficient, ventilation and perfusion in a given lung region must be which of the followi…
back: Upper lobes receive both ventilation and perfusion at rest, though gravity and disease can create regional mismatch.
extra: Anatomic regions are being excluded from exchange.

front:
A 68-year-old researcher studies a lung preparation in which one small alveolar duct is blocked. Before obstruction, regional gas exchange is efficient and ventilation and perfusion volumes are compatible. After obstruction, gas exchange in the affected units falls even though total circuit flow remains stable, and microscopy shows intact capillaries surrounding those alveoli.

Which of the following regional relationships most directly explains the new inefficiency?
back: Ventilation decreases while perfusion remains present
extra: Efficient exchange requires compatible ventilation and perfusion. Airway obstruction reduces ventilation while capillary flow persists, so blood crosses the region without matching exposure to fresh alveolar gas.

front: Why is “Perfusion decreases while ventilation remains present” wrong here? A 68-year-old researcher studies a lung preparation in which one small alveolar duct is blocked. Before obstruction, reg…
back: The capillary bed is still perfused, while the blocked airway prevents fresh gas from reaching the affected alveoli. The primary change is reduced ventilation relative to perfusion.
extra: The perfusion-limited pattern is being substituted for the airway obstruction described.

front: Why is “Ventilation and perfusion increase in matched proportions” wrong here? A 68-year-old researcher studies a lung preparation in which one small alveolar duct is blocked. Before obstruction, reg…
back: A blocked airway cannot increase ventilation. Matching both flows would preserve their relationship rather than create the regional imbalance described.
extra: A matched increase is being inferred despite the documented airway obstruction.

front: Why is “Ventilation and perfusion decrease in matched proportions” wrong here? A 68-year-old researcher studies a lung preparation in which one small alveolar duct is blocked. Before obstruction, reg…
back: The stem states that capillary blood flow continues. A matched fall in both flows would not describe perfused alveoli isolated from fresh gas.
extra: A proportional reduction is being confused with selective loss of ventilation.

front:
A male neonate born at 28 weeks of gestation develops increasing work of breathing, expiratory grunting, and cyanosis within hours of delivery. His alveoli tend to collapse at the end of each expiration.

Deficient secretion by which of the following cells is most directly responsible for this condition?
back: Type II alveolar cells
extra: Type II alveolar cells secrete pulmonary surfactant, which reduces the surface tension of the alveoli; surfactant levels are not generally adequate until about the eighth month of pregnancy, so a 28-week neonate's alveoli collapse.

front: Why is “Type I alveolar cells” wrong here? A male neonate born at 28 weeks of gestation develops increasing work of breathing, expiratory grunting, and cyanosis wi…
back: Type I alveolar cells are squamous epithelial cells forming most of the alveolar surface for gas exchange; they do not secrete surfactant.
extra: The gas-exchange lining cell is being credited with surfactant secretion.

front: Why is “Alveolar macrophages” wrong here? A male neonate born at 28 weeks of gestation develops increasing work of breathing, expiratory grunting, and cyanosis wi…
back: Alveolar macrophages remove pathogens and debris from the alveolus; they do not produce surfactant.
extra: An immune phagocyte is being assigned a secretory surfactant role.

front: Why is “Bronchiolar secretory cells” wrong here? A male neonate born at 28 weeks of gestation develops increasing work of breathing, expiratory grunting, and cyanosis wi…
back: Bronchiolar secretory cells act in the small airways, not the alveoli; alveolar surface tension is controlled by type II alveolar cell surfactant.
extra: A conducting-zone secretory cell is being confused with the alveolar surfactant source.

front:
A 71-year-old woman with lobar pneumonia has consolidation of the right lower lobe: the alveoli in that region are filled with fluid, but blood flow through its capillaries is preserved.

Which of the following best describes gas exchange in the affected region?
back: Ventilation and perfusion are mismatched, so regional blood is poorly oxygenated
extra: For gas exchange to be efficient, ventilation and perfusion must be compatible; fluid-blocked alveoli abolish local ventilation while perfusion continues, so the imbalance leaves the blood poorly oxygenated.

front: Why is “Ventilation and perfusion are both increased, improving local oxygen uptake” wrong here? A 71-year-old woman with lobar pneumonia has consolidation of the right lower lobe: the alveoli in that region are fille…
back: Fluid-filled alveoli cannot ventilate, and perfusion is preserved rather than increased; exchange worsens, not improves.
extra: A compensatory improvement is being assumed where anatomy prevents it.

front: Why is “Perfusion ceases in the region, so no deoxygenated blood reaches it” wrong here? A 71-year-old woman with lobar pneumonia has consolidation of the right lower lobe: the alveoli in that region are fille…
back: Blood flow through the consolidated region continues, which is precisely why the ventilation-perfusion imbalance impairs oxygenation.
extra: The stem states perfusion is preserved; complete shunting off of blood flow is being assumed.

front: Why is “Oxygen diffuses normally because the alveolar partial pressure is unchanged” wrong here? A 71-year-old woman with lobar pneumonia has consolidation of the right lower lobe: the alveoli in that region are fille…
back: Fluid blocking the alveoli prevents fresh air from maintaining alveolar oxygen pressure, so the diffusion gradient cannot be sustained.
extra: Alveolar oxygen tension is being assumed normal in fluid-filled alveoli.

front: During spirometry testing of a healthy 35-year-old woman, the following values are recorded: tidal volume 500 mL, inspiratory reserve volume 3,000 mL, expiratory reserve volume 1,100 mL, and residual volume 1,200 mL. Which of the following is her vital capacity?
extra: Vital capacity is the sum of all volumes except residual volume (TV + ERV + IRV): 500 + 1,100 + 3,000 = 4,600 mL, within the normal 4,000-5,000 mL range.

front: Why is “1,600 mL” wrong here? During spirometry testing of a healthy 35-year-old woman, the following values are recorded: tidal volume 500 mL, inspir…
back: Vital capacity is the sum of tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, and expiratory reserve volume; omitting the inspiratory reserve underestimates it.
extra: Only tidal and expiratory reserve volumes are being summed.

front: Why is “3,500 mL” wrong here? During spirometry testing of a healthy 35-year-old woman, the following values are recorded: tidal volume 500 mL, inspir…
back: Tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume gives inspiratory capacity (3,500 mL), not vital capacity, which also includes the expiratory reserve.
extra: The expiratory reserve volume is being omitted from the sum.

front: Why is “4,100 mL” wrong here? During spirometry testing of a healthy 35-year-old woman, the following values are recorded: tidal volume 500 mL, inspir…
back: The two reserve volumes alone (4,100 mL) exclude the tidal volume; vital capacity includes all three.
extra: Tidal volume is being omitted from the sum.
